items.question: A small amount of copper(II) oxide powder is added to warm dilute sulfuric acid and the mixture is stirred. What is seen? Effervescence, and the solution stays colourless. A white precipitate forms in a colourless solution. A pink-brown solid forms and the solution stays colourless. The black solid disappears and a blue solution forms.
items.ms: CuO(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + H₂O(l): a base reacts with the acid to form a salt and water, so no gas forms; the black oxide dissolves and Cu²⁺(aq) is blue. A describes a metal or a carbonate with an acid; B a precipitation reaction (e.g. barium ions with sulfate ions); C the copper formed in a displacement reaction.
items.why: Observation MCQs on reactions of acids recur (May2024 Q13, Jan2020 Q10(a)); a metal oxide with an acid has not been the context.
keywords: Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance

items.name: Ionic and full equations linked to test-tube observations
path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 1 Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance
C1.12 - relate ionic and full equati
items.question: Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to yellow-orange aqueous iron(III) chloride. Which gives the correct ionic equation and observation? Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s); an orange-brown precipitate forms Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s); a green precipitate forms Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(aq); the solution turns colourless and no solid forms Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → NaCl(s); a white precipitate forms
items.ms: Fe³⁺ and OH⁻ ions combine to form insoluble iron(III) hydroxide, an orange-brown precipitate; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions. B: a green precipitate is iron(II) hydroxide, from Fe²⁺. C: iron(III) hydroxide is insoluble, so its state symbol is (s) and a precipitate is seen. D: sodium chloride is soluble; its ions are the spectator ions.
items.why: Precipitation MCQs recur (Oct2022 Q2, May2024 Q12, Jan2020 Q10(a)); linking the ionic equation and its state symbols to what is seen has not been asked as an MCQ.
keywords: Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance

items.name: Ionic and full equations linked to test-tube observations
path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 1 Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance
C1.12 - relate ionic and full equati
items.question: A student adds lumps of barium carbonate to an excess of dilute sulfuric acid. At first there is effervescence, but this soon stops, even though barium carbonate remains. Write the ionic equation for the reaction. Include state symbols. Suggest why the effervescence soon stops.
items.ms: BaCO₃ + 2H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄ + CO₂ + H₂O (species and balancing) State symbols: BaCO₃(s), H⁺(aq), SO₄²⁻(aq), BaSO₄(s), CO₂(g), H₂O(l) Insoluble barium sulfate forms a layer on the barium carbonate, which stops the acid reaching it
items.why: C1.12 has come up in 14 of 21 sessions; an acid reaction that also forms a precipitate (acid and precipitation reactions in one) has not been asked.
keywords: Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.1 - and be able to interpret evi
items.question: A crystal of potassium manganate(VII), KMnO₄, is placed in the centre of a piece of damp filter paper on a microscope slide. The ends of the paper are connected to a 20 V direct current supply for 15 minutes. What is seen? A purple colour moves towards the negative electrode only. A purple colour moves towards the positive electrode only. A purple colour moves towards both electrodes. The purple colour spreads out evenly in all directions.
items.ms: B: the MnO₄⁻ ion is purple and negatively charged, so it migrates to the positive electrode; K⁺ ions are colourless. A assumes the coloured ion is positive. C assumes both ions are coloured. D describes diffusion only and ignores the migration of ions in the electric field.
items.why: C3.1 has come up in 15 of 21 sessions; the migration MCQs (Oct2023, May2023, Jan2022) all used copper(II) chromate(VI), so the spec's own potassium manganate(VII) microscope-slide practical is the likeliest new version.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.1 - and be able to interpret evi
items.question: Which observation is the best evidence that solid sodium chloride consists of ions? It has a high melting temperature. It dissolves in water. It conducts electricity when molten but not when solid. It forms cube-shaped crystals.
items.ms: C: the solid does not conduct because the ions are fixed in the lattice; when molten the ions are free to move and carry the current. A: giant covalent substances such as diamond also have high melting temperatures. B: many covalent substances, such as sugar, dissolve in water. D: crystal shape alone does not show that charged particles are present.
items.why: Conductivity in different states is the most-asked evidence for ions (Oct2022 Q14(c), Jan2024 Q20(c), Jan2026 Q21(e)); the Oct2022 report says students confuse it with 'no delocalised electrons'.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.2 - describe the formation of io
items.question: Calcium phosphide, Ca₃P₂, is an ionic compound. It is used in some marine distress flares because it reacts with water to release phosphine, which catches fire in air. Describe, in terms of electrons, how calcium atoms and phosphorus atoms form the ions in calcium phosphide.
items.ms: Each calcium atom loses two (outer / 4s) electrons to form a Ca²⁺ ion Each phosphorus atom gains three electrons (into its 3p sub-shell) to form a P³⁻ ion (Overall) three calcium atoms transfer six electrons to two phosphorus atoms
items.why: C3.2 has been asked only as formula MCQs (Jan2026 Q3, Jan2022 Q1(a)); describing ion formation in terms of electrons, the spec's own wording, has not been set for a 2+/3− compound.

items.name: Dot-and-cross diagrams for ions
path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.3 - draw dot-and-cross diagrams
items.question: A dot-and-cross diagram for magnesium nitride, Mg₃N₂, shows the outer electrons only. Dots (•) represent electrons that came from nitrogen atoms and crosses (×) represent electrons that came from magnesium atoms. How many crosses are shown in the outer shell of each nitride ion? 2 3 5 6
items.ms: B: a nitrogen atom has 5 outer electrons and gains 3 from magnesium atoms to form N³⁻ with 8 outer electrons, so each nitride ion shows 5 dots and 3 crosses. A is the number lost by one magnesium atom. C is the number of dots. D is the total lost by three magnesium atoms, which is shared between two nitride ions.
items.why: Dot-and-cross diagrams of ionic compounds came up in 7 sessions (twice in Jan2026); counting the electrons gained by a 3− ion has not been asked and targets the 'partially filled ion' error in the Oct2021 and Jan2020 reports.

items.name: Ionic lattices
path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.4 - describe ionic crystals as g
items.question: Which is the best description of the structure of solid calcium fluoride, CaF₂? a giant lattice of Ca²⁺ and F⁻ ions, each ion attracted to the oppositely charged ions around it a giant lattice of calcium and fluorine atoms joined by covalent bonds separate CaF₂ molecules held together by weak forces between the molecules a lattice of Ca²⁺ ions in a sea of delocalised electrons
items.ms: A: calcium fluoride is a giant ionic lattice held by electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in all directions. B describes a giant covalent structure. C describes a simple molecular substance; there are no CaF₂ molecules. D describes a metal.
items.why: C3.4 is asked in 11 of 21 sessions, usually as 'giant ionic lattice'; the Jan2023 report penalised 'molecule' and 'macromolecule' for an ionic solid.

items.name: Ionic lattices
path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.4 - describe ionic crystals as g
items.question: Potassium bromide has the same lattice structure as sodium chloride. How many bromide ions are nearest neighbours of each potassium ion in the lattice? 1 4 6 8
items.ms: C: in the sodium chloride lattice each cation is surrounded by six anions (above, below, left, right, front and back). A treats KBr as a molecule. B counts only the neighbours in one plane. D is the arrangement in caesium chloride.
items.why: Drawing the sodium chloride lattice was asked in Jun2025 Q23(a)(iv); counting nearest neighbours in the same lattice is the natural MCQ follow-up and has not been asked.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.5 - that ionic bonding is the re
items.question: Which is the best description of ionic bonding? the strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions the transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom the electrostatic attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons the electrostatic attraction between two nuclei and a shared pair of electrons
items.ms: A: ionic bonding is the strong net electrostatic attraction between ions of opposite charge. B describes how the ions form, not the bond. C is metallic bonding. D is covalent bonding.
items.why: Defining ionic bonding came up in Oct2025 Q24(b) and Jun2025 Q23(a)(i); electron transfer and the metallic and covalent definitions are the common wrong answers.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.5 - that ionic bonding is the re
items.question: A crystal of sodium chloride shatters when it is struck sharply with a hammer. Which is the best explanation? The force breaks the covalent bonds between the sodium and chlorine atoms. The delocalised electrons can no longer hold the layers of ions together. The layers of ions slide over each other without the bonding being broken. A layer of ions is displaced so that ions with the same charge are next to each other and repel.
items.ms: D: the net attraction in the lattice depends on each ion being surrounded by oppositely charged ions; a small shift brings like charges together and the repulsion splits the crystal. A: the bonding is ionic, not covalent. B: there are no delocalised electrons in an ionic solid. C explains the malleability of metals.
items.why: Only the attraction between ions has been examined for C3.5; the 'net' attraction in the spec implies repulsion between like ions, which brittleness tests and which has never been asked.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.6 - the effects of ionic radius
items.question: Magnesium oxide melts at 2852 °C and calcium oxide melts at 2613 °C. Which is the best explanation for this difference? The Mg²⁺ ion has a greater charge than the Ca²⁺ ion. The Mg²⁺ ion is smaller than the Ca²⁺ ion, so it attracts the O²⁻ ions more strongly. Magnesium has a higher first ionisation energy than calcium. The forces between MgO molecules are stronger than those between CaO molecules.
items.ms: B: both cations are 2+, but Mg²⁺ has fewer electron shells so it is smaller; the oxide ions are closer to its centre and the electrostatic attraction is stronger, so more energy is needed to melt the solid. A: the charges are the same. C: ionisation energy is a property of the atoms, not of the bonding in the lattice. D: both are giant ionic lattices with no molecules.
items.why: C3.6 comes up in 9 of 21 sessions; the Jun2023 and Jan2024 reports criticise answers about atoms, ionisation energy or molecules instead of the size and charge of the ions.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.6 - the effects of ionic radius
items.question: Which list shows the compounds in order of increasing strength of ionic bonding? MgO, NaF, NaCl, KCl KCl, NaF, NaCl, MgO NaF, NaCl, KCl, MgO KCl, NaCl, NaF, MgO
items.ms: D: KCl has the largest ions with single charges (weakest); Na⁺ is smaller than K⁺; F⁻ is smaller than Cl⁻; MgO has 2+ and 2− ions (strongest). A is the order of decreasing strength. B places NaF before NaCl. C ignores the effect of cation size and puts KCl after NaCl.
items.why: Ranking ionic compounds by bond strength (Oct2025 Q2, Jan2022 Q2, Oct2019 Q8) recurs every few sessions; a list of four tests charge and radius together.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.7 - reasons for the trends in io
items.question: Which is the best explanation for the increase in ionic radius down Group 2, from Be²⁺ to Ba²⁺? The number of protons increases. The charge on the ion increases. The number of occupied electron shells increases. The ions become less polarising.
items.ms: C: each ion down the group has one more occupied shell, so the outer electrons are further from the nucleus. A: more protons on their own would pull the electrons closer. B: all the ions are 2+. D is a consequence of the larger radius, not its cause.
items.why: C3.7 is asked in 14 of 21 sessions; the trend down a group is in the spec but recent questions have all been on isoelectronic series, so it is due.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.7 - reasons for the trends in io
items.question: The ions O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ are isoelectronic. Which is the reason for the decrease in ionic radius from O²⁻ to Mg²⁺? The number of electrons decreases. The number of occupied electron shells decreases. The shielding by inner electrons increases. The number of protons increases but the number of electrons stays the same.
items.ms: D: each ion has 10 electrons in the same shells, but the nuclear charge rises from 8 to 12, so the electrons are attracted more strongly and pulled closer. A and B: isoelectronic ions have the same number of electrons in the same shells. C: the shielding is about the same because the electron arrangement is the same.
items.why: The isoelectronic N³⁻ to Al³⁺ series is the most-asked C3.7 item (Jan2023 Q24(a), May2024 Q11, Jan2022 Q4); the Jan2026 mark scheme needs 'more protons, same number of electrons'.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.8 - the meaning of the term polarisation' as appl
items.question: Aluminium fluoride, AlF₃, is a typical ionic solid that sublimes at 1290 °C. Aluminium iodide, AlI₃, melts at 189 °C and its bonding has considerable covalent character. State what is meant by the term polarisation, as applied to an anion. Explain why the bonding in aluminium iodide has more covalent character than the bonding in aluminium fluoride.
items.ms: Distortion of the electron cloud / electron density of the anion by a (nearby) cation The iodide ion is larger than the fluoride ion (and both have a single negative charge) so the electron cloud of the iodide ion is more easily distorted / polarised by the Al³⁺ ion, giving more electron density between the ions
items.why: C3.8 is asked in 6 of 21 sessions; the Jan2023 report found 70% scored nothing on fluoride polarisation and few mentioned distortion, so a definition plus an anion comparison is likely.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.9 - that the polarising power of
items.question: Which anion is the most easily polarised? F⁻ Cl⁻ O²⁻ S²⁻
items.ms: D: the sulfide ion is large and has a 2− charge, so its outer electron cloud is furthest from the nucleus and most easily distorted. A is the smallest, least polarisable anion. B is large but has only a single charge. C has a 2− charge but is much smaller than S²⁻.
items.why: Anion polarisability was asked only in Jan2022 Q6 and Jun2021 Q9; the Jan2023 report found 70% scored nothing on why the fluoride ion is hard to polarise.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.9 - that the polarising power of
items.question: Beryllium chloride has much more covalent character than barium chloride. Which is the best explanation? Be²⁺ has a much smaller radius than Ba²⁺ but the same charge, so it distorts the electron cloud of the chloride ion more. Be²⁺ has a greater charge than Ba²⁺, so it is more polarising. Be²⁺ is more easily polarised than Ba²⁺ because it is smaller. The chloride ion is smaller in beryllium chloride, so it is more easily polarised.
items.ms: A: polarising power depends on charge and radius; with the same 2+ charge, the very small Be²⁺ has the higher charge density and polarises the chloride ion, drawing electron density between the ions. B: both ions are 2+. C confuses the polarising power of the cation with polarisability. D: the chloride ion is the same in both compounds, and a smaller anion would be less polarisable.
items.why: BeCl₂ against CaCl₂ covalent character was asked in Oct2021 Q12(f); the reports note confusion between charge and charge density and between the cation and the anion.

items.name: Covalent bonding: definition and evidence
path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.10 - that covalent bonding is the
items.question: The diagrams show four electron density maps. The dots show the positions of the nuclei. Which map represents a molecule of chlorine, Cl₂? W X Y Z
items.ms: B: in Cl₂ the bonding pair is shared equally, so the contours enclose both nuclei (high electron density between them) and the map is symmetrical. A shows two separate ions of different size (ionic bonding). C encloses both nuclei but is unsymmetrical, as in a polar molecule such as HCl. D shows two separate atoms with no electron density between them.
items.why: Electron density maps are named in spec 3.10(ii) and were asked in Jun2019 Q23(a) and as MCQs for NaCl and HCl; picking the map of a non-polar covalent molecule from all four types has not been set.

items.name: Covalent bonding: definition and evidence
path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.10 - that covalent bonding is the
items.question: Silicon carbide, SiC, is used in cutting discs. It is very hard, does not melt below 2700 °C and does not conduct electricity. Which structure is best supported by these properties? separate SiC molecules held together by weak forces between the molecules a giant lattice of atoms held together by strong covalent bonds a giant lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons layers of atoms with only weak forces between the layers
items.ms: B: hardness and a very high melting temperature need many strong bonds throughout the structure, and no conduction means no mobile electrons or ions: a giant covalent (atomic) lattice. A would have a low melting temperature. C would conduct electricity. D would be soft and slippery, like graphite.
items.why: Giant covalent properties as evidence for covalent bonding (spec 3.10(i)) appeared with SiO₂ in Oct2021 Q13(b) and Jun2022 Q21(c); silicon carbide is a fresh example.

items.name: Dot-and-cross diagrams for covalent species; dative bonds
path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.11 - draw dot-and-cross diagrams
items.question: How many lone pairs of electrons are there in one molecule of nitrogen trifluoride, NF₃? Include the lone pairs on every atom. 1 3 9 10
items.ms: D: nitrogen has one lone pair and each of the three fluorine atoms has three lone pairs: 1 + 3 × 3 = 10. A counts only the nitrogen. B is the number of bonding pairs. C counts only the fluorine atoms.
items.why: C3.11 is asked in every session; counting lone pairs (Oct2020 Q13, H₂S) and the reports' 'lone pairs missing on the outer atoms' error make a whole-molecule count likely.

items.name: Dot-and-cross diagrams for covalent species; dative bonds
path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.11 - draw dot-and-cross diagrams
items.question: In the vapour at 180 °C, aluminium chloride exists as Al₂Cl₆ molecules. How many dative covalent bonds are there in one Al₂Cl₆ molecule? 1 2 4 6
items.ms: B: two AlCl₃ units join when a chlorine atom of each unit donates a lone pair to the aluminium atom of the other, so there are two dative bonds. A forms only one link. C counts all four bridging Al–Cl bonds, two of which are ordinary covalent bonds. D counts every chlorine atom.
items.why: Al₂Cl₆ is named in the spec and was asked in Jan2019, Jan2023, Jun2022 and Oct2024; the reports say students add Al–Al bonds or too many dative bonds.

items.name: Dot-and-cross diagrams for covalent species; dative bonds
path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.11 - draw dot-and-cross diagrams
items.question: Ammonia borane, H₃NBH₃, is a white solid that is being investigated as a way of storing hydrogen for fuel cells. It can be thought of as an ammonia molecule bonded to a borane molecule, BH₃: NH₃ + BH₃ → H₃NBH₃ The bond between the nitrogen atom and the boron atom is a dative covalent bond. State what is meant by the term dative covalent bond. Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for ammonia borane. Use dots (•) for electrons from nitrogen, crosses (×) for electrons from boron and circles (o) for electrons from hydrogen. Show outer electrons only. Predict the H–B–H bond angle in a borane molecule, BH₃, and in ammonia borane. Justify your answers. Calculate the percentage by mass of hydrogen in ammonia borane. Give your answer to three significant figures. When ammonia borane is heated to about 150 °C, each mole releases two moles of hydrogen gas. Calculate the volume of hydrogen, in dm³ measured at r.t.p., released when 5.00 g of ammonia borane is heated to 150 °C. [Molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹] When ammonia borane is heated strongly, it eventually forms boron nitride, BN. Boron nitride exists in two forms. Hexagonal boron nitride has layers of hexagonal rings of alternating boron and nitrogen atoms, similar to graphite. It is used as a lubricant at high temperatures and is an electrical insulator. Cubic boron nitride has a structure similar to diamond. It is used in cutting tools. Discuss the structure and bonding of the two forms of boron nitride and how they explain these uses and properties. Compare boron nitride with graphite and diamond where relevant.
items.ms: A covalent bond / shared pair of electrons in which both electrons come from the same atom Three N–H and three B–H bonding pairs, each with one electron from each atom The N–B bonding pair shown as two dots (both electrons from nitrogen) and no lone pairs on nitrogen or boron BH₃: 120° Boron in BH₃ has three bonding pairs and no lone pairs, which repel to be as far apart as possible (trigonal planar) Ammonia borane: 109.5° Boron now has four bonding pairs (including the dative bond) and no lone pairs, which repel equally (tetrahedral around boron) M(H₃NBH₃) = 14.0 + 10.8 + 6 × 1.0 = 30.8 (g mol⁻¹) % H = 6.0 ÷ 30.8 × 100 = 19.5 % n(H₃NBH₃) = 5.00 ÷ 30.8 = 0.1623 mol n(H₂) = 2 × 0.1623 = 0.3247 mol V(H₂) = 0.3247 × 24.0 = 7.79 dm³ IC1 Hexagonal BN: each boron atom is covalently bonded to three nitrogen atoms (and each N to three B) in flat layers, a giant covalent lattice IC2 There are only weak forces between the layers, so the layers slide over each other and it acts as a lubricant, as graphite does IC3 Many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt either form, so both have very high melting temperatures and hexagonal BN remains a solid lubricant at high temperatures IC4 Unlike graphite, hexagonal BN has no delocalised electrons that can move: the electrons are held in localised (polar) B–N bonds / on the more electronegative nitrogen atoms, so it does not conduct IC5 Cubic BN: each atom is covalently bonded to four others in a tetrahedral arrangement, a giant three-dimensional lattice like diamond IC6 Strong covalent bonds in all directions and no layers that can slide make cubic BN very hard, so it is used in cutting tools, as diamond is
items.why: C3.11 is asked in every session; dative bonds (NH₄⁺, Al₂Cl₆, SbCl₅) recur and the reports note donor and acceptor errors; boron nitride lets the C3.12 giant-structure ideas be tested in a new context.

items.name: Giant carbon structures: graphite, diamond, graphene
path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.12 - describe the different struc
items.question: Which row gives the number of other carbon atoms that each carbon atom is covalently bonded to? diamond 4, graphite 3, graphene 3 diamond 4, graphite 3, graphene 4 diamond 3, graphite 4, graphene 3 diamond 4, graphite 4, graphene 3
items.ms: A: diamond is a tetrahedral network (4); graphite is made of layers of hexagons (3); graphene is a single layer of graphite (3). B gives graphene four bonds. C swaps diamond and graphite. D gives graphite four bonds.
items.why: C3.12 is asked in 14 of 21 sessions; the number of bonds per carbon is the core marking point in every graphite and diamond mark scheme (Jun2024 Q17(c), Jun2019 Q23(e)).

items.name: Giant carbon structures: graphite, diamond, graphene
path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.12 - describe the different struc
items.question: Graphite is used as a dry lubricant. Which is the best explanation for this use? The covalent bonds within each layer are weak. Graphite has delocalised electrons that can move. There are only weak forces between the layers, so the layers can slide over each other. Each carbon atom is bonded to only three others, so the atoms can move past each other.
items.ms: C: the layers are held together only by weak forces, so they slide easily. A: the covalent bonds within the layers are strong. B explains electrical conductivity, not lubrication. D: the atoms within a layer are fixed by strong covalent bonds.
items.why: Applications of each carbon structure are in the spec; graphite as a lubricant has not been asked since 2019, and the Jun2019 report flags 'weak bonds within the layers'.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.13 - the meaning of the term elec
items.question: What is meant by the term electronegativity? the ability of an atom to attract the bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond the energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms the ability of an atom to gain an electron and form a negative ion the attraction between the nucleus of an isolated atom and its outer electrons
items.ms: A is the definition. B is the first ionisation energy. C describes forming an anion, not a bond. D refers to an isolated atom; electronegativity applies to atoms in a covalent bond.
items.why: C3.13 is asked in 11 of 21 sessions, so far only through bond polarity; definitions are listed as a weakness in several examiner reports and this one has not been asked directly.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.13 - the meaning of the term elec
items.question: Some electronegativity values are given. H 2.1 C 2.5 N 3.0 Si 1.8 S 2.5 In which molecule do the hydrogen atoms carry a partial negative charge (δ−)? CH₄ NH₃ SiH₄ H₂S
items.ms: C: silicon (1.8) is less electronegative than hydrogen (2.1), so the bonding electrons are drawn towards hydrogen, which becomes δ−. In A, B and D the other atom (2.5, 3.0 and 2.5) is more electronegative than hydrogen, so hydrogen is δ+.
items.why: Bond polarity from electronegativity (Jun2021 Q11, Jun2019 Q2) recurs; a hydride in which hydrogen is δ− is the likeliest unfamiliar twist.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.14 - that ionic and covalent bond
items.question: The table shows the electronegativities of some elements on the Pauling scale. Use the data to explain how the type of bonding changes across the series of oxides Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃ and SiO₂.
items.ms: The electronegativity difference between the element and oxygen decreases (from 2.6 in Na₂O to 1.7 in SiO₂) so the bonding becomes less ionic / more covalent (polar covalent), changing gradually along a continuum with no sudden change from ionic to covalent
items.why: The bonding continuum was examined through electronegativity differences in Jun2023 Q20(a)(iv), where the report criticised cut-off values; a series of four oxides tests the gradual change.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.15 - distinguish between polar bo
items.question: Which of these linear molecules is polar? BeCl₂ CO₂ CS₂ OCS
items.ms: D: in O=C=S the C=O bond is much more polar than the C=S bond (oxygen is more electronegative than sulfur), so the dipoles do not cancel. A, B and C are linear and symmetrical, so their bond dipoles cancel.
items.why: Identifying the polar molecule is asked almost every session (Oct2025 Q9, Jan2024 Q5, May2023 Q14); a linear but unsymmetrical molecule is an untested twist on the CO₂ example.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.15 - distinguish between polar bo
items.question: Which molecule is not polar? CH₂F₂ SiF₄ NF₃ SF₂
items.ms: B: SiF₄ is tetrahedral with four identical polar bonds, so the dipoles cancel. A is tetrahedral but has two different kinds of bond, so the dipoles do not cancel. C is pyramidal and D is bent (V-shaped), so they are polar.
items.why: Choosing the non-polar molecule (Jan2022 Q8, Oct2021 Q9) recurs; these four need the shape and the electronegativity together.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.15 - distinguish between polar bo
items.question: A teacher demonstrates the effect of an electrostatic force on jets of liquids. A thin jet of each liquid runs from a burette past a charged rod, as shown in the diagram. The table shows the results. Suggest why the jet of cyclohexane is not deflected. Predict the Cl–C–Cl bond angle in a molecule of tetrachloroethene. Explain why the jet of tetrachloroethene is not deflected but the jet of trichloroethene is deflected. Refer to the shapes of the molecules in your answer. The jet of water bends towards the rod whether the rod is positively or negatively charged. Explain why. 1,2-Dichloroethene, CHCl=CHCl, exists as two geometric isomers, P and Q, shown in the diagram. Give the name of isomer Q, using E–Z notation. Predict which isomer, P or Q, would be deflected by the charged rod. Justify your answer.
items.ms: Carbon and hydrogen have similar electronegativities, so the C–H bonds are (almost) non-polar and cyclohexane molecules have no (permanent) dipole 120° Chlorine is more electronegative than carbon, so the C–Cl bonds are polar (Cδ+ Clδ−) Tetrachloroethene is planar and symmetrical, so the bond dipoles cancel and there is no overall (permanent) dipole In trichloroethene one chlorine is replaced by hydrogen, so the molecule is not symmetrical, the dipoles do not cancel and the molecule is polar Water molecules are polar / have a permanent dipole, with δ− on the oxygen atom and δ+ on the hydrogen atoms The molecules turn so that the end with the opposite charge to the rod is nearest to it, so there is always an attraction (E)-1,2-dichloroethene P (is deflected / is polar) In P both chlorine atoms (δ−) are on the same side of the C=C bond, so the bond dipoles do not cancel / one side of the molecule is δ− and the other δ+ In Q the C–Cl dipoles point in opposite directions, so they cancel and Q is non-polar
items.why: C3.15 is asked in 18 of 21 sessions but the jets-of-liquid practical has appeared only as MCQs (May2024 Q9, Oct2022 Q8); geometric isomers with different polarities link it to topic 5.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.16 - the principles of the electr
items.question: Which shows the order of the strength of repulsion between pairs of electrons? bond pair–bond pair > lone pair–bond pair > lone pair–lone pair lone pair–bond pair > lone pair–lone pair > bond pair–bond pair lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair lone pair–lone pair > bond pair–bond pair > lone pair–bond pair
items.ms: C: lone pairs are held closer to the central atom and spread out more, so lone pair–lone pair repulsion is greatest and bond pair–bond pair repulsion is least. A is the reverse order. B and D put the middle repulsion in the wrong place.
items.why: Lone-pair repulsion is a marking point in the C3.16 mark schemes (Jan2026 Q22(b)); the Jan2022 report says students quote it without understanding.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.16 - the principles of the electr
items.question: A molecule XH₂ has an H–X–H bond angle of about 104.5°. There are no multiple bonds in the molecule. How many lone pairs of electrons are there on the central atom, X? 0 1 2 3
items.ms: C: four pairs (two bonding, two lone) give a tetrahedral arrangement squeezed to about 104.5°, as in water. A: two pairs would give 180°. B: three pairs would give a bent shape with an angle a little under 120°. D: five pairs with three lone pairs would give a linear molecule (180°).
items.why: C3.16 is hot (16 of 21 sessions); working back from a bond angle to the number of lone pairs reverses the usual question.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.16 - the principles of the electr
items.question: Hydrogen cyanide, HCN, and methanal, HCHO, are small molecules that contain multiple bonds. Their shapes can be predicted using electron-pair repulsion theory. State the main principles of electron-pair repulsion theory. Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for a molecule of hydrogen cyanide. Show outer electrons only. Predict the H–C–N bond angle in hydrogen cyanide. Justify your answer. The diagram shows the displayed formula of methanal. The H–C–H bond angle, x, is 116.5°. Explain why the bond angles around the carbon atom in methanal are close to 120°. Suggest why angle x is slightly less than 120°.
items.ms: The pairs of electrons around the central atom repel each other They arrange themselves as far apart as possible to minimise repulsion Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs (lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair) A double or triple bond counts as one region of electron density / the shape depends on the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs A C–H single bond (one shared pair) and a C≡N triple bond (three shared pairs) One lone pair on the nitrogen atom and no lone pair on the carbon atom 180° There are two regions of electron density around the carbon atom (the triple bond counts as one region) and no lone pairs, so they repel to be as far apart as possible There are three regions of electron density (two C–H bonds and the C=O double bond) and no lone pairs around the carbon atom, which repel to be as far apart as possible (trigonal planar) The C=O double bond contains two pairs of electrons / has a greater electron density than a C–H bond so it repels the C–H bonding pairs more strongly than they repel each other, pushing the two C–H bonds closer together
items.why: C3.16 is hot (16 of 21 sessions); the Jun2022 mark scheme accepts regions of electron density for multiple bonds, and the effect of a double bond on a bond angle has not been asked.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.17 - the terms bond length' and bond angle'
items.question: Hydrazine, N₂H₄, is used as a fuel in the small rocket thrusters that keep satellites in position. The diagram shows the displayed formulae of hydrazine, diazene and nitrogen, with the nitrogen–nitrogen bond length in each molecule. The diagram does not show the shapes of the molecules. State what is meant by the term bond length. State what is meant by the term bond angle. Suggest why the nitrogen–nitrogen bond length decreases from hydrazine to nitrogen. Predict the H–N–H bond angle in hydrazine. Justify your answer.
items.ms: The (average) distance between the nuclei of two (covalently) bonded atoms The angle between two (covalent) bonds from the same atom The number of shared pairs of electrons between the nitrogen atoms increases (one, two, three) / there is greater electron density between the nuclei so there is a stronger (electrostatic) attraction between the shared electrons and the two nuclei, which pulls the nuclei closer together 107° Each nitrogen atom has three bonding pairs and one lone pair of electrons (four pairs in total) The lone pair repels more than the bonding pairs, so the angle is less than 109.5°
items.why: C3.17 has been asked in only 3 of 21 sessions and never as the two definitions; the angle in hydrazine links it to the hot C3.19.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.18 - and be able to explain the s
items.question: Which molecule has bond angles of 90° and 120°? BCl₃ PCl₅ (gas) SF₆ C₂H₄
items.ms: B: gaseous PCl₅ is trigonal bipyramidal, with 120° between the equatorial bonds and 90° between axial and equatorial bonds. A and D have angles of 120° only. C is octahedral, with angles of 90° (and 180°).
items.why: C3.18 is asked in 20 of 21 sessions; the Jan2020 report found the 90° and 120° angles of PCl₅ were not known.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.18 - and be able to explain the s
items.question: Which pair of molecules have the same shape? BeCl₂ and CO₂ BCl₃ and NH₃ CO₂ and H₂O NH₃ and NH₄⁺
items.ms: A: both are linear: BeCl₂ has two bonding pairs and CO₂ two double-bond regions around the central atom. B: BCl₃ is trigonal planar but NH₃ is pyramidal (lone pair). C: H₂O is bent because of two lone pairs. D: NH₄⁺ is tetrahedral.
items.why: Comparing shapes of the spec-list molecules (Oct2020 Q15, Jan2023 Q13) recurs; the distractor pairs test the effect of lone pairs.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.18 - and be able to explain the s
items.question: Several gases are used to make computer chips. Boron trichloride, BCl₃, and sulfur hexafluoride, SF₆, are used to etch the surface of silicon wafers. Silane, SiH₄, reacts with ammonia, NH₃, at high temperature to deposit a thin layer of silicon nitride, Si₃N₄, on the wafer. Hydrogen is also formed. Complete the table. The row for silane has been completed for you. Explain why the H–N–H bond angle in ammonia is smaller than the H–Si–H bond angle in silane. Write the equation for the reaction of silane with ammonia to form silicon nitride and hydrogen. Include state symbols. A wafer is coated using 90.0 cm³ of silane, measured at r.t.p. All of the silane reacts. Calculate the mass, in grams, of silicon nitride formed. [Molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹] Silicon nitride does not melt below 1900 °C and is an electrical insulator. Explain these properties in terms of the structure and bonding of silicon nitride.
items.ms: BCl₃: 3, 0, trigonal planar, 120° NH₃: 3, 1, (trigonal) pyramidal, 107° SF₆: 6, 0, octahedral, 90° Both molecules have four pairs of electrons around the central atom Silane has four bonding pairs; ammonia has three bonding pairs and one lone pair The lone pair repels more than the bonding pairs, so the bonding pairs in ammonia are pushed closer together and the angle is reduced 3SiH₄ + 4NH₃ → Si₃N₄ + 12H₂ State symbols: SiH₄(g), NH₃(g), Si₃N₄(s), H₂(g) n(SiH₄) = 90.0 ÷ 24 000 = 3.75 × 10⁻³ mol n(Si₃N₄) = 3.75 × 10⁻³ ÷ 3 = 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol mass = 1.25 × 10⁻³ × 140.3 = 0.175 g Giant covalent lattice / giant atomic structure Many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it, which needs a lot of energy There are no delocalised electrons or mobile ions (all the outer electrons are in localised covalent bonds)
items.why: C3.18 is asked in 20 of 21 sessions, usually as a table of pairs, shape and angle (Jan2021 Q19(a), Oct2019 Q24(c)) followed by the effect of a lone pair (Jun2025 Q23(b), Oct2025 Q17(a)).

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.19 - apply the electron-pair repu
items.question: Which molecule or ion is trigonal pyramidal? AlCl₃ BF₃ CH₃⁺ PF₃
items.ms: D: phosphorus has three bonding pairs and one lone pair, like nitrogen in NH₃, so PF₃ is trigonal pyramidal. A, B and C have three bonding pairs and no lone pair on the central atom, so they are trigonal planar.
items.why: 'Trigonal pyramidal' for AlCl₃ or BF₃ is a named error in the Jan2023 report; PF₃ is a direct analogue of NH₃.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.19 - apply the electron-pair repu
items.question: The amide ion, NH₂⁻, forms when sodium reacts with ammonia. What is the expected H–N–H bond angle in NH₂⁻? 104.5° 107° 109.5° 120°
items.ms: A: nitrogen has 5 + 1 + 2 = 8 outer electrons: two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, like water, so about 104.5°. B assumes one lone pair, as in NH₃. C ignores the extra repulsion of the lone pairs. D assumes three regions and no lone pairs.
items.why: Analogues of water (OF₂, May2024 Q7(c)) and of NH₃ recur in C3.19; the amide ion is an analogous ion not yet used.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.19 - apply the electron-pair repu
items.question: Until 1962 the noble gases were thought to form no compounds. Xenon is now known to react with fluorine to form XeF₂, XeF₄ and XeF₆. A xenon atom has eight electrons in its outer shell. Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for a molecule of xenon tetrafluoride, XeF₄. Show outer electrons only. Predict the shape of a molecule of XeF₄ and its F–Xe–F bond angle. Justify your answer. Explain whether a molecule of XeF₄ is polar. In a preparation, 0.524 g of xenon reacted with excess fluorine to form 0.701 g of XeF₄. Xe(g) + 2F₂(g) → XeF₄(s) Calculate the percentage yield of XeF₄. Xenon tetrafluoride reacts with antimony pentafluoride to form an ionic compound. XeF₄ + SbF₅ → [XeF₃]⁺[SbF₆]⁻ Predict the shape of the SbF₆⁻ ion and its F–Sb–F bond angle. Deduce the number of bonding pairs and the number of lone pairs of electrons around the xenon atom in the XeF₃⁺ ion. Show your working.
items.ms: Four Xe–F bonding pairs Two lone pairs on the xenon atom and three lone pairs on each fluorine atom Six pairs of electrons around the xenon atom: four bonding pairs and two lone pairs The electron pairs repel to be as far apart as possible, giving an octahedral arrangement (as in SF₆) The two lone pairs are opposite each other (at 180°) because lone pair–lone pair repulsion is the greatest Square planar, 90° The Xe–F bonds are polar because fluorine is more electronegative than xenon The molecule is symmetrical (square planar), so the bond dipoles cancel and the molecule is not polar n(Xe) = 0.524 ÷ 131.3 = 3.991 × 10⁻³ mol Theoretical mass of XeF₄ = 3.991 × 10⁻³ × 207.3 = 0.827 g Percentage yield = 0.701 ÷ 0.827 × 100 = 84.7 % Octahedral 90° Xe has 8 − 1 = 7 outer electrons of its own, plus 3 electrons shared from the fluorine atoms = 10 electrons / 5 pairs 3 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs
items.why: Unfamiliar molecules with five or six electron pairs (SF₄ and S₂F₁₀ in Jan2025, TlCl₄³⁻ in Oct2024) are the recent C3.19 pattern; a square planar molecule with two lone pairs has not yet been asked.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.20 - that metals consist of giant
items.question: Which is the best description of the structure of solid magnesium? a giant lattice of Mg²⁺ ions in a sea of delocalised electrons a giant lattice of magnesium atoms joined by covalent bonds a giant lattice of Mg²⁺ ions and electrons, all held in fixed positions Mg₂ molecules held together by weak forces
items.ms: A: each magnesium atom releases its two outer electrons, which are delocalised over the lattice of Mg²⁺ ions. B describes a giant covalent structure. C: the electrons are not fixed, they are delocalised. D: magnesium has no molecules.
items.why: C3.20 is asked in 12 of 21 sessions (Jan2024 Q9, Oct2021 Q14(c)); the Jun2019 report found diagrams of metals that looked ionic or covalent.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.20 - that metals consist of giant
items.question: A student draws a diagram of the metallic bonding in aluminium. The diagram shows 12 aluminium ions. How many delocalised electrons should the diagram show? 12 24 36 156
items.ms: C: each aluminium atom (Group 13) loses its three outer electrons to form Al³⁺, so 12 × 3 = 36 electrons are delocalised. A assumes one electron per ion. B assumes Al²⁺. D uses all 13 electrons of each atom.
items.why: Metallic lattice diagrams (Jun2019 Q23(d), Jun2024 Q15(c), Jun2025 Q23(c)) are marked on the number of delocalised electrons per ion, and the Jun2019 report found too many electrons drawn.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.21 - that metallic bonding is the
items.question: Which list shows the metals in order of increasing strength of metallic bonding? Mg, Na, K Na, K, Mg K, Mg, Na K, Na, Mg
items.ms: D: K⁺ is larger than Na⁺ (weaker attraction to the delocalised electrons); Mg²⁺ is smaller still, has a 2+ charge and gives two delocalised electrons per ion, so magnesium has the strongest metallic bonding. A is the decreasing order. B puts sodium below potassium. C puts magnesium in the middle.
items.why: Comparing metallic bonding strength (Jan2022 Q22(a) Mg against Na, May2023 Q12 Be against Ba) recurs.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.21 - that metallic bonding is the
items.question: Calcium melts at 842 °C but potassium melts at 63 °C. Which is the best explanation? Calcium atoms are larger than potassium atoms, so there is more attraction. Calcium has a higher first ionisation energy than potassium. Each Ca²⁺ ion has a greater charge than a K⁺ ion and there are more delocalised electrons per ion, so the electrostatic attraction is stronger. Calcium has covalent bonds between its atoms, but potassium has metallic bonds.
items.ms: C: stronger attraction between the 2+ ions and twice as many delocalised electrons means more energy is needed to melt calcium. A: calcium atoms are smaller, and larger particles would give weaker attraction. B: ionisation energy does not measure the strength of metallic bonding. D: both are metals with metallic bonding.
items.why: The Jan2026 Q21(b) mark scheme needs the higher ionic charge and more delocalised electrons; atom size and ionisation energy are the reports' common wrong reasons.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.22 - use the models in 3.20 and 3
items.question: Which statement explains why a metal conducts electricity both when solid and when molten? The metal ions are free to move in both states. The delocalised electrons can move through the structure in both states. Electrons are released from the metal ions only when a voltage is applied. The metal ions and the delocalised electrons both carry the current in the liquid but not in the solid.
items.ms: B: the delocalised electrons are mobile in the solid and the liquid and carry the charge. A: the ions are fixed in the solid, and conduction by a metal does not depend on moving ions. C: the electrons are already delocalised. D: the current in a metal is carried by electrons only.
items.why: Metallic conduction is asked in 14 of 21 sessions (Jan2026 Q20(b), Jan2020 Q19(b)); 'ions move' is the error the Jan2026 Q21(e) mark scheme rejects.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 3 Bonding and Structure
C3.22 - use the models in 3.20 and 3
items.question: Copper is ductile: it can be drawn out into thin wires. Which is the best explanation? The layers of copper ions can slide over each other and the delocalised electrons still hold them together. The copper ions repel each other strongly, so the metal spreads out into a wire. The covalent bonds between the copper atoms are weak, so they break and re-form easily. The delocalised electrons can move, so the wire can carry a current.
items.ms: A: when the layers of ions slide, the delocalised electrons still attract all the ions, so the metallic bonding is not broken. B: the attraction between the ions and the electrons holds the metal together. C: copper has metallic, not covalent, bonding. D is true but explains conductivity, not ductility.
items.why: Malleability and alloys were asked in Jun2019 Q23(d) and Jun2024 Q15(c); ductility for wires is an untested version of the same idea.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 5 Alkenes
C5.1 - the general formula of alken
items.question: Myrcene, C₁₀H₁₆, is found in bay leaves. Its skeletal formula is shown. How many σ bonds and how many π bonds are there in one molecule of myrcene? 9 σ bonds and 3 π bonds 22 σ bonds and 3 π bonds 25 σ bonds and 3 π bonds 28 σ bonds and 0 π bonds
items.ms: Myrcene has 9 carbon–carbon bonds (3 of them C=C) and 16 C–H bonds. Each single bond is one σ bond and each C=C is one σ bond and one π bond: σ = 9 + 16 = 25, π = 3. A counts only the carbon–carbon bonds. B counts each C=C as a π bond only. D counts each C=C as two σ bonds.
items.why: Counting σ and π bonds in an unfamiliar skeletal formula was set as an MCQ in Jan2026, Jan2025, Oct2021, Jan2020 and Oct2019.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 5 Alkenes
C5.1 - the general formula of alken
items.question: A hydrocarbon has the molecular formula C₈H₁₄. Which could it be? an alkane an alkene with one C=C bond and no ring a cycloalkane with one ring a cycloalkene with one ring and one C=C bond
items.ms: Alkanes are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (C₈H₁₈). Alkenes with one C=C and cycloalkanes with one ring are both CₙH₂ₙ (C₈H₁₆). A cycloalkene with one ring and one C=C has two fewer hydrogen atoms again, CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ = C₈H₁₄.
items.why: General formulae of alkenes and cycloalkenes were tested in Oct2024 Q15(a) and Jun2021 Q23(a); comparing four series at once is the likely next twist.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 5 Alkenes
C5.1 - the general formula of alken
items.question: When decane is cracked, one of the products is a gaseous alkene, X. A 0.700 g sample of X occupies 300 cm³ at room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.). [Molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹] Deduce the molecular formula of X. Show your working.
items.ms: n(X) = 300 ÷ 24 000 = 0.0125 (mol) and M = 0.700 ÷ 0.0125 = 56 (g mol⁻¹) alkenes are CₙH₂ₙ, so 14n = 56 and n = 4: X is C₄H₈
items.why: Jun2021 Q23(a) deduced an alkene's formula from its molar mass; giving the molar mass through a gas volume (C1.8) is the expected synoptic step.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 5 Alkenes
C5.2 - explain geometric isomerism
items.question: Which compound exists as E and Z isomers? 2-methylbut-2-ene 1,1-dichloropropene 3-ethylpent-2-ene 3-methylpent-2-ene
items.ms: In 3-methylpent-2-ene, CH₃CH=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, C2 carries H and CH₃ and C3 carries CH₃ and C₂H₅: two different groups on each carbon of the C=C. A: C2 carries two CH₃ groups. B: C1 carries two Cl atoms. C: C3 carries two C₂H₅ groups.
items.why: Choosing the alkene with geometric isomers came up in Jan2026 Q19, Jun2025 Q18 and Jan2023 Q20; branched names test the 'two different groups on each carbon' rule.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 5 Alkenes
C5.2 - explain geometric isomerism
items.question: Hepta-2,5-diene has the structure CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH=CHCH₃. How many different geometric isomers of hepta-2,5-diene are there? 1 2 3 4
items.ms: Each C=C can be E or Z, giving EE, ZZ and EZ. The molecule is symmetrical, so 2E,5Z and 2Z,5E are the same compound: 3 isomers. D counts 2 × 2 without spotting the symmetry. B considers only one C=C. A ignores geometric isomerism.
items.why: Counting geometric isomers in molecules with several C=C bonds (α-farnesene Jan2021, ocimene Jan2022) is examined beyond the spec wording; a symmetrical diene is the untested twist.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 5 Alkenes
C5.2 - explain geometric isomerism
items.question: Muscalure is the sex pheromone of the female housefly and is used in fly traps. Muscalure is (Z)-tricos-9-ene, an unbranched alkene with one C=C bond: CH₃(CH₂)₇CH=CH(CH₂)₁₂CH₃ Give the molecular formula of muscalure. The C=C bond in muscalure consists of a σ bond and a π bond. Explain, in terms of the π bond, why there is restricted rotation about the C=C bond. Dec-1-ene, CH₂=CH(CH₂)₇CH₃, is another unbranched alkene. Explain why muscalure has geometric isomers but dec-1-ene does not. Draw the structure of muscalure around the C=C bond to show the Z arrangement. You may write R for CH₃(CH₂)₇– and R′ for –(CH₂)₁₂CH₃. Muscalure made in industry contains some of the E-isomer. Both isomers react with hydrogen. Give the name of a suitable catalyst for this reaction. Explain why the E-isomer and the Z-isomer of tricos-9-ene form the same product with hydrogen. A fly trap contains 5.0 mg of muscalure. Calculate the number of muscalure molecules in the trap. [Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹]
items.ms: C₂₃H₄₆ the π bond forms by the sideways overlap of (two) p orbitals, with electron density above and below the (σ) bond axis rotation about the C=C would move the p orbitals out of line so the overlap is lost / the π bond would have to break (which needs a lot of energy) muscalure: each carbon atom of the C=C is bonded to two different groups (an H atom and an alkyl chain) dec-1-ene: one carbon of the C=C (C1) is bonded to two identical atoms (two H atoms) C=C with H and R on one carbon and H and R′ on the other, R and R′ on the same side of the C=C nickel / Ni both form tricosane / C₂₃H₄₈ / CH₃(CH₂)₂₁CH₃ (the C=C becomes a C–C single bond) there is free rotation about a C–C single bond, so the product has no geometric isomers M(C₂₃H₄₆) = 322 (g mol⁻¹) and n = 5.0 × 10⁻³ ÷ 322 = 1.55 × 10⁻⁵ (mol) number of molecules = 1.55 × 10⁻⁵ × 6.02 × 10²³ = 9.3 × 10¹⁸
items.why: Why geometric isomers exist (restricted rotation, two different groups) was asked in Oct2025, Jan2024, Oct2023 and Jan2021; linking restricted rotation to π overlap (Oct2025 Q23(b)) and the loss of isomerism on hydrogenation is the likely new angle.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 5 Alkenes
C5.3 - the E-Z naming system for ge
items.question: What is the name of the compound shown? E-3-chloropent-2-ene Z-3-chloropent-2-ene E-3-chloropent-3-ene Z-3-chloropent-3-ene
items.ms: On C2, CH₃ has priority over H; on C3, Cl (atomic number 17) has priority over C₂H₅ (C, atomic number 6). CH₃ and Cl are on opposite sides of the C=C, so the isomer is E. The chain is numbered to give the C=C the lowest locant, 2. B follows the carbon chain (both chain ends on the same side) instead of the priority groups; C and D number the chain from the wrong end.
items.why: Naming a drawn halogenoalkene with E or Z came up in Jun2022 Q18, May2023 Q17 and Jan2025 Q20; a drawing in which the carbon chain looks 'cis' but the isomer is E is the likeliest trap.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 5 Alkenes
C5.3 - the E-Z naming system for ge
items.question: In the E–Z naming system, each atom or group attached to a carbon atom of a C=C bond is given a priority. Which shows the groups in order of decreasing priority? –Br > –CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ > –Cl > –F –CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ > –Br > –Cl > –F –Br > –Cl > –F > –CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ –F > –Cl > –Br > –CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃
items.ms: Priority depends on the atomic number of the atom directly attached to the C=C carbon: Br (35) > Cl (17) > F (9) > C (6). A ranks by the mass of the whole group (C₄H₉ = 57); B by the size of the group; D by electronegativity.
items.why: The Jan2021 examiners' report says candidates ranked groups by mass rather than by atomic number; a priority-order MCQ tests this directly.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 5 Alkenes
C5.3 - the E-Z naming system for ge
items.question: The refrigerant HCFO-1224yd is 1-chloro-2,3,3,3-tetrafluoropropene, CF₃CF=CHCl. One of its geometric isomers is shown. Explain why the cis–trans naming system cannot be used to name the geometric isomers of this compound. Deduce whether the isomer shown is the E-isomer or the Z-isomer. Justify your answer.
items.ms: the four atoms or groups on the C=C (F, CF₃, H and Cl) are all different, so there is no pair of identical atoms or groups (one on each carbon) to compare F has a higher priority than CF₃ and Cl has a higher priority than H, because the atom attached to the C=C has a higher atomic number the higher-priority atoms, F and Cl, are on the same side of the C=C, so it is the Z-isomer
items.why: E/Z for a molecule where cis–trans fails was asked as an MCQ in Oct2025 Q12; the spec's 'why cis–trans breaks down' has not had its own written mark, and a group (CF₃) heavier than the higher-priority atom (F) is the known trap.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 5 Alkenes
C5.4 - describe the reactions of al
items.question: 3-Methylbut-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH(CH₃)₂, is shaken with acidified potassium manganate(VII) at room temperature. What is the organic product? 3-methylbutan-2-ol 3-methylbutane-1,2-diol 3-methylbutane-1,1-diol 3-methylbutane-1,3-diol

items.question: In the first step of the mechanism for the reaction of hydrogen bromide with ethene, two curly arrows are drawn. Which pair of curly arrows is correct? arrow 1 from the C=C bond to the Br atom; arrow 2 from the H–Br bond to the H atom arrow 1 from the C=C bond to the H atom; arrow 2 from the H–Br bond to the Br atom arrow 1 from the H atom to the C=C bond; arrow 2 from the H–Br bond to the Br atom arrow 1 from the C=C bond to the H atom; arrow 2 from the Br atom to the H–Br bond

items.question: 1-Methylcyclohexene reacts with hydrogen bromide. What is the major product? 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane (bromomethyl)cyclohexane 1,2-dibromo-1-methylcyclohexane
items.ms: H adds to C2, giving a tertiary carbocation at C1 (bonded to three carbon atoms), which is more stable than the secondary carbocation formed if H adds to C1; Br⁻ then bonds to C1. B comes from the less stable secondary carbocation (minor product). C puts Br on a carbon that was not part of the C=C. D is a product of bromine, not hydrogen bromide.
items.why: Major products from unfamiliar alkenes via tertiary carbocations (Jun2022 Q22(c), Oct2022 Q15(c)) are a regular C5.6 test.

items.question: This question is about electrophilic addition reactions of alkenes. A bromine molecule is non-polar. Explain how a bromine molecule becomes polarised as it approaches the C=C bond of an alkene. Bromine reacts with but-2-ene at room temperature to form 2,3-dibromobutane. Draw the mechanism for this reaction. Include curly arrows, and relevant dipoles, lone pairs and charges. When ethene is bubbled through an aqueous solution of bromine and sodium chloride, the products include 1,2-dibromoethane and 1-bromo-2-chloroethane, but no 1,2-dichloroethane forms. Explain how these results support the mechanism of electrophilic addition. Hydrogen bromide reacts with pent-2-ene to give two products in similar amounts, but with 2-methylbut-2-ene it gives one major product. Explain these observations. Refer to the intermediates formed and name the products. Iodine bromide, IBr, reacts with 2-methylpropene, (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, by electrophilic addition. Explain which atom in the I–Br molecule carries the partial positive charge (δ+). Draw the structure of the major product. Justify your answer.
items.ms: the high electron density of the π bond / C=C repels the electrons in the Br–Br bond, so the Br atom nearer the C=C becomes δ+ (and the other δ−) / an induced dipole forms induced dipole on the bromine molecule, Brδ+–Brδ− curly arrow from the C=C to the Brδ+ atom and curly arrow from the Br–Br bond to (or just beyond) the Brδ− atom correct carbocation intermediate, CH₃CHBrC⁺HCH₃ Br⁻ with a lone pair and a full negative charge and curly arrow from the lone pair to C⁺ the first step is attack on the C=C by Brδ+ from Br₂ (the electrophile), so every product contains Br on one carbon this forms a carbocation intermediate, CH₂BrCH₂⁺, in a separate step the carbocation can then be attacked by any negative ion present: Br⁻ gives 1,2-dibromoethane and Cl⁻ gives 1-bromo-2-chloroethane Cl⁻ cannot start the reaction (it is not an electrophile / it is repelled by the π electrons), so no 1,2-dichloroethane forms IC1 In both reactions the Hδ+ atom of HBr bonds to one carbon of the C=C, forming a carbocation; Br⁻ then bonds to the positive carbon IC2 Pent-2-ene: H adding to C3 gives CH₃C⁺HCH₂CH₂CH₃ and H adding to C2 gives CH₃CH₂C⁺HCH₂CH₃; both are secondary carbocations IC3 The two secondary carbocations have similar stability (two alkyl groups on each C⁺), so 2-bromopentane and 3-bromopentane form in similar amounts IC4 2-Methylbut-2-ene: H adding to C3 gives the tertiary carbocation (CH₃)₂C⁺CH₂CH₃; H adding to C2 gives the secondary carbocation (CH₃)₂CHC⁺HCH₃ IC5 A tertiary carbocation is more stable than a secondary one (three alkyl groups release electron density towards C⁺), so it forms in preference IC6 Major product 2-bromo-2-methylbutane; minor product 2-bromo-3-methylbutane I is δ+ because Br is more electronegative than I (CH₃)₂CBrCH₂I: Br on the carbon bonded to the two CH₃ groups and I on the CH₂ carbon Iδ+ bonds to the CH₂ carbon to give the tertiary carbocation (CH₃)₂C⁺CH₂I, which is more stable than the primary carbocation; Br⁻ then bonds to C⁺
items.why: C5.6 has come up in 20 of 21 sessions and carries 5% of the unit's marks; the spec's 'giving evidence' for the mechanism and the case of two equally stable secondary carbocations have never been asked, while unsymmetrical electrophiles (BrCl Jan2021, ICl Jun2021) recur.

items.question: Aluminium has atomic number 13. Which statement about an atom of ²⁷Al is correct? The neutrons have a total relative mass of 14. The nucleus has a relative charge of +27. The electrons have a total relative mass of 13. The atom has a relative charge of +13.
items.ms: ²⁷Al has 13 protons, 27 − 13 = 14 neutrons and 13 electrons. Each neutron has a relative mass of 1, so the neutrons have a total relative mass of 14. B uses the mass number for the nuclear charge (it is +13, from the protons only); C gives the electron a relative mass of 1 instead of about 1/1840; D ignores the 13 electrons (relative charge −1 each), which make the atom neutral.

items.question: Which pair of species have the same mass number but different atomic numbers? ¹²C and ¹⁴C ¹⁶O and ¹⁶O²⁻ ³⁹K and ⁴⁰Ca ⁴⁰Ar and ⁴⁰K
items.ms: Mass number = number of protons + neutrons; atomic number = number of protons. ⁴⁰Ar (atomic number 18) and ⁴⁰K (atomic number 19) both have mass number 40. A are isotopes (same atomic number, different mass numbers); B have the same nucleus (an atom and its ion); C have the same number of neutrons (20), not the same mass number.

items.ms: Protons = atomic number = 27; neutrons = 59 − 27 = 32; a 2+ ion has lost two electrons, so it has 27 − 2 = 25 electrons. B ignores the charge; C adds two electrons (as for a 2− ion); D gives the mass number as the number of neutrons.

items.question: Heavy water, ²H₂O, contains the hydrogen isotope ²H (deuterium) in place of ¹H. Both kinds of water molecule contain ¹⁶O. Which is the same for a molecule of ²H₂O and a molecule of ¹H₂O? the total number of electrons the total number of neutrons the relative molecular mass the total number of nucleons
items.ms: Isotopes have the same number of protons and so, in neutral atoms, the same number of electrons: both molecules have 1 + 1 + 8 = 10 electrons. ²H has one neutron and ¹H has none, so ²H₂O has 10 neutrons and ¹H₂O has 8 (B); the relative molecular masses (C) and the numbers of nucleons (D) are 20 and 18.
items.why: Isotope questions are always about single atoms (Jan2026 Q25(a), Jan2022 Q20(b), Jun2021 Q1); applying the definition to molecules that contain different isotopes has not been asked.

items.question: Phosphorus has only one isotope, ³¹P. The mass spectrum of phosphorus vapour has peaks at m/z = 31, 62, 93 and 124. What is the formula of the molecules in phosphorus vapour? P P₂ P₃ P₄
items.ms: The peak with the largest m/z is the molecular ion, P₄⁺: 124 ÷ 31 = 4. The peaks at m/z = 31, 62 and 93 are fragment ions (P⁺, P₂⁺ and P₃⁺) formed when molecular ions break up; A, B and C each take a fragment for the molecule.

items.question: Titanium is used to make strong, low-density alloys for aircraft. A sample of titanium was vaporised and analysed in a mass spectrometer. The mass spectrum of the 1+ ions formed is shown. Describe how the titanium atoms are ionised in the mass spectrometer. Include an equation, with state symbols, for the formation of a ⁴⁸Ti⁺ ion. Calculate the relative atomic mass of titanium in this sample. Give your answer to two decimal places. When the full range of m/z values was recorded, a small peak was also seen at m/z = 24.5. Identify the ion responsible for this peak. Explain how this ion gives a peak at m/z = 24.5. Suggest why the peaks from 2+ ions are much smaller than the peaks from 1+ ions. The ions ⁴⁶Ti⁺, ⁵⁰Ti⁺ and ⁴⁸Ti²⁺ all pass through the magnetic field of the mass spectrometer. State which of these ions is deflected the most. Justify your answer. Explain how the detector allows the relative abundance of each isotope to be measured. Titanium-50 is used to make beams of ions in experiments to make new elements. A sample of titanium enriched in ⁵⁰Ti contains only ⁴⁸Ti and ⁵⁰Ti. Its relative atomic mass is 49.6. Calculate the percentage abundance of ⁵⁰Ti in this sample.
items.ms: (Atoms) bombarded with high-energy / high-speed electrons (from an electron gun), which knock out an electron ⁴⁸Ti(g) + e⁻ → ⁴⁸Ti⁺(g) + 2e⁻ (46 × 8.2) + (47 × 7.4) + (48 × 73.7) + (49 × 5.4) + (50 × 5.3) = 4792.2 4792.2 ÷ 100 = 47.92 ⁴⁹Ti²⁺ m/z = mass ÷ charge = 49 ÷ 2 = 24.5 Removing a second electron needs more energy / the second ionisation energy is greater than the first because the second electron is removed from a positive ion, which attracts it more strongly so (far) fewer atoms form 2+ ions than 1+ ions ⁴⁸Ti²⁺ It has the smallest m/z (48 ÷ 2 = 24) / the smaller the mass-to-charge ratio, the greater the deflection The positive ions hit the detector and gain electrons / are discharged, producing an (electric) current The size of the current is proportional to the number of ions with that m/z, so a larger current means a greater abundance 48(100 − x) + 50x = 4960 (or equivalent with fractions) x = 80.0%

items.question: Which is the definition of the first ionisation energy of an element? The energy change when one electron is added to each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1− ions. The energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions. The energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of the element in its standard state to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions. The energy needed to remove all the outer electrons from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous positive ions.
items.ms: First ionisation energy: one electron is removed from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms, forming one mole of gaseous 1+ ions, e.g. Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻. A describes adding electrons to form negative ions, which is not an ionisation energy; C starts from the element in its standard state, so it would also include the energy needed to form gaseous atoms; D removes all the outer electrons, not one electron per atom.
items.why: C2.8 has come up in 17 of 21 sessions; the definition of first ionisation energy is a 3-mark structured item (Oct2025 Q22(a)) and the ERs report confusion with adding electrons (Jan2020, Jan2021), but it has not been an MCQ.

items.question: All ionisation energies are endothermic. Which statement explains why? Energy must be supplied to overcome the attraction between the nucleus and the electron being removed. Energy must be supplied to break the bonds between the atoms in the element. Energy must be supplied because the electron being removed repels the nucleus. Energy must be supplied to overcome the repulsion between the electron being removed and the other electrons.
items.ms: The negative electron is attracted to the positive nucleus, so energy must be supplied to remove it. B: ionisation energies start from gaseous atoms, so no bonds in the element are broken; C: the electron and the nucleus attract, they do not repel; D: repulsion between electrons makes an electron easier to remove, not harder.

C2.10 - how ionisation energies are
items.question: Which element has a lower first ionisation energy than the element immediately before it in the Periodic Table? calcium gallium germanium krypton
items.ms: Gallium ([Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p¹) loses an electron from the 4p sub-shell, which is higher in energy (and partly shielded by the 4s electrons) than the 4s electron removed from zinc ([Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s²), so gallium (579 kJ mol⁻¹) is lower than zinc (906 kJ mol⁻¹). Calcium (after potassium), germanium (after gallium) and krypton (after bromine) follow the general increase: the nuclear charge increases and the electron is removed from the same sub-shell with similar shielding.
items.why: C2.10 has come up in 20 of 21 sessions, with the Mg → Al decrease asked often (Oct2025 Q14(f), Jun2025 Q21(c)); the same sub-shell effect in Period 4 (elements up to Kr are in the spec) has not been asked.

items.question: The gaseous species F⁻, Ne, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ all have the electronic configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. Which species needs the most energy to remove one electron? F⁻ Ne Na⁺ Mg²⁺
items.ms: In each species the electron is removed from the same 2p sub-shell with the same shielding (by the two 1s electrons), so the energy needed depends on the nuclear charge. Mg²⁺ has the most protons (12), so its 2p electrons are attracted most strongly. F⁻ (9 protons), Ne (10) and Na⁺ (11) have smaller nuclear charges.
items.why: Spec 2.10 names the number of protons as one of three factors; past questions change the shell or sub-shell (Jan2024 Q1, Oct2023 Q6), so an isoelectronic set, in which only the nuclear charge changes, is an unasked angle.

items.question: The table shows the first ionisation energies of the elements with atomic numbers 11 to 20. Plot a graph of first ionisation energy against atomic number on the grid. Join the points with straight lines. Explain the general increase in first ionisation energy from sodium to argon. Explain why the first ionisation energy of aluminium is lower than that of magnesium. Explain why the first ionisation energy of sulfur is lower than that of phosphorus. Explain why there is a large decrease in first ionisation energy from argon to potassium. The second ionisation energy of sodium is 4562 kJ mol⁻¹. The second ionisation energy of magnesium is 1451 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain why the second ionisation energy of sodium is much greater than that of magnesium.

items.question: Which feature of the first ionisation energies of the elements from sodium to potassium provides evidence for the existence of sub-shells? the general increase from sodium to argon the decrease from magnesium to aluminium the large decrease from argon to potassium the first ionisation energy of potassium being lower than that of sodium
items.ms: Aluminium's outer electron is in the 3p sub-shell, which is higher in energy than magnesium's 3s, so the first ionisation energy falls: evidence that the third shell is divided into sub-shells. A is caused by the increasing nuclear charge within one shell; C and D are evidence for a new quantum shell, not for sub-shells.

items.question: Which statement about the shapes of the orbitals in the second quantum shell is correct? The three 2p orbitals are each dumbbell-shaped, with their axes at right angles to each other. The 2s orbital is dumbbell-shaped and each 2p orbital is spherical. The three 2p orbitals are each dumbbell-shaped and all lie along the same axis. Each 2p orbital is a circular path that the electrons follow around the nucleus.
items.ms: An s orbital is spherical; each p orbital is dumbbell-shaped (two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus) and the three p orbitals lie along the x, y and z axes, at 90° to each other. B swaps the shapes; C puts all three p orbitals on one axis; D describes an orbit, not an orbital (a region where there is a high probability of finding the electrons).

items.question: Which gaseous species has exactly three unpaired electrons in its ground state? Cl⁺ P⁻ S⁺ Si
items.ms: S⁺ has 15 electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³. The three 3p electrons occupy separate orbitals before any pairing, so there are three unpaired electrons. Cl⁺ and P⁻ have 16 electrons (3p⁴: one pair and two unpaired electrons); Si is 3p² (two unpaired electrons).

items.question: Selenium has the electronic configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁴. Which element would be expected to have chemical properties most similar to those of selenium? arsenic bromine sulfur krypton
items.ms: Chemical properties are determined by the electronic configuration, especially of the outer shell. Sulfur (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴) has the same outer configuration, s² p⁴, as selenium (4s² 4p⁴). Arsenic (4s² 4p³), bromine (4s² 4p⁵) and krypton (4s² 4p⁶) are in the same period, so they have the same number of shells but a different outer configuration.

items.question: Between which two neighbouring elements in Period 2 is there the largest decrease in melting temperature? lithium and beryllium boron and carbon carbon and nitrogen oxygen and fluorine
items.ms: Carbon (diamond or graphite) has a giant covalent structure, so many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it; nitrogen is simple molecular (N₂), so only weak intermolecular forces are overcome. Suggest why the melting temperatures decrease in the order sulfur > phosphorus > chlorine > argon. Boron is the Period 2 element in the same group as aluminium. Its melting temperature is 2349 K. Suggest why the melting temperature of boron is so much higher than that of aluminium.
items.ms: Sodium: giant metallic (lattice); metallic bonding / attraction between Na⁺ ions and delocalised electrons Chlorine: simple molecular (Cl₂); (weak) intermolecular forces / London forces Metallic bonding is the attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons From Na to Al the charge on the ions increases (Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺) and the number of delocalised electrons per atom increases (1, 2, 3) The ions also become smaller, so the attraction is stronger and more energy is needed to overcome it Silicon has a giant covalent structure / lattice with (many) strong covalent bonds between the atoms Phosphorus is simple molecular (P₄) with (weak) intermolecular forces between the molecules Much more energy is needed to break the covalent bonds in silicon than to overcome the intermolecular forces in phosphorus Sulfur, phosphorus and chlorine are simple molecular (S₈, P₄, Cl₂) and argon exists as single atoms, so only (weak) intermolecular forces are overcome on melting The larger the molecule / the more electrons per molecule (S₈ > P₄ > Cl₂ > Ar), the stronger the intermolecular forces Boron has a giant covalent structure (not metallic), with strong covalent bonds between the atoms Many covalent bonds must be broken, which needs more energy than overcoming the metallic bonding in aluminium
items.why: C2.18(i) has come up in 12 of 21 sessions, most often as silicon against phosphorus (Jan2022 Q22(b), Oct2019 Q24(b)); the metals' rise from Na to Al and a Period 2 comparison (boron's giant covalent structure was rewarded in Oct2024 Q20(c)) give the fresh parts.

items.question: Dichloromethane is a toxic, volatile solvent. Which change to an experiment that uses dichloromethane reduces the risk but does not change the hazard of the substance used? heating the dichloromethane so that the reaction is faster using a larger volume of dichloromethane so that the reaction is easier to see replacing dichloromethane with a less toxic solvent carrying out the experiment in a fume cupboard

items.question: Pentane, C₅H₁₂, and hexadecane, C₁₆H₃₄, are both flammable alkanes. Which statement explains why pentane is the greater fire hazard in a laboratory at room temperature? Pentane has a lower boiling temperature, so more flammable vapour forms above the liquid. Pentane is unsaturated, so it reacts more readily with oxygen. Pentane has more carbon atoms in each molecule, so it releases more energy per mole when it burns. Hexadecane is not flammable, because its molecules are too large to react with oxygen.

items.question: Bromine is more electronegative than carbon. Which pair of species forms when the C–Br bond in 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr, breaks heterolytically? (CH₃)₃C• and Br• (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br⁻ (CH₃)₃C⁻ and Br⁺ (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br•

items.question: Which description of the curly arrows for the homolytic fission of a Cl–Cl bond is correct? one double-headed curly arrow from the Cl–Cl bond to one of the chlorine atoms one curly half-arrow from one chlorine atom to the other chlorine atom two curly half-arrows, each starting at the Cl–Cl bond and ending at a different chlorine atom two double-headed curly arrows, each starting at the Cl–Cl bond and ending at a different chlorine atom
