items.question: Hydroxyl radicals, •OH, form in the lower atmosphere in sunlight. They remove methane, a greenhouse gas, from the air. Hydrogen peroxide, H–O–O–H, forms hydroxyl radicals when its O–O bond breaks in sunlight. Use curly half-arrows to show the homolytic fission of the O–O bond in hydrogen peroxide. Show the products. Explain why •OH is described as a free radical. Refer to the electrons in the species in your answer. The first step in the removal of methane by hydroxyl radicals is CH₄ + •OH → •CH₃ + H₂O State, with a reason, whether the C–H bond in methane breaks homolytically or heterolytically in this step. This step is similar to a propagation step in the reaction of methane with chlorine in ultraviolet light. Write the equation for that propagation step. In pure water a very small proportion of the O–H bonds break: H₂O → H⁺ + OH⁻ Explain, in terms of the bonding electrons, how the fission of the O–H bond in this reaction differs from the fission of the O–O bond in (a). Explain why the O–H bond breaks to give H⁺ and OH⁻ rather than H⁻ and OH⁺. Which of the species OH⁻, H₂O, H⁺ and Cl⁻ can act as an electrophile? Explain your answer by referring to the definition of an electrophile. The average concentration of hydroxyl radicals in the lower atmosphere is about 1.0 × 10⁶ radicals per cm³. items.question: Which species is a free radical? CN⁻ CO NO NO⁺
items.ms: A free radical has an unpaired electron. NO has 7 + 8 = 15 electrons, an odd number, so one is unpaired. CN⁻ (6 + 7 + 1 = 14), CO (6 + 8 = 14) and NO⁺ (7 + 8 − 1 = 14) all have an even number of electrons, all paired.
items.why: Jan2026 Q19 asked which OH species is a radical; NO, an engine pollutant (C4.13), tests the same definition by counting electrons instead of spotting a printed dot.

items.question: Crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation. Some of the fractions are then cracked or reformed. Explain how fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions. A student cracks liquid paraffin in the laboratory using the apparatus shown. Liquid paraffin is a mixture of alkanes with 18 to 30 carbon atoms in each molecule. State the purpose of the aluminium oxide. Suggest why the first test tube of gas collected is thrown away. Explain why the delivery tube must be removed from the water before the student stops heating. The gas collected decolourises bromine water. State what this shows about the gas. One alkane in liquid paraffin is icosane, C₂₀H₄₂. Write the equation for the cracking of one molecule of icosane to form decane and ethene only. In one experiment, 1.20 g of liquid paraffin produced 168 cm³ of gas, measured at room temperature and pressure. Assume that the liquid paraffin is icosane only, that it cracks as in (c)(i) and that the gas collected is ethene only. Calculate the percentage by mass of the liquid paraffin that was cracked. [Molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹] In industry, the heavier fractions from fractional distillation are cracked. Explain why oil companies crack these fractions. Heptane is reformed into 2,3-dimethylpentane for use in petrol. Draw the skeletal formula of 2,3-dimethylpentane. Give one reason why 2,3-dimethylpentane is a better fuel for petrol engines than heptane.
items.ms: crude oil is heated so that it vaporises (and passes into a column) there is a temperature gradient in the column: hottest at the bottom, coolest at the top fractions condense at different heights (where the temperature falls below their boiling temperature): the higher the boiling temperature, the lower in the column catalyst it contains (mainly) air displaced from the apparatus as the boiling tube cools, the gas inside contracts / the pressure inside falls so water would be sucked back into the hot boiling tube, which could crack (shatter) it contains a C=C double bond / it contains an alkene / it is unsaturated C₂₀H₄₂ → C₁₀H₂₂ + 5C₂H₄ amount of ethene = 168 ÷ 24 000 = 7.00 × 10⁻³ mol amount of icosane = 7.00 × 10⁻³ ÷ 5 = 1.40 × 10⁻³ mol, so mass = 1.40 × 10⁻³ × 282.0 = 0.3948 g percentage cracked = 0.3948 ÷ 1.20 × 100 = 32.9% demand for shorter-chain fractions (such as petrol) is greater than the supply from fractional distillation / the heavier fractions are produced in excess of demand cracking produces alkenes (such as ethene) used to make polymers / other chemicals shorter-chain alkanes are more useful fuels (they ignite and burn more easily) five-carbon zig-zag chain with methyl branches on carbons 2 and 3 (seven carbon atoms in total) it burns more smoothly / more efficiently / is less likely to cause knocking (pre-ignition, pinking) / has a higher octane number

items.question: Which change would increase the mass of carbon monoxide and carbon particulates in the exhaust gases of a diesel engine? decreasing the ratio of air to fuel increasing the ratio of air to fuel removing sulfur compounds from the fuel removing nitrogen from the air supplied to the engine
items.ms: Less air means less oxygen, so combustion is less complete and more CO and carbon (soot) form. B gives more complete combustion. C reduces sulfur dioxide only. D would reduce oxides of nitrogen only.
items.why: Incomplete combustion in a limited supply of oxygen is asked regularly (Jun2021 Q21(a)(i), Jan2024 Q17); linking each pollutant to its cause is the reasoning the spec wants.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 4 Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes
C4.14 - the problems arising from po
items.question: Large ships burn heavy fuel oil, a mixture of long-chain alkanes that also contains sulfur compounds. International rules limit the sulfur content of the fuel to 0.50% by mass. A ship burns 45 tonnes of fuel oil containing 0.50% sulfur by mass. Calculate the maximum mass, in tonnes, of sulfur dioxide that forms. Assume that all the sulfur is converted into sulfur dioxide. Explain how the sulfur dioxide emitted by the ship can lead to acid rain. Include an equation in your answer. The exhaust gases also contain carbon monoxide, which can build up in the engine room. Explain why carbon monoxide is toxic.
items.ms: mass of sulfur = 45 × 0.50 ÷ 100 = 0.225 tonnes mass of SO₂ = 0.225 × 64.1 ÷ 32.1 = 0.449 tonnes sulfur dioxide dissolves in / reacts with water (in clouds or rain) SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ carbon monoxide binds (strongly / irreversibly) to haemoglobin (in red blood cells) so less oxygen is carried by the blood to the cells / tissues
items.why: C4.14 has come up in 5 of 21 sessions, only as a 1-mark CO MCQ (Oct2022) and why CO is toxic (Oct2021); the acidity of sulfur oxides has never been asked as an equation, and the shipping sulfur limit is a fresh real context.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 4 Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes
C4.15 - discuss the reasons for deve
items.question: Bioethanol made by fermenting sugar cane can replace some of the petrol used in cars. Which statement best explains why bioethanol is a more sustainable fuel than petrol? The sugar cane can be regrown every year, so the fuel is renewable. Bioethanol does not release carbon dioxide when it burns. Bioethanol is biodegradable. Bioethanol releases more energy per gram than petrol when it burns.
items.ms: Sustainability depends on whether the source is renewable: sugar cane can be regrown, but crude oil is finite. B: ethanol releases CO₂ when it burns. C: biodegradability is not a reason (Jun2023 ER). D: ethanol releases less energy per gram than petrol.
items.why: C4.15 was last asked in Oct2023 (E10 sustainability); the Jun2023 ER lists 'biodegradable' and 'releases no CO₂' as the common wrong answers, which are the distractors here.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 4 Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes
C4.16 - apply the concept of carbon
items.question: Hydrogen forms only water when it burns. Which method of producing hydrogen would make it closest to a carbon-neutral fuel? reacting methane with steam electrolysis of water using electricity from a coal-fired power station electrolysis of water using electricity from wind turbines heating coal with steam
items.ms: Carbon neutrality depends on the net CO₂ released over the whole process; electrolysis powered by wind releases (almost) no CO₂. A and D use fossil fuels as the source of the hydrogen and release CO₂. B releases CO₂ when the electricity is generated.
items.why: C4.16 names hydrogen as a fuel to judge, but past papers asked about plant-based fuels (Jun2019) and a general statement (Jan2021); the Oct2021 MS notes hydrogen is carbon neutral only if its production is.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 4 Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes
C4.17 - the reactions of alkanes wit
items.question: 20 cm³ of a gaseous alkane needs exactly 130 cm³ of oxygen for complete combustion. Both volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure. Which alkane is it? methane ethane propane butane
items.ms: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + ½(3n + 1)O₂ → nCO₂ + (n + 1)H₂O. 130 ÷ 20 = 6.5 = ½(3n + 1), so n = 4: butane. Methane needs 2, ethane 3.5 and propane 5 volumes of oxygen per volume of alkane.
items.why: C4.17 has come up in 12 of 21 sessions, mostly as combustion equations; using the balanced equation with gas volumes joins it to the C1.8 skill that every paper tests.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 4 Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes
C4.17 - the reactions of alkanes wit
items.question: Propane reacts with excess bromine in ultraviolet light until every hydrogen atom has been replaced. Which equation represents the overall reaction? C₃H₈ + Br₂ → C₃H₇Br + HBr C₃H₈ + 8Br₂ → C₃Br₈ + 8HBr C₃H₈ + 4Br₂ → C₃Br₈ + 4H₂ C₃H₈ + 4Br₂ → C₃H₈Br₈
items.ms: Each substitution replaces one H atom with one Br atom, uses one Br₂ and forms one HBr: eight substitutions need 8Br₂ and give 8HBr. A is a single substitution. C: hydrogen gas is not a product. D: alkanes are saturated and do not undergo addition.
items.why: Overall equations for alkane halogenation were MCQs in Oct2022 and Jan2022; the Jan2020 ER reported candidates ignoring 'a large excess of bromine', which this item targets.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 4 Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes
C4.18 - the mechanism of the free ra
items.question: When methane reacts with chlorine in ultraviolet light, the absorption of one photon can lead to thousands of molecules of chloromethane being formed. Which statement best explains this? Each propagation step uses up one free radical and forms another. Each termination step forms two free radicals. Ultraviolet light breaks the C–H bonds in methane as well as the Cl–Cl bonds. Each chlorine molecule splits into four free radicals.
items.ms: Propagation steps regenerate a radical (Cl• + CH₄ → •CH₃ + HCl; •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•), so a chain reaction continues until a termination step. B: termination removes radicals. C: ultraviolet light breaks the Cl–Cl bond in initiation; C–H bonds are broken by Cl• in propagation. D: Cl₂ → 2Cl•.
items.why: Oct2025 Q13(c) asked what distinguishes termination from propagation; why one initiation leads to many product molecules is the chain idea behind it, not yet asked directly.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 4 Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes
C4.18 - the mechanism of the free ra
items.question: When butane reacts with chlorine in ultraviolet light, two different butyl radicals can form. Which hydrocarbon cannot form in a termination step of this reaction? octane 3-methylheptane 3,4-dimethylhexane 2,5-dimethylhexane
items.ms: The radicals are CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂• and CH₃C•HCH₂CH₃. Two of the first give octane (A); one of each gives 3-methylheptane (B); two of the second give 3,4-dimethylhexane (C). 2,5-Dimethylhexane, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂CH(CH₃)₂, would need (CH₃)₂CHCH₂• radicals, which form from 2-methylpropane.
items.why: Termination steps that form a hydrocarbon recur (Jun2025: two butyl radicals give octane; Jan2019 ER); seeing that the second butyl radical gives branched C₈ isomers is the extension not yet asked.

path: Unit 1 Structure, Bonding and Introduction to Organic Chemistry
Topic 4 Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes
C4.18 - the mechanism of the free ra
items.question: 2,2-Dimethylpropane, C(CH₃)₄, is a minor component of natural gas. It reacts with chlorine to form 1-chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane, (CH₃)₃CCH₂Cl, and hydrogen chloride. Name the mechanism of this reaction. The first step of the mechanism is the initiation step. State the essential condition for the initiation step. Show the initiation step, using curly half-arrows to show the movement of electrons. Give the two propagation steps that form 1-chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane. Use structural formulae. A small amount of a hydrocarbon with the molecular formula C₁₀H₂₂ also forms, in a termination step. Give the equation for this termination step and the IUPAC name of the hydrocarbon. 2,2-Dimethylpropane forms only one monochlorinated product, C₅H₁₁Cl. Its structural isomer 2-methylbutane forms four different monochlorinated products. Explain this difference. The organic product mixture also contains compounds with two or more chlorine atoms. Explain why this reaction is of limited use for making 1-chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane. One of these compounds contains 50.4% chlorine by mass. Deduce its molecular formula. Show your working.
items.ms: (free) radical substitution ultraviolet (UV) light / sunlight Cl–Cl with two curly half-arrows, each from the bond to a different Cl atom 2Cl• (dots shown) Cl• + C(CH₃)₄ → (CH₃)₃CCH₂• + HCl (CH₃)₃CCH₂• + Cl₂ → (CH₃)₃CCH₂Cl + Cl• 2(CH₃)₃CCH₂• → (CH₃)₃CCH₂CH₂C(CH₃)₃ 2,2,5,5-tetramethylhexane in 2,2-dimethylpropane all 12 hydrogen atoms are equivalent (all in identical CH₃ groups on the same carbon), so replacing any one of them gives the same product in 2-methylbutane the hydrogen atoms are on carbon atoms in four different positions (environments), so Cl can replace H in four different positions further substitution occurs (Cl• attacks the chloroalkane), giving a mixture of products / more than one substitution product molar mass of C₅H₁₂₋ₓClₓ = 72.0 + 34.5x / correct use of percentage by mass x = 2 gives 71.0 ÷ 141.0 × 100 = 50.4% C₅H₁₀Cl₂
items.why: C4.18 is the hottest point in the topic (19 of 21 sessions, 5.1% of marks), set with ethane, propane, butane, hexane and isooctane; a highly symmetrical alkane tests whether students apply the steps rather than recall them (Oct2023 ER), and further substitution with a % by mass link echoes Jan2020 and Jun2025.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.1 - what is meant by the term oxidation number' a
items.question: In the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻, nitrogen has an oxidation number of +5. What does this value represent? the actual charge on the nitrogen atom in the ion the charge the nitrogen atom would have if the ion were completely ionic the number of electrons in the outer shell of a nitrogen atom the number of covalent bonds formed by the nitrogen atom in the ion
items.ms: B: an oxidation number is the charge an atom would have if the species were fully ionic (N⁵⁺ with three O²⁻ gives an overall charge of 1−). A: the bonds in NO₃⁻ are covalent, so nitrogen carries only a small partial charge, not +5. C: nitrogen does have five outer electrons, but this is a coincidence (nitrogen is −3 in NH₃). D: nitrogen forms four covalent bonds in NO₃⁻ (one double, one single and one dative), not five.
items.why: C8.1 was asked in 8 of 20 sessions; the meaning of an oxidation number was tested through Roman numerals in Jun2024 Q18(b) (MS: 'the charge … if the species were fully ionic') but not yet as a stand-alone MCQ.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.2 - calculate the oxidation numb
items.question: Which row gives the oxidation number of hydrogen in potassium hydride, KH, of oxygen in potassium peroxide, K₂O₂, and of oxygen in oxygen difluoride, OF₂? H in KH: +1; O in K₂O₂: −2; O in OF₂: −2 H in KH: +1; O in K₂O₂: −1; O in OF₂: +2 H in KH: −1; O in K₂O₂: −2; O in OF₂: −2 H in KH: −1; O in K₂O₂: −1; O in OF₂: +2
items.ms: D: in a metal hydride hydrogen is −1 (K is +1); in a peroxide each O is −1 (2(+1) + 2x = 0); fluorine is always −1, so O in OF₂ is +2. A applies the usual values (H +1, O −2) throughout; B misses the hydride; C misses the peroxide and the OF₂ exception.
items.why: C8.2 came up in 16 of 20 sessions, almost always as a 1-mark MCQ (Jan2024 Q6 used NaH and H₂O₂ as options); OF₂, where fluorine forces oxygen to be positive, has not been used.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.2 - calculate the oxidation numb
items.question: Sodium tetrahydridoborate, NaBH₄, is a metal hydride used as a reducing agent. It contains Na⁺ and BH₄⁻ ions. Hydrogen has the same oxidation number in NaBH₄ as in sodium hydride, NaH. What is the oxidation number of boron in NaBH₄? −5 −4 +3 +4
items.ms: C: Na is +1 and each H is −1, as in NaH, so +1 + x + 4(−1) = 0 and x = +3. A takes H as +1 (1 + x + 4 = 0). B takes H as +1 and leaves out sodium (x + 4 = 0). D takes H as −1 but leaves out sodium (x − 4 = 0).
items.why: C8.2 is hot (16 of 20 sessions); the spec names metal hydrides, but past MCQs have only used NaH as a distractor (Jan2024 Q6), so a complex hydride is a likely next step.

C8.2 - calculate the oxidation numb
items.question: Lithium hydride, LiH, is an ionic compound. It reacts with water to release hydrogen. LiH(s) + H₂O(l) → LiOH(aq) + H₂(g) Give the oxidation number of hydrogen in LiH, in H₂O and in H₂. Explain why this reaction is a redox reaction but not a disproportionation reaction.
items.ms: LiH: −1; H₂O: +1; H₂: 0 (all three needed) Hydrogen in LiH / H⁻ is oxidised (−1 → 0) and hydrogen in H₂O is reduced (+1 → 0), so the hydrogen oxidised and the hydrogen reduced are in two different species
items.why: C8.2 is hot (16 of 20 sessions) and the spec names metal hydrides, but hydrogen at −1 has only been an MCQ option (Jan2024 Q6); the H⁻ + H₂O reaction also tests the 'two species' idea of Jun2022 Q16(b).

items.ms: lead(IV) oxide sodium nitrate(III)

Its anion contains one bismuth atom and three oxygen atoms. Give the formula of sodium bismuthate(V). Calcium phosphate(V) is the main mineral in bones. The phosphate(V) ion contains one phosphorus atom and four oxygen atoms. Give the formula of calcium phosphate(V).

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.5 - oxidation and reduction in t
items.question: In which reaction is nitrogen reduced? 2NO₂(g) + 4CO(g) → N₂(g) + 4CO₂(g) 4NH₃(g) + 5O₂(g) → 4NO(g) + 6H₂O(g) NH₃(g) + HCl(g) → NH₄Cl(s) 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g)
items.ms: A: N goes from +4 in NO₂ to 0 in N₂, a decrease, so nitrogen is reduced (carbon is oxidised from +2 to +4). B: N rises from −3 to +2, so it is oxidised. C: N is −3 in NH₃ and in NH₄⁺; this is an acid–base reaction, not redox. D: N rises from +2 to +4 (oxidised).
items.why: C8.5 has come up in 18 of 20 sessions, often as an MCQ on which reaction is (not) redox or which element is oxidised (Jan2026 Q8, Jan2024 Q7); nitrogen oxides from exhausts were the context in Jan2020 Q18.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.5 - oxidation and reduction in t
items.question: Silicon can be made by heating silicon dioxide with magnesium. SiO₂(s) + 2Mg(s) → Si(s) + 2MgO(s) How many moles of electrons are transferred for each mole of silicon formed? 1 mol 2 mol 4 mol 8 mol
items.ms: C: Si goes from +4 to 0, gaining 4 electrons per atom; the two Mg atoms each lose 2 electrons (0 → +2), also 4 in total. A gives the amount of silicon formed, not of electrons. B is the number lost by one Mg atom. D adds the electrons lost to the electrons gained, counting each one twice.
items.why: C8.5 asks for redox in terms of electron transfer as well as oxidation number, applied to s- and p-block elements; reduction by a Group 2 metal was set in Oct2022 Q23 (TiCl₄ + Mg), but counting the electrons transferred has not been asked.

items.name: to 8.9 Redox, oxidising and reducing agents, disproportionation, metals/non-metals
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.5 - oxidation and reduction in t
items.question: Car airbags inflate when sodium azide, NaN₃, decomposes rapidly to form nitrogen. Reaction 1 2NaN₃(s) → 2Na(s) + 3N₂(g) The sodium formed is dangerous, so the airbag pellets also contain potassium nitrate and silicon dioxide. Reaction 2 10Na(s) + 2KNO₃(s) → K₂O(s) + 5Na₂O(s) + N₂(g) Reaction 3 Na₂O(s) + SiO₂(s) → Na₂SiO₃(s) Consider Reaction 1. Deduce the oxidation number of nitrogen in sodium azide, NaN₃. Explain, in terms of electron transfer, which element is oxidised and which element is reduced in Reaction 1. A driver's airbag needs 60.0 dm³ of nitrogen, measured at room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.). Calculate the minimum mass of sodium azide needed, assuming all the nitrogen comes from Reaction 1. [Molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹] Consider Reaction 2. State the role of potassium nitrate in Reaction 2. Show that, in Reaction 2, the total number of electrons lost by the sodium atoms is equal to the total number of electrons gained by the nitrogen atoms. Explain, using oxidation numbers, why Reaction 3 is not a redox reaction. Suggest why the sodium oxide formed in Reaction 2 must not escape into the car. Include an equation in your answer.
items.ms: −⅓ Sodium (ions, Na⁺) gain electrons, so sodium is reduced (+1 → 0) Nitrogen / the azide ions lose electrons, so nitrogen is oxidised (−⅓ → 0) n(N₂) = 60.0 ÷ 24.0 = 2.50 mol n(NaN₃) = 2.50 × 2/3 = 1.67 mol mass = 1.667 × 65.0 = 108 g oxidising agent / oxidant 10 Na atoms each lose 1 electron (0 → +1): 10 electrons lost 2 N atoms each gain 5 electrons (+5 in KNO₃ → 0 in N₂): 10 electrons gained Na stays +1, Si stays +4 and O stays −2, so no element changes oxidation number Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH Sodium oxide reacts with water / moisture in the air, eyes or skin to form sodium hydroxide, which is corrosive / strongly alkaline
items.why: C8.5 is hot (18 of 20 sessions) and is usually set inside a longer question on a redox process in context (Oct2022 Q23 titanium, Jan2020 Q18 urea and NOₓ); airbags combine s- and p-block redox, a fractional oxidation number and a gas-volume calculation.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.6 - that oxidising agents gain e
items.question: Which species can act only as a reducing agent in redox reactions? Cl₂ H₂O₂ SO₂ I⁻
items.ms: D: iodine in I⁻ is −1, its lowest oxidation number, so I⁻ can only lose electrons (be oxidised): it can only be a reducing agent. A: Cl₂ (0) can gain electrons (to Cl⁻) or lose them (to ClO⁻), as in its disproportionation. B: O in H₂O₂ is −1, between −2 and 0, so H₂O₂ can be an oxidising or a reducing agent. C: S in SO₂ is +4; it can be oxidised to +6 (SO₄²⁻) or reduced (for example to S, 0).
items.why: C8.6 was asked in 9 of 20 sessions, always about one given reaction (Jan2026 Q9(b), Oct2025 Q2); linking 'reducing agents lose electrons' to an element's lowest oxidation number is an untested angle.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.7 - that a disproportionation re
items.question: Which equation represents a disproportionation reaction? IO₃⁻(aq) + 5I⁻(aq) + 6H⁺(aq) → 3I₂(aq) + 3H₂O(l) 3HNO₂(aq) → HNO₃(aq) + 2NO(g) + H₂O(l) 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g) N₂O₄(g) → 2NO₂(g)
items.ms: B: nitrogen in HNO₂ (+3) is both oxidised, to +5 in HNO₃, and reduced, to +2 in NO: one species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced. A: iodine is oxidised (−1 → 0 in I⁻) and reduced (+5 → 0 in IO₃⁻), but in two different species. C: nitrogen is oxidised and oxygen is reduced (two different elements). D: nitrogen stays +4, so it is not a redox reaction.
items.why: Disproportionation (C8.7) came up in all 20 sessions and 'which equation is (not) disproportionation' is its commonest MCQ (Jan2026 Q7 and Q8, Jan2025 Q10, Oct2023 Q7); a non-chlorine example with a two-species distractor is the likely variant.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.7 - that a disproportionation re
items.question: White phosphorus reacts with hot sodium hydroxide solution. P₄(s) + 3OH⁻(aq) + 3H₂O(l) → PH₃(g) + 3H₂PO₂⁻(aq) What is the ratio of the number of phosphorus atoms oxidised to the number of phosphorus atoms reduced? 1 : 3 3 : 4 1 : 1 3 : 1
items.ms: D: P goes from 0 in P₄ to −3 in PH₃ (one atom reduced) and to +1 in H₂PO₂⁻ (three atoms oxidised), so 3 : 1; check: 3 × 1 electron lost = 1 × 3 electrons gained. A inverts the ratio. B compares the atoms oxidised with all four P atoms. C assumes equal numbers, as in the reaction of chlorine with cold alkali.
items.why: C8.7 is examined every session; the spec allows reactions analogous to those of chlorine, and a p-block disproportionation in alkali with unequal numbers of atoms oxidised and reduced has not been asked.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.7 - that a disproportionation re
items.question: Hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂, is sold as an aqueous solution for bleaching hair and for cleaning wounds. In solution it slowly decomposes. 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g) The decomposition can be represented by two half-equations in acidic solution. Write the half-equation for the oxidation of hydrogen peroxide to oxygen. Write the half-equation for the reduction of hydrogen peroxide to water. Show how your two half-equations combine to give the equation for the decomposition. Hydrogen peroxide oxidises iodide ions to iodine in acidic solution. It also reduces manganate(VII) ions, MnO₄⁻, to manganese(II) ions, Mn²⁺, and is itself oxidised to oxygen. Explain, in terms of oxidation numbers and electron transfer, why hydrogen peroxide can act both as an oxidising agent and as a reducing agent, and why its decomposition is a disproportionation reaction. Use the two reactions above as examples. Equations are not required. Hair bleach is sold as '20 volume' hydrogen peroxide. 1.00 cm³ of this solution releases 20.0 cm³ of oxygen, measured at r.t.p., when it decomposes completely. Calculate the concentration, in mol dm⁻³, of hydrogen peroxide in 20 volume solution. [Molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹] Concentrated hydrogen peroxide and methanol, CH₃OH, have been used together as a rocket propellant. CH₃OH(l) + 3H₂O₂(l) → CO₂(g) + 5H₂O(g) Use oxidation numbers to identify the element that is oxidised in this reaction. Use the mean bond enthalpies in the table to calculate the enthalpy change for this reaction, assuming that all the reactants and products are gases. The structures are CH₃–O–H, H–O–O–H, O=C=O and H–O–H. Hydrogen peroxide was once made by adding barium peroxide to cold dilute sulfuric acid. BaO₂(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + H₂O₂(aq) Explain, using oxidation numbers, whether this is a redox reaction.
items.ms: H₂O₂ → O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ H₂O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2H₂O Adding the half-equations: 2H⁺ and 2e⁻ cancel, giving 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ IC1 Oxygen in H₂O₂ has oxidation number −1, between 0 (in O₂) and −2 (in H₂O) IC2 So H₂O₂ can gain electrons and be reduced (O: −1 → −2): it acts as an oxidising agent IC3 With iodide ions, H₂O₂ takes electrons from I⁻: iodine is oxidised from −1 to 0 while oxygen is reduced from −1 to −2 IC4 H₂O₂ can also lose electrons and be oxidised (O: −1 → 0, forming O₂): it acts as a reducing agent IC5 With manganate(VII), H₂O₂ gives electrons to MnO₄⁻: manganese is reduced from +7 to +2 while oxygen is oxidised from −1 to 0 IC6 In the decomposition, oxygen in the same species, H₂O₂, is simultaneously oxidised (−1 → 0 in O₂) and reduced (−1 → −2 in H₂O): disproportionation n(O₂) = 20.0 ÷ 24 000 = 8.33 × 10⁻⁴ mol n(H₂O₂) = 2 × 8.33 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.67 × 10⁻³ mol concentration = 1.67 × 10⁻³ ÷ 1.00 × 10⁻³ dm³ = 1.67 mol dm⁻³ Carbon, from −2 in CH₃OH to +4 in CO₂ Bonds broken: (3 × 413) + 358 + 464 + (3 × 146) + (6 × 464) = 5283 (kJ mol⁻¹) Bonds made: (2 × 805) + (10 × 464) = 6250 (kJ mol⁻¹) ΔH = 5283 − 6250 = −967 kJ mol⁻¹ Oxygen is −1 in BaO₂ and in H₂O₂ (Ba stays +2, S +6, H +1 and O in sulfate −2) No element changes oxidation number, so it is not a redox reaction
items.why: Disproportionation (C8.7) has come up in all 20 sessions and was a 6-mark extended answer in Jan2022 Q22(c); hydrogen peroxide (an MCQ in Jan2026 Q10, half-equations in Jun2019 Q19) lets one long question test oxidising agent, reducing agent and disproportionation together.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.8 - that oxidation number is a u
items.question: Three reactions of sulfur compounds are shown. Reaction 1 CaO(s) + SO₂(g) → CaSO₃(s) Reaction 2 4Na₂SO₃(s) → 3Na₂SO₄(s) + Na₂S(s) Reaction 3 2H₂S(g) + SO₂(g) → 3S(s) + 2H₂O(l) Classify each reaction as not redox, redox but not disproportionation, or disproportionation. Justify each answer using the oxidation numbers of sulfur.
items.ms: Reaction 1: not redox, as S is +4 in both SO₂ and CaSO₃ Reaction 2: disproportionation, as S (+4) in Na₂SO₃ is both oxidised, to +6 in Na₂SO₄, and reduced, to −2 in Na₂S Reaction 3: redox but not disproportionation, as S in H₂S (−2) is oxidised to 0 and S in SO₂ (+4) is reduced to 0, so two different species
items.why: C8.8 was last asked in Oct2021 (cool), but classifying reactions by oxidation number underlies the disproportionation questions set every session; one example of each class in Section A is the natural form.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.9 - that metals, in general, form positive ions b
items.question: Calcium is a metal. When heated, it reacts with non-metals such as chlorine, oxygen and nitrogen to form ionic compounds. Write the half-equation for the formation of calcium ions from calcium atoms. Explain, in terms of electrons and oxidation number, why calcium is oxidised when it forms calcium chloride. Calcium reacts with nitrogen to form calcium nitride, Ca₃N₂, which contains nitride ions, N³⁻. Write the half-equation for the formation of nitride ions from nitrogen molecules. Use your half-equations to write the equation for the formation of calcium nitride from its elements. Calcium nitride reacts with water. Ca₃N₂(s) + 6H₂O(l) → 3Ca(OH)₂(s) + 2NH₃(g) State, with a reason, whether this is a redox reaction. Magnesium reacts with silicon to form magnesium silicide, Mg₂Si. Deduce the oxidation number of silicon in Mg₂Si and explain how this shows that silicon is behaving as a non-metal in this reaction.
items.ms: Ca → Ca²⁺ + 2e⁻ Calcium atoms lose (two) electrons The oxidation number of calcium increases (from 0 to +2) N₂ + 6e⁻ → 2N³⁻ 3Ca + N₂ → Ca₃N₂ Not redox, because no element changes oxidation number (N stays −3; Ca +2, H +1, O −2) Si: −4 Silicon has gained electrons / its oxidation number has decreased (from 0), forming a negative ion, as non-metals generally do
items.why: C8.9 has never been asked; it is most likely to appear inside a question on s-block reactions, testing the electron-loss and oxidation-number link that examiners say candidates often reverse (Oct2021 Q21, Oct2024 Q19(b)).

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec

items.question: Sulfite ions are oxidised to sulfate ions in alkaline solution. SO₃²⁻(aq) + xOH⁻(aq) → SO₄²⁻(aq) + yH₂O(l) + ze⁻ What are the values of x, y and z? x = 2, y = 1, z = 2 x = 2, y = 1, z = 4 x = 2, y = 2, z = 2 x = 4, y = 2, z = 2
items.ms: A: sulfur is oxidised from +4 to +6, so 2 electrons are released (z = 2); 2OH⁻ on the left supply one O atom and give one H₂O; charges: −2 − 2 = −2 − 2. B balances the atoms but not the charges (−4 and −6). C does not balance H. D does not balance O or the charges.
items.why: Balancing half-equation MCQs came up in Jan2026 Q9, Oct2023 Q6 and Oct2020 Q6, all in acid or for O₂; an oxidation half-equation in alkaline solution has not been asked.

items.name: Ionic half-equations and full ionic equations
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.10 - write ionic half-equations a
items.question: Sulfur dioxide decolourises acidified potassium manganate(VII) solution. MnO₄⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l) SO₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l) → SO₄²⁻(aq) + 4H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ Which is the overall ionic equation? MnO₄⁻ + SO₂ + 4H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ + 2H₂O 2MnO₄⁻ + 5SO₂ + 2H₂O → 2Mn²⁺ + 5SO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ 2MnO₄⁻ + 5SO₂ + 4H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5SO₄²⁻ + 2H₂O 5MnO₄⁻ + 2SO₂ + 32H⁺ → 5Mn²⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻ + 16H₂O
items.ms: B: multiply the MnO₄⁻ half-equation by 2 and the SO₂ half-equation by 5 so that 10 electrons cancel, then cancel 16H⁺ against 20H⁺ and 8H₂O against 10H₂O. A does not balance the electrons (charge +3 on the left, 0 on the right). C puts the H⁺ and H₂O on the wrong sides, so neither O nor charge balances. D inverts the 2 : 5 ratio, so the charges do not balance.
items.why: C8.10 came up in 10 of 20 sessions; combining two given half-equations was last an MCQ in Jan2022 Q14 (Cu and NO₃⁻), and cancelling H⁺ and H₂O that appear on both sides is the step candidates miss.

items.name: Ionisation energy trend down Groups 1 and 2
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.11 - reasons for the trend in ion
items.question: The table shows the first ionisation energies of three Group 1 elements. Explain why the first ionisation energy decreases from lithium to potassium, even though the nuclear charge increases.
items.ms: The outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus / the atomic radius increases (more shells) There are more inner (filled) shells, so the outer electron is more shielded (from the nucleus) These effects outweigh the increase in nuclear charge, so the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron is weaker and less energy is needed to remove it
items.why: C8.11 is cool (4 of 20 sessions) and has only been asked inside MCQs (Jun2021 Q8, Oct2024 Q4); the 'nuclear charge increases' trap (Jun2022 Q16(a): 'Do not award nuclear charge decreases') makes this the likely written form.

items.name: and 8.13 Reactivity trends and reactions of Group 1/2 with oxygen, chlorine, water
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.12 - reasons for the trend in reactivity of the el
items.question: A student added 0.120 g of calcium to 100 cm³ of water at 20 °C and collected the hydrogen in a gas syringe. The experiment was repeated with 0.263 g of strontium. The graph shows the results. Write the equation for the reaction of strontium with water. Include state symbols. Show, by calculation, that the final volume of hydrogen from strontium is consistent with all of the strontium reacting. [Molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹] Explain why strontium reacts more rapidly with water than calcium does. The experiment was repeated with 0.263 g of barium. Deduce two ways in which the curve for barium would differ from the curve for strontium. Justify each answer.
items.ms: Sr + 2H₂O → Sr(OH)₂ + H₂ State symbols: Sr(s), H₂O(l), Sr(OH)₂(aq), H₂(g) n(Sr) = 0.263 ÷ 87.6 = 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol = n(H₂) V(H₂) = 3.002 × 10⁻³ × 24 000 = 72.1 cm³, which matches the 72 cm³ on the graph Strontium atoms are larger / the outer electrons are in a shell further from the nucleus The outer electrons are more shielded (by inner shells), so they are less strongly attracted to the nucleus So less energy is needed to remove the two outer electrons / the ionisation energies are lower, so strontium forms Sr²⁺ ions more readily Steeper initial gradient / reaches its final volume sooner, because barium is more reactive than strontium Lower final volume, because 0.263 g of barium is fewer moles: 0.263 ÷ 137.3 = 1.92 × 10⁻³ mol, so 46 cm³
items.why: C8.12 (7 of 20 sessions, last Oct2025) is examined through Group 1 and 2 metals with water (Jan2024 Q21(d), Oct2024 Q20(a), Oct2019 Q16); a hydrogen-volume graph comparing two Group 2 metals, with a same-mass prediction for barium, has not been set.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7

items.question: Lithium and sodium are each burned in an excess of oxygen. Which row shows the main product formed by each metal? lithium: Li₂O; sodium: Na₂O lithium: Li₂O; sodium: Na₂O₂ lithium: Li₂O₂; sodium: Na₂O lithium: Li₂O₂; sodium: Na₂O₂
items.ms: B: lithium forms the oxide, Li₂O, but sodium burning in excess oxygen forms mainly the peroxide, Na₂O₂. A ignores the peroxide. C reverses the two products. D: the small Li⁺ ion polarises the peroxide ion too strongly, so lithium does not form Li₂O₂ on burning.
items.why: C8.13 (9 of 20 sessions) asks for the products of Group 1 and 2 metals with oxygen (Oct2025 Q19, and May2023 Q10 on why sodium forms a peroxide); the lithium/sodium contrast as a product row has not been set.

items.question: 0.438 g of strontium reacts completely with water. The solution is made up to 250.0 cm³ with distilled water. What is the concentration of hydroxide ions in the solution? 0.0100 mol dm⁻³ 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ 0.0400 mol dm⁻³ 0.400 mol dm⁻³
items.ms: C: Sr + 2H₂O → Sr(OH)₂ + H₂; n(Sr) = 0.438 ÷ 87.6 = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol, so n(OH⁻) = 0.0100 mol in 0.2500 dm³: 0.0400 mol dm⁻³. A is the amount of OH⁻ in mol, not divided by the volume. B is the concentration of Sr(OH)₂ (misses the two OH⁻ ions). D divides by 0.0250 dm³.
items.why: C8.13 calculations recur (May2023 Q11: NaOH from Na; Jun2021 Q17: H₂ from Li); a Group 2 metal, where each mole gives two moles of OH⁻, is the obvious variant.

items.name: Reactions of Group 1/2 oxides and hydroxides with water and acid
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.14 - the reactions of i oxides of Group 1 and 2 el
items.question: Barium oxide, BaO, is a white solid that reacts with water and with dilute acids. Write the equation for the reaction of barium oxide with water. State symbols are not required. Write the ionic equation for the reaction of solid barium oxide with dilute hydrochloric acid. Include state symbols. Calculate the minimum volume, in cm³, of 0.250 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid needed to react completely with 0.767 g of barium oxide. Solid barium oxide is added to dilute sulfuric acid. The reaction soon stops, even though some of each reactant remains. Explain this observation. Potassium hydroxide solution is neutralised by dilute sulfuric acid. Write the equation for this reaction and the ionic equation for the neutralisation. State symbols are not required.
items.ms: BaO + H₂O → Ba(OH)₂ BaO + 2H⁺ → Ba²⁺ + H₂O State symbols: BaO(s), H⁺(aq), Ba²⁺(aq), H₂O(l) n(BaO) = 0.767 ÷ 153.3 = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol n(HCl) = 2 × 5.00 × 10⁻³ = 1.00 × 10⁻² mol V = 1.00 × 10⁻² ÷ 0.250 = 0.0400 dm³ = 40.0 cm³ Barium sulfate forms, which is insoluble It forms a layer on the surface of the barium oxide, which stops the acid reaching / reacting with the rest of the solid 2KOH + H₂SO₄ → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
items.why: C8.14 (5 of 20 sessions, last Jan2026) is examined through calculations and ionic equations for oxides and hydroxides with acid (Oct2025 Q19(c), Oct2019 Q16(d), Jun2023 Q22(b)); the insoluble sulfate that stops barium oxide reacting with sulfuric acid links it to C8.15 and has not been asked.

items.name: Solubility trends of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.15 - the trends in solubility of
items.question: Samples of 0.1 mol dm⁻³ magnesium chloride solution and 0.1 mol dm⁻³ barium chloride solution are placed in separate test tubes. Which reagent, added to each, gives a white precipitate with the magnesium chloride solution but not with the barium chloride solution? dilute sodium hydroxide solution dilute sulfuric acid sodium sulfate solution dilute hydrochloric acid
items.ms: A: Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble, but the solubility of the hydroxides increases down Group 2, so Ba(OH)₂ stays in solution. B and C give the opposite result: sulfate solubility decreases down the group, so BaSO₄ precipitates but MgSO₄ does not. D gives no precipitate with either solution.
items.why: C8.15 came up in 12 of 20 sessions, mostly as 'which trend' MCQs (May2024 Q11, Oct2025 Q2); using the opposite hydroxide and sulfate trends to tell two Group 2 ions apart has not been asked.

items.name: Thermal stability of Group 1 and 2 nitrates and carbonates
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.16 - the reasons for the trends i
items.question: The table gives the ionic radii of four metal ions. Use the data to predict which carbonate decomposes at the lowest temperature. Li₂CO₃ Na₂CO₃ MgCO₃ SrCO₃
items.ms: C: Mg²⁺ has the higher charge and the smallest radius, so the greatest charge density; it polarises (distorts the electron cloud of) the carbonate ion most, weakening the C–O bonds most. A: Li⁺ is almost as small but has only a 1+ charge. B: Na⁺ is larger with a 1+ charge, so it is the least polarising. D: Sr²⁺ has a 2+ charge but is the largest ion.
items.why: C8.16 came up in all 20 sessions; examiners report confusion over the charge and size of the cations (Jun2022 Q15(a)), and comparing a small Group 1 ion with Group 2 ions using data tests both factors.

items.name: Thermal stability of Group 1 and 2 nitrates and carbonates
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.16 - the reasons for the trends i
items.question: A sample of potassium nitrate, KNO₃, is heated with a Bunsen burner until there is no further change in mass. What is the percentage loss in mass? 15.8% 31.7% 45.5% 53.4%
items.ms: A: Group 1 nitrates other than lithium nitrate give the nitrite and oxygen: 2KNO₃ → 2KNO₂ + O₂. Mass lost per mole of KNO₃ = 16.0 g, and 16.0 ÷ 101.1 × 100 = 15.8%. B loses a whole O₂ per KNO₃. C assumes NO₂ is lost. D assumes decomposition to K₂O, NO₂ and O₂, as for Group 2 nitrates.
items.why: Nitrate decomposition calculations recur (Oct2025 Q4 and Jan2025 Q16(a), both on magnesium nitrate); a Group 1 nitrate, whose different products change the answer, has not been asked.

items.name: Thermal stability of Group 1 and 2 nitrates and carbonates
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.16 - the reasons for the trends i
items.question: Dolomite rock contains magnesium carbonate and calcium carbonate. It is heated in kilns to make 'doloma', a mixture of magnesium oxide and calcium oxide that is used to line steel-making furnaces. A 50.0 mg sample of a powdered dolomite rock was heated at a steady rate and its mass was recorded. The only substances in the rock that change mass on heating are the two carbonates. The graph shows the results. The first loss in mass is due to the decomposition of magnesium carbonate. State why the mass of the sample stays constant between 650 °C and 720 °C. Magnesium carbonate decomposes to magnesium oxide and carbon dioxide. Use the graph to show that the sample contains about 19 mg of magnesium carbonate. Calculate the percentage by mass of calcium carbonate in the sample. Suggest why the percentages of magnesium carbonate and calcium carbonate do not add up to 100%. Explain why magnesium carbonate decomposes at a lower temperature than calcium carbonate. A different rock contains strontium carbonate as well as magnesium carbonate and calcium carbonate. Predict how its graph would differ from the one shown. Justify your prediction. Pure dolomite has the formula CaMg(CO₃)₂. Use the data in the table to calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction CaMg(CO₃)₂(s) → CaO(s) + MgO(s) + 2CO₂(g) Use the graph to calculate the mass of carbon dioxide, in kg, released when 1.00 tonne of this rock is heated to 1000 °C. [1 tonne = 1000 kg] The nitrates of Group 2 show the same trend in thermal stability as the carbonates. A student wrote this explanation. 'Magnesium nitrate decomposes at a lower temperature than barium nitrate because magnesium atoms have a smaller atomic radius and a larger charge than barium atoms. So magnesium is polarised more by the nitrate ion, which weakens the ionic bonds.' Identify three errors in the explanation and give a correction for each.
items.ms: All the magnesium carbonate has decomposed, but the temperature is not yet high enough for the calcium carbonate to decompose Mass of CO₂ lost = 50.0 − 40.0 = 10.0 mg, so n(CO₂) = 10.0 × 10⁻³ ÷ 44.0 = 2.27 × 10⁻⁴ mol = n(MgCO₃) mass of MgCO₃ = 2.27 × 10⁻⁴ × 84.3 = 0.0192 g = 19.2 mg Mass of CO₂ lost in the second step = 40.0 − 28.0 = 12.0 mg, so n(CO₂) = 0.0120 ÷ 44.0 = 2.73 × 10⁻⁴ mol mass of CaCO₃ = 2.73 × 10⁻⁴ × 100.1 = 27.3 mg percentage = 27.3 ÷ 50.0 × 100 = 54.6% The rock contains other substances / impurities (such as sand or clay) that do not decompose Mg²⁺ ion is smaller than Ca²⁺ (and has the same charge), so it has a higher charge density Mg²⁺ polarises / distorts the electron cloud of the carbonate ion more so the C–O bonds in the carbonate ion are weakened more and less energy is needed to break them / to release CO₂ A third loss in mass, at a higher temperature than the calcium carbonate step Sr²⁺ is larger than Ca²⁺ (with the same charge), so it polarises the carbonate ion less and strontium carbonate is more thermally stable Sum for products = −635 + (−602) + 2(−394) = −2025 (kJ mol⁻¹) ΔH = −2025 − (−2326) = +301 kJ mol⁻¹ Total mass lost = 50.0 − 28.0 = 22.0 mg, which is 44.0% of the sample Mass of CO₂ = 0.440 × 1000 = 440 kg 'magnesium atoms … atomic radius': it is the magnesium ion, Mg²⁺, that matters, with a smaller ionic radius than Ba²⁺ 'larger charge': Mg²⁺ and Ba²⁺ have the same charge (2+); Mg²⁺ has the greater charge density because it is smaller 'magnesium is polarised by the nitrate ion': the Mg²⁺ ion polarises / distorts the electron cloud of the nitrate ion 'weakens the ionic bonds': it weakens the (covalent) N–O bonds within the nitrate ion
items.why: C8.16 came up in all 20 sessions (4.6% of the marks); the carbonate explanation is the commonest 3-mark part (Jan2026 Q20(a), Jun2022 Q15(a)), mass-loss calculations recur (May2024 Q18(a)) and 'correct the student's errors' on nitrates was new in Oct2025 Q19(d); a thermal-analysis graph of a carbonate rock with a Hess cycle fits the Section C contemporary-context pattern.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec

items.question: Which pair of solid compounds could not be distinguished from each other by flame tests alone? lithium chloride and strontium chloride sodium chloride and potassium chloride calcium chloride and barium chloride magnesium chloride and potassium chloride
items.ms: A: lithium and strontium compounds both give a red (crimson) flame. B: sodium gives a yellow flame and potassium a lilac flame. C: calcium gives a brick-red (orange-red) flame and barium an apple-green flame. D: magnesium compounds give no flame colour, potassium gives lilac.
items.why: C8.17 is hot (15 of 20 sessions) and its MCQs ask for one colour (Jan2025 Q4) or for the compound giving a red flame (May2024 Q13, Jan2023 Q9, Oct2019 Q8); the limit of a flame test when two metals share a colour has not been asked.

items.name: Flame colours and electron transitions
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.17 - the formation of characteris
items.question: Magnesium compounds give no colour to a Bunsen flame. Which is the best explanation? Electrons in magnesium cannot be promoted to higher energy levels. Electrons in magnesium are promoted to higher energy levels but do not return to lower energy levels. Magnesium ions absorb all the visible light given out by the flame. The energy released as electrons in magnesium return to lower energy levels corresponds to radiation outside the visible region.
items.ms: D: the energy gaps in magnesium are large, so the radiation emitted as excited electrons fall back has a frequency outside the visible range (ultraviolet) and no colour is seen. A: the heat of the flame does promote electrons in magnesium. B: excited electrons always fall back, releasing energy. C: flame colours come from light emitted by the metal, not light absorbed from the flame.
items.why: Electron-transition MCQs recur (Jun2025 Q7, Oct2024 Q6, May2023 Q13, Oct2022 Q8); why a Group 2 compound shows no colour at all, implied by the spec's 'know the flame colours', has not been asked.

items.name: Flame colours and electron transitions
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7

items.question: Sodium chloride gives a yellow flame colour in a flame test. Potassium chloride gives a lilac flame colour. Explain how the yellow colour is produced when sodium chloride is heated in a Bunsen flame. Suggest why sodium chloride and potassium chloride give different flame colours.
items.ms: Electrons are promoted / excited to higher energy levels (by heat energy from the flame) The electrons fall back to lower energy levels, releasing energy as (visible) light of a specific frequency / wavelength The energy gaps between the electron energy levels are different in sodium and potassium, so the light emitted has a different frequency / wavelength / energy
items.why: C8.17 is hot (15 of 20 sessions) and the origin of a flame colour was asked in Jan2026 Q22(a) and Oct2025 Q19(a); why two metals give different colours is the natural extension that has not been asked.

items.name: Experimental procedures: thermal decomposition and flame tests; gas tests
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.18 - experimental procedures to s
items.question: A student investigates the thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates using the apparatus shown. 0.0050 mol of each carbonate is heated strongly and the time taken for the limewater to turn cloudy is measured. Write the equation for the reaction that makes the limewater turn cloudy. Include state symbols. The student takes the delivery tube out of the limewater before stopping the heating. Explain why. Explain why the student uses the same amount, in moles, of each carbonate rather than the same mass. Calculate the mass of barium carbonate that the student should use. State one other variable that the student should control. Suggest two reasons why the time for the limewater to turn cloudy is only an approximate measure of the ease of decomposition. The student then heats 0.0050 mol of calcium nitrate in a clean boiling tube, with the delivery tube taken out of the limewater. Write the equation for the thermal decomposition of calcium nitrate. State symbols are not required. Describe tests, with their results, that would show that both nitrogen dioxide and oxygen are given off.
items.ms: Ca(OH)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O(l) To prevent suck-back: as the boiling tube cools the gas inside contracts, so limewater would be drawn back into the hot boiling tube (which could crack) The carbonates have different molar masses, so equal masses would contain different numbers of moles and could give different amounts of carbon dioxide (not a fair test) 0.0050 × 197.3 = 0.987 g Any one of: same volume / concentration of limewater; same Bunsen flame (gas tap setting, blue flame); same distance between flame and tube; same size of boiling tube; same particle size of solid Air in the boiling tube and delivery tube is pushed through the limewater before any carbon dioxide arrives The first cloudiness is judged by eye / is subjective The time includes the time for the tube and the solid to heat up / heating may not be equal for each carbonate 2Ca(NO₃)₂ → 2CaO + 4NO₂ + O₂ Nitrogen dioxide: brown gas seen and damp blue litmus (or universal indicator) paper turns red Oxygen: a glowing splint relights
items.why: C8.18 is cool (7 of 20 sessions) but Jan2026 Q20(b) and Jan2024 Q21 used the decomposition experiment; the examiners' report says candidates are unfamiliar with it and do not see NO₂ as acidic, so a full procedure question is likely.

items.question: Which is the ionic equation for the reaction of aqueous potassium hydrogencarbonate with dilute nitric acid? CO₃²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) → CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) HCO₃⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) → CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) KHCO₃(aq) + H⁺(aq) → K⁺(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) HCO₃⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → CO₃²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7

items.question: Separate 1.00 g samples of anhydrous sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃, and of sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO₃, are each added to excess dilute hydrochloric acid. Which statement is correct? Sodium hydrogencarbonate gives the larger volume of carbon dioxide and reacts with fewer moles of acid. Sodium hydrogencarbonate gives the larger volume of carbon dioxide and reacts with more moles of acid. Sodium carbonate gives the larger volume of carbon dioxide and reacts with more moles of acid. B: NaHCO₃ needs only one H⁺ per CO₂. C: sodium carbonate uses more acid but, with its larger Mr, gives less CO₂. D: each gives one mole of CO₂ per mole of solid, but 1.00 g contains different amounts of the two solids.
items.why: Mole calculations on these ion tests have been MCQs in each of the last three years (Jan2026 Q5, Oct2025 Q3, Jan2025 Q15); comparing carbonate with hydrogencarbonate quantitatively has not been asked.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7

items.question: A garden fertiliser contains a white solid, W, which is a single ionic compound. The table shows the results of some tests on W. Give the formula of W. Explain why dilute hydrochloric acid is added in Test 3 before the aqueous barium chloride is added in Test 4. Write the ionic equation for the reaction in Test 2. Include state symbols. Write the equation for the formation of the white smoke in Test 2. Include state symbols. Write the ionic equation for the reaction in Test 4. Include state symbols. A 2.50 g sample of the fertiliser is dissolved in water and acidified, and excess aqueous barium chloride is added. The precipitate is filtered, washed, dried and weighed. Its mass is 4.21 g. Calculate the percentage by mass of W in the fertiliser. Assume that W is the only sulfate present.
items.ms: (NH₄)₂SO₄ To remove carbonate ions (as CO₂), which would otherwise also give a white precipitate (of barium carbonate) with barium chloride NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O State symbols: NH₄⁺(aq), OH⁻(aq), NH₃(g), H₂O(l) NH₃(g) + HCl(g) → NH₄Cl(s) Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s) n(BaSO₄) = 4.21 ÷ 233.4 = 0.01804 mol n(W) = 0.01804 mol, so mass of (NH₄)₂SO₄ = 0.01804 × 132.1 = 2.383 g percentage = 2.383 ÷ 2.50 × 100 = 95.3%
items.why: C8.19 is hot (17 of 20 sessions, 3.1% of marks); the digest found no direct question on the ammonium-ion test with sodium hydroxide, so it is the likeliest new angle, set beside the sulfate test and a gravimetric calculation (Jun2022 Q16(e), Oct2023 Q19(a)).

items.question: Lithium hydroxide is used to absorb carbon dioxide from the air in spacecraft. 2LiOH(s) + CO₂(g) → Li₂CO₃(s) + H₂O(l) An astronaut breathes out about 1.00 kg of carbon dioxide each day. Calculate the minimum mass, in kg, of lithium hydroxide needed to absorb this carbon dioxide. Sodium hydroxide reacts with carbon dioxide in the same way. Justify, with a calculation, the use of lithium hydroxide rather than sodium hydroxide in a spacecraft. A sample of used absorbent is analysed. Assume that it contains only lithium hydroxide and lithium carbonate. 2.50 g of the used absorbent is dissolved in distilled water and the solution is made up to 250.0 cm³ in a volumetric flask. This is solution S. The diagram summarises the analysis. Write the ionic equation for the formation of the white precipitate when excess aqueous barium chloride is added to S. Include state symbols. The precipitate from 100.0 cm³ of S has a mass of 1.578 g after drying. Calculate the amount, in moles, of lithium carbonate in 25.0 cm³ of S. [Mr of BaCO₃ = 197.3] 25.0 cm³ portions of S are titrated with 0.350 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid using methyl orange indicator. At the end point both the lithium hydroxide and the lithium carbonate have reacted completely. The mean titre is 23.60 cm³. State the colour change at the end point. Write the equation for the reaction of lithium carbonate with hydrochloric acid. State symbols are not required. Calculate the amount, in moles, of lithium hydroxide in 25.0 cm³ of S. Calculate the concentration of lithium hydroxide in S, in g dm⁻³. Calculate the percentage of the original lithium hydroxide in the sample that has been converted into lithium carbonate. The mass of the precipitate in (c)(ii) was found by difference, using a balance with an uncertainty of ±0.001 g for each reading. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mass of the precipitate. Describe how a flame test could be carried out on the used absorbent to show that it contains lithium. Give the expected result.
items.ms: n(CO₂) = 1000 ÷ 44.0 = 22.7 mol n(LiOH) = 2 × 22.7 = 45.5 mol mass of LiOH = 45.5 × 23.9 = 1090 g = 1.09 kg mass of NaOH needed = 45.5 × 40.0 = 1820 g = 1.82 kg a smaller mass of lithium hydroxide is needed (because its Mr is lower), so less mass has to be launched Ba²⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) → BaCO₃(s) n(BaCO₃) = 1.578 ÷ 197.3 = 7.998 × 10⁻³ mol = n(Li₂CO₃) in 100.0 cm³ n(Li₂CO₃) in 25.0 cm³ = 7.998 × 10⁻³ ÷ 4 = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol yellow to orange Li₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2LiCl + CO₂ + H₂O n(HCl) = 0.350 × 23.60 ÷ 1000 = 8.26 × 10⁻³ mol n(HCl) reacting with Li₂CO₃ = 2 × 2.00 × 10⁻³ = 4.00 × 10⁻³ mol n(LiOH) = 8.26 × 10⁻³ − 4.00 × 10⁻³ = 4.26 × 10⁻³ mol 4.26 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 × 23.9 = 4.07 g dm⁻³ LiOH originally present (in 25.0 cm³) = 4.26 × 10⁻³ + 2 × 2.00 × 10⁻³ = 8.26 × 10⁻³ mol percentage converted = 4.00 × 10⁻³ ÷ 8.26 × 10⁻³ × 100 = 48.4% 2 × 0.001 ÷ 1.578 × 100 = 0.13% Dip a clean nichrome / platinum wire (cleaned with concentrated hydrochloric acid) into the solid (moistened with concentrated hydrochloric acid) and hold it in a hot / blue / non-luminous Bunsen flame red / crimson flame

items.question: A student is given hydrochloric acid with a concentration of about 1 mol dm⁻³ and is asked to find its exact concentration. • 25.0 cm³ of the acid is pipetted into a 250.0 cm³ volumetric flask and the solution is made up to the mark with distilled water. • 25.0 cm³ portions of the diluted acid are titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide solution, using phenolphthalein indicator. items.question: In a titration, a 25.0 cm³ pipette has an uncertainty of ±0.06 cm³ and each burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³. The mean titre is 22.40 cm³. The concentration of the solution in the pipette is calculated from these two volumes and a concentration whose uncertainty can be ignored. What is the overall percentage uncertainty in the calculated concentration? 0.22% 0.45% 0.69% 0.93%
items.ms: C: pipette 0.06 ÷ 25.0 × 100 = 0.24%; titre (two readings) 2 × 0.05 ÷ 22.40 × 100 = 0.45%; percentage uncertainties add, 0.24 + 0.45 = 0.69%. A uses one burette reading and ignores the pipette. B ignores the pipette. D doubles the pipette uncertainty as well.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec

items.question: Sulfamic acid, H₂NSO₃H, is a white crystalline solid used as a primary standard. It is a monoprotic acid. H₂NSO₃H(aq) + NaOH(aq) → H₂NSO₃Na(aq) + H₂O(l) A student prepares a standard solution of sulfamic acid and uses it to find the concentration of a solution of sodium hydroxide. [Mr of H₂NSO₃H = 97.1] Suggest why a standard solution is not made by weighing out solid sodium hydroxide. Describe how the student should prepare 250.0 cm³ of a solution of sulfamic acid with a concentration close to 0.100 mol dm⁻³ and known accurately. Include a calculation of the mass of sulfamic acid needed. The student dissolves 2.391 g of sulfamic acid and makes the solution up to 250.0 cm³. A 25.0 cm³ portion of the sodium hydroxide solution needs a mean titre of 23.65 cm³ of the sulfamic acid solution. Calculate the concentration, in mol dm⁻³, of the sodium hydroxide solution.
items.ms: Solid sodium hydroxide absorbs water (vapour) and / or carbon dioxide from the air, so the mass weighed is not all sodium hydroxide IC1 mass needed = 0.100 × 0.2500 × 97.1 = 2.43 g (about 2.4 g) IC2 weigh the solid in a weighing bottle on a (2 or 3 d.p.) balance, tip it into a beaker and reweigh the bottle, so the mass transferred is known (weighing by difference) IC3 dissolve the solid in a small volume of distilled / deionised water in the beaker, stirring with a glass rod IC4 transfer the solution to a 250.0 cm³ volumetric flask using a funnel IC5 rinse the beaker, glass rod and funnel with distilled water and add all the washings to the flask IC6 add distilled water until the bottom of the meniscus is on the graduation mark (at eye level, last drops from a dropping pipette), then stopper and invert the flask several times to mix [H₂NSO₃H] = 2.391 ÷ 97.1 ÷ 0.2500 = 0.09850 mol dm⁻³ n(H₂NSO₃H) in titre = 0.09850 × 23.65 ÷ 1000 = 2.330 × 10⁻³ mol = n(NaOH) [NaOH] = 2.330 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0932 mol dm⁻³
items.why: Core Practical 4 has been examined only once (Jan2026) and the digest found no question asking for the preparation of the standard solution step by step; a 6-mark method description is the likeliest first appearance.

Topic 8 Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
C8.24 - reasons for the trends for G
items.question: Why is chlorine a stronger oxidising agent than bromine? A chlorine atom has more protons than a bromine atom. Chlorine molecules have stronger London forces between them than bromine molecules. A chlorine atom has more electrons in its outer shell than a bromine atom. An electron gained by a chlorine atom enters a shell closer to the nucleus, with less shielding, so it is attracted more strongly.
items.ms: D: a chlorine atom has one fewer occupied shell, so the nucleus attracts an incoming electron more strongly and chlorine gains electrons (is reduced) more readily. A: bromine has more protons (35) than chlorine (17). B: chlorine has weaker London forces, and intermolecular forces do not decide oxidising power. C: both atoms have seven outer electrons.
items.why: Reactivity down Group 7 (8.24iii) appears in trend tables (Jan2024 Q12) but the reason for it has not been asked, unlike the electronegativity reason (Jan2026 Q18(a), Jun2022 Q16(a)).

items.question: A student mixes each of aqueous chlorine, aqueous bromine and aqueous iodine, in turn, with aqueous solutions of the potassium halides of the other two halogens, making six mixtures. In how many of the six mixtures does a redox reaction take place? 2 3 4 6
items.ms: B: a halogen oxidises the halide ions of the halogens below it, so Cl₂ + Br⁻, Cl₂ + I⁻ and Br₂ + I⁻ react; Br₂ + Cl⁻, I₂ + Cl⁻ and I₂ + Br⁻ do not. A misses one of the three reactions (usually Br₂ + I⁻). C and D include reactions of a halogen with the halide ion of a more reactive halogen.
items.why: Displacement reactions recur in every form (Jun2025 Q15(a), Jan2025 Q11, Jan2023 Q11); a whole-grid count tests the full reactivity order at once.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec

items.question: A colourless solution contains one of the ions Cl⁻, Br⁻ or I⁻. A student carries out two tests on separate portions of the solution. Test 1: aqueous bromine is added. Test 2: aqueous chlorine is added. In each test, cyclohexane is then added and the mixture is shaken and left to separate into two layers. The diagram shows the results. Deduce which halide ion is present. Give a reason based on Test 2. Explain why Test 1 on its own would not show whether chloride ions or bromide ions are present.
items.ms: Bromide / Br⁻, because chlorine oxidises bromide ions to bromine, which is orange-red in cyclohexane (chloride would give an almost colourless layer and iodide a purple one) Bromine does not react with (oxidise) chloride ions or bromide ions, so in both cases the orange-red colour is just the bromine that was added, dissolved in the cyclohexane
items.why: C8.25 is hot (15 of 20 sessions) and usually asks for layer colours after a given reaction (Oct2023 Q19(c), Jun2022 Q8); using displacement results to identify an unknown halide, and seeing why one test is not enough, has not been asked.

items.question: Bromine reacts with hot, concentrated aqueous potassium hydroxide in a reaction analogous to that of chlorine with hot alkali. What are the oxidation numbers of bromine in the two bromine-containing products? −1 and +1 −1 and +3 +1 and +5 −1 and +5
items.ms: D: 3Br₂ + 6KOH → 5KBr + KBrO₃ + 3H₂O; bromine is reduced to −1 in KBr and oxidised to +5 in KBrO₃ (disproportionation). A gives the products with cold dilute alkali (KBr and KBrO). B: +3 would be KBrO₂, which is not formed. C has no product in which bromine is reduced, so it cannot be a disproportionation.

items.question: In which reaction does the halogen-containing reactant act as a reducing agent? NaCl(s) + H₂SO₄(l) → NaHSO₄(s) + HCl(g) HBr(g) + NH₃(g) → NH₄Br(s) HI(g) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) 8HI(g) + H₂SO₄(l) → 4I₂(s) + H₂S(g) + 4H₂O(l)
items.ms: D: iodine's oxidation number rises from −1 in HI to 0 in I₂ while sulfur's falls from +6 in H₂SO₄ to −2 in H₂S, so HI is the reducing agent. A, B and C are acid–base (proton-transfer) reactions: no oxidation number changes and the halogen stays at −1.

items.question: Three bottles, P, Q and R, each contain one of the white solids potassium chloride, potassium bromide and potassium iodide, but their labels have been lost. A student dissolves a sample of each solid in distilled water, adds dilute nitric acid and then aqueous silver nitrate. The results are shown in the table. Explain why dilute hydrochloric acid must not be used in place of dilute nitric acid. Write the ionic equation for the formation of the precipitate from Q. Include state symbols. The colours of the precipitates from P and R can be hard to tell apart. Describe how aqueous ammonia could be used to confirm which of P and R is potassium chloride. Concentrated sulfuric acid is added to a sample of solid potassium bromide. State two observations. Write the equation for the reaction in which hydrogen bromide is formed. Hydrogen bromide then reduces some of the sulfuric acid to sulfur dioxide. Write the equation for this reaction and use oxidation numbers to show which element is oxidised and which is reduced. The misty fumes form when hydrogen bromide meets water vapour in the air. Write an equation to show hydrogen bromide forming an acid when it dissolves in water. Include state symbols.
items.ms: Hydrochloric acid adds chloride ions, which would give a white precipitate (of silver chloride) whichever halide was present Ag⁺ + I⁻ → AgI State symbols: Ag⁺(aq), I⁻(aq), AgI(s) Add dilute (aqueous) ammonia to each precipitate: the precipitate from R (AgCl) dissolves The precipitate from P (AgBr) does not dissolve in dilute ammonia (it dissolves only in concentrated ammonia) misty / steamy (white) fumes orange / red-brown / brown fumes or vapour choking / pungent gas (SO₂) KBr + H₂SO₄ → KHSO₄ + HBr 2HBr + H₂SO₄ → Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O Br oxidised from −1 to 0 and S reduced from +6 to +4 An iodide ion is larger than a chloride ion / has more electron shells so its outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, and are less strongly attracted so iodide ions lose electrons more readily: iodide (HI) is the stronger reducing agent HBr(g) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq)

C10.1 - classify reactions (includin
items.question: Which reaction is both a substitution reaction and a hydrolysis reaction? CH₃CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Br CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O CH₃CH₂Br + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH + HBr
items.ms: In D water breaks the C–Br bond and an OH group replaces the Br atom: a substitution in which water is the reagent, so it is also a hydrolysis. A is a substitution, but the reagent is ammonia, not water. B is an addition (hydration): water adds across the C=C bond and nothing is replaced. C is an elimination; water is a product, not a reactant.

C10.13 - understand, in terms of bond
items.question: Under the same conditions, 1-bromopropane is hydrolysed faster than 1-chloropropane. Which is the best explanation? The C–Br bond is more polar than the C–Cl bond, so the carbon atom is attacked more readily. The C–Br bond enthalpy is higher, so more energy is released when the C–Br bond breaks. The C–Br bond enthalpy is lower, so the activation energy is lower and a greater proportion of collisions have enough energy to react. The bromide ion is a better nucleophile than the chloride ion.
items.ms: Less energy is needed to break the C–Br bond, so the activation energy is lower and more molecules have energy ≥ Eₐ (C). A: bromine is less electronegative than chlorine, so C–Br is less polar; polarity does not explain the order. B: bond breaking is endothermic, and C–Br is the weaker bond. D: the halide ion is the leaving group, not the nucleophile.
items.why: C10.13 has come up in 15 of 20 sessions, with 'best explanation' MCQs in Oct2025, Jun2025 and Oct2023; linking the lower bond enthalpy to a lower activation energy (C9.2) is the step not yet tested.

items.question: A student warmed 1-chlorobutane, 1-bromobutane and 1-iodobutane separately with silver nitrate in aqueous ethanol and measured the time, t, for a precipitate to appear. The student then plotted 1/t for each compound against the bond enthalpy of its carbon–halogen bond. Which graph, W, X, Y or Z, shows the expected results? W X Y Z
items.ms: 1/t is a measure of the rate. The C–I bond has the lowest bond enthalpy and 1-iodobutane reacts fastest (largest 1/t); the C–Cl bond has the highest bond enthalpy and reacts slowest, so 1/t falls as the bond enthalpy rises: graph X (B). A (W) is the graph of t, not 1/t, or the 'stronger bond reacts faster' error. C (Y) assumes the halogen has no effect. D (Z) puts 1-bromobutane fastest.
items.why: C10.13 has come up in 15 of 20 sessions as text MCQs on the halogen trend (Oct2025, Jun2025, Jan2024); reading the trend from a graph of rate (1/time, C9.3) against bond enthalpy has not been asked.

C10.13 - understand, in terms of bond
items.question: This question is about the hydrolysis of chloroethane, bromoethane and iodoethane. The table gives some mean bond enthalpies from the Data Booklet. The three halogenoalkanes are warmed separately with silver nitrate in aqueous ethanol. State the order in which the precipitates appear and explain this order in terms of bond enthalpy. The Pauling electronegativity values are: C 2.5, Cl 3.0, Br 2.8, I 2.5. A student suggested that chloroethane should be hydrolysed fastest. Explain why the student made this suggestion and why it is incorrect. The equation for the hydrolysis of a halogenoalkane, with all species as gases, is CH₃CH₂X + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH + HX Calculate the enthalpy change for this reaction when X is Br, using the bond enthalpies in the table. Calculated in the same way, ΔH is +20 kJ mol⁻¹ when X is Cl and +35 kJ mol⁻¹ when X is I. Explain why these enthalpy changes do not explain the order of the rates in (a). Explain why the C–I bond has a lower bond enthalpy than the C–Cl bond.
items.ms: iodoethane first, then bromoethane, then chloroethane the C–I bond enthalpy (228) is the lowest (C–Br 290, C–Cl 346 kJ mol⁻¹), so the least energy is needed to break the C–I bond and it breaks most easily Cl has the largest electronegativity difference from C (0.5), so C–Cl is the most polar bond and its carbon atom has the largest δ+, which would attract the nucleophile most strongly but the C–I bond is (almost) non-polar (difference 0) and iodoethane reacts fastest, so the bond enthalpy, not the bond polarity, decides the rate bonds broken: C–Br + O–H = 290 + 464 = 754 and bonds made: C–O + H–Br = 358 + 366 = 724 ΔH = 754 − 724 = +30 kJ mol⁻¹ the iodoalkane has the most endothermic ΔH yet reacts fastest: the rate depends on the activation energy, which depends on the energy needed to break the C–X bond, not on the overall enthalpy change the iodine atom is larger / has more electron shells, so the bonding pair of electrons is further from the iodine nucleus (and more shielded) and is attracted less strongly than the bonding pair in C–Cl
items.why: C10.13 has come up in 15 of 20 sessions, mostly as 'why does the iodoalkane react fastest'; the polarity-versus-bond-enthalpy argument and showing that ΔH does not control the rate have not been asked.

items.question: 2-Chloro-2-methylpropane is prepared by shaking 2-methylpropan-2-ol with excess concentrated hydrochloric acid at room temperature. Step 1 12.0 cm³ of 2-methylpropan-2-ol and 40 cm³ of concentrated hydrochloric acid are shaken in a stoppered separating funnel for 20 minutes. The tap is opened from time to time. Step 2 The mixture is left to settle into two layers. The organic layer is kept and the aqueous layer is discarded. Step 3 Sodium hydrogencarbonate solution is added to the organic layer and the funnel is shaken. The aqueous layer is discarded. Step 4 The organic layer is run into a dry conical flask and a drying agent is added. Step 5 The dried liquid is distilled and the fraction boiling between 49 °C and 53 °C is collected. Some data are shown in the table. Write the equation for the reaction. Use structural formulae. The diagram shows the separating funnel at the end of step 2. Identify the layer, P or Q, that contains the 2-chloro-2-methylpropane. Justify your answer using the data in the table. Give the reason for adding sodium hydrogencarbonate solution in step 3, and explain why the tap must be opened frequently while the funnel is shaken in this step. Name a suitable drying agent for step 4. The student obtained 8.07 g of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane. Calculate the percentage yield. Give your answer to three significant figures.
items.ms: (CH₃)₃COH + HCl → (CH₃)₃CCl + H₂O P (the upper layer), because 2-chloro-2-methylpropane is less dense than the (aqueous) acid / 0.85 g cm⁻³ is less than 1.18 g cm⁻³ To neutralise / remove the (excess) hydrochloric acid left in the organic layer Carbon dioxide gas is produced, so the pressure builds up (and could force out the stopper); opening the tap releases the gas (anhydrous) sodium sulfate / magnesium sulfate / calcium chloride / calcium sulfate Mass of 2-methylpropan-2-ol = 12.0 × 0.78 = 9.36 g, so moles = 9.36 ÷ 74.0 = 0.1265 mol Maximum mass of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane = 0.1265 × 92.5 = 11.70 g Percentage yield = 8.07 ÷ 11.70 × 100 = 69.0%
items.why: Core Practical 6 has been asked in only 1 of 20 sessions (last Jan2024) and no paper has yet asked the whole method; the digest flags the drying agent and the NaHCO₃ wash, and yield calculations appear in nearly every paper.

items.question: What is the systematic name of the alcohol CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH(OH)CH₃? 1,2-dimethylbutan-1-ol 3-methylpent-2-ol 3-methylpentan-2-ol 3-methylpentan-4-ol
items.ms: The longest chain that contains the C–OH carbon has five carbon atoms (pentan-). It is numbered from the end nearer the –OH, so the –OH is on C2 and the methyl branch on C3: 3-methylpentan-2-ol. A does not use the longest chain (the CH₃ next to the C–OH carbon is part of the chain, not a branch); B leaves out the 'an' of pentan-; D numbers the chain from the wrong end, giving the –OH a higher number than necessary.
items.why: Alcohol nomenclature (C10.15) has come up in 13 of 20 sessions; Oct2024 Q12 asked the name of a branched secondary alcohol, and the Jun2021 mark scheme rejects names that leave out the 'an' (4-methylhex-2-ol).

items.question: Which compound is a structural isomer of 2-methylbutan-2-ol? 2-methylpropan-2-ol 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol cyclopentanol pentan-2-one
items.ms: 2-methylbutan-2-ol is C₅H₁₂O. 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol, (CH₃)₃CCH₂OH, is also C₅H₁₂O but has a different structure, so it is a structural isomer. A is C₄H₁₀O (one carbon atom fewer); C is C₅H₁₀O because forming the ring needs two fewer hydrogen atoms; D is C₅H₁₀O (the ketone has two hydrogen atoms fewer than the alcohol).
items.why: Isomers of alcohols recur (Oct2019, Oct2022 and Jan2023 tables; Jan2024 Q16 counted cyclic alcohol isomers); C₅ alcohols set against a ring alcohol and a ketone with the same number of carbon atoms have not been tested.

items.question: Which of these alcohols is a secondary alcohol? (CH₃)₃CCH₂OH (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃ cyclohexanol, C₆H₁₁OH
items.ms: In cyclohexanol the carbon atom bonded to the –OH is bonded to two other carbon atoms (its neighbours in the ring) and one hydrogen atom, so it is secondary. A and B are primary: the C–OH carbon is bonded to only one other carbon atom, even though the chains are branched. C is tertiary: the C–OH carbon is bonded to three carbon atoms and no hydrogen atom.
items.why: Classification (C10.16) was asked in 13 of 20 sessions (Oct2021 and Oct2023 MCQs picked the tertiary alcohol); the Oct2022 report found candidates think 'primary' means the OH is at the end of the chain, which branched primary alcohols and a ring alcohol test.

items.question: Which reagents are used to convert butan-1-ol into 1-iodobutane? red phosphorus and iodine iodine and ultraviolet light aqueous potassium iodide potassium iodide and concentrated sulfuric acid
items.ms: Red phosphorus and iodine react to form phosphorus(III) iodide in the mixture, and this replaces the –OH group by –I. B is the condition for free-radical substitution of an alkane, not for replacing an –OH group; C: iodide ions in water do not replace the –OH of an alcohol; D: concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises iodide ions (and hydrogen iodide) to iodine, so very little hydrogen iodide is available.
items.why: C10.17 is hot (15 of 20 sessions); the chlorinating and brominating reagents have both been asked (Jan2024 Q18, Jun2021 Q18(a)) but the red phosphorus and iodine route named in the spec has not.

items.question: 0.00500 mol of propane-1,2,3-triol, CH₂(OH)CH(OH)CH₂OH, reacts with excess phosphorus(V) chloride. All the –OH groups react. What volume of hydrogen chloride, measured at r.t.p., is produced? [Molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹] 0.120 dm³ 0.360 dm³ 0.600 dm³ 1.80 dm³
