A assumes only one –OH group reacts; C counts all five chlorine atoms of one PCl₅ as HCl; D counts all five chlorine atoms of each of the three PCl₅ molecules.

items.name: Oxidation of alcohols with acidified potassium dichromate(VI)
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec

items.question: Which alcohol, when heated under reflux with excess potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid, forms an organic product with the molecular formula C₄H₈O? butan-1-ol butan-2-ol 2-methylpropan-1-ol 2-methylpropan-2-ol
items.ms: Butan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol and is oxidised to the ketone butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃ (C₄H₈O), which is not oxidised further. A and C are primary alcohols: under reflux with excess oxidising agent they are oxidised all the way to carboxylic acids (butanoic acid and 2-methylpropanoic acid, C₄H₈O₂), not to the aldehydes. D is a tertiary alcohol and is not oxidised, so the organic compound is still C₄H₁₀O.
items.why: C10.18 is the most-asked point in this topic (17 of 20 sessions); Jun2025 Q12(b) asked which compound gives a ketone, and the Jan2025 report shows the reflux / distillation distinction for primary alcohols is still misunderstood.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec

items.question: Which compound does not change the colour of acidified potassium dichromate(VI) solution when they are warmed together? 2-methylbutan-2-ol 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol propanal cyclohexanol
items.ms: 2-methylbutan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol: there is no hydrogen atom on the C–OH carbon, so it is not oxidised and the solution stays orange. B is a (branched) primary alcohol and D is a secondary alcohol, so both are oxidised; C is an aldehyde and is oxidised to propanoic acid. With B, C and D the orange solution turns green.
items.why: The Oct2022 report found over half of candidates did not know that tertiary alcohols are not oxidised, and Oct2023 Q13(b) asked which reagent reacts with tertiary alcohols; a heavily branched primary alcohol and an aldehyde are the natural distractors.

items.question: Menthol, C₁₀H₂₀O, is an alcohol obtained from mint oil. It is oxidised to menthone, C₁₀H₁₈O, by heating it with potassium dichromate(VI) and dilute sulfuric acid. The skeletal formula of menthol is shown. Classify menthol as a primary, secondary or tertiary alcohol. Give a reason for your answer. State the colour change seen during the reaction. Give the oxidation number of chromium in the species responsible for each colour. Draw the skeletal formula of menthone. Explain why menthone is not oxidised further, even when it is heated under reflux with excess oxidising agent. Use the Data Booklet to give two differences between the infrared spectra of menthol and menthone. The half-equations for the reaction are: C₁₀H₂₀O → C₁₀H₁₈O + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O Use them to write the overall ionic equation for the reaction. State symbols are not required. Calculate the minimum mass of potassium dichromate(VI), K₂Cr₂O₇, needed to oxidise 7.80 g of menthol. Use relative atomic masses: H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0, K = 39.1, Cr = 52.0
items.ms: Secondary, because the carbon atom bonded to the –OH group is bonded to two other carbon atoms / one hydrogen atom Orange to green +6 (in Cr₂O₇²⁻) and +3 (in Cr³⁺) The ring structure of menthol with the C–OH replaced by C=O (all other groups unchanged) Menthone is a ketone: there is no hydrogen atom on the carbonyl (C=O) carbon that can be removed Menthol has an O–H absorption at 3750–3200 cm⁻¹ that is absent from the spectrum of menthone Menthone has a C=O absorption at 1720–1700 cm⁻¹ that is absent from the spectrum of menthol Ratio of 3C₁₀H₂₀O to 1Cr₂O₇²⁻ (forming 3C₁₀H₁₈O and 2Cr³⁺) 3C₁₀H₂₀O + Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 8H⁺ → 3C₁₀H₁₈O + 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O (H⁺ cancelled correctly) Moles of menthol = 7.80 ÷ 156.0 = 0.0500 mol Moles of K₂Cr₂O₇ = 0.0500 ÷ 3 = 0.01667 mol Mass = 0.01667 × 294.2 = 4.90 g
items.why: C10.18 is the most often asked point in the topic (17 of 20 sessions, 4.4% of marks); the full ionic equation from the dichromate half-equation and a reacting-mass calculation for the oxidising agent have not yet been set, and a cyclic natural-product alcohol is a typical unfamiliar Section B context.

To check the purity of the product, the student distils it, heating the flask with an electric heater, and records the temperature at which the liquid boils. Explain why a water bath would not be suitable for heating the flask in this distillation. The product distilled over the range 96 °C to 108 °C. Explain what this shows about the product.

items.name: Core Practical 7: oxidation of propan-1-ol to propanal and propanoic acid
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 10 Organic Chemistry: Halogenoalkanes, Alcohols
C10.20 - CORE PRACTICAL 7 The oxidation of propan-1-ol
items.question: In Core Practical 7, propan-1-ol is oxidised to propanal using potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid. The propanal is distilled off as it forms. The diagram shows the apparatus that a student set up. Anti-bumping granules were added to the flask. Some boiling temperatures are given in the table. Write the equation for the oxidation of propan-1-ol to propanal. Use [O] to represent the oxidising agent. Identify two errors in the way the apparatus is set up. State how each error should be corrected. Explain why propanal can be separated from the reaction mixture by distillation as it forms. Refer to the intermolecular forces in propanal and in propan-1-ol. Suggest why the receiving flask is cooled in ice. Describe a chemical test to show that the distillate contains an aldehyde. Give the result. Propanoic acid is made from propan-1-ol by heating under reflux with excess oxidising agent instead. Explain why heating under reflux produces propanoic acid rather than propanal.
items.ms: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CH₂CHO + H₂O The thermometer bulb is in the liquid: it should be level with the side arm (where the vapour enters the condenser) The water enters the condenser at the top: it should enter at the lower end (and leave at the upper end) Propan-1-ol molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other (as they have an O–H group) Propanal molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other (no hydrogen bonded to oxygen); there are only London forces and permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces between them So less energy is needed to separate propanal molecules / propanal has the lowest boiling temperature, so it boils off as soon as it forms while the propan-1-ol stays in the flask Propanal is volatile / has a low boiling temperature (49 °C), so cooling stops it evaporating from the receiver Warm with Benedict's solution / Fehling's solution Blue solution forms a red / red-brown / orange precipitate The condenser returns the propanal (vapour) to the flask, so it stays in contact with the oxidising agent and is oxidised further to propanoic acid
items.why: Core Practical 7 has been examined through reflux versus distillation (Jun2021, Jan2025, Jan2026) but never through the apparatus itself; spotting set-up errors and the hydrogen-bonding reason why propanal distils out are the likeliest new angles.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec

items.question: The mass spectrum of butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, has peaks at m/z = 72, 57, 43 and 29. Which species is responsible for the peak at m/z = 57? CH₃CO⁺ C₄H₉⁺ CH₃CH₂CO CH₃CH₂CO⁺
items.ms: Breaking the bond between the C=O carbon and the CH₃ group gives the ion CH₃CH₂CO⁺ (3 × 12 + 5 × 1 + 16 = 57). A is the ion responsible for the peak at m/z = 43. B also has a mass of 57 but cannot form from butanone, which has only eight hydrogen atoms in its molecule. C has the right mass but is not charged, so it is not detected.
items.why: Mass spectra (C10.21) came up in 13 of 20 sessions, usually as fragment MCQs on propanone and the propanols (Jun2021, Oct2024, Oct2025); butanone and an uncharged-fragment distractor reflect the mark schemes' penalty for missing charges.

items.question: Use the Data Booklet. Which bond causes a very broad absorption across the range 3300–2500 cm⁻¹ in an infrared spectrum? O–H in alcohols N–H in amines O–H in carboxylic acids C–H in alkanes
items.ms: The hydrogen-bonded O–H in carboxylic acids absorbs over a very wide range, 3300–2500 cm⁻¹. A: the O–H in alcohols absorbs at 3750–3200 cm⁻¹; B: N–H in amines absorbs at 3500–3300 cm⁻¹; D: C–H in alkanes absorbs in a much narrower band, about 2962–2853 cm⁻¹.

items.question: The infrared spectrum of a compound has a strong absorption at 1730 cm⁻¹ and two weaker absorptions at 2820 cm⁻¹ and 2720 cm⁻¹. There is no broad absorption above 3000 cm⁻¹. Use the Data Booklet to identify the compound. butanal butanone butan-1-ol butanoic acid
items.ms: 2820 cm⁻¹ and 2720 cm⁻¹ lie in the two aldehyde C–H ranges (2900–2820 and 2775–2700 cm⁻¹), and 1730 cm⁻¹ is in the aldehyde C=O range (1740–1720 cm⁻¹). B: a ketone C=O absorbs at 1720–1700 cm⁻¹ and a ketone has no aldehyde C–H absorptions; C would show a broad O–H absorption at 3750–3200 cm⁻¹ and no C=O; D would show a very broad O–H absorption at 3300–2500 cm⁻¹.
items.why: Oct2024 Q15 and Oct2021 Q1 identified compounds from IR data; the two aldehyde C–H absorptions (10.22i), which separate an aldehyde from a ketone, have not yet been the deciding evidence.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec

C10.23 - CORE PRACTICAL 8 Analysis of some inorganic a
items.question: In Core Practical 8, a student identifies some unknown compounds by chemical tests. Two white solids, R and S, are each one of: lithium carbonate, lithium nitrate, sodium carbonate, sodium nitrate. The results of two tests are shown in the table. Identify R and S. Write the equation for the thermal decomposition of R. Include state symbols. Explain why R and S decompose in different ways when they are heated. Four colourless liquids, W, X, Y and Z, are each one of: propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol, propanoic acid. The student adds phosphorus(V) chloride to a sample of each liquid. State what is observed. Write the equation for the reaction with propan-1-ol, and explain why this test cannot identify the four liquids. Devise a sequence of chemical tests that would identify each of the four liquids. Give the reagents and the expected observations for each test.
items.ms: R is lithium nitrate S is sodium nitrate 4LiNO₃ → 2Li₂O + 4NO₂ + O₂ (correct species and balancing) State symbols: LiNO₃(s), Li₂O(s), NO₂(g), O₂(g) The Li⁺ ion is smaller (has a higher charge density) than Na⁺, so it polarises (distorts the electron cloud of) the nitrate ion more, weakening its N–O bonds Misty / steamy (white) fumes with all four liquids CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + PCl₅ → CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl + POCl₃ + HCl All four compounds contain an –OH group, so they all give the same result IC1 Add sodium hydrogencarbonate (or sodium carbonate) solution to each liquid: only propanoic acid gives effervescence (of CO₂, which turns limewater milky) IC2 Warm each of the other three liquids with potassium dichromate(VI) and dilute sulfuric acid IC3 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary) leaves the solution orange; propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol turn it from orange to green IC4 Oxidise propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol again, distilling off the product as it forms (alcohol in excess) IC5 Warm each distillate with Benedict's (or Fehling's) solution: the distillate from propan-1-ol (propanal) gives a red precipitate IC6 The distillate from propan-2-ol (propanone) gives no change / the solution stays blue
items.why: Core Practical 8 has never been the main point of a question, but its tests are examined piecemeal (flame tests and nitrate decomposition in Topic 8, PCl₅ in Jun2019 and Jun2025, dichromate and Fehling's for alcohols); after the Jun2024 six-mark choice of a test for –OH, a six-mark plan to identify four liquids is the likeliest first full appearance.

items.question: Enthalpy changes of reactions in solution are often measured in an open polystyrene cup. Explain why the heat energy change measured in an open polystyrene cup is an enthalpy change. Data books list standard enthalpy changes. State the pressure and the temperature that are used for standard enthalpy changes.
items.ms: The cup is open to the atmosphere, so the pressure is constant, and an enthalpy change is the heat energy change measured at constant pressure 100 kPa and (a stated temperature, usually) 298 K
items.why: C6.1 has never been the main point of a question; standard conditions were asked inside a definition in Jun2022 Q18(a)(i), and 'measured at constant pressure' is the one part of its wording never tested.

items.question: Solid barium hydroxide-8-water and solid ammonium chloride are stirred together in a beaker. A smell of ammonia is produced and the beaker becomes so cold that a film of water underneath it freezes. Ba(OH)₂·8H₂O(s) + 2NH₄Cl(s) → BaCl₂(aq) + 2NH₃(g) + 10H₂O(l) State the sign of ΔrH for this reaction. Justify your answer using the observations. A student writes: 'In this reaction the products have less energy than the reactants, because energy is used up.' Explain why the student's statement is incorrect.
items.ms: Positive, because the temperature falls / heat energy is taken in from the surroundings, so the reaction is endothermic The products have more enthalpy than the reactants / ΔrH = H(products) − H(reactants) is positive, because heat energy is taken in from the surroundings (energy is transferred, not used up)
items.why: C6.2 was tested in 7 of 20 sessions, mostly as MCQ rows for neutralisation (Jan2022, Oct2020); an endothermic reaction that cools its surroundings, and the 'energy is used up' misconception, have not been asked.

items.question: The enthalpy level diagram shows the enthalpy changes when hydrogen burns in oxygen to form water as a gas and as a liquid. What is the enthalpy change, in kJ mol⁻¹, for H₂O(l) → H₂O(g)? −88.0 −44.0 +44.0 +88.0
items.ms: C: on the diagram 2H₂O(l) lies 571.6 − 483.6 = 88.0 kJ below 2H₂O(g), so 2H₂O(l) → 2H₂O(g) is an upward (endothermic) change of +88.0 kJ; for one mole of water ΔH = +88.0 ÷ 2 = +44.0 kJ mol⁻¹. A and B have the wrong sign (they are for condensation, which goes down the diagram). D is for 2 mol of water, not the 1 mol in the equation.
items.why: C6.3 has come up in 10 of 20 sessions, always as a profile or diagram to pick (Jan2026, May2023, Jun2021); reading a value off a diagram with two product levels has not been asked.

items.question: Which equation represents the reaction whose enthalpy change is the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation, ΔneutH, for sulfuric acid and potassium hydroxide? items.question: For which reaction is the standard enthalpy change both the standard enthalpy change of combustion of one substance and the standard enthalpy change of formation of another? H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(g) C(graphite) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g) C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g) 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)
items.ms: C: one mole of carbon in its standard state burns completely, and one mole of CO₂ forms from its elements in their standard states. D involves 2 mol of each substance, so its ΔH is twice each value.
items.why: Jan2024 Q22(a) asked why a reaction 'can also be called' an enthalpy change of formation and Jan2026 Q2 tested these definitions; a reaction that fits two definitions at once is the likely next twist.

items.name: Calculating energy transferred and ΔH from calorimetry (mcΔT)
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec

C6.5 - use experimental data to cal
items.question: An instant cold pack contains 4.00 g of ammonium nitrate and 50.0 g of water, kept apart. When the pack is squeezed, the solid dissolves. NH₄NO₃(s) + aq → NH₄⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq) ΔsolH = +25.7 kJ mol⁻¹ The water is at 21.0 °C at the start. Assume that no heat is exchanged with the surroundings, that the mass of the solution is 50.0 g and that its specific heat capacity is 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. [Mr of NH₄NO₃ = 80.0] What is the lowest temperature reached? 6.1 °C 14.9 °C 15.3 °C 27.1 °C
items.ms: B: n = 4.00 ÷ 80.0 = 0.0500 mol; energy taken in = 0.0500 × 25 700 = 1285 J; ΔT = 1285 ÷ (50.0 × 4.18) = 6.15 °C. The change is endothermic, so the temperature falls to 21.0 − 6.15 = 14.9 °C. A is the temperature change, not the final temperature. C uses 54.0 g (water + solid), which the stem rules out. D adds the temperature change, as if the change were exothermic.
items.why: C6.5 has come up in 18 of 20 sessions; working back from ΔH to a final temperature (Jan2021 hand warmer, Oct2025 biopropanol) has only been asked for exothermic changes.

items.question: 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ nitric acid is mixed with 50.0 cm³ of 1.20 mol dm⁻³ potassium hydroxide solution in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises by 6.6 °C. Assume that the density of the mixture is 1.00 g cm⁻³ and its specific heat capacity is 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Which expression gives the enthalpy change of neutralisation, in J mol⁻¹? −(50.0 × 4.18 × 6.6) ÷ 0.0500 −(100.0 × 4.18 × 6.6) ÷ 0.0600 −(100.0 × 4.18 × 6.6) ÷ 0.110 −(100.0 × 4.18 × 6.6) ÷ 0.0500
items.ms: D: all 100.0 g of the mixture is heated, and the acid (0.0500 mol) is the limiting reagent, so 0.0500 mol of water forms; the alkali (0.0600 mol) is in excess. A uses the mass of one solution only. B uses the moles of the reagent in excess. C adds the moles of acid and alkali.

items.question: A student compares ethanol and propan-1-ol as fuels for a camping stove. Each alcohol is burned in a spirit burner under a copper can containing 200 g of water, and the temperature rise of the water is measured. The table shows the results. [Specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹; Mr: ethanol 46.0, propan-1-ol 60.0] Calculate the energy transferred to the water when the ethanol was burned. The standard enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol is −1367 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the percentage of the energy released by burning the ethanol that was transferred to the water. Calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of propan-1-ol from the student's results. Assume that the same percentage of the energy released is transferred to the water as for ethanol. Give your answer to three significant figures, with a sign and units. Suggest one reason why the percentage of the energy transferred to the water may not be the same for the two alcohols.
items.ms: 200 × 4.18 × 21.3 = 17 807 J / 17.8 kJ Moles of ethanol = 0.92 ÷ 46.0 = 0.0200 (mol) Energy released = 0.0200 × 1367 = 27.3 kJ / 27 340 J Percentage = 17.8 ÷ 27.34 × 100 = 65.1 % Energy transferred to the water = 200 × 4.18 × 24.0 = 20 064 J Energy released by the propan-1-ol = 20 064 ÷ 0.651 = 30 800 J / 30.8 kJ Moles of propan-1-ol = 0.90 ÷ 60.0 = 0.0150 (mol) ΔcH = −30.8 ÷ 0.0150 = −2050 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative sign, units and 3 s.f.) Propan-1-ol may undergo more incomplete combustion (a sootier flame / soot on the can) The flames may be different sizes or at different distances from the can The burning times are different, so different amounts of heat are lost to the surroundings
items.why: Combustion calorimetry of alcohols is the most-asked C6.5 context (Oct2021, Jan2022, Jun2022, Oct2025); using a known fuel to find the fraction of energy reaching the water (Jun2023 Q20 asked an efficiency) and then correcting a second fuel with it has not been asked.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 6 Energetics

items.question: Flameless ration heaters are used to heat food for soldiers and campers. The heater is a pad of magnesium powder mixed with a little iron and sodium chloride. When water is added, the magnesium reacts quickly and the pad becomes hot. Equation 1 Mg(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Mg(OH)₂(s) + H₂(g) [Ar of Mg = 24.3] Explain, in terms of oxidation numbers, why the reaction in Equation 1 is a redox reaction. Calcium reacts with cold water much faster than magnesium does. Explain why the reactivity of the Group 2 elements increases down the group. A student finds ΔrH for Equation 1 indirectly. In experiment 1, 0.200 g of magnesium ribbon is added to 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises by 17.9 °C. In experiment 2, magnesium hydroxide is added to the same volume of the same acid. The student calculates that ΔH₂ = −107 kJ mol⁻¹. The Hess cycle links the two experiments to Equation 1. Show by calculation that the hydrochloric acid is in excess in experiment 1. Calculate ΔH₁, in kJ mol⁻¹. Assume that the density of the solution is 1.00 g cm⁻³ and its specific heat capacity is 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Write the ionic equation, including state symbols, for the reaction in experiment 2. State one observation the student would make in experiment 2. Use the Hess cycle and your answer to (c)(ii) to calculate ΔrH for Equation 1. Use the standard enthalpy changes of formation in the table to calculate another value for ΔrH for Equation 1. The value of ΔH₁ from experiment 1 is less exothermic than the true value. Suggest two reasons for this, other than heat loss to the surroundings. A ration heater contains 7.50 g of magnesium. It is used to heat a 250 g pouch of food that starts at 15.0 °C. Only 45 % of the energy released is transferred to the food. Use ΔrH = −352.9 kJ mol⁻¹ to calculate the final temperature of the food. [Specific heat capacity of the food = 3.50 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹] The heater bag has a vent and the instructions say that it must not be used in an enclosed space. Suggest why.
items.ms: Magnesium is oxidised: its oxidation number increases from 0 to +2 Hydrogen is reduced: its oxidation number decreases from +1 (in H₂O) to 0 (in H₂) Down the group the atoms have more (occupied) shells / larger atomic radius / more shielding, so the outer electrons are further from the nucleus so the outer electrons are less strongly attracted and are lost more easily / the ionisation energies decrease Mol Mg = 0.200 ÷ 24.3 = 0.00823; mol HCl = 0.0500, which is more than the 2 × 0.00823 = 0.0165 (mol) needed Energy transferred = 50.0 × 4.18 × 17.9 = 3741 J ΔH₁ = −3.741 ÷ 0.00823 = −455 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative sign, 2 or 3 s.f.) Mg(OH)₂(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2H₂O(l) The white solid dissolves / disappears A colourless solution forms The temperature rises ΔrH = ΔH₁ − ΔH₂ = −455 − (−107) = −348 kJ mol⁻¹ ΔrH = −924.5 − 2(−285.8) = −352.9 kJ mol⁻¹ The magnesium ribbon is coated with magnesium oxide, so fewer moles of magnesium react than calculated from the mass Some energy is absorbed by the cup / thermometer, which is not included in the calculation The escaping hydrogen carries spray / water vapour (and so energy) out of the cup Energy released = (7.50 ÷ 24.3) × 352.9 = 0.309 × 352.9 = 108.9 kJ Temperature rise = 0.45 × 108 900 ÷ (250 × 3.50) = 56.0 °C Final temperature = 15.0 + 56.0 = 71.0 °C Hydrogen is produced, which is flammable / forms an explosive mixture with air
items.why: Section C is a contemporary context with routine Unit 2 ideas and 3–6 marks of calculation (Oct2025 self-heating can with CaO, biopropanol); a magnesium ration heater links Group 2 redox, an indirect Hess determination like Jun2025 Q17, and working back to a temperature.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec

items.question: Nitrogen dioxide forms from nitrogen and oxygen in car engines. N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g) ΔrH = +180.6 kJ mol⁻¹ 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g) ΔrH = −114.2 kJ mol⁻¹ What is the standard enthalpy change of formation of NO₂(g), in kJ mol⁻¹? +33.2 +66.4 +147.4 +294.8
items.ms: A: adding the equations gives N₂(g) + 2O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g), ΔH = +180.6 + (−114.2) = +66.4 kJ; ΔfH is for one mole of NO₂, so +66.4 ÷ 2 = +33.2 kJ mol⁻¹. B is for 2 mol of NO₂. C subtracts the second value and halves. D subtracts the second value and does not halve.
items.why: Combining given equations was asked in Jan2026 Q14 and in Jan2021 and Jan2023 structured parts; a target that must also be halved to match the definition is a trap not yet used.

items.question: Methanol is made from synthesis gas, a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen. Under standard conditions the reaction is: CO(g) + 2H₂(g) → CH₃OH(l) ΔrH The table shows some standard enthalpy changes of combustion. Give the meaning of the term standard enthalpy change of combustion. Write the equation, including state symbols, for the reaction whose enthalpy change is the standard enthalpy change of combustion of carbon monoxide. A Hess cycle can be used to find ΔrH from the enthalpy changes of combustion. Complete the Hess cycle. Write the formulae of the products, with state symbols, in the box and label the two downward arrows with the enthalpy changes they represent. Calculate ΔrH. The standard enthalpy change of formation of carbon monoxide is −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹. Use this value and your answer to (c)(ii) to calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation of methanol. Use the bond enthalpies in the table to calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction when all the substances are gases. CO(g) + 2H₂(g) → CH₃OH(g) Give two reasons why your answer to (e) is different from your answer to (c)(ii). Methanol and hydrogen are both possible fuels for cars. Calculate the energy released, in kJ, when 1.00 g of each fuel burns completely. [Mr: CH₃OH = 32.0; H₂ = 2.0] 1.00 dm³ of liquid methanol has a mass of 792 g. 1.00 dm³ of hydrogen gas at room temperature and pressure has a mass of 0.0833 g. Use these data and your answers to (g) to explain why methanol is a more practical fuel for cars than hydrogen.
items.ms: The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is burned completely in oxygen under standard conditions (100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K), with all substances in their standard states CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g) Box: CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) Left arrow: ΔcH(CO) + 2ΔcH(H₂) (or −283.0 + 2(−285.8)) and right arrow: ΔcH(CH₃OH) ΔrH = [−283.0 + 2(−285.8)] − (−726.0) = −128.6 kJ mol⁻¹ ΔrH = ΔfH(CH₃OH) − ΔfH(CO), because ΔfH of H₂ is zero ΔfH(CH₃OH) = −128.6 + (−110.5) = −239.1 kJ mol⁻¹ Bonds broken: 1077 + 2(436) = 1949 (kJ) Bonds made: 3(413) + 358 + 464 = 2061 (kJ) ΔH = 1949 − 2061 = −112 kJ mol⁻¹ In (c)(ii) methanol is a liquid but in (e) it is a gas, so the energy released when methanol condenses is not included in (e) The C–H, C–O and O–H values are mean bond enthalpies, averaged over many compounds, not the exact values in methanol Methanol: 726.0 ÷ 32.0 = 22.7 kJ (per gram) Hydrogen: 285.8 ÷ 2.0 = 143 kJ (per gram) Energy per dm³: methanol 792 × 22.7 = 1.80 × 10⁴ kJ; hydrogen 0.0833 × 143 = 11.9 kJ Methanol releases far more energy per unit volume (about 1500 times), so a much smaller fuel tank is needed / hydrogen would have to be compressed to high pressure or liquefied
items.why: Hess cycles from combustion data recur (Oct2021 Q19(c) ethanal, Oct2020 Q13) and usually sit beside a bond-enthalpy estimate and its limitations (Jun2023 Q20); a cycle with a compound (CO) among the reactants, then used to find Δ_{f}H, has not been set.

items.question: In Core Practical 2, the enthalpy change for the thermal decomposition of potassium hydrogencarbonate, ΔrH, is found indirectly. 2KHCO₃(s) → K₂CO₃(s) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) ΔrH Both solids react with dilute hydrochloric acid. Reaction 1: K₂CO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) ΔH₁ Reaction 2: KHCO₃(s) + HCl(aq) → KCl(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) ΔH₂ Explain why ΔrH cannot be measured directly. Describe how a student should carry out experiments to determine ΔH₁ and ΔH₂, and how the results are used to calculate ΔrH. The student is given anhydrous potassium carbonate, potassium hydrogencarbonate, 2.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid and normal laboratory apparatus. In reaction 1, 4.15 g of K₂CO₃ was added to 40.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. The temperature rose by 5.7 °C. Calculate ΔH₁, in kJ mol⁻¹. Assume that the density of the solution is 1.00 g cm⁻³ and its specific heat capacity is 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. [Mr of K₂CO₃ = 138.2] In reaction 2, ΔH₂ = +30.6 kJ mol⁻¹. Use Hess's law and your answer to (c) to calculate ΔrH for the thermal decomposition of potassium hydrogencarbonate. In both reactions the measured temperature change is smaller than it would be if no heat were exchanged with the surroundings. Deduce whether the value of ΔrH in (d) is too high or too low. Justify your answer.
items.ms: The solid has to be heated (strongly) to decompose, so the temperature change of the reaction cannot be measured / energy is being supplied while it reacts IC1 Measure a known volume (e.g. 40.0 cm³) of the acid, in excess, with a burette / pipette / measuring cylinder into a polystyrene cup (supported in a beaker) IC2 Weigh about 3–4 g of K₂CO₃ in a weighing bottle and reweigh the empty bottle after adding the solid, to find the mass added (by difference) IC3 Record the temperature of the acid (every 30 s for a few minutes) until it is steady IC4 Add the solid in small portions (so that acid spray is not lost in the effervescence), stir, and record the temperature at regular intervals / the highest temperature reached IC5 Repeat with a known mass of KHCO₃ and the same volume of fresh acid; the temperature falls in reaction 2 IC6 For each reaction, energy = mass of acid × 4.18 × ΔT and ΔH = −energy ÷ moles of solid (in kJ mol⁻¹); then ΔrH = 2ΔH₂ − ΔH₁ by Hess's law Energy transferred = 40.0 × 4.18 × 5.7 = 953 J Moles of K₂CO₃ = 4.15 ÷ 138.2 = 0.0300 (mol) ΔH₁ = −0.953 ÷ 0.0300 = −31.7 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative sign) ΔrH = 2ΔH₂ − ΔH₁ (or a correct Hess cycle) = 2(+30.6) − (−31.7) = +92.9 kJ mol⁻¹ Too low (less endothermic): ΔH₁ is less negative and ΔH₂ is less positive than the true values, so 2ΔH₂ − ΔH₁ is smaller
items.why: Core Practical 2 underlies Jan2020 Q15, Oct2024 Q16(b) and Jun2025 Q17(b) (hydrated salts, MgO/MgCO₃) and Jan2026 Q13 used KHCO₃ in an MCQ; the potassium hydrogencarbonate practical itself has not been a structured question, and a 6-mark practical description was set in Jan2026 Q20(b).

items.name: Evaluating experiments: errors, uncertainty, assumptions, graphs and cooling-curve corrections
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 6 Energetics
C6.8 - evaluate the results obtaine
items.question: A student mixes 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid with 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide solution in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises by 6.8 °C. Each thermometer reading has an uncertainty of ±0.5 °C. Which change to the method would reduce the percentage uncertainty in the temperature change? using 50.0 cm³ of each solution instead of 25.0 cm³ measuring each solution with a burette instead of a measuring cylinder using 2.00 mol dm⁻³ solutions of both reagents recording the temperature every 15 seconds instead of every 30 seconds
items.ms: C: twice as much acid and alkali react in the same mass of solution, so ΔT doubles (about 13.6 °C) while each reading still has ±0.5 °C, so the percentage uncertainty halves. A doubles both the energy released and the mass heated, so ΔT does not change. B reduces the uncertainty in the volumes, not in the temperature change. D gives more readings, but each has the same uncertainty.
items.why: Percentage uncertainty in ΔT was a calculation MCQ in Jun2025 Q1(b) and Jan2023 Q1(a); how to reduce it, part of the spec's 'comment on sources of uncertainty', has not been asked.

items.name: Evaluating experiments: errors, uncertainty, assumptions, graphs and cooling-curve corrections
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 6 Energetics
C6.8 - evaluate the results obtaine
items.question: A student finds the enthalpy change of solution of potassium chloride, which is endothermic. A weighed sample is dissolved in water in a polystyrene cup and the largest fall in temperature is measured. Which of these would make the calculated value of ΔsolH more positive than the true value? Heat energy is transferred from the surroundings to the solution during the experiment. The thermometer reads 0.5 °C too high at every temperature. Some of the weighed solid is left in the weighing boat, but the mass weighed is used in the calculation. The specific heat capacity of the solution is less than the value of 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ used in the calculation.
items.ms: D: the real energy taken in is m × c × ΔT with the smaller c, so using 4.18 overestimates the energy and the value is too positive. A: heat gained from the surroundings makes the temperature fall smaller, so ΔsolH is less positive. B: a constant error cancels when ΔT is found by subtraction. C: fewer moles dissolve than the mass used suggests, so dividing by too many moles makes ΔsolH less positive.
items.why: Effects of errors were asked in May2023 Q2(b) (wrong c) and Jan2023 Q1(c) for exothermic reactions; an endothermic case, where the direction of each error reverses, has not been tested.

items.name: Evaluating experiments: errors, uncertainty, assumptions, graphs and cooling-curve corrections
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 6 Energetics
C6.8 - evaluate the results obtaine
items.question: A student investigates the reaction between iron and copper(II) sulfate solution. Fe(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + Cu(s) 50.0 cm³ of 0.400 mol dm⁻³ copper(II) sulfate solution is placed in a polystyrene cup and its temperature is measured every minute. At 3.0 minutes, 2.00 g of iron powder is added and the mixture is stirred. The temperature is then measured every minute until 10.0 minutes. The graph shows the results. Show by calculation that the iron is in excess. [Ar of Fe = 55.8] Draw suitable lines on the graph and use them to determine the temperature change at 3.0 minutes. Explain why the temperature change is found in this way, rather than from the highest temperature recorded. Calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction, in kJ mol⁻¹. Assume that the density of the solution is 1.00 g cm⁻³ and its specific heat capacity is 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Each temperature reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 °C. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in your temperature change from (b). State one assumption, other than those given in (d), that is made in the calculation in (d).
items.ms: Mol Fe = 2.00 ÷ 55.8 = 0.0358 and mol CuSO₄ = 0.0500 × 0.400 = 0.0200, so the iron is in excess (1 : 1 ratio) Horizontal straight line through the points from 0 to 2 minutes, extended to 3.0 minutes Straight line of best fit through the points from 5 to 10 minutes, extrapolated back to 3.0 minutes ΔT = 34.2 − 20.2 = 14.0 °C Heat is lost to the surroundings while the reaction is taking place (it is not instantaneous), so extrapolating gives the temperature that would be reached if the reaction were instantaneous / with no heat loss Energy transferred = 50.0 × 4.18 × 14.0 = 2926 J ΔH = −2.926 ÷ 0.0200 = −146 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative sign and units) (2 × 0.05) ÷ 14.0 × 100 = 0.71 % All the energy released is transferred to the solution (none to the cup, thermometer or solids) All the copper(II) sulfate reacts / the reaction goes to completion The heat capacity of the solids (iron and copper) is negligible
items.why: Drawing lines and extrapolating a cooling curve was asked in Jun2021 Q19(c) and Jun2024 Q17(a), and percentage uncertainty in ΔT in Jun2022 Q18(b)(ii); the zinc version of this displacement was an MCQ in Jun2023, so iron is the fresh context.

items.question: Ammonia is being tested as a carbon-free fuel for ships. 4NH₃(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2N₂(g) + 6H₂O(g) Use the bond enthalpies in the table to calculate the enthalpy change, in kJ mol⁻¹, for this reaction. −1272 −202 +1272 +1512
items.ms: A: bonds broken = 12 N–H + 3 O=O = 12(391) + 3(498) = 6186 kJ; bonds made = 2 N≡N + 12 O–H = 2(945) + 12(464) = 7458 kJ; ΔH = 6186 − 7458 = −1272 kJ mol⁻¹. B uses N=N instead of N≡N for nitrogen. C is bonds made − bonds broken. D counts only one O–H bond per water molecule.
items.why: Bond-enthalpy calculations appear in 18 of 20 sessions (Jan2026 Q15, Oct2025 Q13); ammonia as a carbon-free fuel that forms N≡N has not been used.

items.name: Bond enthalpy and mean bond enthalpy; calculations and limitations
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 6 Energetics
C6.9 - the terms bond enthalpy and
items.question: The mean bond enthalpy of the C–H bond is +413 kJ mol⁻¹. Which statement is correct? 413 kJ is released when one mole of C–H bonds is broken. The enthalpy change for CH₄(g) → C(g) + 4H(g) is exactly +1652 kJ mol⁻¹. It is an average of the bond enthalpies of C–H bonds in a range of different compounds in the gaseous state. It is the enthalpy change for CH₄(g) → CH₃(g) + H(g).
items.ms: C: a mean bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break one mole of a bond in the gas phase, averaged over many different compounds. A: breaking bonds always needs energy. B: 4 × 413 is only an estimate for methane, because 413 is an average. D: this is the enthalpy change for breaking the first C–H bond in methane only, which is not the same as the mean.
items.why: The meaning of mean bond enthalpy was asked in Oct2021 Q19(b)(i), and Oct2023 Q1 and Oct2020 Q1 tested what a bond enthalpy value represents; the 'exact or average' distinction suits an MCQ.

items.name: Bond enthalpy and mean bond enthalpy; calculations and limitations

items.question: Dimethyl ether, CH₃OCH₃, is a gas at room temperature. It is being developed as a fuel for diesel engines. Its displayed formula is shown. Give the meaning of the term mean bond enthalpy. Dimethyl ether burns completely in oxygen. Write the equation for the complete combustion of one mole of dimethyl ether, with all the substances in the gaseous state. Include state symbols. Use your equation and the mean bond enthalpies in the table to calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of dimethyl ether. The standard enthalpy change of combustion of dimethyl ether is −1460 kJ mol⁻¹. Give two reasons why the value calculated in (b)(ii) is different from this value.
items.ms: The energy required to break one mole of a (specified) bond with all species in the gaseous state averaged over a range of different compounds CH₃OCH₃(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(g) Bonds broken: 6(413) + 2(358) + 3(498) = 4688 (kJ) Bonds made: 4(805) + 6(464) = 6004 (kJ) ΔH = 4688 − 6004 = −1316 kJ mol⁻¹ Mean bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds, not the values for the bonds in dimethyl ether Under standard conditions water is a liquid, but the calculation forms steam, so the energy released when the steam condenses is not included
items.why: Combustion enthalpies from mean bond enthalpies were asked in Oct2019 (butan-1-ol), Oct2021 (ethanol) and Jun2023 (octane), each followed by 'why the value differs'; a fuel that is itself a gas, so only the water's state matters, has not been used.

items.name: Calculating mean bond enthalpies from ΔrH
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 6 Energetics
C6.10 - calculate mean bond enthalpi
items.question: Nitrogen trifluoride, NF₃, is used to clean equipment for making computer chips. N₂(g) + 3F₂(g) → 2NF₃(g) ΔrH = −264 kJ mol⁻¹ Bond enthalpies / kJ mol⁻¹: N≡N 945; F–F 158 What is the mean bond enthalpy of the N–F bond, in kJ mol⁻¹? +192.5 +280.5 +561.0 +841.5
items.ms: B: bonds broken = 945 + 3(158) = 1419 kJ; −264 = 1419 − 6E(N–F), so 6E(N–F) = 1683 and E(N–F) = +280.5 kJ mol⁻¹ (two NF₃ molecules contain six N–F bonds). A uses 1419 − 264. C divides by 3 (one NF₃ only). D divides by 2.
items.why: C6.10 has come up in 9 of 20 sessions (May2024 Q4 and Jan2020 Q3 N–H, Jan2024 Q24 S–F); two moles of product, giving six bonds, is the trap the examiners' reports single out.

path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 6 Energetics
C6.10 - calculate mean bond enthalpi
items.question: The enthalpy changes of atomisation of two gaseous alkanes are shown. CH₄(g) → C(g) + 4H(g) ΔH = +1664 kJ mol⁻¹ C₂H₆(g) → 2C(g) + 6H(g) ΔH = +2826 kJ mol⁻¹ Assume that the C–H bond enthalpy is the same in both compounds. What is the bond enthalpy of the C–C bond in ethane, in kJ mol⁻¹? +330 +404 +502 +1162
items.ms: A: E(C–H) = 1664 ÷ 4 = 416 kJ mol⁻¹; ethane has six C–H bonds and one C–C bond, so E(C–C) = 2826 − 6(416) = +330 kJ mol⁻¹. B divides 2826 by 7, treating every bond as the same. C is 2 × 1664 − 2826 (it compares ethane with 2CH₄ the wrong way round). D subtracts the methane value once.
items.why: Jun2022 Q18(c) found C–H, O–H, C–O and C–C step by step from atomisation enthalpies and Jan2026 Q19(b) asked for an unknown bond; a two-alkane version fits an MCQ.

items.question: The table shows some standard enthalpy changes. Calculate the mean bond enthalpy of the C–Cl bond in tetrachloromethane, CCl₄(g). The Data Booklet value of the mean bond enthalpy of C–Cl is +346 kJ mol⁻¹. Suggest why this value is different from your answer to (a).
items.ms: Enthalpy change for CCl₄(g) → C(g) + 4Cl(g) = +95.7 + 716.7 + 4(121.7) = +1299.2 (kJ mol⁻¹) Mean C–Cl bond enthalpy = 1299.2 ÷ 4 = +325 kJ mol⁻¹ The Data Booklet value is an average over many different compounds containing C–Cl bonds, whereas (a) is the value in CCl₄ only (the strength of a bond depends on the other atoms in the molecule)
items.why: Jun2022 Q18(c) and Jan2026 Q19(b) asked for bond enthalpies from atomisation and reaction data; dividing by the number of bonds is the step the examiners' reports say is most often missed.

items.name: Bond enthalpy and which bond breaks first / rate
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 6 Energetics
C6.11 - that bond enthalpy data gives some indication
items.question: The table shows some bond enthalpies. A red-hot wire is lowered into a gas jar of hydrogen iodide. Purple fumes appear around the wire. When the experiment is repeated with hydrogen chloride, there is no visible change. Write the equation, including state symbols, for the reaction that takes place in the hydrogen iodide. Explain, using data from the table, why hydrogen iodide decomposes but hydrogen chloride does not. Fluoroalkanes are used as refrigerants because they are very unreactive. For example, 1,1,1,2-tetrafluoroethane, CF₃CH₂F, is not hydrolysed when it is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide, but chloroalkanes are. Explain this difference, using data from the table. A mixture of nitrogen and hydrogen does not react at room temperature, even though the reaction is exothermic. N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) ΔrH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹ Explain, using data from the table, why there is no reaction at room temperature.
items.ms: 2HI(g) → H₂(g) + I₂(g) The H–I bond enthalpy (298 kJ mol⁻¹) is much lower than the H–Cl bond enthalpy (432 kJ mol⁻¹) / the H–I bond is weaker than the H–Cl bond so the H–I bond breaks easily at the temperature of the wire / the activation energy is low enough for a fast reaction, but very few H–Cl bonds break The C–F bond has a higher bond enthalpy (467 kJ mol⁻¹) than the C–Cl bond (346 kJ mol⁻¹) / C–F is the stronger bond so the activation energy for breaking C–F is very high and (almost) no collisions have enough energy, so the rate of hydrolysis is negligible The N≡N bond (945 kJ mol⁻¹) is very strong / has a very high bond enthalpy and must be broken for the reaction to take place so the activation energy is very high At room temperature (almost) no molecules have energy ≥ Ea / very few collisions are successful, so the rate is (almost) zero A negative ΔrH only shows that the products have less enthalpy than the reactants; it says nothing about the rate
items.why: C6.11 has never been the main point of a question, though 'C–I is weaker than C–Cl' is asked almost every year under C10.13 (Jun2022, Jan2022, Oct2024, Jun2024); predicting which molecule breaks up on heating, and why a strong bond makes an exothermic reaction slow at room temperature, are the untested parts of its wording.

items.name: Collision theory: concentration, temperature, pressure, surface area
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 9 Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria
C9.1 - understand, in terms of the
items.question: Which change increases the rate of a reaction mainly because a greater proportion of the collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy? increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution increasing the pressure of a gaseous reaction mixture using a powdered solid in place of lumps of the same mass increasing the temperature
items.ms: At a higher temperature the particles have more kinetic energy, so a much larger proportion of collisions have energy ≥ Ea; the small rise in collision frequency is a minor effect. A, B and C increase the number of collisions per unit time (more particles per unit volume or more exposed surface) but do not change the proportion of collisions with energy ≥ Ea.
items.why: C9.1 has come up in 15 of 20 sessions, often as 'which change does not affect the rate' (Jun2019 Q1, May2024 Q3(a)); separating the frequency effect from the energy effect is the distinction the examiners say candidates confuse.

items.name: Collision theory: concentration, temperature, pressure, surface area
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 9 Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria

items.question: Excess zinc granules react with 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid at 20 °C. Zn(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + H₂(g) Which change increases the initial rate of reaction but does not change the total volume of hydrogen produced? using 100 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid using 25 cm³ of 2.0 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid using 50 cm³ of 2.0 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid using 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid at 10 °C
items.ms: Zinc is in excess, so the volume of hydrogen depends only on the amount of acid. B: 25 × 2.0 = 50 mmol, the same as 50 × 1.0, but the higher concentration gives more frequent collisions, so the initial rate increases. A: same concentration, so the same initial rate, but twice the acid gives twice the hydrogen. C: faster, but 100 mmol of acid doubles the volume. D: same volume, but the lower temperature decreases the rate.
items.why: Jun2025 Q9 asked how particle size and acid volume affect both the rate and the total gas volume, and the Jun2022 ER notes candidates who kept the final volume unchanged when the acid changed; separating concentration from amount is the next step.

items.name: Collision theory: concentration, temperature, pressure, surface area
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 9 Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria

items.question: A pile of flour burns slowly when it is heated in air, but a fine cloud of flour dust in air can explode if it is ignited by a spark. Explain, in terms of collision theory, why the flour dust reacts so much faster than the pile of flour.
items.ms: The dust has a (much) larger surface area / more of the flour is exposed to the oxygen in the air so there are more frequent collisions between oxygen molecules and the flour / more (successful) collisions per unit time
items.why: C9.1 is asked in 15 of 20 sessions; surface area has been examined only through a catalyst (Oct2021 Q22(f)(i)), and the Jan2025 mark scheme insists on 'collisions per unit time'.

items.name: Activation energy
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 9 Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria
C9.2 - that reactions take place on
items.question: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen does not react at room temperature, although the reaction to form water is very exothermic. Which is the best explanation? Very few collisions between hydrogen and oxygen molecules have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy. Hydrogen and oxygen molecules do not collide at room temperature. The bonds in water molecules are weaker than the bonds in hydrogen and oxygen molecules. The enthalpy change of the reaction is positive at room temperature.
items.ms: A reaction only happens when colliding molecules have at least the activation energy; at room temperature almost no collisions do, so the rate is negligible. B: gas molecules collide all the time. C: an exothermic reaction forms stronger bonds than it breaks. D: ΔH is negative (exothermic) at room temperature too.
items.why: C9.2 is asked in 10 of 20 sessions, mostly by reading E_{a} off a profile (Oct2025 Q1, Jan2021 Q1); the idea that a very exothermic reaction can still be too slow to observe has not been tested directly.

items.name: Rates from 1/time and from gradients of graphs
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 9 Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria
C9.3 - calculate the rate of a reac
items.question: Magnesium carbonate reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid in a conical flask standing on a balance. Carbon dioxide escapes from the flask. The graph shows the loss in mass of the flask and its contents against time. A tangent has been drawn to the curve at 40 s. What is the rate of reaction at 40 s? 0.0055 g s⁻¹ 0.010 g s⁻¹ 0.017 g s⁻¹ 0.10 g s⁻¹
items.ms: Gradient of the tangent, e.g. (1.37 − 0.26) ÷ (110 − 0) = 0.010 g s⁻¹. A is the average rate over the whole reaction (1.10 g ÷ 200 s); C divides the loss in mass at 40 s by the time (0.66 ÷ 40), which is the average rate over the first 40 s, not the rate at 40 s; D is a power-of-ten slip.
items.why: The rate at a given time from a tangent is a regular MCQ (Oct2025 Q12, May2024 Q3(b), Oct2022 Q16); a loss-in-mass graph has not yet been used.

items.name: Rates from 1/time and from gradients of graphs
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 9 Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria
C9.3 - calculate the rate of a reac
items.question: Excess magnesium ribbon is added to 40.0 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid. Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g) At one instant, hydrogen is being produced at a rate of 0.48 cm³ s⁻¹, measured at r.t.p. What is the rate of decrease of the concentration of hydrochloric acid at this instant? [Molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹] 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
items.ms: H₂: 0.48 ÷ 24 000 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol s⁻¹; HCl is used twice as fast, 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol s⁻¹; ÷ 0.0400 dm³ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. A is the rate of formation of H₂ in mol s⁻¹; B is the rate of loss of HCl in mol s⁻¹ (not divided by the volume); C leaves out the 2 : 1 ratio.
items.why: Oct2020 Q5(b) converted a gas-volume gradient into mol s⁻¹ and Jan2025 Q8(b) asked for the units of rate; combining the mole ratio with a change in concentration is the likely harder version.

items.name: Rates from 1/time and from gradients of graphs
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 9 Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria
C9.3 - calculate the rate of a reac
items.question: A student investigated the rate of the reaction between calcium and water. A 0.100 g sample of calcium granules was added to an excess of water in a conical flask connected to a gas syringe. The volume of hydrogen was recorded every 10 seconds at room temperature and pressure. The graph shows the results. Write the equation for the reaction of calcium with water. Include state symbols. Show that the final volume of hydrogen should be about 60 cm³. [Ar: Ca = 40.1. Molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹] Use the graph to determine the rate of reaction at 30 s. Show your working on the graph. The experiment was repeated with 0.100 g of calcium in much smaller pieces. Half of the final volume of hydrogen was collected in 12 s, compared with 30 s in the first experiment. Calculate the relative rate, 1/time, for each experiment, using the time taken to collect half of the final volume. Explain the difference in rate, and state the effect, if any, on the final volume of hydrogen.
items.ms: Ca(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g) Amount of Ca = amount of H₂ = 0.100 ÷ 40.1 = 2.494 × 10⁻³ mol Volume = 2.494 × 10⁻³ × 24 000 = 59.9 cm³ Tangent drawn to the curve at t = 30 s Gradient calculated from the tangent, e.g. (50.7 − 9.2) ÷ (60 − 0) Rate = 0.69 cm³ s⁻¹ (range 0.60 to 0.80) with units 1/30 = 0.033 s⁻¹ and 1/12 = 0.083 s⁻¹ Smaller pieces have a larger surface area, so there are more frequent collisions between water molecules and calcium (more collisions per unit time) The final volume is the same (59.9 cm³) because the same amount of calcium is used (and water is in excess)
items.why: C9.3 is asked in 9 of 20 sessions: a tangent rate and 1/t rates were set in Jun2022 Q15(b) and Jan2025 Q17(b), and the spec allows the rate 'at a time t'; a Group 2 metal with water is a fresh gas-syringe context from topic 8.

items.name: Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution: effect of temperature
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 9 Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria
C9.4 - qualitatively, in terms of t
items.question: A sealed container holds a sample of a gas at a constant temperature. More of the same gas is added and the temperature is kept the same. What happens to the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution of molecular energies, drawn as the number of molecules against energy? peak higher; energy at the peak unchanged peak higher; energy at the peak increases peak height unchanged; energy at the peak unchanged peak lower; energy at the peak increases
items.ms: The shape of the distribution depends only on temperature, so the most probable energy is unchanged; with more molecules the number at every energy increases, so the area under the curve and the peak height increase. B and D describe a change of temperature (D is a temperature rise); C would be true only if the fraction of molecules were plotted.
items.why: M-B MCQs appear in 13 of 20 sessions, almost always about temperature (Jan2026 Q11, Oct2025 Q6, May2024 Q1(b)); changing the number of molecules at constant temperature (part of Jan2023 Q17(b)) is the untested half.

items.name: Role of catalysts: alternative route, lower Ea
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 9 Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria

items.question: A catalyst is added to a reversible reaction that is at equilibrium in a closed system at constant temperature. Which statement is correct? It increases the rate of the forward reaction only. It increases the equilibrium yield of the product. It increases the rates of the forward and backward reactions by the same factor. It increases the activation energy of the backward reaction.
items.ms: The catalyst provides an alternative route that is used in both directions, lowering the activation energy of the forward and the backward reaction, so both rates increase equally; the position of equilibrium (and the yield) is unchanged and equilibrium is simply reached sooner. A and B describe a shift in the equilibrium, which a catalyst does not cause; D: the activation energy of the backward reaction is lowered, not raised.
items.why: Catalyst-and-equilibrium MCQs came up in Oct2025 Q3 and Jun2025 Q11(b); the statement form tests the misconception that a catalyst speeds up only the forward reaction.

items.question: In polluted air, sulfur dioxide is oxidised to sulfur trioxide, which then forms sulfuric acid in rain. 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g) ΔH = −196 kJ mol⁻¹ Without a catalyst this reaction is extremely slow. items.question: The diagram shows the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution of the energies of the molecules in a gas at a constant temperature. Ea is the activation energy of the uncatalysed reaction and Ecat is the activation energy of the catalysed reaction. Which area represents the molecules that have enough energy to react when the catalyst is present but not when it is absent? P Q R Q and R
items.ms: With the catalyst, molecules with energy ≥ Ecat can react (Q and R); without it only those with energy ≥ Ea can (R). The extra molecules have energies between Ecat and Ea: area Q. P cannot react either way; R can react with or without the catalyst; Q and R are all the molecules that can react with the catalyst.

items.question: Dinitrogen monoxide, N₂O, is a powerful greenhouse gas that forms as a by-product in nitric acid plants. items.question: Two sealed flasks of the same volume are kept at 800 K. Flask 1 initially contains 1.0 mol of carbon monoxide and 1.0 mol of steam. Flask 2 initially contains 1.0 mol of carbon dioxide and 1.0 mol of hydrogen. CO(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO₂(g) + H₂(g) Which statement is correct when both flasks have reached equilibrium? Flask 1 contains no carbon monoxide. Flask 1 contains more carbon dioxide than flask 2. The two flasks contain the same amount of each of the four gases. A: the reaction is reversible and does not go to completion. B: the equilibrium mixtures are identical. D: the equilibrium is dynamic; both reactions continue at equal rates.

items.question: Bromine water is orange. It contains the equilibrium Br₂(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HOBr(aq) + H⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) Which substance, added in a small amount, makes the orange colour deeper? aqueous silver nitrate dilute sodium hydroxide solid sodium carbonate solid potassium bromide
items.ms: Adding Br⁻ ions increases [Br⁻], so the equilibrium moves to the left and more Br₂ forms. A removes Br⁻ as a precipitate of AgBr; B removes H⁺ (OH⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O); C removes H⁺ (forming CO₂ and water). In A, B and C the equilibrium moves to the right and the colour fades.

items.name: Le Chatelier: temperature, pressure, concentration
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 9 Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria
C9.10 - predict and justify the qual
items.question: Nitrogen dioxide, NO₂, is a brown gas. Dinitrogen tetroxide, N₂O₄, is colourless. They form an equilibrium mixture. 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g) Use the standard enthalpy changes of formation in the table to calculate the enthalpy change of the forward reaction. A sealed glass tube containing the equilibrium mixture at room temperature is placed in iced water. State and explain what is seen. Some of the equilibrium mixture is in a sealed gas syringe at constant temperature. The plunger is pushed in quickly so that the volume of gas is halved, and it is then held in place. At first the brown colour becomes darker. Over the next few seconds it becomes paler, but it remains darker than it was before the plunger was pushed in. Explain these observations. In a different experiment, the equilibrium mixture was kept in a sealed container of fixed volume. Two separate changes were made, at times t₁ and t₂. The graph shows how the concentrations of NO₂ and N₂O₄ changed. Identify the change made at t₁ and the change made at t₂. Justify your answers. When the temperature of the equilibrium mixture is increased, the rates of both the forward and the backward reactions increase, but the position of equilibrium moves to the left. Suggest why.
items.ms: ΔH = 9.2 − (2 × 33.2) = −57.2 kJ mol⁻¹ The brown colour becomes paler The forward reaction is exothermic, so lowering the temperature moves the equilibrium to the right (the exothermic direction) and the concentration of NO₂ decreases At first the same number of NO₂ molecules is in a smaller volume, so the concentration of NO₂ increases and the colour is darker The pressure has increased, so the equilibrium moves to the side with fewer gas molecules / moles 2 mol of gas on the left and 1 mol on the right, so the equilibrium moves to the right and some NO₂ is converted into N₂O₄ (the colour becomes paler) The shift only partly opposes the change, so the concentration of NO₂ remains higher than it was originally t₁: (some) N₂O₄ was added Only [N₂O₄] increases suddenly at t₁; [NO₂] then rises gradually as the equilibrium moves to the left, using up some of the added N₂O₄ t₂: the temperature was increased Neither concentration changes suddenly at t₂ (so not an addition or removal of a gas); [NO₂] increases and [N₂O₄] decreases, so the equilibrium moves to the left, the endothermic direction At a higher temperature more molecules have energy ≥ the activation energy of each reaction, so both rates increase The backward (endothermic) reaction has the larger activation energy, so its rate increases more; the backward rate is greater than the forward rate until a new equilibrium (with more NO₂) is reached
items.why: C9.10 has come up in 19 of 20 sessions (3.7% of the marks); NO₂/N₂O₄ is a named spec demonstration, and the two-stage colour change on compression and changes read off a concentration–time graph have not been asked.

items.question: In an industrial process, a gas mixture passes over a catalyst for a fixed time and then leaves the reactor before equilibrium is reached. The table shows, at four temperatures, the equilibrium yield of the product and the percentage of this equilibrium yield that is reached in the reactor. At which temperature is the yield of product leaving the reactor greatest? 350 °C 400 °C 450 °C 500 °C
items.ms: Yield leaving the reactor = equilibrium yield × fraction reached: 350 °C 24.0%, 400 °C 38.5%, 450 °C 46.4%, 500 °C 42.8%, so 450 °C. A has the highest equilibrium yield, but the rate is too slow for much of it to be reached; D comes closest to equilibrium (fastest rate), but the equilibrium yield is low. This is why a compromise temperature is used.

items.question: In the Haber process, only about 15% of the nitrogen and hydrogen is converted into ammonia each time the gases pass through the reactor, but about 98% is converted overall. N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) Which is the best explanation? The unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are separated from the ammonia and passed through the reactor again. The iron catalyst increases the equilibrium yield of ammonia to 98%. The high pressure moves the position of equilibrium so far to the right that the reaction goes to completion. Ammonia is removed inside the reactor as it forms, so the reaction goes to completion in a single pass.
items.ms: Ammonia is condensed out of the gas leaving the reactor and the unreacted N₂ and H₂ are recycled, so almost all of it is converted eventually. B: a catalyst does not change the equilibrium yield. C: the equilibrium does not go to completion (only 15% per pass). D contradicts the 15% conversion per pass; the ammonia is removed after the gases leave the reactor.

items.name: Compromise between yield and rate in industry
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 9 Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria
C9.11 - evaluate data to explain the
items.question: Large amounts of hydrogen chloride are formed as a by-product when chlorine is used to make plastics such as PVC. In the Deacon process, this hydrogen chloride is oxidised back to chlorine. 4HCl(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2Cl₂(g) + 2H₂O(g) Use oxidation numbers to show that this is a redox reaction. Identify the element that is oxidised and the element that is reduced. Use the mean bond enthalpies in the table to calculate the enthalpy change of the forward reaction. The value of ΔH calculated from standard enthalpy changes of formation is −114 kJ mol⁻¹. Give a reason why your answer to (b) is different from this value. The table shows the equilibrium conversion of hydrogen chloride into chlorine at different temperatures and pressures, for a 4 : 1 mole ratio of HCl to O₂. Use the data to describe and explain the effect of increasing the pressure on the equilibrium conversion. The original Deacon process used a copper(II) chloride catalyst at 450 °C and a pressure of about 1 atm. Discuss the choice of these conditions. Use the data in the table and your answer to (b). Modern plants use a ruthenium(IV) oxide catalyst, which gives a fast enough rate at 300 °C. Explain two ways in which this makes the process more sustainable. In one plant, 7.30 tonnes of hydrogen chloride are fed into the reactor each hour, and 80.0% of it is converted into chlorine. Calculate the mass, in tonnes, of chlorine produced each hour. [Ar: H = 1.0, Cl = 35.5. 1 tonne = 10⁶ g]
items.ms: Chlorine is oxidised: −1 in HCl → 0 in Cl₂ Oxygen is reduced: 0 in O₂ → −2 in H₂O Bonds broken: (4 × 432) + 498 = 2226 (kJ mol⁻¹) Bonds made: (2 × 243) + (4 × 464) = 2342 (kJ mol⁻¹) ΔH = 2226 − 2342 = −116 kJ mol⁻¹ The O–H bond enthalpy is a mean (average) value from a range of compounds, not the value for H₂O itself At every temperature the conversion is greater at 5 atm than at 1 atm (e.g. 71% → 78% at 450 °C) There are 5 mol of gas on the left and 4 mol on the right, so a higher pressure moves the equilibrium to the right (the side with fewer gas molecules) IC1 The forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH negative), so a lower temperature gives a higher equilibrium conversion (e.g. 87% at 300 °C compared with 71% at 450 °C, at 1 atm) IC2 At a lower temperature the rate is too slow, because fewer molecules have energy ≥ Ea / there are fewer successful collisions per unit time IC3 So 450 °C is a compromise between an acceptable rate and an acceptable equilibrium conversion IC4 A higher pressure would increase the conversion and the rate, but the gain in conversion is small (e.g. 71% → 78% at 450 °C) and does not justify the cost of compressors / thick-walled reactors / energy for compression (or the greater risk of leaks of toxic HCl and Cl₂) IC5 The catalyst increases the rate by providing an alternative route with a lower activation energy, so a lower temperature can be used; it does not change the equilibrium conversion IC6 Unreacted HCl and O₂ are separated and recycled, so the overall conversion is high even though the conversion in each pass is incomplete A lower temperature is used, so less energy / fuel is needed for heating / less CO₂ is released The equilibrium conversion is higher at 300 °C (87% compared with 71% at 450 °C), so more chlorine is made per pass / less unreacted HCl has to be separated and recycled The catalyst is not used up / can be used for a long time Amount of HCl = 7.30 × 10⁶ ÷ 36.5 = 2.00 × 10⁵ mol Amount of Cl₂ = 2.00 × 10⁵ × 0.800 ÷ 2 = 8.00 × 10⁴ mol Mass of Cl₂ = 8.00 × 10⁴ × 71.0 = 5.68 × 10⁶ g = 5.68 tonnes

items.name: London forces, permanent dipole–dipole interactions, hydrogen bonds
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 7 Intermolecular Forces
C7.1 - the nature of the following
items.question: Which statement describes how London forces arise between two molecules? A lone pair of electrons on one molecule is attracted to a δ+ hydrogen atom on a neighbouring molecule. The permanent dipole of one molecule attracts the permanent dipole of a neighbouring molecule. An uneven distribution of electrons at one instant in one molecule induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule. A pair of electrons is shared between two neighbouring molecules.
items.ms: London forces come from an instantaneous dipole (electrons unevenly spread at one moment) inducing a dipole in a neighbouring molecule; the two dipoles attract. A describes a hydrogen bond; B describes permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces; D describes a covalent bond, which is not an intermolecular force.
items.why: C7.1 has come up in all 20 sessions; Oct2024 asked how London forces arise in a structured part, but no MCQ has yet tested the mechanism against the other forces.

items.name: London forces, permanent dipole–dipole interactions, hydrogen bonds

items.question: Which substance has permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces, but no hydrogen bonds, between its molecules in the liquid state? CH₃CH₂OH CH₃OCH₃ CH₃CH₂CH₃ CH₃NH₂
items.ms: Methoxymethane has polar C–O bonds arranged at an angle, so its molecules have a permanent dipole, but no H atom is bonded to O, so it cannot form hydrogen bonds. A (O–H) and D (N–H) form hydrogen bonds; C is a non-polar alkane with London forces only.
items.why: MCQs on which forces act in a liquid recur (Jan2022, Jan2023, Oct2023); an ether, polar but with no O–H bond, has not been used.

items.question: Tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, and trichloromethane, CHCl₃, are both liquids at room temperature. CCl₄ molecules are non-polar but CHCl₃ molecules are polar. Explain why tetrachloromethane has the higher boiling temperature, even though there are no permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces between its molecules.
items.ms: CCl₄ has more electrons (74 compared with 58 in CHCl₃) so the London forces between CCl₄ molecules are stronger / larger instantaneous and induced dipoles form the extra London forces in CCl₄ are greater than the permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces in CHCl₃, so more energy is needed to separate CCl₄ molecules
items.why: C7.1 has come up in all 20 sessions; London forces outweighing a dipole was asked for ICl v water (Jan2026) and 1-iodopropane (Oct2021), but a non-polar liquid boiling above its polar analogue has not been asked.

items.name: Hydrogen bonding in H₂O, NH₃, HF
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 7 Intermolecular Forces
C7.2 - the interactions in molecule
items.question: Which statement about a hydrogen bond between two water molecules, O–H···O, is correct? The hydrogen bond forms between a lone pair on the hydrogen atom and the oxygen atom of the other molecule. The hydrogen bond is shorter than the covalent O–H bond. The hydrogen bond is stronger than the covalent O–H bond. The three atoms O–H···O lie in a straight line.
items.ms: The hydrogen bond lines up with the covalent O–H bond, so O–H···O is linear (180°). A: the lone pair is on the oxygen atom, not on hydrogen; B: the hydrogen bond is longer than the covalent O–H bond; C: a hydrogen bond is much weaker than a covalent O–H bond.
items.why: C7.2 has come up in 19 of 20 sessions; the linear O–H···O arrangement was tested through diagrams (Jun2019, Jan2025) but never as a statement MCQ with length and strength distractors.

items.question: Ammonia is very soluble in water. Which hydrogen bonds can form between ammonia molecules and water molecules? (··· represents a hydrogen bond) N–H···O only O–H···N only both N–H···O and O–H···N neither: only London forces and permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces form
items.ms: Each molecule has an H atom bonded to a very electronegative atom (N or O) and a lone pair on N or O, so hydrogen bonds form both ways: a δ+ H of ammonia to a lone pair on the O of water (N–H···O) and a δ+ H of water to the lone pair on N (O–H···N). A and B each miss one direction; D ignores the N–H and O–H bonds and lone pairs.
items.why: Hydrogen bonding between two different molecules has been asked only for alcohols with water (May2023, Jun2021); ammonia acting as both donor and acceptor has not been tested.

items.question: Hydrogen fluoride, HF, boils at 20 °C. Hydrogen bonds form between the molecules in liquid hydrogen fluoride. Draw a diagram to show a hydrogen bond between two molecules of hydrogen fluoride. Include the relevant lone pair of electrons, the partial charges and the value of the F–H···F bond angle. Hydrogen chloride does not form hydrogen bonds between its molecules. Give a reason why.
items.ms: Hydrogen bond (dotted or dashed line) from a lone pair on the F atom of one molecule to the H atom of the other molecule, with δ+ on H and δ− on F F–H···F shown as a straight line with the angle labelled 180° Chlorine is not electronegative enough (much less electronegative than F), so the H atom in HCl is not sufficiently δ+
items.why: Liquid HF is named in spec 7.2, but hydrogen-bond drawings have always been of water or alcohols (Jan2025, Oct2019, Jun2021); the Jun2022 report says candidates wrongly give hydrogen bonds to the other hydrogen halides.

items.name: Anomalous properties of water: melting/boiling point, density of ice
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 7 Intermolecular Forces
C7.3 - the following anomalous prop
items.question: Solid ammonia sinks in liquid ammonia, but ice floats on liquid water. Explain, in terms of hydrogen bonding, why ice is less dense than liquid water.
items.ms: In ice each water molecule forms (four) hydrogen bonds, which hold the molecules in a rigid, open (tetrahedral) lattice with the molecules further apart When ice melts some hydrogen bonds break, the open structure collapses and the molecules move closer together, so the same mass occupies a smaller volume
items.why: C7.3 is cool (5 of 20 sessions, last Oct2025); the density of ice has appeared only in MCQ statements and in Jan2025's data comparison, never as a direct explanation.

items.question: Fluoromethane, CH₃F, is used to etch silicon chips. The fluorine atom in a fluoromethane molecule has three lone pairs of electrons. Explain why fluoromethane molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other. Deduce whether a fluoromethane molecule can form a hydrogen bond with a water molecule. Justify your answer.
items.ms: No hydrogen atom is bonded to the fluorine atom: the H atoms are bonded to carbon, so they are not sufficiently δ+ Yes, because a lone pair on the F atom of CH₃F can form a hydrogen bond with a δ+ H atom of a water molecule (O–H···F)
items.why: C7.4 MCQs (7 of 20 sessions) ask whether a compound hydrogen bonds with itself, and Jan2023 used (CH₃)₃CF as a distractor; whether such a molecule can hydrogen bond to water has never been asked.

items.question: Which shows the hydrogen halides in order of increasing boiling temperature? HCl < HBr < HI < HF HF < HCl < HBr < HI HI < HBr < HCl < HF HCl < HF < HBr < HI
items.ms: London forces increase from HCl to HI as the number of electrons increases, so HCl < HBr < HI; HF also has hydrogen bonds, which are much stronger, so it has the highest boiling temperature (20 °C). B ignores hydrogen bonding in HF; C reverses the London-force trend; D underestimates the effect of hydrogen bonding in HF.
items.why: The hydrogen halide trend (spec 7.5iv) appeared in Jun2022, Oct2024 and Jan2025, but the full order with HF's position has not been an MCQ.

items.question: Each of these compounds has 50 electrons in one molecule. Which compound is the most volatile? pentan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂OH 2-methylbutan-2-ol, CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)₂OH hexane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ 2,2-dimethylbutane, CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)₃
items.ms: The most volatile compound has the weakest intermolecular forces (lowest boiling temperature). The alcohols also have hydrogen bonds, so the answer is an alkane; with the same number of electrons, the branched 2,2-dimethylbutane has fewer points of contact between molecules and weaker London forces (boiling temperature 50 °C) than hexane (69 °C). A has the least volatile (138 °C); B is branched but still hydrogen bonds (102 °C); C is the straight-chain isomer.
items.why: Isomer boiling-temperature MCQs recur (Oct2025, Jun2025, Oct2024, May2024); the spec's word 'volatility' and combining branching with the alcohol–alkane difference have not been used.

items.question: The enthalpy change of vaporisation, ΔvapH, is the enthalpy change when one mole of a liquid is converted into gas at its boiling temperature. A student used the apparatus shown to measure ΔvapH for ethanol. The ethanol in the insulated flask was already boiling when the timing started. The ethanol vapour was condensed and collected in a beaker on a balance. The heater supplied energy at a rate of 50.0 W (50.0 J s⁻¹) for 300 s. In this time 16.6 g of ethanol, C₂H₅OH, was collected. Calculate ΔvapH for ethanol, in kJ mol⁻¹. Include a sign in your answer. The data-book value of ΔvapH for ethanol is +38.6 kJ mol⁻¹. Suggest why the student's value is greater than the data-book value. The table shows data-book values of ΔvapH for three liquids. Explain why ΔvapH for ethanol is greater than that for hexane, even though hexane molecules have more electrons. Explain why water has the greatest ΔvapH of the three liquids, even though it has the fewest electrons.
items.ms: Energy supplied = 50.0 × 300 = 15 000 J / 15.0 kJ Amount of ethanol = 16.6 ÷ 46.0 = 0.361 mol ΔvapH = 15.0 ÷ 0.361 = +41.6 kJ mol⁻¹ Some energy from the heater is lost to the surroundings, so less ethanol is vaporised / collected than expected Hexane has only London forces, although these are stronger than the London forces in ethanol (more electrons) Ethanol molecules also form hydrogen bonds (from the O–H group) Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than London forces, so more energy is needed to separate ethanol molecules (this outweighs the weaker London forces) Each water molecule has two δ+ H atoms and two lone pairs, so it can form (on average) two hydrogen bonds An ethanol molecule has only one δ+ H atom, so it forms (on average) one hydrogen bond; water has more hydrogen bonds per molecule, so more energy is needed to separate its molecules
items.why: C7.5 is asked every session, always through boiling temperatures; the spec's suggested practical on the enthalpy change of vaporisation and Δ_{vap}H data have not been used.

items.question: The graph shows the boiling temperatures of the first seven straight-chain alkanes and the first five straight-chain alcohols, plotted against the number of electrons in one molecule. In each alcohol the OH group is on the end carbon atom. Explain why the boiling temperatures of the alkanes increase as the number of electrons increases. Hexan-1-ol, CH₃(CH₂)₅OH, is the next alcohol in the series. Use the graph to estimate the boiling temperature of hexan-1-ol. Compare and explain the boiling temperatures of the alcohols and of the alkanes that have the same number of electrons. Your answer should explain how the difference between their boiling temperatures changes as the number of electrons increases. Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane, C(CH₃)₄, both have the molecular formula C₅H₁₂. Pentane boils at 36 °C and 2,2-dimethylpropane boils at 10 °C. Explain why 2,2-dimethylpropane has the lower boiling temperature.
items.ms: More electrons, so larger instantaneous and induced dipoles / stronger London forces between the molecules so more energy is needed to overcome the London forces / to separate the molecules Hexan-1-ol has 58 electrons Extending the alcohol line: 158 °C IC1 Alkanes have only London forces between their molecules IC2 Alcohols have London forces, permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces and hydrogen bonds (from the O–H group) IC3 An alcohol and an alkane with the same number of electrons have similar London forces IC4 Hydrogen bonds are stronger than London forces, so more energy is needed to separate alcohol molecules and each alcohol boils higher, e.g. methanol 65 °C and ethane −89 °C at 18 electrons IC5 As the number of electrons increases, the London forces increase in both series and become a larger part of the intermolecular forces IC6 Each alcohol still has only one OH group, so the hydrogen bonding stays about the same and the difference falls (from about 154 °C at 18 electrons to about 69 °C at 50 electrons) Both have the same number of electrons, but 2,2-dimethylpropane is branched / more compact / spherical so there are fewer points of contact / a smaller surface area of contact between molecules, so the London forces are weaker so less energy is needed to separate the molecules
items.why: C7.5 has come up in all 20 sessions with 6-mark answers in Oct2025 and Jan2026; alcohols versus alkanes with the same number of electrons (7.5iii) has never been shown as two series on one graph, and the narrowing gap has never been asked.
