items.question: Equal volumes of two liquids are shaken together and left to stand. Which pair of liquids forms two separate layers? ethanol and water 1-chlorobutane and water hexane and cyclohexane propanone and water
items.ms: 1-chlorobutane is polar but cannot form hydrogen bonds with water; the hydrogen bonds between water molecules are stronger than the attractions that would form between water and 1-chlorobutane, so the liquids do not mix. A and D form hydrogen bonds with water (the O–H of ethanol; lone pairs on the O of propanone); in C both liquids have only London forces of similar strength, so they mix.
items.why: Spec 7.6iii (water a poor solvent for polar halogenoalkanes) was tested only through Jan2025's best-solvent MCQ; immiscibility has not been asked directly.

items.name: Choice of solvents: water for ionic compounds and alcohols; poor solvent for halogenoalkanes; non-aqueous solvents
path: Unit 2 Energetics, Group Chemistry, Halogenoalkanes and Analytical Tec
Topic 7 Intermolecular Forces
C7.6 - factors that influence the c
items.question: Solid sulfur consists of non-polar S₈ molecules. In which solvent is sulfur most soluble? carbon disulfide, CS₂ ethanol, C₂H₅OH water dilute hydrochloric acid
items.ms: Sulfur molecules attract each other only by London forces. CS₂ is non-polar with only London forces, so the London forces formed between S₈ and CS₂ are similar to those broken. Ethanol, water and dilute hydrochloric acid all contain hydrogen bonds, which are not replaced by the weak attractions they would form with S₈.
items.why: Best-solvent MCQs recur (Jan2025, Jan2024, Jan2022); a non-hydrocarbon non-aqueous solvent for a non-polar solid (spec 7.6iv) has not been used.

items.question: The table shows the solubility in water at 20 °C of four straight-chain alcohols. In each alcohol the OH group is on the end carbon atom. Explain why the solubility of the alcohols in water decreases from propan-1-ol to hexan-1-ol. Calculate the concentration, in mol dm⁻³, of a saturated solution of pentan-1-ol at 20 °C. Assume that 100 g of water gives 100 cm³ of solution. Hexan-1-ol mixes completely with hexane. State the main type of intermolecular force between hexan-1-ol molecules and hexane molecules. A solution of butan-1-ol in water can be 'salted out' by dissolving solid potassium carbonate, K₂CO₃, in it. The butan-1-ol then separates as an upper layer. Complete the diagram to show how water molecules are arranged around the potassium ion and around the carbonate ion in the solution. Show two water molecules around each ion. Suggest why dissolving potassium carbonate causes the butan-1-ol to separate from the water.
items.ms: The OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules The hydrocarbon chain cannot form hydrogen bonds with water / forms only (weaker) London forces with water As the chain gets longer, more hydrogen bonds between water molecules must be broken to make room for it, and this energy is not regained There is still only one OH group per molecule, so hydrogen bonding to water becomes a smaller part of the attraction / the non-polar part of the molecule gets larger Amount of pentan-1-ol = 2.2 ÷ 88.0 = 0.025 mol Concentration = 0.025 ÷ 0.100 = 0.25 mol dm⁻³ London forces At least two water molecules with the O atom closest to K⁺ At least two water molecules with an H atom closest to the CO₃²⁻ ion The K⁺ and CO₃²⁻ ions are strongly hydrated / the attractions between the ions and water molecules are stronger than the hydrogen bonds between water and butan-1-ol so fewer water molecules are available to form hydrogen bonds with butan-1-ol, which forms a separate layer
items.why: Alcohol–water mixing (Jan2021, Oct2025) and hydration diagrams (Jun2021, Oct2024, Jan2026) recur; the fall in solubility with chain length and salting out have not been asked.

items.question: Rock salt is spread on roads in winter to melt ice. At very low temperatures anhydrous calcium chloride, CaCl₂, is often used instead, because energy is released when it dissolves. A student added 5.55 g of anhydrous calcium chloride to 50.0 g of water in a polystyrene cup, stirred, and recorded the highest temperature reached (Experiment 1). The student then repeated the experiment with hydrated calcium chloride, CaCl₂·6H₂O (Experiment 2). The results are shown. Calculate the enthalpy change, in kJ mol⁻¹, when one mole of anhydrous calcium chloride dissolves in Experiment 1. Assume that only the water changes temperature. [specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹] The enthalpy change when one mole of CaCl₂·6H₂O dissolves, calculated from Experiment 2, is +15.0 kJ mol⁻¹. Use a Hess cycle and your answer to (a)(i) to calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction CaCl₂(s) + 6H₂O(l) → CaCl₂·6H₂O(s) Each temperature reading has an uncertainty of ±0.1 °C. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the temperature change in Experiment 1. A data-book value for the enthalpy change when one mole of anhydrous calcium chloride dissolves is −81.3 kJ mol⁻¹. Give one reason, other than heat loss to the surroundings, why the student's value in (a)(i) is less exothermic. In solid CaCl₂·6H₂O, each calcium ion is surrounded by six water molecules, with the oxygen atom of each water molecule closest to the calcium ion. Explain why the water molecules are arranged in this way. Suggest why dissolving anhydrous calcium chloride is exothermic but dissolving hydrated calcium chloride is endothermic. Aircraft are de-iced with a mixture of water and propane-1,2-diol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂OH. The displayed formula of propane-1,2-diol is shown. Explain why propane-1,2-diol mixes with water in all proportions. Include a diagram showing one hydrogen bond between a propane-1,2-diol molecule and a water molecule. Propane-1,2-diol (boiling temperature 188 °C) and butan-1-ol (boiling temperature 118 °C) have the same number of electrons in one molecule. Explain why propane-1,2-diol has the higher boiling temperature. Water running off roads treated with calcium chloride contains chloride ions. Give the reagents and the observation for the test for chloride ions, and write the ionic equation, including state symbols, for the reaction.
items.ms: Energy transferred = 50.0 × 4.18 × 18.2 = 3803.8 J Amount of CaCl₂ = 5.55 ÷ 111.1 = 0.04995 mol ΔH = −3.8038 ÷ 0.04995 = −76.1 kJ mol⁻¹ Hess cycle with CaCl₂(s) + 6H₂O(l) and CaCl₂·6H₂O(s) both going to CaCl₂(aq) / Ca²⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq) ΔH = ΔH(Experiment 1) − ΔH(Experiment 2) = −76.1 − (+15.0) = −91.1 kJ mol⁻¹ (2 × 0.1) ÷ 18.2 × 100 = 1.1 % The anhydrous calcium chloride had absorbed water (vapour) from the air before it was weighed, so fewer moles of CaCl₂ were used / some of it was already hydrated Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so water is polar with δ− on O and δ+ on H The δ− oxygen atom (with its lone pairs) is attracted to the positive Ca²⁺ ion (the δ+ H atoms would be repelled) When anhydrous CaCl₂ dissolves, strong new attractions form between the ions and water molecules (the ions become hydrated), releasing more energy than is needed to break up the ionic lattice In CaCl₂·6H₂O the Ca²⁺ ions are already surrounded by water molecules, so less energy is released on dissolving, and this is less than the energy needed to separate the ions Propane-1,2-diol forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules (using its OH groups) Diagram: hydrogen bond from a lone pair on an O atom of one molecule to a δ+ H atom bonded to O in the other molecule, with O–H···O at 180° The hydrogen bonds formed between propane-1,2-diol and water are similar in strength to the hydrogen bonds broken in the pure liquids Same number of electrons, so the London forces are similar Propane-1,2-diol has two OH groups, so it forms more hydrogen bonds per molecule and more energy is needed to separate the molecules Dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate solution; white precipitate Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)
items.why: Section C often pairs a calorimetry/Hess calculation with intermolecular forces (Jan2026 Q23: MgCl₂ hydration); the spec's suggested practical on temperature changes when salts dissolve has not been used.

items.name: Definition of a transition metal
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 17 Transition Metals and their Chemistry
C17.1 - that transition metals are d
items.question: Cadmium, Cd, is a d-block element in Period 5. Its only stable ion is Cd²⁺, which has the electronic configuration [Kr]4d¹⁰. Which statement about cadmium is correct? Cadmium is a transition metal because it is in the d-block. Cadmium is a transition metal because a cadmium atom has electrons in its 4d subshell. Cadmium is not a transition metal because it is in Period 5, not Period 4. Cadmium is not a transition metal because its only stable ion has a completely filled d subshell.
items.ms: A transition metal forms at least one stable ion with an incompletely filled d subshell; Cd²⁺ (4d¹⁰) is full, so cadmium is a d-block element but not a transition metal (like zinc). A and B confuse 'd-block' (where the last electron goes) with 'transition metal'. C: the definition does not depend on the period (platinum, in Period 6, is a transition metal).
items.why: C17.1 MCQs came up in 8 of 17 sessions and the Jun2023 report says candidates could not explain why mercury is d-block but not transition; a Period 5 analogue of zinc has not been used.

items.name: Definition of a transition metal
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 17 Transition Metals and their Chemistry
C17.1 - that transition metals are d
items.question: How many of the ten Period 4 d-block elements, scandium to zinc, are transition metals? 7 8 9 10
items.ms: Titanium to copper (8 elements) each form at least one stable ion with an incompletely filled 3d subshell (for copper, Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹). Scandium (Sc³⁺, 3d⁰) and zinc (Zn²⁺, 3d¹⁰) are not. A also leaves out copper (thinking only of Cu⁺, 3d¹⁰); C leaves out only one of Sc and Zn; D counts every d-block element.
items.why: Jan2026 and Jan2025 asked which named elements are transition metals; counting the whole row tests both exceptions and the copper trap in one item.

items.name: Electronic configurations of Sc–Zn atoms and ions
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 17 Transition Metals and their Chemistry
C17.2 - deduce the electronic config
items.question: How many unpaired electrons are there in a Co²⁺ ion in its ground state? (Atomic number of cobalt = 27) 1 3 5 7
items.ms: Co is [Ar]3d⁷4s²; the 4s electrons are lost first, so Co²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁷. Seven electrons in five 3d orbitals: each orbital takes one electron before any pairing, so two orbitals are full and three hold one electron: 3 unpaired. A pairs electrons before every orbital is singly filled; C removes two 3d electrons instead of the 4s electrons ([Ar]3d⁵4s²); D is the number of 3d electrons.
items.why: Electrons-in-boxes for ions recur (Jan2025 Fe²⁺, Jan2023 Mn²⁺) and the reports say 4s is often left occupied; counting unpaired electrons in Co²⁺ tests both points in a new way.

items.name: Electronic configurations of Sc–Zn atoms and ions
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 17 Transition Metals and their Chemistry
C17.2 - deduce the electronic config
items.question: An ion X³⁺ of a Period 4 element has the electronic configuration [Ar]3d⁶. What is element X? iron cobalt nickel copper
items.ms: X³⁺ has 18 + 6 = 24 electrons, so the atom has 27: cobalt (Co is [Ar]3d⁷4s²; Co³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶). A: Fe²⁺, not Fe³⁺, is [Ar]3d⁶ (Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵). C: Ni³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁷. D: Cu³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁸.
items.why: Jan2026 Q4 and Jun2025 Q4 asked the configuration of a given ion; working back from a configuration and a charge to the element has not been asked.

items.name: Electronic configurations of Sc–Zn atoms and ions
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 17 Transition Metals and their Chemistry
C17.2 - deduce the electronic config
items.question: The graph shows the second ionisation energies of the Period 4 d-block elements, scandium to zinc. Complete the table to show the electronic configurations of the species. Explain why the second ionisation energy of chromium is greater than that of manganese. Use your answers to (a). Identify the other element whose second ionisation energy is higher than the general trend suggests. Explain your answer in terms of electronic configurations. Scandium is a d-block element but it is not a transition metal. Its only ion is Sc³⁺. Explain why scandium is not a transition metal.
items.ms: Cr: [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ Cr⁺: [Ar]3d⁵ and Mn⁺: [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ For chromium the second electron is removed from the 3d subshell, but for manganese it is removed from the 4s subshell The 4s electron is further from the nucleus / more shielded, so it is held less strongly than a 3d electron Removing an electron from Cr⁺ breaks the (stable) half-filled 3d⁵ subshell, whereas Mn²⁺ keeps the half-filled 3d⁵ arrangement Copper / Cu Cu⁺ is [Ar]3d¹⁰, so the second electron is removed from a full 3d subshell (whereas Zn⁺, [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹, loses a 4s electron) Sc³⁺ is [Ar] / has an empty 3d subshell, so scandium forms no (stable) ion with an incompletely filled d subshell
items.why: Configurations are asked in 12 of 17 sessions and successive ionisation energies appeared in the Jan2024 and Jan2025 MCQs; using second ionisation energies across Sc–Zn to show the chromium and copper anomalies has never been asked.

items.name: Variable oxidation numbers
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 17 Transition Metals and their Chemistry

items.question: For each of the elements scandium to manganese, the maximum oxidation number in its compounds is equal to the number of 4s electrons in the atom. the number of unpaired electrons in the atom. the number of 3d electrons in the atom. the total number of 3d and 4s electrons in the atom.
items.ms: Sc (3d¹4s²) +3, Ti +4, V +5, Cr (3d⁵4s¹) +6, Mn (3d⁵4s²) +7: the 3d and 4s electrons are close in energy, so all of them can be lost or used in bonding. A gives +2 for most; B fails for Mn (5 unpaired, maximum +7) and V (3 unpaired, maximum +5); C gives +5 for Mn.
items.why: Oct2022 asked the highest oxidation state of vanadium from its configuration and Oct2020 the maximum for chromium; the general rule across Sc–Mn has not been tested.

items.question: Manganese shows every oxidation number from +2 to +7 in its compounds. Complete the table to show the oxidation number of manganese in each species. The table shows the first eight ionisation energies of manganese and of calcium. Write the equation, with state symbols, for the third ionisation energy of manganese. Use the data to explain why manganese has a maximum oxidation number of +7, while calcium shows only the +2 oxidation number in its compounds. The electronic configurations are: Mn [Ar]3d⁵4s²; Ca [Ar]4s². Solutions of manganese(II) sulfate are stable in air, but a solution of iron(II) sulfate slowly turns from pale green to yellow-brown in air as iron(III) ions form. Explain this difference using the electronic configurations of the ions involved. In aqueous solution, manganese in the +7 oxidation state exists as the manganate(VII) ion, MnO₄⁻, and not as Mn⁷⁺ ions. Suggest why Mn⁷⁺ ions do not exist in aqueous solution.
items.ms: At least three correct All five correct: +7, +6, +4, +3, +2 Mn²⁺(g) → Mn³⁺(g) + e⁻ Calcium: there is a large increase between the 2nd and 3rd ionisation energies (1145 to 4912 kJ mol⁻¹) because the 3rd electron would come from the inner 3p subshell, closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so calcium loses only its two 4s electrons Manganese: the ionisation energies rise steadily from the 1st to the 7th, with no large jump, because the 3d and 4s electrons are close in energy The large jump is between the 7th and 8th ionisation energies (an increase of about 7300 kJ mol⁻¹, compared with about 2000 for each earlier step) because the 8th electron is in the 3p subshell, so the maximum is +7 (all seven 3d and 4s electrons) The energy needed to remove more electrons is recovered by lattice / hydration energies or by forming covalent bonds (e.g. in MnO₄⁻) Mn²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵ and Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵: both have a half-filled 3d subshell Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶, so it is (easily) oxidised by oxygen in the air to Fe³⁺, which has the more stable half-filled 3d subshell Oxidising Mn²⁺ to Mn³⁺ would remove an electron from the stable half-filled 3d subshell (giving 3d⁴), so Mn²⁺ is not easily oxidised In Fe²⁺ one 3d orbital holds a pair of electrons, and the repulsion between them makes one of these electrons easier to remove Mn⁷⁺ would be very small and highly charged / would have a very high charge density so it would strongly polarise water molecules (O–H bonds) and bond covalently to oxygen, releasing H⁺ ions / the energy to remove seven electrons could not be recovered by hydration
items.why: C17.3 is hot (14 of 17 sessions); the Mn²⁺/Fe²⁺ half-filled-subshell argument recurs (Jan2023, Jan2025) and the oxo-ion argument was asked for V⁵⁺ in Jan2023, but not for Mn(VII) or with ionisation-energy data.

items.question: Which species cannot act as a ligand? CH₃NH₃⁺ CO H₂S SCN⁻
items.ms: A ligand must have a lone pair of electrons to donate to the metal ion. In CH₃NH₃⁺ the lone pair on nitrogen has been used to bond to H⁺, so the ion has no lone pair. CO has a lone pair on carbon, H₂S two lone pairs on sulfur, and SCN⁻ lone pairs on S and N.
items.why: Oct2020 (NH₄⁺) and Jan2025 (C₂H₆) asked which species cannot be a ligand; a protonated amine links to the amines in this unit and has not been used.

items.question: Which statement describes each bond between the cobalt ion and a ligand in [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺? an ionic bond between Co³⁺ and an NH₃ molecule a covalent bond in which Co³⁺ and the nitrogen atom each provide one electron a dative covalent bond in which Co³⁺ provides both electrons a dative covalent bond in which the nitrogen atom provides both electrons
items.ms: Each NH₃ donates the lone pair on its nitrogen atom to Co³⁺, forming a dative (coordinate) covalent bond. A: NH₃ is neutral, so there is no ionic bond; B describes an ordinary covalent bond; C reverses the direction of donation (the metal ion accepts the pair).
items.why: Dative bonding is hot (13 of 17 sessions); Jan2021 and Jan2022 asked the bond type, and the Oct2023 report says the lone pair must be said to come from the donor atom.

The Ni(CO)₄ vapour is then passed over nickel pellets heated to 230 °C, where it decomposes and pure nickel is deposited. items.question: Which statement about the d-orbitals of a transition metal ion in an octahedral complex is correct? The ligands split each d-orbital into two orbitals of different energy. The ligands split the five d-orbitals into two groups of different energy. The ligands raise all five d-orbitals to the same higher energy. Light is emitted when an electron moves from a higher to a lower d-orbital, and this gives the colour.
items.ms: The ligands' lone pairs affect the d-orbitals unequally, so the five d-orbitals split into a lower and a higher group. A is the error the reports penalise (a single d-orbital does not split); C would give no energy gap; D confuses absorption with emission: the colour seen is the light that is not absorbed.
items.why: Explaining colour is warm (10 of 17 sessions) and reports from Jan2022 to Oct2024 penalise 'a d orbital splits' and 'light is emitted'; this item targets both errors.

items.question: Two complex ions of the same metal ion, X and Y, absorb visible light most strongly at 620 nm and 470 nm respectively. Which statement is correct? The energy gap between the split d-orbitals is larger in X than in Y. The energy gap between the split d-orbitals is larger in Y than in X. Y absorbs light of lower frequency than X. X and Y must contain the metal in different oxidation states.
items.ms: A shorter wavelength means a higher frequency and a higher photon energy, so Y (470 nm) has the larger d-orbital splitting. A reverses this; C: 470 nm light has a higher frequency than 620 nm light; D: a different ligand or coordination number could also change the splitting.
items.why: Oct2025 Q13(d) linked a colour to the wavelength absorbed; relating the wavelength of maximum absorption to the size of the energy gap has not been asked.

items.question: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate contains [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ ions. When excess aqueous ammonia is added, [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ ions form. The graph shows the absorption spectra of solutions of the two complex ions with the same concentration of copper(II). Explain why a solution of [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ ions is blue and why the colour of the solution changes when [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ ions form. Use information from the graph in your answer. The energy gap, ΔE, between the split d-orbitals is related to the wavelength, λ, of maximum absorption by ΔE = hc/λ. Use the graph to calculate the energy gap, in kJ mol⁻¹, for [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺. [h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹] [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ is used to find the percentage by mass of copper in a garden fungicide, a powder containing hydrated copper(II) sulfate and zinc sulfate. • 1.50 g of the fungicide is dissolved in water and the solution is made up to 250.0 cm³ with distilled water. • 25.0 cm³ of this solution is transferred to a 50.0 cm³ volumetric flask, excess aqueous ammonia is added and the solution is made up to the mark. • The absorbance of this solution is measured with a colorimeter set at 600 nm. It is 0.31. A calibration graph was made using standard solutions of copper(II) ions treated with excess ammonia in the same way. Explain why the colorimeter is set at 600 nm. Use the absorption spectra to suggest two reasons why the analysis uses [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ rather than [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺. Use the calibration graph to calculate the percentage by mass of copper in the fungicide. Zinc ions also form a complex ion with ammonia. Explain why the zinc sulfate in the fungicide does not affect the absorbance reading. A second batch of the fungicide is contaminated with nickel(II) sulfate. Nickel(II) ions form the blue-violet complex ion [Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺ with excess ammonia. Suggest the effect of the nickel on the calculated percentage of copper. Explain your answer.
items.ms: IC1 Cu²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁹: it has an incompletely filled 3d subshell IC2 The ligands split the 3d orbitals into two groups of different energy IC3 Light is absorbed and its energy promotes an electron from a lower-energy to a higher-energy d-orbital (the photon energy equals the energy gap) IC4 [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ absorbs mainly red / orange light (maximum near 800 nm, just beyond the red end of the visible region); the other wavelengths are transmitted, so the solution looks blue IC5 Ammonia ligands split the d-orbitals by a different (larger) amount than water, so the energy gap is larger IC6 So [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ absorbs a shorter wavelength / higher frequency (maximum at 600 nm, yellow-orange) and absorbs more strongly, so a different, deeper (blue-violet) colour is seen λ = 600 nm = 6.00 × 10⁻⁷ m (read from the graph) ΔE = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸ ÷ 6.00 × 10⁻⁷ = 3.32 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (for one ion) × 6.02 × 10²³ ÷ 1000 = 200 kJ mol⁻¹ 600 nm is the wavelength of maximum absorbance of [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺, so the measurement is most sensitive (largest change in absorbance with concentration) The ammine complex absorbs much more strongly (higher absorbance at the same concentration), so the method is more sensitive / more accurate for dilute solutions The absorption maximum of [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (about 800 nm) is outside the visible region, so a colorimeter using visible light would detect only weak absorption Concentration in the 50.0 cm³ flask, read from the graph, = 10.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ Concentration in the 250.0 cm³ solution = 2 × 10.3 × 10⁻³ = 2.06 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ n(Cu) in 250.0 cm³ = 2.06 × 10⁻² × 0.2500 = 5.15 × 10⁻³ mol mass of Cu = 5.15 × 10⁻³ × 63.5 = 0.327 g percentage = 0.327 ÷ 1.50 × 100 = 21.8% Zn²⁺ is [Ar]3d¹⁰ / has a full 3d subshell so no electron can be promoted from a lower to a higher d-orbital (no d–d transitions): the zinc complex does not absorb visible light / is colourless The calculated percentage of copper would be too high because [Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺ is coloured and also absorbs light at (around) 600 nm, increasing the absorbance
items.why: The colour 6-mark recurs (Oct2021, Jan2026) and colorimetry is 'beyond spec but examined' (Jun2021, Oct2024); an absorption spectrum with its wavelength of maximum absorption and the energy gap has never been asked.

items.question: Aqueous solutions containing Sc³⁺ ions and Zn²⁺ ions are both colourless. Which row gives the reason for each ion? Sc³⁺: its 3d subshell is empty; Zn²⁺: its 3d subshell is full Sc³⁺: its 3d subshell is full; Zn²⁺: its 3d subshell is empty Sc³⁺: water does not split its d-orbitals; Zn²⁺: its 3d subshell is full Sc³⁺: its 3d subshell is empty; Zn²⁺: water does not split its d-orbitals

B reverses the configurations; C and D use 'the d-orbitals are not split', which the mark schemes do not accept.
items.why: C17.9 MCQs recur (Jun2025, Jan2023, Jun2021); pairing the d⁰ and d¹⁰ cases in one item is new, and the mark schemes reject 'the d-orbitals are not split'.

items.question: Iron(III) ions form the octahedral ion [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ with water but the tetrahedral ion [FeCl₄]⁻ with chloride ions. Which statement explains why only four chloride ions bond to the iron(III) ion? Chloride ions are larger than water molecules, so there is not enough space for six around the iron(III) ion. path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry

items.question: Cisplatin is supplied for cancer treatment as a single isomer and not mixed with its isomer transplatin. Which statement explains this? Transplatin is tetrahedral, so it cannot bind to DNA. In transplatin the two chloride ligands are opposite each other, so it cannot bind to DNA in the same way as cisplatin. Cisplatin and transplatin are optical isomers, and only one of them rotates plane-polarised light. Transplatin cannot undergo ligand exchange with water molecules.
items.ms: Both isomers are square planar. In cisplatin the two Cl⁻ ligands are adjacent (90°), so after ligand exchange the platinum binds to two neighbouring bases on the same DNA strand; in transplatin they are at 180° and cannot do this, so the trans isomer is not effective. A: transplatin is square planar; C: they are geometric (cis/trans), not optical, isomers; D: transplatin also exchanges Cl⁻ for H₂O.
items.why: Cisplatin appears in most recent sessions (Jan2026, Jun2025, Jan2024); the spec's 'single isomer' clause was asked only in Jan2024 Q17(b)(iii) as a written part.

items.question: Which row is correct for cisplatin, [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]? two Cl–Pt–N bond angles of 90°; Cl–Pt–Cl bond angle 90° two Cl–Pt–N bond angles of 90°; Cl–Pt–Cl bond angle 180° four Cl–Pt–N bond angles of 90°; Cl–Pt–Cl bond angle 90° four Cl–Pt–N bond angles of 90°; Cl–Pt–Cl bond angle 180°
items.ms: Cisplatin is square planar with the two Cl⁻ ligands next to each other: Cl–Pt–Cl = 90°. Each Cl is at 90° to one N and at 180° to the other, so there are two 90° Cl–Pt–N angles. D describes transplatin; B and C are impossible combinations for a square planar Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂.
items.why: Jan2026 asked two MCQs on the structure of Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂; reasoning about the bond angles of the cis isomer in detail is a harder angle not yet asked.

items.question: How many molecules of 1,2-diaminoethane, H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂, are needed to replace all six water ligands in [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺? 1 2 3 6
items.ms: Each 1,2-diaminoethane is bidentate (one lone pair on each nitrogen atom), so 3 molecules form the 6 dative bonds. D treats it as monodentate; B as tridentate; A as hexadentate.

items.question: Chromium(III) ions form a complex ion with EDTA⁴⁻ ions in which the coordination number of chromium is 6. What is the formula of this complex ion? [Cr(EDTA)]⁺ [Cr(EDTA)₂]⁵⁻ [Cr(EDTA)₃]⁹⁻ [Cr(EDTA)]⁻
items.ms: EDTA⁴⁻ is hexadentate, so one EDTA⁴⁻ provides all six dative bonds: charge = +3 − 4 = −1. A has the sign of the charge wrong; B treats EDTA⁴⁻ as tridentate (two ligands); C treats it as bidentate (three ligands).

items.question: EDTA⁴⁻ is a hexadentate ligand. Its structure is shown. State what is meant by the term hexadentate. Identify the six atoms in EDTA⁴⁻ that form dative bonds to a metal ion. Aqueous cobalt(II) ions, [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺, react with EDTA⁴⁻ ions to form a complex ion in which all the water ligands have been replaced. Write the ionic equation for this reaction. Include state symbols. State the coordination number of cobalt and the shape of the complex ion formed. A student used this reaction to find the value of x in hydrated cobalt(II) nitrate, Co(NO₃)₂·xH₂O. • 2.62 g of the crystals were dissolved in water and the solution was made up to 250.0 cm³. • 25.0 cm³ portions of this solution were titrated with 0.0450 mol dm⁻³ EDTA⁴⁻ solution, using an indicator. The results are shown. Calculate the mean titre, using only concordant titres. Calculate the value of x. Show your working. Each burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mean titre. The crystals had been stored in a warm room and had lost some of their water of crystallisation before they were weighed. State and explain the effect on the value of x calculated. The indicator forms a yellow complex with cobalt(II) ions. The free indicator is violet. At the end point the colour changes from yellow to violet. Explain this colour change. Lead poisoning is treated by injecting a solution of the calcium complex Na₂[Ca(EDTA)]. Lead(II) ions in the body replace the calcium ions in the complex, and the lead complex is excreted in urine. Suggest why lead(II) ions replace the calcium ions in the complex. Suggest why the solution injected contains Na₂[Ca(EDTA)] and not Na₄EDTA.
items.ms: (A ligand that) forms six dative (covalent) bonds to one metal ion / donates six lone pairs from six different atoms The two nitrogen atoms and four (negatively charged) oxygen atoms, one from each –COO⁻ group [Co(EDTA)]²⁻ as the product, with the correct charge [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺(aq) + EDTA⁴⁻(aq) → [Co(EDTA)]²⁻(aq) + 6H₂O(l): balanced with 6H₂O, with state symbols 6 and octahedral (20.05 + 19.95 + 20.00) ÷ 3 = 20.00 cm³ n(EDTA⁴⁻) = 0.0450 × 20.00 ÷ 1000 = 9.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol n(Co²⁺) in 250.0 cm³ = 9.00 × 10⁻⁴ × 10 = 9.00 × 10⁻³ mol (1 : 1 ratio) M(Co(NO₃)₂·xH₂O) = 2.62 ÷ 9.00 × 10⁻³ = 291 g mol⁻¹ mass of water per mole = 291 − 182.9 = 108 g x = 108 ÷ 18.0 = 6 (2 × 0.05) ÷ 20.00 × 100 = 0.50% x would be lower (than the true value) because each gram of the sample contains more cobalt, so the titre is larger and the calculated molar mass is smaller EDTA⁴⁻ forms a more stable complex with cobalt(II) than the indicator does, so it replaces the indicator (ligand exchange) as it is added At the end point all the cobalt(II) ions are bonded to EDTA⁴⁻, so the indicator is free and its violet colour is seen EDTA⁴⁻ forms a more stable complex with Pb²⁺ than with Ca²⁺ (larger equilibrium constant) Free EDTA⁴⁻ would also bind / remove calcium ions from the blood / body lowering the concentration of calcium ions in the blood, which is harmful / with calcium already bound, only metal ions that form more stable complexes (such as Pb²⁺) are removed
items.why: C17.16 is hot (15 of 17 sessions) and EDTA⁴⁻ chelation appeared in Jan2025 Q20(c) (chromium poisoning); an EDTA titration to find water of crystallisation and the Ca–EDTA treatment for lead poisoning are new synoptic angles for Section C.

items.name: Haemoglobin, ligand exchange with CO
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry

items.question: Haemoglobin, Hb, is an iron(II) complex containing a polydentate ligand. In the lungs, an oxygen molecule bonds to each iron(II) ion. Carbon monoxide can take the place of the oxygen: HbO₂ + CO ⇌ HbCO + O₂ K ≈ 2 × 10² at body temperature Explain, in terms of ligand exchange and the value of K, why breathing air that contains only 0.1% carbon monoxide can be fatal.
items.ms: Carbon monoxide replaces the oxygen molecule as a ligand on the iron(II) ion (ligand exchange) CO bonds more strongly to Fe²⁺ / forms a more stable complex (K is large, so the equilibrium lies to the right even when [CO] is low), so less oxygen is carried to the cells
items.why: CO poisoning was asked in Oct2023 (2 marks) and as MCQs in Oct2021, Oct2022 and Oct2025; using the size of K to explain why a low level of CO is dangerous has not been asked.

items.question: Ammonium vanadate(V), NH₄VO₃, dissolves in dilute sulfuric acid to form a solution containing VO₂⁺ ions. When excess zinc powder is added, the vanadium is reduced in stages to the +2 oxidation state. Complete the table by giving the colour of each vanadium species in aqueous solution. A few minutes after the zinc is added the solution looks green, although no vanadium(III) ions have formed yet. Suggest why the solution looks green.
items.ms: Any two colours correct All four correct: VO₂⁺ yellow; VO²⁺ blue; V³⁺ green; V²⁺ violet It contains a mixture of yellow VO₂⁺ and blue VO²⁺ ions
items.why: Vanadium colours were MCQs in Jun2025, Jan2025 and May2024; the green mixture of yellow VO₂⁺ and blue VO²⁺, which the Oct2020 report shows candidates confuse with V³⁺, has never been asked.

items.question: Some standard electrode potentials are shown. VO₂⁺(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ VO²⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) E° = +1.00 V VO²⁺(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ V³⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) E° = +0.34 V V³⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ V²⁺(aq) E° = −0.26 V I₂(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2I⁻(aq) E° = +0.54 V Fe³⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Fe²⁺(aq) E° = +0.77 V Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Ag(s) E° = +0.80 V Which reaction is thermodynamically feasible under standard conditions? VO²⁺ + Fe²⁺ + 2H⁺ → V³⁺ + Fe³⁺ + H₂O VO²⁺ + Ag⁺ + H₂O → VO₂⁺ + Ag + 2H⁺ 2VO₂⁺ + 2I⁻ + 4H⁺ → 2VO²⁺ + I₂ + 2H₂O 2V³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2V²⁺ + I₂
items.ms: E°cell = E°(couple reduced) − E°(couple oxidised). C: +1.00 − (+0.54) = +0.46 V, positive, so feasible. A: +0.34 − (+0.77) = −0.43 V; B: +0.80 − (+1.00) = −0.20 V (Ag⁺ cannot oxidise VO²⁺); D: −0.26 − (+0.54) = −0.80 V. All three are negative, so not feasible.
items.why: C17.19 has come up in 7 of 17 sessions, always as choosing reductants or oxidants from E° values (Oct2022, Jan2023, Oct2025); a straight feasibility check across four vanadium reactions has not been set as an MCQ.

items.question: Use these standard electrode potentials. Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Zn(s) E° = −0.76 V V³⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ V²⁺(aq) E° = −0.26 V Sn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Sn(s) E° = −0.14 V VO²⁺(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ V³⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) E° = +0.34 V Fe³⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Fe²⁺(aq) E° = +0.77 V VO₂⁺(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ VO²⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) E° = +1.00 V MnO₄⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) + 5e⁻ ⇌ Mn²⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l) E° = +1.51 V A violet solution of V²⁺ ions in dilute acid is mixed with an excess of a solution containing one of these ions. Which ion oxidises V²⁺ to V³⁺ but no further? Zn²⁺ Sn²⁺ Fe³⁺ MnO₄⁻
items.ms: Sn²⁺: V²⁺ → V³⁺ has E°cell = −0.14 − (−0.26) = +0.12 V (feasible) but V³⁺ → VO²⁺ has −0.14 − (+0.34) = −0.48 V (not feasible), so oxidation stops at V³⁺. A: −0.76 − (−0.26) = −0.50 V, no reaction. C: Fe³⁺ also oxidises V³⁺ to VO²⁺ (+0.43 V) so it goes on to vanadium(IV) (stopping there, −0.23 V). D: MnO₄⁻ oxidises all the way to VO₂⁺ (+1.51 − 1.00 = +0.51 V).
items.why: Oxidation of V²⁺ and V³⁺ by chosen oxidants was asked only in Oct2020 (structured); every recent item has been about reducing vanadium(V), so an oxidant that stops at V³⁺ is a likely surprise.

items.question: Zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid reduce orange dichromate(VI) ions to a blue solution of chromium(II) ions. When the blue solution is exposed to air it turns green. Cr³⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Cr²⁺(aq) E° = −0.41 V O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻ ⇌ 2H₂O(l) E° = +1.23 V Which row gives E°cell for the reaction that turns the solution green, and the change in the oxidation number of chromium? E°cell = +0.82 V; chromium +2 → +3 E°cell = +1.64 V; chromium +2 → +3 E°cell = +1.64 V; chromium +2 → +6 E°cell = +1.64 V; chromium +3 → +2
items.ms: Oxygen oxidises Cr²⁺ to green Cr³⁺ (+2 → +3): 4Cr²⁺ + O₂ + 4H⁺ → 4Cr³⁺ + 2H₂O, E°cell = +1.23 − (−0.41) = +1.64 V. A subtracts 0.41 instead of −0.41; C would give orange Cr₂O₇²⁻, not a green solution; D has chromium being reduced, but O₂ is an oxidising agent.
items.why: C17.20 has come up in 8 of 17 sessions (last Jan2026), always about reducing dichromate(VI); why Cr²⁺ must be kept from air, judged by E°cell, has not been asked.

items.question: Which sequence of reagents converts chromium(III) ions, Cr³⁺(aq), into dichromate(VI) ions, Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq)? excess NaOH(aq), then H₂O₂(aq) and warm, then dilute H₂SO₄(aq) dilute H₂SO₄(aq), then H₂O₂(aq) and warm, then excess NaOH(aq) excess NaOH(aq), then zinc powder, then dilute H₂SO₄(aq) excess concentrated NH₃(aq), then dilute H₂SO₄(aq)
items.ms: Excess alkali gives [Cr(OH)₆]³⁻, which H₂O₂ oxidises in alkaline solution to yellow CrO₄²⁻ (E°cell = +0.88 − (−0.13) = +1.01 V); acidifying then shifts 2CrO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H₂O to the right, giving orange dichromate(VI). B ends in alkali, so the final product is chromate(VI), not dichromate(VI); C uses zinc, a reducing agent; D has no oxidising agent (ammonia only forms [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺ by ligand exchange, chromium stays +3).
items.why: Spec 17.20(ii) (alkaline H₂O₂, then acidify) was tested only by the Jun2023 MCQ equation and Jan2025 Q20(a)(i), where many omitted H₂O₂; the order of reagents is the likeliest MCQ angle.

items.question: Potassium dichromate(VI) solution is orange. It contains this equilibrium. Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ 2CrO₄²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) When aqueous barium nitrate is added to the orange solution, a yellow precipitate of barium chromate(VI), BaCrO₄, forms and the pH of the mixture decreases. Explain, with reference to the equilibrium, why the pH of the mixture decreases.
items.ms: Barium ions remove chromate(VI) ions from the solution as the insoluble BaCrO₄ / [CrO₄²⁻] decreases so the position of equilibrium shifts to the right (to replace chromate(VI) ions), producing more H⁺ ions, so [H⁺] increases
items.why: C17.21 has come up in 5 of 17 sessions (Oct2025 asked the effect of alkali, Jan2021 the reverse equation); removing chromate(VI) by precipitation is an unasked way to test the same equilibrium.

items.question: Which hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess aqueous ammonia but not in excess aqueous sodium hydroxide? chromium(III) hydroxide iron(III) hydroxide copper(II) hydroxide zinc hydroxide
items.ms: Copper(II) hydroxide dissolves in excess ammonia by ligand exchange to give deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺, but it is not amphoteric, so it does not dissolve in excess NaOH. A and D are amphoteric and also form ammine complexes, so they dissolve in both reagents; B dissolves in neither.
items.why: Hydroxide solubility in excess reagents recurs (Jan2023 Q4 asked which dissolves in both); the reverse case, ammonia only, has not been asked.

path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry

items.question: Aqueous ammonia is added drop by drop, until in excess, to aqueous iron(III) chloride. Which observations are made? a red-brown precipitate forms, which dissolves in excess ammonia to give a deep red solution a green precipitate forms, which slowly turns brown at its surface a red-brown precipitate forms, which slowly turns green at its surface a red-brown precipitate forms, which does not dissolve in excess ammonia
items.ms: Ammonia acts only as a base here: [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ + 3NH₃ → [Fe(OH)₃(H₂O)₃] + 3NH₄⁺, giving red-brown iron(III) hydroxide, which does not form an ammine complex and is not amphoteric. A assumes ligand exchange; B describes iron(II); C reverses the air oxidation of iron(II) hydroxide.
items.why: C17.22 has come up in 15 of 17 sessions; the Oct2020 and Jun2024 examiner reports describe candidates giving ligand exchange for Fe³⁺ with ammonia instead of precipitation.

items.question: A technician finds four unlabelled bottles, W, X, Y and Z. Each contains an aqueous solution of one of these compounds. chromium(III) sulfate manganese(II) sulfate iron(II) sulfate cobalt(II) sulfate nickel(II) sulfate zinc sulfate The table shows the results of tests on each solution. Identify the metal ion in each of the solutions W, X, Y and Z. Write the ionic equation for the formation of the off-white precipitate when a few drops of NaOH(aq) are added to solution W. Include state symbols. The precipitate from W darkens to brown, starting at its surface. Suggest why. Write an equation, starting from the hexaaqua ion, for the reaction that forms the blue solution when excess aqueous ammonia is added to X. State the type of reaction. Explain why solution Z is colourless. A student tests aqueous iron(II) sulfate and aqueous iron(III) chloride with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Compare and contrast the observations when aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to each solution, first a few drops and then in excess, and the mixtures are then left to stand in air. Include equations in your answer.
items.ms: W: Mn²⁺ / manganese(II) X: Ni²⁺ / nickel(II) Y: Co²⁺ / cobalt(II) Z: Zn²⁺ / zinc Correct formulae: [Mn(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → [Mn(OH)₂(H₂O)₄] + 2H₂O Balanced, with state symbols (aq) + (aq) → (s) + (l) Manganese(II) is oxidised (to a higher oxidation state, e.g. +3 or +4, which is brown) by oxygen in the air, which is in contact with the surface of the precipitate first [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 6NH₃ → [Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺ + 6H₂O Ligand exchange / ligand substitution Zn²⁺ has a full 3d subshell (3d¹⁰), so no electrons can be promoted between the split d orbitals / no d–d transitions, so no visible light is absorbed IC1 Iron(II) sulfate is a pale green solution and gives a green precipitate IC2 Iron(III) chloride is a yellow / orange / yellow-brown solution and gives a red-brown / orange-brown precipitate IC3 [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → [Fe(OH)₂(H₂O)₄] + 2H₂O IC4 [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → [Fe(OH)₃(H₂O)₃] + 3H₂O IC5 Both are deprotonation (acid–base) reactions, and neither precipitate dissolves in excess NaOH (neither hydroxide is amphoteric) IC6 On standing in air the green precipitate turns (orange-)brown, starting at the surface, as iron(II) is oxidised to iron(III) by oxygen; the iron(III) precipitate does not change
items.why: C17.22 has come up in 15 of 17 sessions; the 6-mark answers have covered cobalt (Jan2022), nickel (Jun2022) and copper (Jun2025), so iron(II) against iron(III) is the likeliest next, and manganese(II) has not been examined.

items.question: In which reaction does a metal hydroxide act as a Brønsted–Lowry acid? [Zn(OH)₂(H₂O)₄](s) + 2OH⁻(aq) → [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻(aq) + 4H₂O(l) [Zn(OH)₂(H₂O)₄](s) + 2H⁺(aq) → [Zn(H₂O)₆]²⁺(aq) [Cu(OH)₂(H₂O)₄](s) + 2H⁺(aq) → [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺(aq) [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → [Fe(OH)₃(H₂O)₃](s) + 3H₂O(l)
items.ms: In A the zinc hydroxide donates protons (from its water ligands) to hydroxide ions, so it is acting as an acid; with B this shows zinc hydroxide is amphoteric. In B and C the hydroxide accepts protons (acts as a base). In D the proton donor is the hexaaqua ion, not a metal hydroxide.
items.why: Amphoteric MCQs recur (Oct2024 Cr(OH)₃, Jan2026 Zn(OH)₂), and asking which equation shows the hydroxide acting as an acid tests the meaning rather than the label.

items.question: A few drops of aqueous ammonia are added to pink aqueous cobalt(II) chloride, and a blue precipitate forms. Which row gives the type of reaction and the cobalt-containing product? ligand exchange; [Co(NH₃)₆]²⁺ ligand exchange; [Co(OH)₂(H₂O)₄] deprotonation; [Co(NH₃)₆]²⁺ deprotonation; [Co(OH)₂(H₂O)₄]

[Co(NH₃)₆]²⁺ (A, C) is the straw-coloured complex formed by ligand exchange in excess ammonia; B pairs the precipitate with the wrong reaction type.

items.question: Chromium(III) sulfate dissolves in water to form a green solution containing [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ ions. The scheme shows some reactions of these ions. A solution of chromium(III) sulfate has a pH of about 3. Write an equation to show why the solution is acidic. A solution with the same concentration of [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ ions is much less acidic. Explain why [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is more acidic than [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺. Write the ionic equation for the formation of precipitate A from [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ ions. State the type of reaction in (c). Precipitate A is amphoteric. Write an equation for the reaction of A with excess OH⁻ ions to form B, and an equation for the reaction of A with H⁺ ions. Use your equations to explain what is meant by amphoteric. Give the formula of the complex ion in C. Write an equation for its formation from [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ and state the type of reaction. A solution contains both Fe³⁺(aq) and Cr³⁺(aq) ions. Suggest how aqueous sodium hydroxide could be used to obtain a solution that contains chromium but no iron. Explain your answer.
items.ms: [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ + H₂O ⇌ [Cr(H₂O)₅(OH)]²⁺ + H₃O⁺ Cr³⁺ has a greater charge (and is smaller), so it has a higher charge density so it polarises / withdraws electron density from the O–H bonds of the water ligands more, weakening them so that H⁺ ions are released more readily Formula of A: [Cr(OH)₃(H₂O)₃] [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → [Cr(OH)₃(H₂O)₃] + 3H₂O (balanced) Deprotonation / acid–base [Cr(OH)₃(H₂O)₃] + 3OH⁻ → [Cr(OH)₆]³⁻ + 3H₂O [Cr(OH)₃(H₂O)₃] + 3H⁺ → [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ A reacts with both acids and bases (alkalis): it accepts H⁺ ions in the second reaction and donates H⁺ ions to OH⁻ ions in the first [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺ [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ + 6NH₃ → [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺ + 6H₂O Ligand exchange / ligand substitution Add excess NaOH(aq), then filter and keep the filtrate Iron(III) hydroxide is not amphoteric, so it stays as a red-brown precipitate, while chromium(III) hydroxide dissolves as [Cr(OH)₆]³⁻, which passes through the filter paper
items.why: C17.23 has come up in 14 of 17 sessions, mostly for zinc and as MCQs; chromium(III) amphoteric equations and the acidity of a 3+ hexaaqua ion have only been asked in parts (Oct2024 MCQ, Jun2025 Q16(b)), so a full chromium scheme is likely.

items.question: Concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Which row describes the type of reaction and the colour change? ligand exchange; blue to yellow-green ligand exchange; blue to deep blue redox; blue to yellow-green deprotonation; blue solution to pale blue precipitate
items.ms: Chloride ions replace the water ligands: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ → [CuCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O. [CuCl₄]²⁻ is yellow, so the solution looks yellow-green. items.question: A little aqueous ammonia is added to aqueous copper(II) sulfate and a pale blue precipitate forms. Excess aqueous ammonia is then added. Which equation represents the reaction of the precipitate with the excess ammonia? [Cu(OH)₂(H₂O)₄] + 2NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₂(H₂O)₄]²⁺ + 2OH⁻ [Cu(OH)₂(H₂O)₄] + 6NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₆]²⁺ + 2OH⁻ + 4H₂O [Cu(OH)₂(H₂O)₄] + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + 2OH⁻ + 2H₂O [Cu(OH)₂(H₂O)₄] + 4NH₄⁺ → [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + 2H⁺ + 4H₂O
items.ms: The deep blue complex is [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺: four ammonia ligands replace the two hydroxide and two water ligands. All four equations balance, but A has only two ammine ligands, B gives [Cu(NH₃)₆]²⁺ (a common error), and D uses ammonium ions, which have no lone pair and cannot act as ligands.
items.why: Spec 17.24(i) names the route via Cu(OH)₂(H₂O)₄; May2023 Q12 asked the overall equation from Cu²⁺, and the Jan2021 examiner report notes [Cu(NH₃)₆]²⁺ as a frequent wrong answer.

items.question: In these equations, en represents the bidentate ligand H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂. Which reaction has the most negative entropy change of the system, ΔSsystem? [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ → [CoCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O [Cu(en)₂(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + 2en [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ + EDTA⁴⁻ → [Fe(EDTA)]⁻ + 6H₂O [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 6NH₃ → [Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺ + 6H₂O
items.ms: Count the particles in solution. B: 5 → 3, a decrease, so ΔSsystem is negative (bidentate ligands replaced by monodentate ones, the reverse of the chelate effect). A: 5 → 7 and C: 2 → 7, both increases; D: 7 → 7, so ΔSsystem is close to zero.
items.why: C17.25 has come up in 10 of 17 sessions, always for a chelate replacing monodentate ligands (Oct2021 asked the most positive ΔS); the reverse direction has not been asked.

items.question: The ethanedioate ion, C₂O₄²⁻, is a bidentate ligand. It reacts with hexaaquairon(III) ions. [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ + 3C₂O₄²⁻ → X + 6H₂O Which row gives the increase in the number of particles in solution and the charge on the complex ion X? increase of 3; X is 3+ increase of 3; X is 6− increase of 6; X is 3− increase of 3; X is 3−
items.ms: Particles: 1 + 3 = 4 on the left, 1 + 6 = 7 on the right, an increase of 3, so ΔSsystem is positive. Charge: +3 + 3 × (−2) = −3, so X is [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻. A ignores the charges of the ligands; B ignores the charge of Fe³⁺; C counts only the water molecules released.
items.why: Particle counting with polyatomic anion ligands was the hardest step in Jun2022 Q15(d) and Oct2023 Q19(e); a tris(ethanedioato) complex also needs the charge on the complex.

items.question: Cobalt(II) ions catalyse the oxidation of tartrate ions by hydrogen peroxide. A little pink cobalt(II) chloride solution is added to a solution of potassium sodium tartrate and hydrogen peroxide at 70 °C. The mixture turns green and effervesces vigorously. When the effervescence stops, the mixture turns pink again. Some standard electrode potentials are given in the table. The reaction profile for the uncatalysed reaction is shown. Draw, on the same axes, the reaction profile for the reaction catalysed by cobalt(II) ions. Calculate E°cell for the oxidation of Co²⁺(aq) ions by hydrogen peroxide. Use your answer to suggest why cobalt(II) is still oxidised in this experiment. Iron is the catalyst in the Haber process. N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) Compare and contrast the way solid iron acts as a catalyst in the Haber process with the way cobalt(II) ions act as a catalyst in the tartrate reaction. Refer to the observations in the tartrate reaction. Suggest why zinc chloride does not catalyse the tartrate reaction. The iron catalyst in the Haber process is used in a finely divided, porous form. Explain why.
items.ms: Two humps (two steps), each with a maximum lower than the uncatalysed maximum A minimum between the two humps (the intermediate, cobalt(III)), with the curve starting at the reactant level and finishing at the product level E°cell = +1.77 − (+1.81) = −0.04 V, so the oxidation of Co²⁺(aq) is not feasible under standard conditions The conditions are not standard: cobalt is bonded to tartrate ligands rather than water, which changes the electrode potential / the temperature is 70 °C / concentrations are not 1 mol dm⁻³ IC1 Both provide an alternative route (mechanism) with a lower activation energy, and both are regenerated / unchanged at the end IC2 Iron is a heterogeneous catalyst: a solid, in a different phase from the gaseous reactants; Co²⁺(aq) is homogeneous: in the same (aqueous) phase as the reactants IC3 N₂ and H₂ molecules are adsorbed onto the surface of the iron, their bonds are weakened, they react, and the ammonia desorbs IC4 Co²⁺ is oxidised (by H₂O₂) to cobalt(III), the green intermediate IC5 Cobalt(III) is reduced back to Co²⁺ (by the tartrate), so the pink colour returns when the reaction is over IC6 Cobalt can act in this way because it has variable oxidation states (+2 and +3), whereas the iron works by providing a surface (its oxidation state does not change) Zinc has only one oxidation state (+2) in its compounds, so Zn²⁺ cannot be oxidised (or reduced) to form an intermediate and then be regenerated The reaction occurs on the surface of the catalyst and this form has a larger surface area, so more molecules can be adsorbed at once / more active sites
items.why: C17.26 is a cool point (4 of 17), but heterogeneous against homogeneous catalysis is a recurring 6-mark topic (Oct2020, Jan2021, Jan2026); the cobalt–tartrate reaction has appeared only as a Jun2025 MCQ, and the negative E°cell and a two-step profile have not been asked.

C17.27 - that a heterogeneous catalyst is in a differe
items.question: Solid iron catalyses the reaction between nitrogen and hydrogen gases in the Haber process. Which statement about this catalyst is correct? The iron is in the same phase as the reactants. Nitrogen and hydrogen molecules are absorbed into the iron, where they react. Nitrogen and hydrogen molecules are adsorbed onto the surface of the iron, where they react. The iron increases the equilibrium yield of ammonia.
items.ms: A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants (solid with gases) and the reaction occurs at its surface after adsorption. A is the definition of a homogeneous catalyst; B confuses absorption (into the bulk) with adsorption (onto the surface); D: a catalyst speeds up both directions equally and does not change the equilibrium yield.
items.why: C17.27 has come up in 9 of 17 sessions; 'absorbed' for 'adsorbed' is penalised in the Jan2025 and Oct2025 mark schemes.

items.question: Vanadium(V) oxide, V₂O₅, catalyses the oxidation of sulfur dioxide in the Contact process. 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) Which row describes the type of catalyst and the oxidation number of vanadium immediately after V₂O₅ has reacted with sulfur dioxide? heterogeneous; +4 heterogeneous; +6 homogeneous; +4 homogeneous; +6
items.ms: V₂O₅ is a solid and the reactants are gases, so it is heterogeneous. SO₂ reduces it: V₂O₅ + SO₂ → V₂O₄ + SO₃ (vanadium +5 → +4); then V₂O₄ + ½O₂ → V₂O₅ regenerates it. B: +6 would mean SO₂ had oxidised the vanadium, but SO₂ is the reducing agent; C and D: changing oxidation number does not make a catalyst homogeneous.
items.why: C17.28 has come up in 8 of 17 sessions, usually as oxidation-number MCQs; the Jan2021 examiner report notes V₂O₅ wrongly called homogeneous, so pairing the type with the oxidation number is likely.

items.question: A catalytic converter in a car exhaust contains a thin layer of rhodium on a ceramic support. Carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide from the engine react on the surface of the rhodium. Write the equation for the reaction between carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide in the catalytic converter. State symbols are not required. Explain why the rhodium would stop working as a catalyst if the product molecules were held strongly on its surface.
items.ms: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂ The products would not desorb, so the (active) sites on the surface stay occupied and no more CO / NO molecules can be adsorbed
items.why: C17.29 has come up in 6 of 17 sessions (last Jan2026); the Jan2021 examiner report says the desorption of products is the step most often left out.

C17.30 - that a homogeneous catalyst
items.question: Which statement about a homogeneous catalyst is correct? It is in a different phase from the reactants, and the reaction occurs on its surface. It lowers the activation energy of the single step of the uncatalysed reaction. It is permanently changed to a different oxidation state during the reaction. It is in the same phase as the reactants, and the reaction proceeds via an intermediate species.
items.ms: D is the definition in the specification: same phase, and the catalysed route goes through an intermediate (for example Fe³⁺ when Fe²⁺ catalyses the S₂O₈²⁻/I⁻ reaction). A describes a heterogeneous catalyst; B: the catalyst provides a different route with more steps, it does not lower the barrier of the original step; C: a catalyst is regenerated, so any change in oxidation state is reversed.
items.why: C17.30 has come up in 11 of 17 sessions; the spec wording (same phase, intermediate species) has not been tested directly as a statement MCQ.

items.question: Copper(II) ions catalyse the reaction between iron(III) ions and thiosulfate ions. 2Fe³⁺(aq) + 2S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → 2Fe²⁺(aq) + S₄O₆²⁻(aq) The catalysed reaction takes place in two steps. Step 1 2Cu²⁺(aq) + 2S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → 2Cu⁺(aq) + S₄O₆²⁻(aq) Step 2 2Cu⁺(aq) + 2Fe³⁺(aq) → 2Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Fe²⁺(aq) Which species is the intermediate? Cu²⁺ Cu⁺ Fe²⁺ S₄O₆²⁻
items.ms: Cu⁺ is formed in step 1 and used up in step 2, so it is the intermediate. Cu²⁺ (A) is used in step 1 and regenerated in step 2, so it is the catalyst; Fe²⁺ (C) and S₄O₆²⁻ (D) are products of the overall reaction.
items.why: Identifying the roles of species in a multi-step catalytic mechanism recurs (Oct2022 Q9, Jan2026 Q23(c)); a copper(II)/copper(I) cycle is an unseen context.

C17.31 - the role of Fe2+ ions in cat
items.question: Iron(II) ions catalyse the reaction between peroxodisulfate ions and iodide ions. S₂O₈²⁻(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2SO₄²⁻(aq) + I₂(aq) S₂O₈²⁻(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2SO₄²⁻(aq) E° = +2.01 V Co³⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Co²⁺(aq) E° = +1.81 V I₂(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2I⁻(aq) E° = +0.54 V Sn⁴⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Sn²⁺(aq) E° = +0.15 V Cr³⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Cr²⁺(aq) E° = −0.41 V Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Zn(s) E° = −0.76 V Use these standard electrode potentials to decide which ion could also catalyse this reaction. Co²⁺ Cr²⁺ Sn²⁺ Zn²⁺
items.ms: The catalyst must be oxidised by S₂O₈²⁻ and its oxidised form must then oxidise I⁻, so its E° must lie between +0.54 and +2.01 V. Co²⁺: +2.01 − 1.81 = +0.20 V, then Co³⁺ with I⁻: +1.81 − 0.54 = +1.27 V; both feasible. B and C are oxidised by S₂O₈²⁻, but Cr³⁺ and Sn⁴⁺ cannot then oxidise I⁻ (−0.41 − 0.54 = −0.95 V; +0.15 − 0.54 = −0.39 V), so they are not regenerated. D: Zn²⁺ cannot be oxidised to a higher oxidation state.
items.why: Jun2022 asked which ion could catalyse using an E° table; a cobalt couple, away from the iron example, tests the same reasoning in a new context.

path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry

C17.31 - the role of Fe2+ ions in cat
items.question: When Fe²⁺ ions catalyse the reaction between S₂O₈²⁻ and I⁻ ions, the first step is S₂O₈²⁻(aq) + 2Fe²⁺(aq) → 2SO₄²⁻(aq) + 2Fe³⁺(aq) S₂O₈²⁻(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2SO₄²⁻(aq) E° = +2.01 V Fe³⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Fe²⁺(aq) E° = +0.77 V I₂(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2I⁻(aq) E° = +0.54 V What is E°cell for this step? −1.24 V +0.23 V +0.47 V +1.24 V
items.ms: E°cell = E°(S₂O₈²⁻/SO₄²⁻) − E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +2.01 − (+0.77) = +1.24 V. A subtracts the wrong way round; B is E°cell for the second step (Fe³⁺ oxidising I⁻); C wrongly doubles the Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ value because two Fe²⁺ ions react (E° values are not multiplied).
items.why: C17.31 has come up in 9 of 17 sessions (last Jan2026, whose mark scheme used E°cell = +1.24 V and +0.23 V for the two steps).

path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 17 Transition Metals and their Chemistry
C17.32 - the role of Mn2+ ions in aut
items.question: Acidified potassium manganate(VII) reacts with sodium ethanedioate solution at 40 °C. 2MnO₄⁻(aq) + 5C₂O₄²⁻(aq) + 16H⁺(aq) → 2Mn²⁺(aq) + 10CO₂(g) + 8H₂O(l) The reaction was followed with a colorimeter. The absorbance of the mixture is proportional to the concentration of manganate(VII) ions. The graph shows the results. Explain the shape of the graph. The experiment is repeated with some manganese(II) sulfate added at the start. All other conditions are the same. Sketch, on the graph, the curve you would expect.
items.ms: The rate is slow at the start because no Mn²⁺ (catalyst) is present at first / the uncatalysed reaction is between two negative ions, which repel, so it has a high activation energy The rate increases (the curve gets steeper) as Mn²⁺ ions are formed, because the product Mn²⁺ catalyses the reaction (autocatalysis) The rate then decreases and the absorbance levels off at zero as the concentration of MnO₄⁻ (and C₂O₄²⁻) falls, until all the manganate(VII) has reacted The greatest rate (steepest part) is at about 150–250 s, where enough Mn²⁺ has formed but much MnO₄⁻ remains Curve starting at the same absorbance (0.80) and falling steeply from the start, with no slow initial section, reaching zero sooner
items.why: Mn²⁺ autocatalysis has come up in 6 of 17 sessions (graph-based in Jan2023, Oct2024 and Jan2026); an absorbance–time curve, and a sketch for Mn²⁺ added at the start, have not been asked.

items.name: Core Practical 14: preparation of a transition metal complex
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 17 Transition Metals and their Chemistry
C17.33 - CORE PRACTICAL 14 The preparation of a transi
items.question: A student prepared crystals of tetraamminecopper(II) sulfate monohydrate, [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄·H₂O, using this method. Step 1 Dissolve 3.00 g of copper(II) sulfate-5-water, CuSO₄·5H₂O, in the minimum volume of distilled water in a small beaker. Step 2 In a fume cupboard, add concentrated aqueous ammonia drop by drop, with stirring, until the precipitate that forms at first has just dissolved, then add 2 cm³ more. Step 3 Slowly add 10 cm³ of ethanol and cool the beaker in an ice bath until crystals form. Step 4 Filter off the crystals under reduced pressure and wash them with a little ice-cold ethanol. Step 5 Dry the crystals between filter papers and weigh them. Mass of dry crystals = 2.47 g Describe what the student would see in Step 2. Explain the observations in Step 2 in terms of how the ammonia reacts in each stage. Give a reason why Step 2 is carried out in a fume cupboard. Explain why ethanol is added in Step 3. Explain why the crystals are washed with ice-cold ethanol, rather than with water, in Step 4. Calculate the percentage yield of [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄·H₂O. Use relative atomic masses from the Data Booklet and give your answer to three significant figures. The student checked the ammonia content of the crystals. • 0.300 g of the crystals was warmed with an excess of aqueous sodium hydroxide. All of the ammonia given off was absorbed in 50.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid, which is an excess. NH₃(g) + HCl(aq) → NH₄Cl(aq) • The resulting solution was made up to 100.0 cm³ with distilled water in a volumetric flask. • 25.0 cm³ portions of this solution were titrated with 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide solution, using a suitable indicator. Give a reason why the solution was made up to 100.0 cm³ and 25.0 cm³ portions titrated, rather than titrating all of the solution. Calculate the percentage by mass of ammonia in the crystals. Use only the concordant titres. Deduce whether your answer is consistent with the formula [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄·H₂O. Suggest one reason why the percentage of ammonia found is slightly lower than expected.
items.ms: (Pale) blue precipitate forms (at first) The precipitate dissolves to give a deep blue / dark blue solution At first ammonia acts as a base, removing H⁺ ions from water ligands of [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (deprotonation) forming neutral, insoluble copper(II) hydroxide, [Cu(OH)₂(H₂O)₄] In excess, ammonia acts as a ligand: the lone pair on nitrogen forms dative bonds to Cu²⁺, replacing water / hydroxide ligands (ligand exchange) to give soluble [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ Concentrated ammonia gives off ammonia gas, which is toxic / corrosive / irritates the eyes and lungs The complex is less soluble in ethanol (than in water), so adding ethanol makes it crystallise out (increasing the yield) Washing removes soluble impurities (e.g. excess ammonia or ammonium salts in the remaining solution) from the surface of the crystals The product is less soluble in ethanol, and less soluble when cold, so less of it dissolves and is lost than with water Ethanol evaporates quickly, so the crystals dry faster Mᵣ(CuSO₄·5H₂O) = 249.6 and n = 3.00 ÷ 249.6 = 0.01202 mol Mᵣ([Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄·H₂O) = 245.6; theoretical mass = 0.01202 × 245.6 = 2.952 g % yield = 2.47 ÷ 2.952 × 100 = 83.7% So that the titration can be repeated (several times) to obtain concordant titres Mean concordant titre = (25.75 + 25.65) ÷ 2 = 25.70 cm³ n(HCl) left in 25.0 cm³ = n(NaOH) = 0.0500 × 25.70 ÷ 1000 = 1.285 × 10⁻³ mol n(HCl) left in 100.0 cm³ = 4 × 1.285 × 10⁻³ = 5.14 × 10⁻³ mol n(NH₃) = n(HCl) reacted = 0.0100 − 0.00514 = 4.860 × 10⁻³ mol mass of NH₃ = 4.860 × 10⁻³ × 17.0 = 0.0826 g; % NH₃ = 0.0826 ÷ 0.300 × 100 = 27.5% Expected % NH₃ = 4 × 17.0 ÷ 245.6 × 100 = 27.7%, which is very close to 27.5%, so the result is consistent with four NH₃ per formula Some ammonia escaped / was not absorbed by the acid / not all the ammonia was driven off The crystals were still damp (with water or ethanol) / contained some unreacted copper(II) sulfate or other impurity
items.why: Core Practical 14 has never been examined in WCH15 (only formula and hydrate calculations on prepared salts, e.g. Jan2023, Jan2025), so the tetraamminecopper(II) sulfate preparation, with a yield and a check of the ammonia content by back titration, is the likeliest first appearance.

items.name: Oxidation and reduction; oxidation numbers (s, p, d block)
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 16 Redox Equilibria
C16.1 - the terms oxidation and redu
items.question: Sodium hydride, NaH, is an ionic compound that contains the hydride ion, H⁻. It reacts with water. NaH(s) + H₂O(l) → NaOH(aq) + H₂(g) Which statement about this reaction is correct? The hydride ion is oxidised and a hydrogen atom from the water molecule is reduced. The hydride ion is reduced and a hydrogen atom from the water molecule is oxidised. Sodium is oxidised from 0 to +1. It is not a redox reaction because the oxidation number of sodium does not change.
items.ms: A: hydrogen in H⁻ goes from −1 to 0 in H₂ (loses an electron, oxidised); one hydrogen of H₂O goes from +1 to 0 (gains an electron, reduced). B reverses the two changes. C: sodium is already +1 in NaH and stays +1 in NaOH. D: a reaction is redox if any element changes oxidation number, and hydrogen does.
items.why: Oxidation-number MCQs came up in 9 of 17 sessions (latest Jun 2025), always on p- or d-block species; the spec's s-block case (a metal hydride, H = −1) has never been used.

items.name: Oxidation and reduction; oxidation numbers (s, p, d block)
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 16 Redox Equilibria
C16.1 - the terms oxidation and redu
items.question: Which change is a reduction? CrO₄²⁻ → Cr₂O₇²⁻ SO₃²⁻ → SO₄²⁻ ClO⁻ → Cl⁻ MnO₄²⁻ → MnO₄⁻
items.ms: C: chlorine goes from +1 in ClO⁻ to −1 in Cl⁻, a decrease in oxidation number (gain of electrons), so it is a reduction. A: chromium is +6 in both ions, so this is not redox. B: sulfur goes from +4 to +6 (oxidation). D: manganese goes from +6 to +7 (oxidation).
items.why: Oct 2020 Q14–Q16 and Jun 2024 Q2 tested oxidation numbers across several species; this set mixes p- and d-block ions and includes the non-redox chromate–dichromate change (Jan 2025 Q20(a)(iv)).

path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry

items.question: Potassium ferrate(VI), K₂FeO₄, is a powerful oxidising agent used in water treatment. In acidic solution the ferrate(VI) ion decomposes. 4FeO₄²⁻(aq) + 20H⁺(aq) → 4Fe³⁺(aq) + 3O₂(g) + 10H₂O(l) Explain, in terms of oxidation numbers, why this is a redox reaction.
items.ms: Iron is reduced from +6 (in FeO₄²⁻) to +3 (in Fe³⁺) Oxygen is oxidised from −2 (in FeO₄²⁻) to 0 (in O₂)

items.question: The standard electrode potential of the Pb²⁺(aq)|Pb(s) half-cell is −0.13 V. Explain what is meant by this statement.
items.ms: The (maximum) potential difference / emf of a cell made by connecting the Pb²⁺|Pb half-cell to a standard hydrogen electrode measured under standard conditions: 1.00 mol dm⁻³ Pb²⁺ (and H⁺), hydrogen at 100 kPa and 298 K The negative sign shows that the lead electrode is the negative electrode / lead releases electrons more readily than hydrogen does

path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry

C16.3 - that the standard electrode
items.question: The electrolyte for a standard V³⁺|V²⁺ half-cell contains V³⁺ ions at a concentration of 1.00 mol dm⁻³. What mass of vanadium(III) sulfate, V₂(SO₄)₃, provides the V³⁺ ions in 200 cm³ of this electrolyte? [Mr of V₂(SO₄)₃ = 390.1] 26.0 g 39.0 g 78.0 g 195 g
items.ms: B: n(V³⁺) = 1.00 × 0.200 = 0.200 mol; each V₂(SO₄)₃ gives two V³⁺, so n(V₂(SO₄)₃) = 0.100 mol and mass = 0.100 × 390.1 = 39.0 g. A divides by 3 (the number of sulfate ions). C ignores the two V³⁺ per formula unit. D uses 1.00 dm³ instead of 200 cm³.
items.why: The mass of a salt for a standard half-cell is the most frequent C16.3 MCQ (Jan 2026, Jun 2025, Jan 2024, Oct 2021), always with two metal ions per formula unit.

path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 16 Redox Equilibria
C16.3 - that the standard electrode
items.question: The standard electrode potential of this half-cell is measured at 298 K. MnO₄⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) + 5e⁻ ⇌ Mn²⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l) Which concentrations are needed in the half-cell? [MnO₄⁻] = 1.00, [Mn²⁺] = 1.00 and [H⁺] = 8.00 mol dm⁻³ [MnO₄⁻] = 1.00 and [H⁺] = 1.00 mol dm⁻³, with no Mn²⁺ present [MnO₄⁻] = 1.00 and [Mn²⁺] = 1.00 mol dm⁻³, with no acid added [MnO₄⁻] = 1.00, [Mn²⁺] = 1.00 and [H⁺] = 1.00 mol dm⁻³
items.ms: D: standard conditions need every ion in the half-equation at 1.00 mol dm⁻³, including H⁺, whatever its coefficient. A uses the coefficient 8. B leaves out the reduced form, but both manganese species must be present for the equilibrium. C leaves out H⁺, which is in the half-equation, so its concentration affects the potential.
items.why: Standard conditions are tested in 13 of 17 sessions, but only through hydrogen pressure and metal-ion concentrations; that H⁺ in a half-equation must also be 1.00 mol dm⁻³ has never been asked.

items.question: A student set up a cell to measure the standard electrode potential of the Zn²⁺(aq)|Zn(s) half-cell. • Zinc half-cell: a zinc strip in 0.500 mol dm⁻³ zinc sulfate solution. • Hydrogen electrode: a platinum electrode in 2.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid, with hydrogen gas bubbled over it at the standard pressure. • The half-cells were joined by a salt bridge and a high-resistance voltmeter. The temperature of the laboratory was 20 °C. Give two changes the student must make so that the voltmeter reading is the standard electrode potential of the zinc half-cell.
items.ms: Use 1.00 mol dm⁻³ zinc sulfate / Zn²⁺(aq) (not 0.500 mol dm⁻³) Use 1.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid / H⁺(aq) (not 2.00 mol dm⁻³) Carry out the measurement at 298 K / 25 °C (not 20 °C)

items.name: Standard hydrogen electrode; why a reference is needed
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 16 Redox Equilibria
C16.4 - the features of the standard
items.question: A standard hydrogen electrode is connected in turn to a standard Zn²⁺(aq)|Zn(s) half-cell (E° = −0.76 V) and to a standard Cu²⁺(aq)|Cu(s) half-cell (E° = +0.34 V). In each cell a small current is allowed to flow. Which row describes the reaction at the platinum surface of the hydrogen electrode in each cell? with zinc: H⁺ ions are reduced to H₂; with copper: H₂ is oxidised to H⁺ ions with zinc: H₂ is oxidised to H⁺ ions; with copper: H⁺ ions are reduced to H₂ H⁺ ions are reduced to H₂ in both cells H₂ is oxidised to H⁺ ions in both cells
items.ms: A: Zn²⁺|Zn is more negative than the SHE, so zinc is oxidised and the hydrogen electrode is the positive electrode, where 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. Cu²⁺|Cu is more positive, so Cu²⁺ is reduced and the hydrogen electrode is the negative electrode, where H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻. B reverses both. C and D assume that the reference electrode always reacts in the same direction; its 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂ equilibrium can go either way.
items.why: C16.4 MCQs have asked only fixed features of the SHE (Oct 2022 pressure, Oct 2021 acid, Jan 2021 platinum black); how the SHE behaves against more and less positive half-cells has not been asked.

items.name: Standard hydrogen electrode; why a reference is needed
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 16 Redox Equilibria
C16.4 - the features of the standard
items.question: A standard hydrogen electrode is connected to a Cu²⁺(aq)|Cu(s) half-cell under standard conditions. The voltmeter reads 0.34 V. Which change to the hydrogen electrode would change the voltmeter reading? using a larger platinum electrode using a larger volume of the same acid bubbling the hydrogen gas faster, at the same pressure adding distilled water to the acid to dilute it tenfold
items.ms: D: [H⁺] falls to 0.100 mol dm⁻³, so the 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂ equilibrium shifts and the electrode is no longer standard. The size of the electrode (A), the volume of acid (B) and the flow rate of hydrogen at the same pressure (C) do not change any concentration, pressure or temperature, so the reading is unchanged.
items.why: SHE features were MCQs in Oct 2022, Oct 2021 and Jan 2021 (pressure, acid, platinum black); this asks which feature actually fixes its potential.

items.question: The diagram shows the apparatus used to measure the standard electrode potential of the Ni²⁺(aq)|Ni(s) half-cell. The voltmeter has a very high resistance. Identify A, B and C. Give the pressure or concentration where relevant. Explain why the potential of the Ni²⁺|Ni half-cell has to be measured against a reference electrode such as the standard hydrogen electrode. The voltmeter reading was 0.25 V and the nickel electrode was the negative electrode. State the standard electrode potential of the Ni²⁺|Ni half-cell. Explain why the voltmeter must have a very high resistance. In many laboratories the standard hydrogen electrode is replaced by a silver/silver chloride reference electrode. This is a silver wire coated with silver chloride, dipping into 1.00 mol dm⁻³ potassium chloride solution inside a glass tube with a porous plug at the bottom. AgCl(s) + e⁻ ⇌ Ag(s) + Cl⁻(aq) E = +0.22 V A Co²⁺(aq)|Co(s) half-cell was connected to the silver/silver chloride electrode. The emf was 0.50 V and the cobalt electrode was negative. Calculate the standard electrode potential of the Co²⁺|Co half-cell. Give two advantages of the silver/silver chloride electrode over the standard hydrogen electrode.
items.ms: A: hydrogen gas at 100 kPa B: platinum (coated with platinum black) C: 1.00 mol dm⁻³ H⁺(aq) / 1.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid The potential of a single electrode / half-cell cannot be measured on its own A voltmeter only measures the potential difference between two electrodes, so a second half-cell is needed Every half-cell is compared with the same reference, which is given the value 0.00 V, so the values can be compared / placed in order −0.25 V So that (almost) no current flows, so no reaction occurs at the electrodes / the concentrations do not change and the maximum potential difference (emf) is measured Ecell = Eright − Eleft / 0.50 = 0.22 − E(Co²⁺|Co) E(Co²⁺|Co) = −0.28 V It does not need a (continuous) supply of hydrogen gas at 100 kPa It does not need a separate salt bridge (the porous plug lets ions through) It has no platinum (black) surface that can be poisoned It is easier to keep at equilibrium / the hydrogen electrode is difficult to keep at equilibrium
items.why: The SHE is examined in 13 of 17 sessions; Jun 2023 Q21(d) compared it with a calomel reference, so another reference electrode and the never-asked 'why is a reference needed' are likely.

items.question: A cell is made from an I₂(aq)|I⁻(aq) half-cell and an Ag⁺(aq)|Ag(s) half-cell. Which electrodes are used? iodine in the I₂|I⁻ half-cell and silver in the Ag⁺|Ag half-cell platinum in both half-cells platinum in the I₂|I⁻ half-cell and silver in the Ag⁺|Ag half-cell silver in the I₂|I⁻ half-cell and platinum in the Ag⁺|Ag half-cell
items.ms: C: the I₂/I⁻ system has no solid that conducts, so an inert platinum electrode is used; a metal in contact with its own ions is its own electrode, so silver is used for Ag⁺|Ag. A: iodine does not conduct electricity. B: the Ag⁺/Ag equilibrium needs silver metal. D: the two electrodes are the wrong way round.
items.why: Choosing electrode materials is the most common C16.5 MCQ (Jan 2026, Jun 2025, Jan 2024, Oct 2022); a halogen/halide half-cell has not been used in it.

path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry

items.question: The standard electrode potential of the Na⁺(aq)|Na(s) half-cell is −2.71 V. This value cannot be measured directly by dipping a sodium electrode into 1.00 mol dm⁻³ Na⁺(aq). What is the reason? Sodium does not conduct electricity well enough to be used as an electrode. Sodium reacts with the water in the solution, so the equilibrium Na⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Na(s) cannot be set up. Sodium salts do not dissolve well enough to give 1.00 mol dm⁻³ Na⁺(aq). A voltmeter cannot measure a potential difference larger than 2 V.
items.ms: B: sodium reacts with water (2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂), so the electrode dissolves and no Na⁺/Na equilibrium is established; the value is found indirectly. A: sodium is a metal and a good conductor. C: sodium salts such as NaCl and NaNO₃ are very soluble. D: voltmeters easily measure several volts.
items.why: C16.5 is asked in 16 of 17 sessions, always with half-cells that can be built; why a reactive metal's value cannot be measured in water is a plausible unseen angle.
