items.name: Core Practical 12: investigating some electrochemical cells
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 16 Redox Equilibria
C16.6 - CORE PRACTICAL 12 Investigating some electroc
items.question: A student carried out Core Practical 12 to investigate some electrochemical cells. Each half-cell was a strip of metal, cleaned with emery paper, in a 1.00 mol dm⁻³ solution of a soluble salt of the same metal. The half-cells were connected by a strip of filter paper soaked in saturated potassium nitrate solution and by a high-resistance voltmeter. The diagram shows the cell made from the zinc and copper half-cells. Explain why each metal strip was cleaned with emery paper immediately before use. The strip of filter paper soaked in potassium nitrate solution acts as a salt bridge. Explain the function of the salt bridge. Suggest why a new strip of soaked filter paper was used for each cell. State the direction in which electrons flow in the external circuit of the cell in the diagram. Give a reason for your answer. The student used the copper half-cell as a reference and connected it to each of the other half-cells in turn. The table shows the results, with the Data Booklet values. E°(Cu²⁺|Cu) = +0.34 V Calculate the electrode potential of each of the four metals from the student's results. The student's value for iron is the furthest from the Data Booklet value. Suggest two reasons for this. The student replaced the voltmeter in the zinc–copper cell with a small lamp and left the cell connected for several hours. Describe what would be seen at each electrode and in the copper(II) sulfate solution. Include a half-equation for the reaction at each electrode. Calculate the emf of a cell made from the zinc and silver half-cells using • the student's results • the Data Booklet values. Write the conventional cell diagram for the cell made from the lead and copper half-cells. The student then made a half-cell containing 1.00 mol dm⁻³ Fe²⁺(aq) and 1.00 mol dm⁻³ Fe³⁺(aq) and connected it to the copper half-cell. Name a suitable electrode for the iron half-cell and predict the emf of this cell. [E°(Fe³⁺|Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V]
items.ms: To remove the oxide layer / impurities from the surface, so that the metal itself is in contact (and in equilibrium) with its ions Ions move through the salt bridge (between the half-cells) to complete the circuit / to balance the charge in each half-cell (keep the solutions electrically neutral) without the two solutions mixing The used strip contains ions from the previous half-cells, which would contaminate (or react with) the solutions of the next cell From zinc to copper (through the wires and voltmeter) because zinc is more easily oxidised / E° of Zn²⁺|Zn is more negative than E° of Cu²⁺|Cu Zinc −0.72 V and iron −0.38 V Lead −0.11 V and silver +0.78 V An oxide (rust) layer forms quickly on the iron surface / was not completely removed Fe²⁺ ions in the solution are oxidised by air to Fe³⁺, so [Fe²⁺] is less than 1.00 mol dm⁻³ The iron reacts slowly with the solution / dissolved oxygen, changing the conditions at the electrode The temperature was not 298 K / the concentrations were not exactly 1.00 mol dm⁻³ The zinc electrode becomes thinner / loses mass: Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ Pink-brown copper is deposited on the copper electrode / the blue colour of the solution fades: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s) From the results: 0.78 − (-0.72) = 1.50 V / 1.06 + 0.44 = 1.50 V From the Data Booklet: 0.80 − (-0.76) = 1.56 V Pb(s) | Pb²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s) Platinum 0.77 − 0.34 = 0.43 V (the Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ electrode is positive)
items.why: Core Practical 12 was examined directly in Oct 2024 (6-mark) and its apparatus in Oct 2023, Jun 2022 and Oct 2025; the Oct 2024 report said answers showed little first-hand experience, so a results-and-method question is likely.

items.name: Calculating E°cell
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 16 Redox Equilibria
C16.7 - calculate a standard emf, Eo
items.question: Sn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Sn(s) E° = −0.14 V Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Ag(s) E° = +0.80 V What is the standard emf of the cell made from these two half-cells? −0.94 V +0.66 V +0.94 V +1.74 V
items.ms: C: E°cell = E°(positive electrode, Ag⁺|Ag) − E°(negative electrode, Sn²⁺|Sn) = +0.80 − (−0.14) = +0.94 V. A subtracts the wrong way round. B subtracts 0.14 instead of adding it. D doubles the silver value because two Ag⁺ react with each Sn; E° values are not multiplied by the coefficients.
items.why: Single E°cell calculations are set in most sessions (Jan 2026 Q2, Jun 2025 Q2(b), Jan 2024 Q2(b)); doubling an E° when balancing is a common error.

items.name: Calculating E°cell
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 16 Redox Equilibria
C16.7 - calculate a standard emf, Eo
items.question: Three metals, P, Q and R, each in a 1.00 mol dm⁻³ solution of its own ions, were used to make two cells under standard conditions. • Cell 1, P and Q: emf = 0.63 V; Q is the positive electrode. • Cell 2, Q and R: emf = 0.47 V; R is the positive electrode. What is the emf of a cell made from P and R? 0.16 V 0.47 V 0.63 V 1.10 V
items.ms: D: E°(Q) = E°(P) + 0.63 V and E°(R) = E°(Q) + 0.47 V, so E°(R) − E°(P) = 0.63 + 0.47 = 1.10 V, with R positive. A subtracts the two emfs, as if R lay between P and Q. B and C are the emfs of the given cells.
items.why: Moving between electrode potentials and cell emfs is asked almost every session (Oct 2023 Q10 signs; Jan 2026 Q1(a) unknown E°); combining two cells without an SHE value is a likely step up.

path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry

items.question: Redox flow batteries store large amounts of electrical energy, for example from wind farms, until it is needed. In an iron–chromium flow battery, two electrolytes are stored in tanks and pumped through a cell, where they are separated by an ion-exchange membrane. Both electrodes are made of carbon felt. • Positive electrolyte: iron(II) chloride and iron(III) chloride in hydrochloric acid. • Negative electrolyte: chromium(II) chloride and chromium(III) chloride in hydrochloric acid. The diagram shows the battery. The table gives some standard electrode potentials. Write the ionic equation for the reaction that takes place when the battery is discharging (supplying electrical energy). Include state symbols. Calculate E°cell for the discharge reaction. Write the conventional cell diagram for the cell when it is discharging. Use C(s) for the carbon electrodes. Identify the reducing agent in the discharge reaction. Justify your answer in terms of oxidation numbers. Give the electronic configurations of the Cr²⁺ and Fe³⁺ ions. Use [Ar] for the electrons in the first three shells. State the colour change of the negative electrolyte as the battery discharges. Explain why the ion-exchange membrane must allow some ions to pass through it but must stop the iron and chromium ions moving from one electrolyte into the other. When the battery is being charged, a small amount of hydrogen gas forms at the negative electrode. Use E° values to explain why. Air must be kept out of the tank of negative electrolyte. Write the ionic equation for the reaction of Cr²⁺ ions with oxygen in acidic solution and calculate E°cell for this reaction. The state of charge of the battery is found by titrating the positive electrolyte. A 10.0 cm³ sample was diluted with distilled water and titrated with 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ potassium dichromate(VI) solution. The mean titre was 18.40 cm³. Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + 14H⁺(aq) + 6Fe²⁺(aq) → 2Cr³⁺(aq) + 6Fe³⁺(aq) + 7H₂O(l) Calculate the concentration of Fe²⁺ ions in the positive electrolyte. The total concentration of iron ions in the positive electrolyte is 1.25 mol dm⁻³. Calculate the percentage of the iron that is present as Fe³⁺ ions. When the battery is fully discharged, all the iron in the positive electrolyte is present as Fe²⁺. Calculate the volume of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ potassium dichromate(VI) solution that would react with a 10.0 cm³ sample of the fully discharged electrolyte. Comment on your answer.
items.ms: Fe³⁺(aq) + Cr²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cr³⁺(aq) E°cell = +0.77 − (-0.41) = +1.18 V C(s) | Cr²⁺(aq), Cr³⁺(aq) || Fe³⁺(aq), Fe²⁺(aq) | C(s) Cr²⁺: the oxidation number of chromium increases from +2 to +3 (it loses an electron to Fe³⁺) Cr²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁴ and Fe³⁺: [Ar] 3d⁵ Blue to green Ions (e.g. H⁺ or Cl⁻) moving through the membrane complete the circuit / keep each electrolyte electrically neutral If Fe³⁺ and Cr²⁺ mixed they would react directly in solution, so the energy would be released as heat rather than as electrical energy / the battery would discharge itself During charging, reduction takes place at the negative electrode: Cr³⁺ + e⁻ → Cr²⁺ (E° = −0.41 V) 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ has a more positive E° (0.00 V), so H⁺ ions (from the HCl) are more easily reduced than Cr³⁺ / Cr²⁺ can reduce H⁺ (E°cell = +0.41 V) 4Cr²⁺(aq) + O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) → 4Cr³⁺(aq) + 2H₂O(l) E°cell = +1.23 − (-0.41) = +1.64 V n(Cr₂O₇²⁻) = 0.0200 × 18.40 ÷ 1000 = 3.68 × 10⁻⁴ mol n(Fe²⁺) = 6 × n(Cr₂O₇²⁻) = 2.208 × 10⁻³ mol [Fe²⁺] = 2.208 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0100 = 0.221 mol dm⁻³ [Fe³⁺] = 1.25 − 0.221 = 1.029 mol dm⁻³ percentage = 1.029 ÷ 1.25 × 100 = 82.3 % n(Fe²⁺) = 1.25 × 0.0100 = 0.0125 mol, n(Cr₂O₇²⁻) = 0.0125 ÷ 6 = 2.08 × 10⁻³ mol, volume = 2.08 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0200 = 104 cm³ This is more than a (50 cm³) burette holds, so a smaller sample (e.g. 5.00 cm³ by pipette) or a more concentrated dichromate(VI) solution should be used
items.why: E°cell is set in 14 of 17 sessions, and Section C always uses an unseen context (rhodium catalysis Jan 2026, carminic acid Oct 2025); a grid-storage flow battery combines E°cell, cell diagrams, membrane function, transition-metal chemistry and a redox titration, as recent Section C questions do.

path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry

C16.9 - the importance of the condit
items.question: A half-cell contains a platinum electrode in a solution in which [Fe³⁺(aq)] = [Fe²⁺(aq)] = 1.00 mol dm⁻³. It is connected by a salt bridge to a standard Zn²⁺(aq)|Zn(s) half-cell. Fe³⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Fe²⁺(aq) E° = +0.77 V Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Zn(s) E° = −0.76 V Solid iron(II) sulfate is then dissolved in the iron half-cell, so that [Fe²⁺(aq)] increases. [Fe³⁺(aq)] does not change. What is the effect on the electrode potential, E, of the iron half-cell and on Ecell? E of the iron half-cell becomes less positive; Ecell decreases E of the iron half-cell becomes less positive; Ecell increases E of the iron half-cell becomes more positive; Ecell increases E of the iron half-cell becomes more positive; Ecell decreases
items.ms: Adding Fe²⁺ shifts Fe³⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Fe²⁺ to the left, so the half-cell has less tendency to gain electrons and E becomes less positive. The iron half-cell is the positive electrode, so Ecell = E(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) − E(Zn²⁺/Zn) decreases. B gets the half-cell right but not its effect on Ecell; C and D assume a higher ion concentration always makes E more positive, which is true only for the oxidised form.
items.why: C16.9 has come up in 11 of 17 sessions; past questions changed the oxidised species (Zn²⁺ diluted, Jan2025; H⁺ in conc. HCl, Oct2023/Oct2024), but changing the reduced form of an ion/ion couple has not been asked.

items.question: The electrode potential, E, of a Zn²⁺(aq)|Zn(s) half-cell at 298 K is given by E = E° + (RT ÷ 2F) ln[Zn²⁺(aq)] where E° = −0.76 V, R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹. This cell is set up at 298 K. For Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu(s), E° = +0.34 V. Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) (0.0100 mol dm⁻³) || Cu²⁺(aq) (1.00 mol dm⁻³) | Cu(s) What is the emf of this cell? +1.04 V +1.13 V +1.16 V +1.22 V
items.ms: E(Zn) = −0.76 + (8.31 × 298 ÷ 193 000) × ln 0.0100 = −0.76 − 0.059 = -0.819 V; Ecell = +0.34 − (-0.819) = +1.16 V. A adds the correction with the wrong sign; B uses log₁₀ instead of ln; D uses RT ÷ F (n = 1), doubling the correction.
items.why: Nernst-type calculations with the expression supplied were set in Oct2020, Jun2022 and Oct2024; a whole cell with one non-standard half-cell has not been asked.

items.question: Jewellers use a concentrated solution of iron(III) nitrate, containing very little iron(II), to etch (dissolve) silver. Fe³⁺(aq) + Ag(s) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Ag⁺(aq) Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Ag(s) E° = +0.80 V Fe³⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Fe²⁺(aq) E° = +0.77 V Calculate E°cell for the reaction of iron(III) ions with silver. Explain why silver dissolves in the etching solution.

items.question: A metal M forms M²⁺ ions. M reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to give hydrogen, but it does not react with iron(II) sulfate solution. Fe²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Fe(s) E° = −0.44 V 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂(g) E° = 0.00 V Which could be the standard electrode potential of the M²⁺(aq)|M(s) half-cell? −0.60 V −0.30 V +0.10 V +0.40 V
items.ms: M reduces H⁺, so E°(M²⁺/M) must be below 0.00 V; M does not reduce Fe²⁺, so E°(M²⁺/M) must be above −0.44 V. Only −0.30 V lies between. With −0.60 V, M + Fe²⁺ would be feasible (E°cell = +0.16 V); with +0.10 V or +0.40 V, the reaction with acid would not be feasible.
items.why: Deducing an unknown electrode potential from observations was asked in Jan2026 Q22(c) and Oct2023 Q11; C16.10 is hot (16 of 17 sessions).

items.question: This question is about the redox chemistry of iron. Use the standard electrode potentials in the table. Iron reacts with bromine to form iron(III) bromide, FeBr₃, but when iron is heated with iodine the product is iron(II) iodide, FeI₂. Write the ionic equation for the oxidation of iron(II) ions by bromine in aqueous solution, and calculate E°cell for this reaction. Explain, using E° values, why iron(III) iodide, FeI₃, cannot be made. Iron(II) ions are usually titrated with potassium manganate(VII) in the presence of dilute sulfuric acid. Explain why dilute sulfuric acid is suitable for acidifying the titration mixture. Use E° values where relevant. Explain why dilute nitric acid would be unsuitable. A sample of iron ore is dissolved in acid to give a solution containing both Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ ions. To find the total iron content, all the Fe³⁺ must first be reduced to Fe²⁺, and the solution is then titrated with manganate(VII). Three possible reducing agents are zinc powder, tin(II) chloride solution and potassium iodide solution. Using E° values from the table, discuss the suitability of each of these reducing agents for this purpose. Include equations and E°cell values in your answer. Iron(II) sulfate solutions slowly turn yellow-brown when left in air. Write the ionic equation for the oxidation of Fe²⁺(aq) by oxygen in acidic solution, and calculate E°cell. When sodium hydroxide solution is added to iron(II) sulfate solution, a green precipitate forms which turns orange-brown at the surface in contact with air. Use E° values to explain why iron(II) solutions for titrations are kept acidified rather than alkaline. Suggest why an acidified iron(II) solution should still be standardised shortly before it is used.
items.ms: 2Fe²⁺ + Br₂ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2Br⁻ E°cell = +1.09 − (+0.77) = +0.32 V Iodine cannot oxidise Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺: E°cell = +0.54 − (+0.77) = −0.23 V, negative Fe³⁺ ions oxidise iodide ions: 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂ E°cell = +0.23 V, positive, so Fe³⁺ and I⁻ cannot exist together / FeI₃ would give FeI₂ and I₂ It supplies the H⁺ ions needed for the reduction of manganate(VII) (MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O) Sulfate ions cannot be oxidised by manganate(VII), as sulfur is already in its highest oxidation state (+6) Sulfate ions do not oxidise Fe²⁺: E°cell = +0.17 − (+0.77) = −0.60 V, negative / not feasible Nitrate ions (in acid) oxidise Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺: E°cell = +0.96 − (+0.77) = +0.19 V So less Fe²⁺ is left to react with manganate(VII) and the titre is too small / the amount of iron calculated is too low IC1 Zinc reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺: Zn + 2Fe³⁺ → Zn²⁺ + 2Fe²⁺, E°cell = +1.53 V IC2 Zinc also reduces Fe²⁺ to Fe: Zn + Fe²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Fe, E°cell = +0.32 V, so any excess zinc must be removed (filtered off) quickly or some iron is lost IC3 Tin(II) reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺: Sn²⁺ + 2Fe³⁺ → Sn⁴⁺ + 2Fe²⁺, E°cell = +0.62 V IC4 Tin(II) cannot reduce Fe²⁺ to Fe: E°cell = −0.44 − (+0.15) = −0.59 V, so reduction stops at Fe²⁺ IC5 Excess Sn²⁺ would itself react with manganate(VII) (E°cell = +1.36 V) and increase the titre, so only a slight excess may be used or the excess must be removed IC6 Iodide reduces Fe³⁺ (2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂, E°cell = +0.23 V) but the excess I⁻ and the I₂ formed interfere: I⁻ is oxidised by manganate(VII) (E°cell = +0.97 V) and the iodine colour hides the end-point, so KI is unsuitable 4Fe²⁺ + O₂ + 4H⁺ → 4Fe³⁺ + 2H₂O E°cell = +1.23 − (+0.77) = +0.46 V In alkali: 4Fe(OH)₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4Fe(OH)₃, E°cell = +0.40 − (−0.56) = +0.96 V +0.96 V is more positive than +0.46 V in acid, so oxidation of iron(II) by air is (thermodynamically) more favourable in alkali; keeping the solution acidic reduces this tendency E°cell in acid is still positive, so Fe²⁺ is slowly oxidised by air and its concentration falls over time
items.why: C16.10 has come up in 16 of 17 sessions; the 6-mark 'which reducing agent' discussion (Jan2023, vanadium) and acid-choice reasoning (Oct2023, Oct2024, dichromate) recur, set here with iron, the halogens and air oxidation, which have not been used.

items.question: Tin(II) ions reduce iron(III) ions. Sn²⁺(aq) + 2Fe³⁺(aq) ⇌ Sn⁴⁺(aq) + 2Fe²⁺(aq) Sn⁴⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Sn²⁺(aq) E° = +0.15 V Fe³⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Fe²⁺(aq) E° = +0.77 V ln K = nFE°cell ÷ RT, where F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹ and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is the value of the equilibrium constant, K, for this reaction at 298 K? 48.3 3.1 × 10¹⁰ 9.7 × 10²⁰ 1.4 × 10³¹
items.ms: E°cell = 0.77 − 0.15 = +0.62 V and n = 2, so ln K = 2 × 96 500 × 0.62 ÷ (8.31 × 298) = 48.3 and K = e48.3 = 9.7 × 10²⁰. A is ln K, not K; B uses n = 1; D adds the two E° values (0.92 V).
items.why: C16.11 has come up in 8 of 17 sessions, mostly as MCQs; Oct2025 Q5 asked for ΔS_{total} and K numerically for the first time, so a K calculation with a different couple is likely.

items.question: Copper reduces silver ions. 2Ag⁺(aq) + Cu(s) ⇌ 2Ag(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) E°cell = +0.46 V The equilibrium constant for this reaction at 298 K is K. The same reaction is written as Ag⁺(aq) + ½Cu(s) ⇌ Ag(s) + ½Cu²⁺(aq) What are E°cell and the equilibrium constant for the reaction written this way, at 298 K? E°cell = +0.46 V; equilibrium constant = √K E°cell = +0.46 V; equilibrium constant = ½K E°cell = +0.23 V; equilibrium constant = √K E°cell = +0.23 V; equilibrium constant = ½K
items.ms: E°cell does not depend on the amounts in the equation, so it stays +0.46 V. ln K = nFE°cell ÷ RT and n halves (2 → 1), so ln K halves and the new constant is √K. B halves K instead of ln K; C and D halve E°cell as if it depended on the amounts.
items.why: Jan2025 Q8 and Oct2023 Q7 asked what E°_{cell} is proportional to; that E°_{cell} stays the same while ln K scales with n when an equation is rewritten has not been asked.

items.question: Cerium(IV) sulfate solution is used as an oxidising agent in titrations. It oxidises iron(II) ions. Ce⁴⁺(aq) + Fe²⁺(aq) → Ce³⁺(aq) + Fe³⁺(aq) ΔStotal = nFE°cell ÷ T and ln K = nFE°cell ÷ RT F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹ R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ Calculate E°cell for the reaction of cerium(IV) ions with iron(II) ions. Calculate ΔStotal for this reaction at 298 K. Include units in your answer. Calculate the value of the equilibrium constant, K, for this reaction at 298 K. Explain what your answers to (b) and (c) show about the suitability of this reaction for a titration. A student writes the equation as 2Ce⁴⁺(aq) + 2Fe²⁺(aq) → 2Ce³⁺(aq) + 2Fe³⁺(aq) State and explain the effect, if any, of writing the equation this way on the values of E°cell and K. Iron(II) ions can also be titrated with acidified dichromate(VI) ions. Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + 14H⁺(aq) + 6Fe²⁺(aq) → 2Cr³⁺(aq) + 6Fe³⁺(aq) + 7H₂O(l) Calculate ΔStotal for this reaction, as written, at 298 K. Explain why it is larger than ΔStotal for the cerium(IV) reaction, even though E°cell is smaller.
items.ms: E°cell = +1.70 − (+0.77) = +0.93 V n = 1 and ΔStotal = 1 × 96 500 × 0.93 ÷ 298 = +301 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ln K = 96 500 × 0.93 ÷ (8.31 × 298) = 36.2 K = e36.2 = 5.5 × 10¹⁵ (no units) ΔStotal is positive and K is very large, so the reaction goes (virtually) to completion So every Ce⁴⁺ added reacts with Fe²⁺ in a 1 : 1 ratio until the Fe²⁺ is used up, giving an accurate end-point / titre E°cell is unchanged (+0.93 V) because an electrode potential does not depend on the amounts in the equation n doubles so ln K doubles and K is squared (≈ 3.0 × 10³¹) E°cell = 1.33 − 0.77 = +0.56 V and n = 6 ΔStotal = 6 × 96 500 × 0.56 ÷ 298 = +1090 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ΔStotal is for the equation as written, in which 6 mol of electrons are transferred (6 mol of Fe²⁺ oxidised); per mole of Fe²⁺ it is only 181 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, less than 301
items.why: C16.11 (8 of 17 sessions) is nearly always a 1-mark MCQ; the digest notes ΔS_{total} = nFE/T has never been needed numerically in a structured question, and Oct2025 Q5 began asking for numbers.

items.question: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) solution is often stored in the laboratory for many months. Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + 14H⁺(aq) + 6e⁻ ⇌ 2Cr³⁺(aq) + 7H₂O(l) E° = +1.33 V O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻ ⇌ 2H₂O(l) E° = +1.23 V Calculate E°cell for the oxidation of water by acidified dichromate(VI) ions. No oxygen is given off by the stored solution. Give one reason why this does not contradict your answer to (a).
items.ms: E°cell = +1.33 − (+1.23) = +0.10 V The reaction has a (very) high activation energy / is (very) slow, so the solution is kinetically stable E°cell is only slightly positive, so under the non-standard conditions in the bottle (for example [Cr₂O₇²⁻] below 1 mol dm⁻³) Ecell may be negative
items.why: C16.12 was last asked in Oct2024 (6 of 17 sessions); past contexts were S₂O₈²⁻/I⁻ and MnO₄⁻/VO²⁺, while the stability of a stored oxidising agent towards water has not been asked.

items.name: Disproportionation
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 16 Redox Equilibria
C16.14 - how standard electrode poten
items.question: Hydrogen peroxide solution slowly decomposes. 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g) The diagram shows standard electrode potentials linking oxygen, hydrogen peroxide and water in acidic solution at 298 K. Each arrow represents a reduction in which the species gains electrons and hydrogen ions. Give the oxidation number of oxygen in O₂, H₂O₂ and H₂O. Use these to explain why the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide is a disproportionation reaction. Use the diagram to write the two half-equations involved, and show that the decomposition is thermodynamically feasible. A bottle of hydrogen peroxide solution can be kept for months with very little decomposition. Explain why this is consistent with your answer to (b). Bromide ions catalyse the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide in acidic solution. In the first step bromide ions are oxidised to bromine; in the second step bromine is reduced back to bromide ions. Br₂(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2Br⁻(aq) E° = +1.09 V Sn⁴⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Sn²⁺(aq) E° = +0.15 V Write an ionic equation for each step and show that both steps are thermodynamically feasible. Explain why the Sn⁴⁺/Sn²⁺ system could not catalyse the decomposition in the same way.
items.ms: O₂ 0, H₂O₂ −1, H₂O −2 Oxygen in H₂O₂ is both oxidised (−1 to 0) and reduced (−1 to −2) in the same reaction H₂O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2H₂O and O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂O₂ E°cell = +1.77 − (+0.68) = +1.09 V, positive so (thermodynamically) feasible The uncatalysed reaction has a high activation energy / is very slow, so H₂O₂ is kinetically stable (although thermodynamically unstable) Step 1: H₂O₂ + 2Br⁻ + 2H⁺ → Br₂ + 2H₂O and E°cell = 1.77 − 1.09 = +0.68 V Step 2: Br₂ + H₂O₂ → 2Br⁻ + O₂ + 2H⁺ and E°cell = 1.09 − 0.68 = +0.41 V E° (+0.15 V) is less positive than +0.68 V, so Sn⁴⁺ cannot oxidise H₂O₂ to O₂ (E°cell = −0.53 V) and Sn²⁺ is not regenerated
items.why: C16.14 (3 of 17 sessions, last Jan2024) has used only copper and manganese species; hydrogen peroxide is the standard non-metal disproportionation, and Latimer-style data were used in Jan2024.

items.question: Iron(II) ethanedioate, FeC₂O₄, is oxidised by acidified potassium manganate(VII). Both ions are oxidised: Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, and C₂O₄²⁻ to CO₂. The manganate(VII) ions are reduced to Mn²⁺. What volume of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄(aq) reacts exactly with 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol of FeC₂O₄? 10.0 cm³ 20.0 cm³ 30.0 cm³ 50.0 cm³
items.ms: Each FeC₂O₄ loses 1 e⁻ (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺) + 2 e⁻ (C₂O₄²⁻ → 2CO₂) = 3 e⁻, so 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol e⁻; each MnO₄⁻ gains 5 e⁻, so n(MnO₄⁻) = 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol and V = 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 0.0200 = 0.0300 dm³ = 30.0 cm³. A counts only Fe²⁺ (1 : 5); B counts only C₂O₄²⁻ (2 : 5); D uses a 1 : 1 ratio.
items.why: C16.15 has come up in all 17 sessions; manganate(VII) with ethanedioate (Jan2024, Jun2025) or with Fe²⁺ is routine, but a reductant in which both ions are oxidised has not been set.

items.question: A solution containing 1.50 × 10⁻³ mol of a metal ion X²⁺ is titrated with 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ acidified potassium manganate(VII). All the X²⁺ ions are oxidised to the same higher oxidation state and the MnO₄⁻ ions are reduced to Mn²⁺. The titre is 12.00 cm³. What is the oxidation number of X after the reaction? +3 +4 +5 +6
items.ms: n(MnO₄⁻) = 0.01200 × 0.0500 = 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol, accepting 5 × 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ = 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol e⁻. Each X²⁺ loses 3.00 × 10⁻³ ÷ 1.50 × 10⁻³ = 2 e⁻, so X goes from +2 to +4. +3 would need a titre of 6.00 cm³, +5 a titre of 18.00 cm³ and +6 a titre of 24.00 cm³.

items.question: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. A student found the percentage by mass of copper in a brass screw. Step 1 1.215 g of brass was dissolved in nitric acid in a fume cupboard. Nitrogen monoxide, NO, was given off. Step 2 The excess nitric acid was neutralised with sodium carbonate solution, a little ethanoic acid was added, and the solution was made up to 250.0 cm³ with deionised water. Step 3 25.0 cm³ portions of this solution were pipetted into conical flasks and 1.00 g of potassium iodide was added to each. A white precipitate of copper(I) iodide formed in a brown solution. 2Cu²⁺(aq) + 4I⁻(aq) → 2CuI(s) + I₂(aq) Step 4 The iodine was titrated with 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ sodium thiosulfate solution, adding starch near the end-point. I₂(aq) + 2S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → 2I⁻(aq) + S₄O₆²⁻(aq) Use these standard electrode potentials where needed. Use the data to explain why copper dissolves in nitric acid but not in dilute hydrochloric acid. Suggest why the excess nitric acid must be removed before Step 3. Calculate E°cell for the reaction 2Cu²⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Cu⁺(aq) + I₂(aq). The reaction in Step 3 still takes place. Explain why. The table shows the student's titration results. The diagram shows the burette readings for titration 3. Use the diagram to complete the table for titration 3. Calculate the mean titre that should be used. Calculate the percentage by mass of copper in the brass. Give your answer to three significant figures. State the colour change at the end-point. Each burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the titre for titration 3. The brass also contained a small amount of iron, which formed Fe³⁺ ions in Step 1. State and explain the effect of this on the calculated percentage of copper. Show by calculation that 1.00 g of potassium iodide is an excess in Step 3.
items.ms: Nitrate ions (with H⁺) oxidise copper: E°cell = +0.96 − (+0.34) = +0.62 V, positive so feasible In hydrochloric acid the only oxidising agent is H⁺: E°cell = 0.00 − (+0.34) = −0.34 V, negative so not feasible Nitrate ions in acid would also oxidise iodide ions to iodine (E°cell = +0.42 V), so the titre would be too large E°cell = +0.15 − (+0.54) = −0.39 V Copper(I) is removed from solution as the insoluble CuI precipitate / [Cu⁺] is very low So Cu²⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Cu⁺ shifts to the right, making E for this system more positive (than +0.54 V), so Ecell becomes positive Final 24.80, initial 0.85, titre 23.95 (cm³) (23.90 + 23.95) ÷ 2 = 23.925 cm³, using the concordant titres 1 and 3 only n(S₂O₃²⁻) = 23.925 × 10⁻³ × 0.0500 = 1.196 × 10⁻³ mol n(Cu²⁺) in 25.0 cm³ = n(S₂O₃²⁻) = 1.196 × 10⁻³ mol (2Cu²⁺ ≡ I₂ ≡ 2S₂O₃²⁻) n(Cu) in 250.0 cm³ = 1.196 × 10⁻² mol mass of Cu = 1.196 × 10⁻² × 63.5 = 0.7596 g % Cu = 0.7596 ÷ 1.215 × 100 = 62.5% blue-black to white / cream / off-white 2 × 0.05 ÷ 23.95 × 100 = 0.42% Fe³⁺ ions also oxidise I⁻ to I₂, as E°cell = +0.77 − (+0.54) = +0.23 V More iodine forms, so the titre is larger and the calculated percentage of copper is too high n(KI) = 1.00 ÷ 166.0 = 6.02 × 10⁻³ mol n(I⁻) needed = 2 × n(Cu²⁺) = 2 × 1.196 × 10⁻³ = 2.39 × 10⁻³ mol, which is less than 6.02 × 10⁻³ mol, so KI is in excess
items.why: C16.15 has come up in all 17 sessions (9.1% of the unit's marks); iodine–thiosulfate calculations appeared in Jan2021 and Oct2025, and the spec's suggested practical (copper in brass by iodine–thiosulfate) has not yet been set as a titration (Jun2022 used a gravimetric method).

The total percentage uncertainty from the apparatus was 2.5%. The manufacturer states that each tablet contains 65.0 mg of iron. Which statement is correct? The result agrees with the manufacturer's value because the two values differ by less than 5%. The difference between the two values is larger than the measurement uncertainty, so it cannot be explained by the apparatus alone. The result agrees with the manufacturer's value within the uncertainty of the measurements. No conclusion can be drawn because a total uncertainty greater than 1% makes the result invalid.
items.ms: 2.5% of 62.8 mg = ±1.6 mg, so the result lies between 61.2 mg and 64.4 mg, which does not include 65.0 mg (the difference, 2.2 mg, is 3.4%). A uses an arbitrary 5% limit instead of the measurement uncertainty; C is wrong because 65.0 mg lies outside the range; D: a 2.5% uncertainty does not make a result invalid, it sets the range for the comparison.
items.why: C16.16 has come up in 7 of 17 sessions, always as calculating percentage uncertainties; the spec's 'implications for the validity of the final results' (comparing with a claimed value) has not been asked.

items.ms: Pipette: 0.04 ÷ 10.0 × 100 = 0.40%; flask: 0.20 ÷ 100.0 × 100 = 0.20%; percentage uncertainties add, giving 0.60%. A is the flask only; B adds the absolute uncertainties (0.04 + 0.20); C is the pipette only.

items.question: In the titration of iodine with sodium thiosulfate solution, starch is not added at the start. It is added when the solution in the conical flask has become pale yellow. Why is the starch not added at the start of the titration? At a high concentration of iodine, the starch–iodine complex releases iodine only slowly, so the end-point would not be sharp. Starch reacts with sodium thiosulfate, so the titre would be too large. Starch oxidises iodide ions to iodine when the concentration of iodine is high. Starch is decomposed by iodine, so none would be left to show the end-point.
items.ms: With a lot of iodine present, iodine is held strongly in the starch complex and released only slowly to the thiosulfate, so the blue-black colour fades gradually and the end-point is unclear or overshot. B: starch does not react with thiosulfate; C: starch is not an oxidising agent; D: starch is not decomposed, the complex forms reversibly.
items.why: C16.17 has come up in 11 of 17 sessions, almost always as end-point colours (Jan2022, Jan2024, Jun2025, Jan2026); when to add the indicator has not been asked.

items.question: Which statement about a fuel cell is correct? The fuel is burned inside the cell and the heat released is converted into electrical energy. The energy released when the fuel reacts with oxygen is used to generate a voltage, without the fuel being burned. The cell stores electrical energy and must be recharged from the mains when the voltage falls. The fuel and oxygen react at the same electrode, which releases electrons into the external circuit.
items.ms: The fuel is oxidised at one electrode and oxygen reduced at the other, so the energy of the reaction appears as a voltage, not as heat from combustion. A describes a power station; C describes a rechargeable battery (a fuel cell runs as long as fuel and oxygen are supplied); D: the fuel and oxygen are kept apart at different electrodes.
items.why: C16.18 has come up in 10 of 17 sessions; the spec wording 'use the energy released on the reaction of a fuel with oxygen to generate a voltage' was the point least often seen in the Jun2024 6-mark answers.

items.question: Methane can be used as the fuel in a fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte. At the negative electrode, methane reacts with water to form carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions. How many moles of electrons are released at the negative electrode for each mole of methane that reacts? 2 4 6 8
items.ms: CH₄ + 2H₂O → CO₂ + 8H⁺ + 8e⁻: carbon goes from −4 to +4. A is the value for each H₂ in a hydrogen cell; B is the number gained by each O₂ at the positive electrode; C is the value for methanol (carbon −2 to +4).

items.question: In a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell with an alkaline electrolyte, hydrogen is supplied to one electrode and oxygen to the other. Which ions are formed at one electrode and used up at the other, and in which direction do they move through the electrolyte? OH⁻ ions, from the oxygen electrode to the hydrogen electrode OH⁻ ions, from the hydrogen electrode to the oxygen electrode H⁺ ions, from the hydrogen electrode to the oxygen electrode H⁺ ions, from the oxygen electrode to the hydrogen electrode
items.ms: OH⁻ is formed at the oxygen (positive) electrode, O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻, and used at the hydrogen (negative) electrode, H₂ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O + 2e⁻, so OH⁻ ions move towards the hydrogen electrode. B reverses the direction; C describes an acidic electrolyte; D is wrong for either electrolyte.
items.why: C16.19 MCQs (12 of 17 sessions) have asked for the half-equation at each electrode, and Oct2025 Q6(a) asked the direction of electron flow; the matching ion flow in the electrolyte is a likely variant.

items.question: At which electrode is water formed in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, and in one with an alkaline electrolyte? acidic electrolyte: negative electrode; alkaline electrolyte: negative electrode acidic electrolyte: negative electrode; alkaline electrolyte: positive electrode acidic electrolyte: positive electrode; alkaline electrolyte: positive electrode acidic electrolyte: positive electrode; alkaline electrolyte: negative electrode
items.ms: Acidic: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O at the positive electrode (H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ at the negative). Alkaline: H₂ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O + 2e⁻ at the negative electrode; at the positive electrode water is used up (O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻). A, B and C each place at least one of these wrongly.
items.why: Jun2022 Q2(b) and Jan2026 Q2 compared acidic and alkaline fuel cells; where the water forms in each has not been asked.

items.question: The Apollo spacecraft used hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells with an alkaline electrolyte of potassium hydroxide solution. The water produced was used by the crew. The diagram shows a simplified fuel cell. 2H₂O(l) + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂(g) + 2OH⁻(aq) E° = −0.83 V O₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) + 4e⁻ ⇌ 4OH⁻(aq) E° = +0.40 V Write the half-equation for the reaction at electrode A, and explain why electrode A is the negative electrode. Calculate E°cell for the fuel cell. Write the overall equation for the reaction in the cell. Include state symbols. When the fuel cell is in use, the concentration of the potassium hydroxide solution slowly decreases unless water is removed. Explain why. ΔStotal = nFE°cell ÷ T, where F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔStotal at 298 K for the reaction of 1 mol of hydrogen with oxygen. Include units. The electrodes are made of porous carbon coated with a platinum catalyst. Explain why a catalyst is needed even though E°cell is large and positive, and why the electrodes are porous. Fuel cells can also use ethanol, C₂H₅OH, with an acidic electrolyte. Ethanol is oxidised to carbon dioxide at the negative electrode. Write the half-equation for the oxidation of ethanol, and the overall equation for the cell reaction. State symbols are not required. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using ethanol rather than hydrogen as the fuel in a fuel-cell car.
items.ms: H₂(g) + 2OH⁻(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + 2e⁻ The H₂O/H₂ system has the more negative E°, so oxidation takes place at A / electrons are released at A and flow from A into the external circuit E°cell = +0.40 − (−0.83) = +1.23 V 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) The OH⁻ ions used at the negative electrode are replaced by the OH⁻ ions formed at the positive electrode, so the amount of OH⁻ does not change Water is a (net) product of the cell reaction, so it dilutes the electrolyte n = 2 and ΔStotal = 2 × 96 500 × 1.23 ÷ 298 = +797 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ Hydrogen and oxygen are kinetically stable / the electrode reactions have a high activation energy, so without a catalyst they would be too slow to give a useful current Porous electrodes have a large surface area where the gas, electrolyte and catalyst meet, so the rate is higher C₂H₅OH + 3H₂O → 2CO₂ + 12H⁺ + 12e⁻ C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O Ethanol is a liquid, so it is easier to store and transport than hydrogen gas (which needs high pressure or a very low temperature / has a low density) Hydrogen is highly flammable / forms explosive mixtures with air and leaks easily; ethanol is less hazardous to store Ethanol can be made from renewable crops by fermentation, whereas most hydrogen is made from fossil fuels (or needs energy for electrolysis) Ethanol produces carbon dioxide (a greenhouse gas) at the point of use, whereas hydrogen produces only water Ethanol cells give a lower current / need more catalyst, as the oxidation of ethanol is slow (and its intermediates poison the platinum)
items.why: C16.19 has come up in 12 of 17 sessions, nearly always as 1-mark MCQs on electrode half-equations; Jun2024 Q18 showed fuel cells can carry a long question, and electrolyte dilution and a second hydrogen-rich fuel have not been asked.

path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 18 Organic Chemistry - Arenes
C18.1 - use thermochemical, X-ray di
items.question: Naphthalene, C₁₀H₈, can be represented by the Kekulé-type structure shown. Naphthalene reacts with hydrogen to form decahydronaphthalene, C₁₀H₁₈. The enthalpy change for this reaction is −333 kJ mol⁻¹. The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −120 kJ mol⁻¹. By how much is naphthalene more stable than the Kekulé-type structure? 27 kJ mol⁻¹ 147 kJ mol⁻¹ 267 kJ mol⁻¹ 933 kJ mol⁻¹
items.ms: C: the structure has five C=C bonds, so the expected value is 5 × (−120) = −600 kJ mol⁻¹; −333 − (−600) = +267, so naphthalene is 267 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable. A uses three C=C bonds, as for benzene (−360). B uses four C=C bonds (−480). D adds the two magnitudes instead of finding the difference.
items.why: C18.1 has come up in 11/17 sessions and hydrogenation-enthalpy comparisons recur (Jan2024, Jan2026 Q19); a fused-ring arene appeared in Oct2024 Q10, but its stabilisation has never been calculated.

items.name: Evidence for the structure and stability of benzene (thermochemical, X-ray, IR)
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 18 Organic Chemistry - Arenes
C18.1 - use thermochemical, X-ray di
items.question: Which observation is not evidence that benzene is more stable than the Kekulé structure, cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene? The standard enthalpy change of formation of benzene is positive. The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of benzene is less exothermic than three times that of cyclohexene. The enthalpy change of combustion of benzene is less exothermic than the value predicted for cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene. The enthalpy change of atomisation of benzene is more endothermic than the value calculated from mean bond enthalpies for cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene.
items.ms: A: a positive ΔfH compares benzene with its elements, not with the Kekulé structure, so it says nothing about delocalisation. B, C and D each compare benzene with the hypothetical triene: less energy released on hydrogenation or combustion, or more energy needed to break benzene into atoms, all mean that benzene is lower in energy (more stable) than the Kekulé structure.
items.why: May2024 Q7 asked which type of data is not used as evidence; atomisation data (as in the Jun2025 Q16(a) bond enthalpy cycle) beside a positive Δ_{f}H tests whether students know the comparison must be with the triene.

items.name: Evidence for the structure and stability of benzene (thermochemical, X-ray, IR)
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 18 Organic Chemistry - Arenes
C18.1 - use thermochemical, X-ray di
items.question: Kekulé suggested that benzene is cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene, with three localised C=C double bonds. Thermochemical, X-ray diffraction and infrared data show that this structure is incorrect. The table shows some standard enthalpy changes of formation at 298 K. Calculate the enthalpy change for each of these hydrogenation reactions. Reaction 1: C₆H₁₀(g) + H₂(g) → C₆H₁₂(g) Reaction 2: C₆H₆(g) + 3H₂(g) → C₆H₁₂(g) Use your answers to (a)(i) to calculate how much more stable benzene is than cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene would be. Complete the enthalpy level diagram for the hydrogenation of benzene and of cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene. Label each level and show the values from (a)(i) and (a)(ii). Explain, in terms of orbitals, why benzene is more stable than cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene. X-ray diffraction shows that all the carbon–carbon bonds in benzene are 0.140 nm long. The C–C bond in cyclohexane is 0.154 nm long and the C=C bond in cyclohexene is 0.134 nm long. Explain how these data are evidence against the Kekulé structure. The infrared spectrum of benzene has absorptions at 3030, 1600 and 1500 cm⁻¹ but no absorption in the range 1669–1645 cm⁻¹. Explain how these data are evidence for the delocalised structure. Use the Data Booklet.
items.ms: ΔH (Reaction 1) = −123.4 − (−4.6) = −118.8 kJ mol⁻¹ ΔH (Reaction 2) = −123.4 − (+82.9) = −206.3 kJ mol⁻¹ expected ΔH of hydrogenation of cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene = 3 × (−118.8) = −356.4 kJ mol⁻¹ −206.3 − (−356.4) = 150 kJ mol⁻¹, so benzene is 150 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable levels for C₆H₆(g) + 3H₂(g) and for cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene + 3H₂(g), both above C₆H₁₂(g), with the triene level the higher downward arrows to C₆H₁₂(g) labelled −356 kJ mol⁻¹ (from the triene) and −206 kJ mol⁻¹ (from benzene) gap between the two upper levels labelled 150 kJ mol⁻¹ (stabilisation / delocalisation energy) the p orbitals on all six carbon atoms overlap (sideways) with those on both neighbours, so the π electrons are delocalised around the ring instead of being localised in three C=C bonds the Kekulé structure would have two different bond lengths: three shorter C=C bonds (0.134 nm) and three longer C–C bonds (0.154 nm) in benzene all six bonds are the same length, in between (intermediate between) C–C and C=C 1669–1645 cm⁻¹ is the range for the C=C stretch in alkenes, so no absorption here means benzene has no localised C=C bonds 1600 and 1500 cm⁻¹ are arene (ring carbon–carbon) absorptions, so the carbon–carbon bonds in benzene are a different type of bond from those in alkenes
items.why: C18.1 has come up in 11/17 sessions; hydrogenation data (Jan2024, Jan2026) and X-ray data recur, but enthalpies of hydrogenation found from Δ_{f}H data, the enthalpy level diagram (badly drawn in Oct2021) and IR evidence (only Jun2025 Q20(c)) are the rarer angles.

items.question: How many σ bonds and how many delocalised π electrons are there in one molecule of methylbenzene, C₆H₅CH₃? 12 σ bonds and 6 delocalised π electrons 15 σ bonds and 3 delocalised π electrons 15 σ bonds and 6 delocalised π electrons 18 σ bonds and 6 delocalised π electrons
items.ms: C: σ bonds = 6 C–C in the ring + 5 ring C–H + 1 ring C–CH₃ + 3 C–H in CH₃ = 15; each ring carbon contributes one p electron, so there are 6 delocalised π electrons. A is the count for benzene. B gives the number of π bonds in a Kekulé structure (3), not the number of electrons. D also counts the three Kekulé π bonds as σ bonds.
items.why: Counting bonds and delocalised electrons was asked in Oct2022 Q10 (σ and π in benzene) and May2023 Q15 (anthracene); a substituted benzene with σ bonds outside the ring has not been used.

items.name: Delocalised model: p-orbital overlap and π bonds
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 18 Organic Chemistry - Arenes

items.question: Which row gives the C–C–C bond angle in benzene and the type of overlap of p orbitals that forms the delocalised π system? 109.5° and end-on overlap 109.5° and sideways overlap 120° and end-on overlap 120° and sideways overlap
items.ms: D: each carbon forms three σ bonds in a planar ring, so the angle is 120°; the p orbitals at right angles to the ring overlap sideways above and below the plane. 109.5° (A, B) is the angle for four σ bonds, as in cyclohexane. End-on (head-on) overlap (A, C) forms σ bonds, not π bonds.
items.why: Orbital-overlap MCQs came up in Oct2020, Jan2021, Oct2024 and Oct2025; pairing the overlap with the planar σ framework tests the part the Jan2024 examiner report says is usually missing.

items.name: Delocalised model: p-orbital overlap and π bonds
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 18 Organic Chemistry - Arenes
C18.2 - that the delocalised model f
items.question: Ethene, C₂H₄, and benzene, C₆H₆, both contain π bonding. Compare the way the π bonding forms in ethene with the way it forms in benzene. You may use labelled diagrams in your answer.
items.ms: in both, p orbitals (one on each carbon atom, at right angles to the plane of the σ bonds) overlap sideways in ethene, the p orbitals on only two carbon atoms overlap, forming one localised π bond (electron density above and below the C–C axis between those two atoms) in benzene, the p orbital on each of the six carbon atoms overlaps with those on both neighbouring carbon atoms forming a ring of delocalised π electron density (six electrons) above and below the plane of the ring
items.why: C18.2 has come up in 10/17 sessions as 'describe the bonding in benzene' (Jan2024 Q13(d), Jun2025 Q16(b)); a direct comparison with the localised π bond of an alkene has not been asked.

items.name: Resistance of benzene to bromination (delocalisation compared with localised π)
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 18 Organic Chemistry - Arenes
C18.3 - why benzene is resistant to
items.question: Benzene reacts with bromine in the presence of iron(III) bromide to form bromobenzene. It does not form the addition product 5,6-dibromocyclohexa-1,3-diene. Which is the best explanation for this? Addition reactions need a nucleophile, but bromine acts as an electrophile. Substitution keeps the delocalised π system, so the product is more stable than the addition product. The C–H bonds in benzene are weaker than its π bonds. Benzene has no π electrons available to attack an electrophile.
items.ms: B: substitution restores the delocalised ring (about 150 kJ mol⁻¹ of stabilisation) whereas addition would destroy it. A: alkenes add bromine by electrophilic addition, so addition does not need a nucleophile. C: the C–H bond breaks only after the electrophile has attacked, and C–H bonds are not weaker than π bonds. D: benzene has six delocalised π electrons and does attack electrophiles.
items.why: Jan2021 Q11 and Jan2026 Q13 asked why benzene needs a catalyst; the Jun2021 Q20(b) marking point 'substitution because the stable benzene ring is retained' has not been asked on its own.

items.name: Resistance of benzene to bromination (delocalisation compared with localised π)
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 18 Organic Chemistry - Arenes
C18.3 - why benzene is resistant to
items.question: Phenylethene, C₆H₅CH=CH₂, reacts rapidly with a solution of bromine in hexane at room temperature, in the dark and without a catalyst. Which describes this reaction? addition across the C=C bond in the side chain addition across a carbon–carbon bond in the ring substitution of a hydrogen atom on the ring substitution of a hydrogen atom in the side chain
items.ms: A: the side-chain C=C has localised π electron density, high enough to polarise Br₂, so bromine adds at once (electrophilic addition) to give C₆H₅CHBrCH₂Br. B: addition to the ring would destroy the stable delocalised system. C: substitution on the ring needs a halogen carrier such as FeBr₃. D: substitution in a side chain is a free-radical reaction that needs UV light.
items.why: C18.3 has come up in 9/17 sessions, always as benzene against cyclohexene or ethene; a molecule with a localised and a delocalised π system side by side has not been asked.

items.name: Resistance of benzene to bromination (delocalisation compared with localised π)
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry

items.question: Cyclohexa-1,4-diene, C₆H₈, has two separate C=C double bonds. Its skeletal formula is shown. Cyclohexa-1,4-diene decolourises bromine water immediately at room temperature. Benzene does not react with bromine water. Explain this difference in reactivity.
items.ms: in cyclohexa-1,4-diene the π electrons are localised in each C=C bond (between two carbon atoms), giving a high electron density that polarises / induces a dipole in Br₂ in benzene the π electrons are delocalised over six carbon atoms, so the electron density is lower and Br₂ is not polarised (enough) / the delocalised ring is very stable, so the activation energy is too high
items.why: Jan2021 Q11 and Jan2026 Q13 asked this comparison as MCQs using ethene; a six-membered diene with two isolated C=C bonds has not been used, and the Oct2023 report says localised electron density is the point usually missed.

items.question: Benzene burns in air with a very smoky flame, but hexane burns with a much cleaner flame. Which is the best explanation? Benzene molecules contain delocalised electrons, which are released as soot. Benzene has a much higher ratio of carbon atoms to hydrogen atoms, so not all of its carbon is oxidised. Benzene is a liquid at room temperature, but hexane is a gas. Benzene releases more energy per mole when it burns completely.
items.ms: B: C₆H₆ has a C : H ratio of 1 : 1 (hexane 1 : 2.3), so there is not enough oxygen to oxidise all the carbon and unburnt carbon forms soot. A: delocalised electrons are not released as soot. C: both are liquids at room temperature. D: hexane releases more energy per mole, and the energy released does not decide whether soot forms.

items.question: Ethylbenzene, C₆H₅CH₂CH₃, is converted industrially into phenylethene, the monomer for poly(phenylethene). In the laboratory, ethylbenzene can be made from benzene by a Friedel–Crafts reaction. Give the formula of the organic reagent and the name of the catalyst needed to make ethylbenzene from benzene. Write an equation for the reaction, using your reagent from (a)(i). The aluminium chloride must be anhydrous and the apparatus must be dry. Suggest why. The catalyst reacts with the organic reagent to form the electrophile. Write an equation for the formation of the electrophile. Explain, in terms of electrons, why aluminium chloride can remove a chloride ion from the organic reagent. When equal amounts in moles of benzene and the organic reagent are used, the product also contains diethylbenzenes, C₆H₄(CH₂CH₃)₂. Draw the skeletal formulae of the three isomers of diethylbenzene. Suggest how ethylbenzene could be separated from the diethylbenzenes. Suggest how the proportion of diethylbenzenes in the product could be reduced. In an experiment, 23.4 g of benzene reacted with an excess of the organic reagent. After purification, 20.1 g of ethylbenzene was obtained. Calculate the percentage yield of ethylbenzene. Industrially, ethylbenzene is made by reacting benzene with ethene in the presence of an acid catalyst, which supplies H⁺ ions. The electrophile is the same as in the laboratory method. Write an equation for the formation of the electrophile from ethene. Write an equation for the overall industrial reaction and explain why its atom economy is higher than that of the laboratory method.
items.ms: CH₃CH₂Cl / C₂H₅Cl aluminium chloride C₆H₆ + CH₃CH₂Cl → C₆H₅CH₂CH₃ + HCl aluminium chloride reacts with / is hydrolysed by water, so it would no longer form the electrophile / act as a catalyst CH₃CH₂Cl + AlCl₃ → CH₃CH₂⁺ + AlCl₄⁻ the Al atom in AlCl₃ has only six electrons in its outer shell, so it accepts a lone pair of electrons from Cl (forming a dative covalent bond in AlCl₄⁻) any two correct isomers (1,2-, 1,3- and 1,4-diethylbenzene) all three correct, with no repeats (fractional) distillation, because ethylbenzene has the lower boiling temperature use a (large) excess of benzene n(benzene) = 23.4 ÷ 78.0 = 0.300 mol n(ethylbenzene) = 20.1 ÷ 106.0 = 0.1896 mol / theoretical mass = 0.300 × 106.0 = 31.8 g percentage yield = 63.2% CH₂=CH₂ + H⁺ → CH₃CH₂⁺ C₆H₆ + CH₂=CH₂ → C₆H₅CH₂CH₃ all the atoms of the reactants end up in ethylbenzene (atom economy 100%), whereas the laboratory method also forms HCl as a by-product
items.why: Friedel–Crafts alkylation was asked in Jun2022, Jun2024, Oct2024 and Jan2025 (where chloroethane was wrongly given for chloromethane); multiple substitution, the dry catalyst and the industrial ethene route have not been asked.

items.question: In the mechanism for the nitration of benzene, where does the first curly arrow start and where does it end? It starts on the N atom of NO₂⁺ and ends on the delocalised ring. It starts on the delocalised ring and ends on the N atom of NO₂⁺. It starts on the delocalised ring and ends on an O atom of NO₂⁺. It starts on a C–H bond of benzene and ends on the N atom of NO₂⁺.
items.ms: B: the electron-rich delocalised ring donates a pair of electrons to the electron-deficient N atom, which carries the positive charge. A reverses the direction: the electrophile has no lone pair to donate. C: the arrow must go to the N atom (an error noted in the Jan2025 report). D: the C–H bond breaks in the second step, after the intermediate has formed.
items.why: An electrophilic substitution mechanism has been set in every session since 2020; the reports list arrows from the electrophile and arrows to O of NO₂⁺ among the commonest errors.

items.question: Which statement about the intermediate formed when NO₂⁺ attacks a benzene ring is correct? It contains six delocalised π electrons. It is a free radical. The positive charge is on the N atom of the NO₂ group. The carbon atom bonded to the NO₂ group has four bonds arranged tetrahedrally.
items.ms: D: the attacked carbon is bonded to H, NO₂ and two ring carbons, so it has four σ bonds (tetrahedral) and is no longer part of the delocalised system. A: only four π electrons remain delocalised, over five carbon atoms. B: it is a carbocation formed by heterolytic attack, with all electrons paired. C: the positive charge is on the ring (inside the horseshoe), not on the NO₂ group, an error noted in the Jan2023 report.
items.why: Oct2025 Q4(d) asked students to pick the structure of the intermediate; describing its features tests the same marking points (charge in the horseshoe, tetrahedral carbon) without a drawing.

items.question: Iodine monochloride, ICl, reacts with benzene in the presence of aluminium chloride. The organic product is iodobenzene, C₆H₅I. Explain why the electrophile is I⁺ and not Cl⁺. Write an equation for the formation of the electrophile.
items.ms: chlorine is more electronegative than iodine, so the I–Cl bond is polarised Iδ+–Clδ− and the chlorine (as Cl⁻) is transferred to AlCl₃, leaving I⁺ ICl + AlCl₃ → I⁺ + AlCl₄⁻
items.why: Electrophile-forming equations are in most C18.5 mark schemes, and unfamiliar electrophiles recur (HCO⁺ in Oct2022, the acylium ion in Oct2025); an interhalogen needing an electronegativity argument has not been set.

items.question: Nitrobenzene is made by warming benzene with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid, keeping the temperature between 50 °C and 55 °C. Most nitrobenzene is used to make dyes and polyurethanes. Write an equation for the formation of the electrophile from nitric acid and sulfuric acid. Explain the role of the concentrated sulfuric acid in this reaction. Draw the mechanism for the reaction of the electrophile with benzene. Explain why the temperature is kept between 50 °C and 55 °C. In a laboratory preparation, 15.0 cm³ of benzene gave 13.8 g of purified nitrobenzene. Density of benzene = 0.877 g cm⁻³ Calculate the percentage yield of nitrobenzene. The crude nitrobenzene is shaken with sodium carbonate solution in a separating funnel, then washed with water, dried and distilled. Explain why the crude product is shaken with sodium carbonate solution, and state what is seen. Name a suitable drying agent. Suggest why methylbenzene is not nitrated at 50–55 °C. Nitrobenzene can be nitrated further to 1,3-dinitrobenzene, but this needs a temperature of about 100 °C. The NO₂ group withdraws electron density from the ring. Suggest why a higher temperature is needed.
items.ms: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻ H₂SO₄ is the stronger acid, so it donates a proton (H⁺) to HNO₃, which then forms NO₂⁺ (and water) H₂SO₄ is regenerated at the end (H⁺ + HSO₄⁻ → H₂SO₄), so it acts as a catalyst curly arrow from on or within the hexagon (delocalised ring) to the N atom of NO₂⁺ intermediate: horseshoe over five carbon atoms with its gap facing the tetrahedral carbon, positive charge inside the horseshoe, and H and NO₂ on the same carbon curly arrow from the C–H bond into the ring (horseshoe) nitrobenzene and H⁺ as the products above 55 °C further substitution occurs / dinitrobenzene forms below 50 °C the rate is too slow mass of benzene = 15.0 × 0.877 = 13.155 g n(benzene) = 13.155 ÷ 78.0 = 0.1687 mol theoretical mass of nitrobenzene = 0.1687 × 123.0 = 20.74 g / n(nitrobenzene) = 13.8 ÷ 123.0 = 0.1122 mol percentage yield = 66.5% to remove / neutralise the acids (HNO₃ and H₂SO₄) left in the product effervescence / bubbles anhydrous calcium chloride / anhydrous magnesium sulfate / anhydrous sodium sulfate the methyl group releases / pushes electrons into the ring (positive inductive effect) so the ring has a higher electron density and attracts the electrophile / NO₂⁺ more readily it is more reactive, so at the higher temperature further nitration would occur (di- / trinitro products form) the ring in nitrobenzene has a lower electron density than benzene, so it attracts / polarises the electrophile less so the activation energy is higher and a higher temperature is needed for a reasonable rate

items.question: 4-Methylphenol is used in disinfectants. Its skeletal formula is shown. 4-Methylphenol reacts with excess bromine water at room temperature in the same way as phenol. The methyl group is not replaced. What is the organic product? 2,6-dibromo-4-methylphenol 2-bromo-4-methylphenol 3,5-dibromo-4-methylphenol 2,3,5,6-tetrabromo-4-methylphenol
items.ms: A: phenol is substituted at the 2-, 4- and 6-positions (next to and opposite the OH group). In 4-methylphenol the 4-position is already taken, so excess bromine water substitutes at the 2- and 6-positions. B: with excess bromine both free positions are substituted. C: the 3- and 5-positions are not substituted in phenol either. D: phenol gives a tribromo product, not substitution of every ring hydrogen.
items.why: Phenol with bromine water has come up in 13/17 sessions, always with phenol itself; applying the 2,4,6-pattern to a substituted phenol is the likeliest unfamiliar twist.

items.question: 2,4,6-Trichlorophenol has been used as an antiseptic and as a wood preservative. It can be made by reacting phenol with chlorine at room temperature. Benzene also reacts with chlorine, but only in the presence of a catalyst. Compare and contrast the reactions of chlorine with benzene and with phenol. Include equations in your answer and explain the difference in reactivity. In an experiment, 4.70 g of phenol reacted completely with chlorine gas and 8.39 g of 2,4,6-trichlorophenol was obtained. Calculate the minimum volume of chlorine, in dm³, measured at room temperature and pressure, needed for this reaction. items.ms: IC1 both are electrophilic substitution reactions: H atoms on the ring are replaced by Cl and the delocalised ring is kept IC2 benzene needs a halogen carrier such as AlCl₃ or FeCl₃ (and warming), which forms the electrophile: Cl₂ + AlCl₃ → Cl⁺ + AlCl₄⁻ IC3 one H is substituted in benzene: C₆H₆ + Cl₂ → C₆H₅Cl + HCl IC4 phenol reacts at room temperature without a catalyst and three H atoms are substituted: C₆H₅OH + 3Cl₂ → C₆H₂Cl₃OH + 3HCl IC5 a lone pair of electrons on the oxygen atom of phenol overlaps with / is delocalised into the π system of the ring IC6 so the ring in phenol has a higher electron density than benzene and it polarises Cl₂ / attracts the electrophile enough to react without a catalyst n(phenol) = 4.70 ÷ 94.0 = 0.0500 mol, so n(Cl₂) = 3 × 0.0500 = 0.150 mol volume = 0.150 × 24.0 = 3.60 dm³ M(C₆H₃Cl₃O) = 197.5 g mol⁻¹, so theoretical mass = 0.0500 × 197.5 = 9.875 g percentage yield = 8.39 ÷ 9.875 × 100 = 85.0% two peaks, because the two ring H atoms (at positions 3 and 5) are in the same environment and the OH hydrogen is in a different one area ratio 2 : 1 (ring H : OH) dipole on Cl₂ (Clδ+–Clδ−), curly arrow from on or within the ring to the Clδ+ atom and curly arrow from the Cl–Cl bond to Clδ− intermediate with H and Cl on the carbon opposite the OH group, a horseshoe facing that carbon and the positive charge inside the horseshoe (Cl⁻ also formed) curly arrow from the C–H bond into the ring, giving 4-chlorophenol and H⁺ (or HCl)

items.question: The phenol content of a disinfectant can be found by reacting the phenol with an excess of bromine and then finding the amount of bromine left over. Stage 1 10.0 cm³ of the disinfectant is diluted to 250.0 cm³ with distilled water in a volumetric flask. Stage 2 25.0 cm³ of the diluted solution is pipetted into a conical flask with a stopper. 50.0 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ potassium bromate(V), KBrO₃, an excess of potassium bromide and dilute sulfuric acid are added. The stopper is replaced and the flask is left for 15 minutes. Bromine forms: BrO₃⁻(aq) + 5Br⁻(aq) + 6H⁺(aq) → 3Br₂(aq) + 3H₂O(l) The bromine reacts with the phenol and some bromine is left over. Stage 3 An excess of potassium iodide solution is added. The bromine left over oxidises iodide ions to iodine. Stage 4 The iodine is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium thiosulfate solution. I₂(aq) + 2S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → 2I⁻(aq) + S₄O₆²⁻(aq) Suggest why an excess of potassium bromide is used in Stage 2. Calculate the amount, in moles, of bromine formed in Stage 2. Use standard electrode potentials from the Data Booklet to show that this reaction is feasible. Give the indicator used in Stage 4 and the colour change at the end point. items.ms: so that all the bromate(V) is converted into bromine / the amount of bromine formed is exactly three times the amount of BrO₃⁻ n(BrO₃⁻) = 0.0500 × 0.0200 = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol, so n(Br₂) = 3 × 1.00 × 10⁻³ = 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol C₆H₂Br₃OH / 2,4,6-tribromophenol as the organic product C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr a white precipitate forms the solution turns / stays yellow-orange (because bromine is in excess) Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂ E°(Br₂/Br⁻) = +1.09 V and E°(I₂/I⁻) = +0.54 V E°cell = +1.09 − (+0.54) = +0.55 V, which is positive, so the reaction is feasible starch blue-black to colourless mean titre = (22.40 + 22.45 + 22.35) ÷ 3 = 22.40 cm³ (rough titre excluded) n(S₂O₃²⁻) = 22.40 × 0.100 ÷ 1000 = 2.240 × 10⁻³ mol n(I₂) = n(Br₂ left over) = 1.120 × 10⁻³ mol n(Br₂) that reacted with phenol = 3.00 × 10⁻³ − 1.120 × 10⁻³ = 1.880 × 10⁻³ mol n(phenol) in 25.0 cm³ = 1.880 × 10⁻³ ÷ 3 = 6.267 × 10⁻⁴ mol n(phenol) in 10.0 cm³ of disinfectant = 6.267 × 10⁻⁴ × 10 = 6.267 × 10⁻³ mol concentration = 6.267 × 10⁻³ × 94.0 ÷ 0.0100 = 58.9 g dm⁻³ less bromine is left to oxidise the iodide ions, so less iodine forms and the titre is smaller so the amount of bromine that appears to have reacted with phenol is larger, and the calculated phenol concentration is too high

items.question: What is the systematic name of the compound with this skeletal formula? N-methylbutanamide N-methylpropanamide pentanamide N-butylmethanamide
items.ms: A: the C=O carbon is C1 of a four-carbon chain (butanamide) and the CH₃ group is bonded to the N atom (N-methyl). B does not count the C=O carbon in the chain. C counts the N-methyl carbon as part of the chain, but a chain cannot continue through the N atom; pentanamide is CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CONH₂. D swaps the two parts: N-butylmethanamide is HCONHCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃.
items.why: Naming amides from skeletal formulae recurs (Jun2025 Q7 N-butylethanamide, Jan2021 Q12 2-methylbutanamide); the Oct2023 examiners' report says IUPAC naming remains very challenging.

items.question: Phenylmethylamine, C₆H₅CH₂NH₂, is a much stronger base than phenylamine, C₆H₅NH₂. Which is the best explanation? The benzene ring in phenylmethylamine releases electrons to the nitrogen atom. In phenylmethylamine the CH₂ group separates the nitrogen atom from the ring, so its lone pair is not delocalised into the ring and is more available to accept a proton. The nitrogen atom in phenylmethylamine has two lone pairs of electrons. The N–H bonds in phenylmethylamine are weaker, so it releases hydrogen ions more easily.
items.ms: B: in phenylamine the nitrogen lone pair overlaps with the delocalised π electrons of the ring, so it is less available to accept H⁺; in phenylmethylamine the CH₂ group prevents this overlap, so it behaves like an alkylamine. A is wrong: the benzene ring does not push electron density onto the nitrogen. C is wrong: an amine nitrogen has one lone pair. D describes an acid (H⁺ donor), not a base (H⁺ acceptor).
items.why: Explaining the base strength of an aromatic amine recurs (Oct2020 Q22(b)(i), Jan2025 Q23(c), Jun2025 Q17(b)); applying the delocalisation argument to an amine whose N is not on the ring is a likely new angle.

items.question: Propylamine, CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂, and trimethylamine, (CH₃)₃N, are isomers. Propylamine boils at 48 °C and trimethylamine boils at 3 °C. Both are very soluble in water. Does trimethylamine form hydrogen bonds between its own molecules in the pure liquid, and with water molecules? own molecules: yes; water: yes own molecules: yes; water: no own molecules: no; water: yes own molecules: no; water: no
items.ms: C: trimethylamine has no H atom bonded to N, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other (hence the much lower boiling temperature than propylamine, whose N–H groups do); but the lone pair on its N atom accepts a hydrogen bond from an O–H group of water, so it dissolves. A and B ignore the missing N–H bond. D ignores the nitrogen lone pair, which is enough for a hydrogen bond with water.

The table shows the pH of aqueous solutions of three aromatic amines. Each solution has a concentration of 0.00500 mol dm⁻³. Suggest an explanation for the differences in pH. Refer to the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom.
items.ms: Hydrogen bond from an H atom of water (O–H) to the lone pair on the N atom of methylamine Hydrogen bond from the H atom of an N–H bond of methylamine to a lone pair on the O atom of water δ+ on the H atoms and δ− on the N and O atoms in the hydrogen bonds AND the hydrogen bond in line with the covalent bond (N···H–O and O···H–N about 180°) The long hydrocarbon chain / (CH₂)₅ section is non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water (only London forces) so the energy released when hexylamine mixes with water is not enough to break the hydrogen bonds between water molecules / the NH₂ group is a much smaller part of the molecule IC1 Make aqueous solutions of the same concentration (e.g. 0.10 mol dm⁻³) of each base, at the same temperature IC2 Measure the pH of each solution with a (calibrated) pH meter IC3 Expected order of pH: butylamine > ammonia > phenylamine; the higher the pH (the greater [OH⁻]), the stronger the base IC4 A base accepts a proton / H⁺ using the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom (forming RNH₃⁺ and OH⁻ ions) IC5 The butyl (alkyl) group is electron-releasing / has a positive inductive effect, so the electron density on the N increases and its lone pair is more available to accept a proton than in ammonia IC6 In phenylamine the N lone pair overlaps with / is delocalised into the π system of the benzene ring, so it is less available to accept a proton than in ammonia The higher the pH, the more OH⁻ ions are formed / the more the amine accepts protons from water, so the stronger the base The CH₃ group is electron-releasing (positive inductive effect), so the electron density on the N is greater and its lone pair is more available to accept a proton than in phenylamine The NO₂ group is electron-withdrawing / draws electron density from the ring and the N atom, so the lone pair is much less available to accept a proton
items.why: C19.3 has come up in 13 of 17 sessions (3.1% of marks); the Jun2025 6-mark explained base strength from given pH values, so the experiment that produces those values is the next angle, while hydrogen bonding with water (Oct2024, Jun2025) recurs and substituted aromatic amines extend the procaine and caffeine comparisons (Jan2025, Jan2021).

items.question: 4-Methylphenylamine is made by heating 1-methyl-4-nitrobenzene under reflux with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid. An excess of sodium hydroxide solution is then added and the amine is separated by steam distillation. Why is the sodium hydroxide solution added? to reduce any 1-methyl-4-nitrobenzene that has not reacted to react with the tin so that it can act as a catalyst again to make the amine more soluble in water so that it can be separated to convert 4-methylphenylammonium ions into 4-methylphenylamine

items.name: Diazotisation and azo coupling
path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 19 Organic Nitrogen Compounds Amines, Amides,

items.question: Benzenediazonium chloride is made by adding sodium nitrite solution to a solution of phenylamine in hydrochloric acid. The temperature is kept below 10 °C. Why is the temperature kept below 10 °C? Above about 10 °C the benzenediazonium ion decomposes, giving off nitrogen and forming phenol. The reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature gives a greater equilibrium yield of the diazonium ion. Above about 10 °C phenylamine would evaporate from the solution. The azo dye made in the next step decomposes above 10 °C.
items.ms: A: the diazonium ion is unstable; above about 10 °C it reacts with water, C₆H₅N₂⁺ + H₂O → C₆H₅OH + N₂ + H⁺, so the yield of dye falls. B: the temperature is not chosen to shift an equilibrium. C: phenylamine boils at 184 °C and is present as its salt in the acid. D: azo dyes are stable at room temperature, and no dye is present at this stage.
items.why: Diazotisation conditions appear in most C19.6 questions (Jan2025 Q9, Jun2025 Q19(a)); the reason for the low temperature has been asked only once (Oct2021 Q21(d)(v)).

items.question: The skeletal formula of an azo dye is shown. Which pair of compounds could be used to make this dye, by diazotising the first compound and then coupling the product with the second? 4-aminophenol and benzoic acid 4-aminobenzoic acid and phenol phenylamine and 4-hydroxybenzoic acid 4-nitrobenzoic acid and phenol
items.ms: B: 4-aminobenzoic acid forms the diazonium ion HOOCC₆H₄N₂⁺, which couples with phenol at the carbon atom opposite (para to) the OH group. A: benzoic acid has a deactivated ring with no OH or NH₂ group, so it does not couple. C: the benzenediazonium ion would couple with 4-hydroxybenzoic acid next to the OH group, giving a dye with OH and COOH on the same ring. D: a nitro compound does not form a diazonium ion; it must first be reduced to the amine.
items.why: Identifying the coupling partner from a dye structure recurs (Oct2024 Q7(c), Jun2025 Q17(d)(i), Oct2021 Q21(d)(iv)); deciding which half of the dye carries the diazonium group has not been asked.

items.question: Disperse Yellow 3 is an azo dye used to colour polyester fabrics. It can be made from phenylamine by the route shown. Steps I to III convert phenylamine into compound A. Give the name or formula of a reagent for Step I. Give the reagents for Step III. State the type of reaction in Step III. In Step IV, compound A is converted into the diazonium ion B. Give the reagents and the temperature for Step IV. Write an equation for the formation of the diazonium ion B from compound A. Use structural formulae for the organic species. In Step V, B couples with 4-methylphenol in alkaline solution. Coupling takes place at the carbon atom next to the OH group of 4-methylphenol. Draw the structure of Disperse Yellow 3. Phenol itself couples at the carbon atom opposite the OH group. Suggest why 4-methylphenol cannot couple at this position. Suggest why Step V is carried out in alkaline solution. In a preparation, 1.50 g of compound A (Mr = 150.0) gave 2.05 g of Disperse Yellow 3 (Mr = 269.0). Calculate the percentage yield. Disperse Yellow 3 can exist as two geometric (E/Z) isomers. Explain why. Methyl orange contains an –SO₃⁻Na⁺ group and dissolves in water. Disperse Yellow 3 is only very slightly soluble in water. Suggest why.
items.ms: ethanoyl chloride / CH₃COCl tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid / Sn and conc HCl reduction sodium nitrite / sodium nitrate(III) / NaNO₂ and hydrochloric acid / HCl between 0 °C and 10 °C / about 5 °C Formula of B: CH₃CONHC₆H₄N₂⁺ / CH₃CONH–C₆H₄–N⁺≡N CH₃CONHC₆H₄NH₂ + HNO₂ + H⁺ → CH₃CONHC₆H₄N₂⁺ + 2H₂O Azo group, –N=N–, joining the two benzene rings, with the CH₃CONH– group on the ring from B –N=N– on the carbon next to the OH group, with the CH₃ group opposite (para to) the OH group That carbon atom (position 4) is already bonded to the CH₃ group (so there is no H atom to be substituted) The OH⁻ ions convert 4-methylphenol into the phenoxide ion, whose ring has a greater electron density / is more reactive towards the (electrophilic) diazonium ion Moles of A = 1.50 ÷ 150.0 = 0.0100 mol, so maximum mass of dye = 0.0100 × 269.0 = 2.69 g Percentage yield = 2.05 ÷ 2.69 × 100 = 76.2% There is restricted rotation about the N=N double bond Each nitrogen atom of the N=N bond has two different groups (an aryl group and a lone pair), so the two aryl groups can be on the same side or on opposite sides of the double bond Disperse Yellow 3 has no ionic group (to be hydrated by water); most of the molecule (two benzene rings, CH₃ group) is non-polar, so it forms few hydrogen bonds with water
items.why: C19.6 carries 3.6% of the unit's marks (12 of 17 sessions), usually as a named dye's synthesis (methyl orange Jun2025, methyl red Jan2026); coupling to a phenol whose para position is blocked, an ethanoyl-protected amine and E/Z isomerism about N=N (last asked Oct2020) are untested angles.

items.question: Which of these would form a polyamide? hexane-1,6-diamine and ethanoyl chloride propenamide, CH₂=CHCONH₂, on its own ethane-1,2-diol and hexanedioyl dichloride butane-1,4-diamine and hexanedioyl dichloride

B: propenamide forms an addition polymer whose amide groups are side groups, not links in the main chain. C forms a polyester (ester links).

items.question: Nylon-6,10 can be made in the laboratory by the 'nylon rope' experiment shown. • 50.0 cm³ of an aqueous solution containing 0.0125 mol of hexane-1,6-diamine, H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂, and some sodium hydroxide is placed in a beaker. • A solution of 2.39 g of decanedioyl dichloride, ClOC(CH₂)₈COCl, in 50.0 cm³ of cyclohexane is poured carefully on top. • Nylon-6,10 forms where the two layers meet. It is pulled out as a continuous thread and wound onto a glass rod. Write the equation for the formation of nylon-6,10 in this experiment. Show the repeat unit of the polymer. State the type of polymerisation, giving a reason. Suggest why the polymer forms only at the boundary between the two layers, sodium hydroxide is added to the aqueous layer. After washing and drying, the mass of nylon-6,10 obtained was 1.97 g. Calculate the percentage yield. In industry, nylon-6,10 is made by heating hexane-1,6-diamine with decanedioic acid, HOOC(CH₂)₈COOH. Calculate the atom economy by mass for making nylon-6,10 by the laboratory method and by the industrial method. Base each calculation on one repeat unit formed from one molecule of each monomer. In the industrial method, the two monomers are first mixed in water at room temperature. They react to form a salt, which is then heated to form the polymer. Give the formula of this salt. Suggest why decanedioyl dichloride, rather than decanedioic acid, is used in the laboratory method. A sample of nylon-6,10 has an average relative molecular mass of 3.10 × 10⁴. Calculate the average number of repeat units in one polymer chain. Nylon-6,10 fibres are strong because of hydrogen bonds between the polymer chains. Draw a diagram to show a hydrogen bond between two nylon-6,10 chains. Show only the atoms close to the hydrogen bond, including lone pairs and relevant dipoles. Nylon-6,10 absorbs much less water than nylon-6,6 and is used for toothbrush bristles. Suggest why nylon-6,10 absorbs less water. Give the structures of the two organic products formed when nylon-6,10 is completely hydrolysed by heating with hydrochloric acid.
items.ms: Repeat unit –[NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₈CO]– with continuation bonds n H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂ + n ClOC(CH₂)₈COCl → –[NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₈CO]ₙ– + 2n HCl Condensation, because a small molecule (HCl) is eliminated as each link forms The diamine is in the aqueous layer and the diacyl dichloride is in the cyclohexane layer; the two liquids are immiscible, so the monomers meet only at the boundary To neutralise the HCl formed, which would otherwise react with / protonate the NH₂ groups of the diamine, so the diamine could no longer react (as a nucleophile) Mr of ClOC(CH₂)₈COCl = 239.0, so moles = 2.39 ÷ 239.0 = 0.0100 mol Decanedioyl dichloride is the limiting reagent (0.0100 mol < 0.0125 mol of diamine) Mr of repeat unit C₁₆H₃₀N₂O₂ = 282.0, so maximum mass = 0.0100 × 282.0 = 2.82 g Percentage yield = 1.97 ÷ 2.82 × 100 = 69.9% Laboratory: 282.0 ÷ (116.0 + 239.0) × 100 = 79.4% Industrial: 282.0 ÷ (116.0 + 202.0) × 100 = 88.7% ⁺H₃N(CH₂)₆NH₃⁺ ⁻OOC(CH₂)₈COO⁻ The acyl chloride is much more reactive, so it forms amide links rapidly with the diamine at room temperature (the acid only forms a salt unless it is heated strongly) 3.10 × 10⁴ ÷ 282.0 = 110 Hydrogen bond from the H of an N–H group in one chain to a lone pair on the O of a C=O group in the other chain δ+ on H and δ− on O (and N), with N–H···O about 180° Nylon-6,10 has fewer amide groups per unit length / per unit mass of chain (longer (CH₂)₈ sections) so there are fewer N–H and C=O groups to form hydrogen bonds with water molecules HOOC(CH₂)₈COOH ⁺H₃N(CH₂)₆NH₃⁺ (2Cl⁻)
items.why: C19.8 has appeared in 16 of 17 sessions; nylon-6,10 (Oct2024 Q11) and nylon monomers (May2023 Q24(c)) recur, and the spec's suggested practical (preparing nylon-6,10) has never been examined, so a Section C question on it with yield, atom economy and hydrogen bonding is a strong prediction.
