items.question: Poly(propenamide) is used in water treatment and as a soil conditioner. What is the repeat unit of poly(propenamide)? –CH₂–CH(CONH₂)– –CH₂–CH₂–CO–NH– –CH=C(CONH₂)– –CH₂–CH(CONH₂)–CH₂–
items.ms: A: the C=C of propenamide, CH₂=CHCONH₂, opens and its two carbon atoms become the main chain, with CONH₂ as a side group. B puts the amide group into the main chain, as in a condensation polyamide. C keeps a C=C double bond, which is used up in addition polymerisation. D includes an extra carbon atom; the repeat unit has only the two carbon atoms of the C=C.
items.why: Repeat-unit MCQs recur in 19.9 (Jun2025 Q10, Jan2025 Q14 poly(ethenol), Oct2024 Q11); poly(propenamide), named in the spec, has not had its repeat unit asked and the Jun2023 report found extra carbon atoms at the continuation bonds.

items.question: Liquid-detergent capsules (liquitabs) are sealed in a thin film of poly(ethenol). The film dissolves when a capsule is put into the water in a washing machine. Plastic bags made of poly(ethene) do not dissolve in water. Explain why poly(ethenol) dissolves in water but poly(ethene) does not.
items.ms: Poly(ethenol) has (many) OH groups (on alternate carbon atoms of the chain), which form hydrogen bonds with water molecules Poly(ethene) is non-polar / has only C–H bonds, so it forms only London forces with water, which cannot replace the hydrogen bonds between water molecules The energy released by hydrogen bonding of poly(ethenol) with water compensates for breaking the hydrogen bonds between poly(ethenol) chains
items.why: C19.10 is cool (4 of 17 sessions); poly(ethenol) laundry bags appeared only as an MCQ (Jun2025 Q14) and the spec's own example, liquid-detergent capsules, has never been asked.

items.question: Solutions of four amino acids are placed in turn in a polarimeter. Each amino acid that has optical isomers is present as a single optical isomer. Which solution does not rotate the plane of plane-polarised monochromatic light? 2-aminobutanoic acid, CH₃CH₂CH(NH₂)COOH 2-amino-2-methylpropanoic acid, (CH₃)₂C(NH₂)COOH 2-amino-3-hydroxypropanoic acid, HOCH₂CH(NH₂)COOH 2-amino-4-methylpentanoic acid, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH(NH₂)COOH
items.ms: B: C2 carries two identical CH₃ groups, so the molecule has no chiral carbon atom and no optical isomers; its solution does not rotate the plane of polarisation. A, C and D each have a chiral C2 (bonded to H, NH₂, COOH and a different R group), so a single optical isomer rotates the plane. In D the carbon atom bonded to two CH₃ groups is not chiral, but C2 is.

items.question: Aspartic acid, HOOCCH₂CH(NH₂)COOH, has Mr = 133.0. A solution containing 0.665 g of aspartic acid is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide solution until all the aspartic acid has been converted into the ion ⁻OOCCH₂CH(NH₂)COO⁻. What volume of the sodium hydroxide solution is needed? 25.0 cm³ 50.0 cm³ 100 cm³ 150 cm³
items.ms: C: n(aspartic acid) = 0.665 ÷ 133.0 = 0.00500 mol; two H⁺ ions are removed from each molecule (from the two COOH groups, or from COOH and NH₃⁺ in the zwitterion), so n(NaOH) = 0.0100 mol and V = 0.0100 ÷ 0.100 = 0.100 dm³ = 100 cm³. A uses the 1 : 2 ratio the wrong way round. B removes only one H⁺. D counts three acidic H atoms (two COOH groups and the NH₃⁺ group of the zwitterion).
items.why: The acid–base behaviour of amino acids is asked almost every session (aspartic acid at pH 12 May2024, serine with NaOH Oct2024); linking it to a titration calculation has not been asked.

items.question: Glutamic acid is an amino acid found in proteins. Its skeletal formula is shown. Monosodium glutamate (MSG), a flavour enhancer, is a sodium salt of glutamic acid. Give the systematic name of glutamic acid. Draw the structure of the zwitterion of glutamic acid. Glutamic acid decomposes at about 200 °C without melting. Pentanedioic acid, HOOC(CH₂)₃COOH, melts at 98 °C. Explain this difference. Draw the structures of the organic species present in a solution of glutamic acid at pH 1 and in a solution at pH 13. Glutamic acid made by bacterial fermentation is a single optical isomer. Glutamic acid made by a chemical synthesis is a racemic mixture. Describe how a polarimeter could be used to show which of two unlabelled solutions of glutamic acid was made by fermentation. Explain the results. Glutamic acid and glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH, form a dipeptide. The COOH group on the same carbon atom as the NH₂ group of glutamic acid forms the peptide link. Draw the structure of this dipeptide. Show the peptide link as a displayed formula. The dipeptide is heated with hydrochloric acid until it is completely hydrolysed. Give the structures of the two organic products in the acidic mixture. The MSG content of a seasoning powder was found. The only nitrogen compound in the powder is MSG, C₅H₈NO₄Na·H₂O (Mr = 187.0). • 2.50 g of the powder was heated with concentrated sulfuric acid, which converted all the nitrogen into ammonium ions. • The mixture was made alkaline and all the ammonia released was passed into 50.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid (an excess). • The remaining acid needed 21.30 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide solution for neutralisation. Calculate the percentage by mass of MSG in the powder.
items.ms: 2-aminopentanedioic acid HOOCCH₂CH₂CH(NH₃⁺)COO⁻ Glutamic acid exists as zwitterions, so there are strong (ionic) attractions between the NH₃⁺ and COO⁻ groups of neighbouring molecules Pentanedioic acid has only hydrogen bonds and London forces between its molecules, which are weaker / need less energy to overcome pH 1: HOOCCH₂CH₂CH(NH₃⁺)COOH pH 13: ⁻OOCCH₂CH₂CH(NH₂)COO⁻ Pass plane-polarised monochromatic light (e.g. from a sodium lamp through a polariser) through each solution in turn Turn the analyser to find the angle of rotation of the plane of polarisation, compared with a tube of water / the solvent The solution from fermentation rotates the plane of polarisation (it is optically active) The racemic mixture gives no (overall) rotation, because it contains equal amounts of the two enantiomers, which rotate the plane by equal amounts in opposite directions Peptide link displayed: –C(=O)–N(–H)– (C=O and N–H shown) Rest of the dipeptide correct: HOOCCH₂CH₂CH(NH₂)CONHCH₂COOH HOOCCH₂CH₂CH(NH₃⁺)COOH ⁺H₃NCH₂COOH n(HCl) at the start = 50.0 × 0.100 ÷ 1000 = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol n(HCl) left = n(NaOH) = 21.30 × 0.100 ÷ 1000 = 2.13 × 10⁻³ mol n(NH₃) = 5.00 × 10⁻³ − 2.13 × 10⁻³ = 2.87 × 10⁻³ mol = n(MSG) (one N per formula unit) Mass of MSG = 2.87 × 10⁻³ × 187.0 = 0.537 g Percentage = 0.537 ÷ 2.50 × 100 = 21.5%

Topic 19 Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides,
C19.12 - CORE PRACTICAL 15 Analysis of some inorganic
items.question: A technician has two unlabelled samples, X and Y. X is a white crystalline inorganic salt. Y is a white crystalline organic solid that melts at 44 °C. The table shows the results of tests on X and Y. Identify X. Justify your answer using the results of Tests 1, 2 and 4. The purity of a sample of X was found by titration. • 0.435 g of X was dissolved in water and the solution was made up to 100.0 cm³. • This solution was added from a burette to 25.0 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ potassium manganate(VII) solution acidified with dilute sulfuric acid, until the purple colour just disappeared. • The mean titre was 20.30 cm³. In acidic solution, 2 mol of manganate(VII) ions react with 5 mol of X. Calculate the percentage purity by mass of X. Use your answer to (a). Deduce the structure of Y. Explain how you use each piece of information from Tests 3, 4 and 5.
items.ms: sodium nitrite / sodium nitrate(III) / NaNO₂ Yellow flame shows Na⁺ (Test 1) AND the anion is nitrite because X forms nitrous acid with the hydrochloric acid, which converts the aromatic amine into a diazonium ion that couples with phenol (Test 4) / because X is a reducing agent that decolourises manganate(VII) (Test 2) n(MnO₄⁻) = 25.0 × 0.0200 ÷ 1000 = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol n(X) in the titre = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ × 5 ÷ 2 = 1.250 × 10⁻³ mol n(X) in 100.0 cm³ = 1.250 × 10⁻³ × 100.0 ÷ 20.30 = 6.158 × 10⁻³ mol Mass of NaNO₂ = 6.158 × 10⁻³ × 69.0 = 0.4249 g, so purity = 0.4249 ÷ 0.435 × 100 = 97.7% Test 3: Y is a base / an amine; it reacts with HCl to form a soluble ionic salt, and NaOH releases the amine again Test 4: an azo dye forms, so Y is a primary aromatic amine (NH₂ group on a benzene ring) m/z = 107: C₆H₄NH₂ accounts for 92, so there is also a CH₃ group on the ring / molecular formula C₇H₉N 5 peaks in the ¹³C NMR spectrum fits 4-methylphenylamine; 2- and 3-methylphenylamine would each give 7 peaks Structure: CH₃C₆H₄NH₂ with the CH₃ and NH₂ groups opposite each other (1,4) on the ring
items.why: Core Practical 15 (C19.12) has never had its own question; Jun2022 Q14(b) and Oct2021 Q18(a) show the likely form, deducing an inorganic and an organic unknown from test results, here linked to the azo-dye test (19.6), a redox titration (16.15) and spectra (20.1).

path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 20 Organic Synthesis
C20.1 - deduce the empirical formula
items.question: 10 cm³ of a gaseous hydrocarbon was mixed with 80 cm³ of oxygen, an excess, and exploded. After cooling to room temperature, the volume of gas was 60 cm³. The volume decreased to 30 cm³ when the gas was passed through aqueous sodium hydroxide. All volumes were measured at the same temperature and pressure. What is the molecular formula of the hydrocarbon? C₃H₄ C₃H₆ C₃H₈ C₄H₈
items.ms: C: the sodium hydroxide absorbs 60 − 30 = 30 cm³ of CO₂, so each molecule has 3 C atoms. The 30 cm³ left is unused oxygen, so 80 − 30 = 50 cm³ of oxygen was used: x + y/4 = 5 gives y = 8 (C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O). A (C₃H₄) and B (C₃H₆) have the right number of carbon atoms but would use only 40 cm³ and 45 cm³ of oxygen; B comes from treating the 30 cm³ contraction on cooling as the volume of water vapour alone. D would give 40 cm³ of CO₂ and use 60 cm³ of oxygen.
items.why: Combustion data are the commonest C20.1 item (MCQs in Jan2021, Jan2025, Jun2025 and Jan2026); the gas-volume version was set as structured parts in Oct2020 and Jan2021 but never as an MCQ.

items.question: The mass spectrum of compound X has peaks in the molecular ion region at m/z = 112, 114 and 116, with relative heights 9 : 6 : 1. Which compound could be X? 1,2-dichloropropane, C₃H₆Cl₂ 1,2-dichloroethane, C₂H₄Cl₂ chlorobenzene, C₆H₅Cl 1,1,1-trichloroethane, C₂H₃Cl₃
items.ms: A: two chlorine atoms (³⁵Cl : ³⁷Cl = 3 : 1) give M, M+2 and M+4 peaks in the ratio 9 : 6 : 1, and C₃H₆³⁵Cl₂ has m/z = 36 + 6 + 70 = 112. B has the right 9 : 6 : 1 pattern but at m/z 98, 100 and 102. C has m/z 112 but only one chlorine atom, so it gives two peaks (112 and 114) in the ratio 3 : 1. D has three chlorine atoms, giving four peaks starting at m/z 132.
items.why: Chlorine isotope patterns were examined in Jun2024 Q15(d), where about 75% of candidates failed; mass spectra appear in about a third of sessions.

items.question: Benzocaine is a local anaesthetic used in throat lozenges. It contains carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen and oxygen only. Its composition by mass is: C 65.5%, H 6.7%, N 8.5%, O 19.4%. The molecular ion peak in the mass spectrum of benzocaine is at m/z = 165. Determine the molecular formula of benzocaine. You must show your working.
items.ms: Divides each percentage by the relative atomic mass: C 65.5 ÷ 12.0 = 5.46, H 6.7 ÷ 1.0 = 6.7, N 8.5 ÷ 14.0 = 0.607, O 19.4 ÷ 16.0 = 1.21 Ratio 9 : 11 : 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is C₉H₁₁NO₂; its Mr is 165, the same as the molecular ion, so the molecular formula is C₉H₁₁NO₂
items.why: Formulae from percentage composition recur in 8 of 17 papers (e.g. Jan2025 Q20(b), Jun2025 Q19(b)); linking the empirical formula to the molecular ion uses the mass-spectrum skill in the same spec point.

items.question: Compound P is used as a flavouring and has a sweet smell like hawthorn blossom. P contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. When 1.80 g of P was burned completely in excess oxygen, 4.75 g of carbon dioxide and 1.08 g of water were formed. Determine the empirical formula of P. You must show your working. The molecular ion peak in the mass spectrum of P is at m/z = 150. Deduce the molecular formula of P. P forms an orange precipitate with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine but gives no silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. The infrared spectrum of P has a strong absorption at 1685 cm⁻¹ and no broad absorption between 3750 cm⁻¹ and 2500 cm⁻¹. Explain what this information shows about the functional groups in P. The table gives the high-resolution proton NMR data for P. The ¹³C NMR spectrum of P has seven peaks. Deduce the structure of P. Draw the structure in the box and explain how you used the NMR data. The mass spectrum of P has a large peak at m/z = 43. Give the formula of the species responsible for this peak. P reacts with methylmagnesium iodide in dry ether. The product is then hydrolysed with dilute acid to form compound Q. Draw the structure of Q.
items.ms: Mass of C = 4.75 × 12.0 ÷ 44.0 = 1.295 g (or moles of C = 4.75 ÷ 44.0 = 0.1080) Mass of H = 1.08 × 2.0 ÷ 18.0 = 0.120 g (or moles of H = 2 × 1.08 ÷ 18.0 = 0.120) Mass of O = 1.80 − 1.295 − 0.120 = 0.385 g, so moles of O = 0.385 ÷ 16.0 = 0.0240 C : H : O = 0.1080 : 0.120 : 0.0240 = 4.5 : 5 : 1, so the empirical formula is C₉H₁₀O₂ Mr of C₉H₁₀O₂ = 150, so the molecular formula is C₉H₁₀O₂ P has a C=O group: orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH / absorption at 1685 cm⁻¹ P is a ketone and not an aldehyde, because it does not react with Tollens' reagent No O–H group, so P is not an alcohol, phenol or carboxylic acid (no broad O–H absorption) So the second oxygen atom is not in an OH group, and not in an ester (an ester C=O absorbs at 1750–1735 cm⁻¹ and gives no precipitate with 2,4-DNPH): it is in an ether, C–O–C, group Peaks at 6.9 and 7.9 ppm, total area 4: four H atoms on a benzene ring, so the ring has two substituents (C₆H₄) 3.9 ppm, area 3, singlet: a CH₃ group bonded to oxygen (CH₃–O) with no H atoms on the adjacent atom 2.6 ppm, area 3, singlet: a CH₃ group next to C=O (CH₃–C=O) with no H atoms on the adjacent atom Seven carbon environments (or two ring peaks each of area 2) means the molecule is symmetrical, so the two groups are on carbons 1 and 4 of the ring (the 1,2- and 1,3-isomers have nine carbon environments) Structure: CH₃O–C₆H₄–COCH₃ with the groups in the 1,4-positions, 1-(4-methoxyphenyl)ethanone CH₃CO⁺ CH₃O–C₆H₄–C(CH₃)₂OH, 1,4-substituted: 2-(4-methoxyphenyl)propan-2-ol
items.why: Combustion data followed by spectra to identify an unknown has come up in Jan2022, Jun2022, Jan2023 and Oct2025; counting ¹³C environments to fix 1,4-substitution echoes Oct2021, and the Grignard follow-on links C20.2.

path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry
Topic 20 Organic Synthesis
C20.2 - methods of increasing the le
items.question: Grignard reagents react with carbonyl compounds, and the products are then hydrolysed with dilute acid to form alcohols. Which alcohol cannot be made in this way? methanol ethanol propan-2-ol 2-methylpropan-2-ol
items.ms: A: the Grignard reagent always adds an alkyl (or aryl) group to the carbonyl carbon, forming a new C–C bond, so the alcohol has at least two carbon atoms; methanol has one. B: CH₃MgBr + methanal; C: CH₃MgBr + ethanal; D: CH₃MgBr + propanone (a ketone gives a tertiary alcohol).
items.why: Grignard + carbonyl MCQs recur (Oct2020 Q11, Jan2023 Q12, May2023 Q20); asking which alcohol is impossible tests the C–C bond-forming idea from the other direction.

items.question: Ethylmagnesium bromide reacts rapidly with water, which is why Grignard reactions are carried out in dry ether. What is the organic product of the reaction of ethylmagnesium bromide with water? butane ethane ethanol ethene
items.ms: B: the ethyl group takes H⁺ from water: CH₃CH₂MgBr + H₂O → CH₃CH₃ + Mg(OH)Br, so the reagent is destroyed. A would need two ethyl groups to join. C: water gives no C–O bond; an alcohol forms only after reaction with a carbonyl compound followed by hydrolysis. D is an elimination product, which is not formed.
items.why: Dry ether is demanded in every Grignard mark scheme and the Jan2025 and Jan2024 examiner reports say candidates did not understand why; the reaction with water itself has never been asked.

It can be made by reacting a Grignard reagent with a carbonyl compound in dry ether, followed by hydrolysis with dilute acid. Give the structural formulae of the Grignard reagent and of the carbonyl compound used to make 3-methylbutan-1-ol.
items.ms: Grignard reagent: (CH₃)₂CHCH₂MgBr Carbonyl compound: HCHO / methanal

items.question: Valproic acid, 2-propylpentanoic acid, is used to treat epilepsy. The diagram shows a laboratory synthesis of valproic acid from 1-bromopropane. Write the equation for the reaction in Step 1. The C–Mg bond in a Grignard reagent is polar. Explain why the carbon atom bonded to magnesium acts as a nucleophile in Step 2. Identify compound X. Give the reagent for Step 3. Give the reagents for Step 5. In one preparation, 20.0 g of 1-bromopropane gave 6.95 g of valproic acid, C₈H₁₆O₂. Calculate the overall percentage yield. Deduce the number of peaks in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of valproic acid.
items.ms: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + Mg → CH₃CH₂CH₂MgBr Magnesium is less electronegative than carbon, so the carbon atom is δ− / has a high electron density so it is attracted to and forms a bond with (donates a pair of electrons to) the δ+ carbon atom of the C=O group in X butanal / CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO phosphorus(V) chloride / PCl₅ carbon dioxide / CO₂ (gas or solid) then dilute acid, e.g. HCl(aq) or H₂SO₄(aq), added after the reaction with CO₂ Moles of 1-bromopropane = 20.0 ÷ 122.9 = 0.1627 Moles of valproic acid = 6.95 ÷ 144.0 = 0.04826 (one mole of valproic acid forms from one mole of 1-bromopropane) Percentage yield = 0.04826 ÷ 0.1627 × 100 = 29.7% 5
items.why: Grignard routes ending with CO₂ then dilute acid are the commonest long C20.2 item (Jan2022, Oct2023, Jan2025, Jan2026); the polarity of the C–Mg bond has only been an MCQ (Oct2022), and a route using two Grignard steps has not been set.

items.question: Triphenylmethanol, (C₆H₅)₃COH, can be prepared in the laboratory from bromobenzene, C₆H₅Br, and benzophenone, (C₆H₅)₂CO. Stage 1 Magnesium turnings, dry ethoxyethane (ether) and bromobenzene are heated gently under reflux, using the apparatus shown, to form phenylmagnesium bromide. Stage 2 A solution of benzophenone in dry ether is added slowly to the cooled mixture. The mixture is then poured onto ice and dilute sulfuric acid. The ether layer is separated and dried, and the ether is distilled off to leave crude triphenylmethanol. Write the equation for the formation of phenylmagnesium bromide in Stage 1. Explain the purpose of the drying tube containing anhydrous calcium chloride. Ether boils at 35 °C. Explain why the mixture in Stage 1 is heated under reflux. Stage 2 Name the type of reaction between phenylmagnesium bromide and benzophenone. Give one reason why the mixture is poured onto ice and dilute sulfuric acid. In one preparation, 2.50 cm³ of bromobenzene (density 1.50 g cm⁻³) was used in Stage 1 and 3.64 g of benzophenone was added in Stage 2. The mass of triphenylmethanol obtained was 3.90 g. Assume that all the bromobenzene was converted into phenylmagnesium bromide and that the magnesium was in excess. Show that benzophenone is the limiting reagent and calculate the percentage yield of triphenylmethanol. Biphenyl, C₆H₅–C₆H₅, forms as a by-product in Stage 1 when some phenylmagnesium bromide reacts with unreacted bromobenzene. Write an equation for the formation of biphenyl. Biphenyl is very soluble in hexane, but triphenylmethanol is almost insoluble in cold hexane. Explain why the crude product is washed with a small volume of cold hexane. The washed solid is then purified by recrystallisation. Describe how this is carried out and explain how it removes impurities. The recrystallised sample melted between 156 °C and 160 °C. Pure triphenylmethanol melts at 162 °C. Comment on the purity of the sample. Explain how the infrared spectrum of the product would show that benzophenone has been converted into triphenylmethanol. Benzophenone and triphenylmethanol both have five peaks in their ¹³C NMR spectra. Explain why triphenylmethanol has only five peaks.
items.ms: C₆H₅Br + Mg → C₆H₅MgBr It stops water vapour in the air from entering the apparatus (the calcium chloride absorbs water) Water would react with (destroy) the Grignard reagent, forming benzene, so the yield would be lower The vapour of the ether (and bromobenzene) condenses and runs back into the flask, so the mixture can be heated for a long time without losing the volatile solvent or reactant nucleophilic addition To hydrolyse the magnesium-containing intermediate, (C₆H₅)₃COMgBr, to the alcohol / to provide H⁺ to form the OH group To dissolve the magnesium salts and remove unreacted magnesium, so the organic layer can be separated The ice absorbs the heat released by the (exothermic) hydrolysis / reaction with acid, so the ether does not boil away Moles of bromobenzene = 2.50 × 1.50 ÷ 156.9 = 0.02390, so 0.02390 mol of C₆H₅MgBr Moles of benzophenone = 3.64 ÷ 182.0 = 0.0200; this is less than 0.0239 and they react 1 : 1, so benzophenone is limiting Maximum mass of triphenylmethanol = 0.0200 × 260.0 = 5.20 g Percentage yield = 3.90 ÷ 5.20 × 100 = 75.0% C₆H₅MgBr + C₆H₅Br → C₆H₅C₆H₅ + MgBr₂ The biphenyl dissolves and is washed away, but very little triphenylmethanol dissolves (cold, small volume), so little product is lost Dissolve the solid in the minimum volume of hot solvent Filter the hot solution to remove insoluble impurities Cool the filtrate so that triphenylmethanol crystallises; the soluble impurities (present in small amounts) stay in solution Filter (under reduced pressure), wash the crystals with a little cold solvent and dry them It is still impure (or damp), because it melts below 162 °C and over a range of temperature No (strong) absorption in the range 1700–1680 cm⁻¹, so there is no C=O (ketone) group left A (broad) absorption in the range 3750–3200 cm⁻¹ shows that the O–H group of the alcohol is present The three phenyl groups are equivalent (in identical environments) Each phenyl group has four carbon environments (the carbon bonded to the central carbon, two ortho, two meta and one para carbon), plus the central C–OH carbon, making five
items.why: Every Grignard mark scheme insists on dry conditions and the Jan2025 report says candidates do not know why; a whole Grignard preparation with limiting reagent, purification and spectra has not been set and links C20.2 with the techniques in C20.5.

items.question: Sulcatone, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₂CH₂COCH₃, is found in the odour of human skin. It can be converted in one step into sulcatol, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₂CH₂CH(OH)CH₃, an insect pheromone. Which reagent should be used? acidified potassium dichromate(VI) hydrogen with a nickel catalyst lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III) in dry ether tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid
items.ms: C: LiAlH₄ reduces the C=O group of the ketone to CH–OH but does not react with the C=C bond. A is an oxidising agent, so no alcohol forms; B would also add hydrogen across the C=C bond; D reduces aromatic nitro compounds to amines and is not used to reduce ketones.
items.why: Choosing a reagent that changes one functional group and leaves another was examined in Oct2024 Q19(d) and Jan2024 Q15(b).

items.question: A reaction mixture in ethoxyethane (ether) must be heated under reflux. The table gives hazard data for ethoxyethane. Which is the most appropriate way to heat the flask? a Bunsen burner with a small flame, in a fume cupboard an electric hotplate with its surface at 300 °C a sand bath at 200 °C on an electric heater a water bath at 50 °C, warmed beforehand, with no flames in the laboratory
items.ms: D: 50 °C is above the boiling temperature, so the ether boils and refluxes, but it is far below the autoignition temperature and there is no flame to ignite the dense vapour as it spreads along the bench. A: any flame can ignite the vapour (flash point −45 °C), even in a fume cupboard. B and C: surfaces at 300 °C and 200 °C are above the autoignition temperature, so the vapour can ignite without a flame.
items.why: C20.3(iv), control measures from hazard data, has only been asked as a hazard-symbol tick box (Jun2024 Q19(a), about 25% scored); using numerical hazard data has never been set.

items.question: 2-Phenylethylamine, C₆H₅CH₂CH₂NH₂, occurs naturally in chocolate. Two routes for making it in the laboratory are shown. Step 5 uses a reaction that is not in your specification. It converts an amide into a primary amine with one fewer carbon atom: RCONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH → RNH₂ + Na₂CO₃ + 2NaBr + 2H₂O Route 1 Give the structure of A and name the type of reaction in Step 1. Write an equation for Step 2. Use [H] to represent the reducing agent. Route 2 Give the reagent for Step 3 and the structure of B. Give the reagent for Step 4 and the structure of C. Calculate the atom economy by mass for Step 5. Compare Route 1 and Route 2. In your answer, use the hazard data in the table and other factors that chemists consider when choosing a synthetic route. 2-Phenylethylamine is a weak base. Write an equation for the reaction of 2-phenylethylamine with hydrochloric acid. Suggest why the product in (e)(i) is much more soluble in water than 2-phenylethylamine.
items.ms: A: C₆H₅CH₂CN nucleophilic substitution C₆H₅CH₂CN + 4[H] → C₆H₅CH₂CH₂NH₂ phosphorus(V) chloride / PCl₅ B: C₆H₅CH₂CH₂COCl (concentrated) ammonia / NH₃ C: C₆H₅CH₂CH₂CONH₂ Sum of Mr of reactants = 149.0 + 159.8 + (4 × 40.0) = 468.8 Atom economy = 121.0 ÷ 468.8 × 100 = 25.8% IC1 Route 1 has two steps but Route 2 has three, so Route 1 is likely to give a higher overall yield (losses at each step) and needs fewer separations IC2 Route 1 uses potassium cyanide, which is very toxic: wear gloves, use a fume cupboard and keep it away from acids, which would release hydrogen cyanide IC3 Step 2 needs dry conditions because LiAlH₄ reacts violently with water releasing flammable hydrogen, and no naked flames because the ether is extremely flammable IC4 Route 2 uses phosphorus(V) chloride (corrosive, gives HCl fumes) and bromine (very toxic, corrosive), so it also needs a fume cupboard and gloves; it avoids cyanide IC5 Step 5 has a low atom economy (25.8%), so Route 2 produces much more waste (sodium carbonate, sodium bromide) IC6 Route 1 adds a carbon atom (7 C to 8 C) while Route 2 removes one (9 C to 8 C), so the choice also depends on the cost and availability of the starting materials / a justified overall conclusion C₆H₅CH₂CH₂NH₂ + HCl → C₆H₅CH₂CH₂NH₃⁺Cl⁻ The product is ionic and its ions are strongly attracted to (hydrated by) polar water molecules, whereas the amine has a large non-polar part (benzene ring and chain)
items.why: Planning routes appears in most sessions and comparing routes was set in Jun2024 Q15(c) and the Jan2024 6-mark answer on hazards and atom economy; using an unfamiliar reaction given in the stem (spec 20.3(ii)) has not yet been set.

path: Unit 5 Transition Metals and Organic Nitrogen Chemistry

items.question: Ibuprofen is a painkiller. It is manufactured from 2-methylpropylbenzene by the three-step BHC process shown. Give the molecular formula of ibuprofen. Step 1 is a Friedel–Crafts acylation. In Step 1, hydrogen fluoride reacts with ethanoic anhydride to form the electrophile, CH₃CO⁺. Write an equation for this reaction. Suggest one advantage of using ethanoic anhydride, rather than ethanoyl chloride, in the industrial process. Step 2 uses hydrogen and a Raney nickel catalyst. Draw the structure of L. Raney nickel is a heterogeneous catalyst. State what is meant by the term heterogeneous. Suggest why hydrogen and nickel are used for Step 2 in industry, rather than lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III). State the atom economy of Step 3. Justify your answer. Atom economy is one measure of the sustainability of a process. Calculate the atom economy by mass of the whole BHC process. Assume that the ethanoic acid formed in Step 1 is a waste product. The older Boots process makes ibuprofen in six steps, with an atom economy of 40.0%. Give two reasons why the BHC process is more sustainable than the Boots process. A plant uses 5.00 tonnes of 2-methylpropylbenzene, C₁₀H₁₄, each day. The overall yield of ibuprofen is 85.0%. Calculate the number of 200 mg ibuprofen tablets that can be made from one day's production. [1 tonne = 1.00 × 10⁶ g] One tablet was dissolved in ethanol and titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide solution. The mean titre was 9.45 cm³. Ibuprofen reacts with sodium hydroxide in a 1 : 1 ratio. Calculate the percentage of the stated 200 mg of ibuprofen that was present in the tablet. The NMR spectra of ibuprofen are recorded. Deduce the number of peaks in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of ibuprofen. The ¹H NMR spectrum of ibuprofen has a doublet with a relative peak area of 6. Identify the hydrogen atoms responsible for this peak and explain why it is a doublet.
items.ms: C₁₃H₁₈O₂ (CH₃CO)₂O + HF → CH₃CO⁺ + CH₃COOH + F⁻ The by-product is ethanoic acid, which can be sold or reused, instead of hydrogen chloride gas (toxic, corrosive) Ethanoic anhydride reacts less vigorously (with water) than ethanoyl chloride, so it is safer to store and handle (CH₃)₂CHCH₂–C₆H₄–CH(OH)CH₃ (1,4-substituted): 1-[4-(2-methylpropyl)phenyl]ethanol The catalyst is in a different phase (state) from the reactants LiAlH₄ is expensive / is used up in the reaction and leaves aluminium and lithium waste, whereas the nickel catalyst is reused LiAlH₄ needs dry ether (extremely flammable) and reacts violently with water, so it is too hazardous on a large scale Hydrogen adds on with 100% atom economy 100%, because it is an addition reaction: all the atoms in L and CO end up in ibuprofen (there is only one product) Sum of Mr of reactants = 134.0 + 102.0 + 2.0 + 28.0 = 266.0 Atom economy = 206.0 ÷ 266.0 × 100 = 77.4% Higher atom economy, so less waste is produced / fewer raw materials are needed per tonne of ibuprofen Fewer steps, so less energy and fewer resources are used and the overall yield is likely to be higher The catalysts (HF, Raney nickel, palladium) are recovered and reused The ethanoic acid by-product can be sold or used, so the effective atom economy is close to 100% Moles of 2-methylpropylbenzene = 5.00 × 10⁶ ÷ 134.0 = 3.731 × 10⁴ Mass of ibuprofen = 3.731 × 10⁴ × 0.850 × 206.0 = 6.534 × 10⁶ g Number of tablets = 6.534 × 10⁶ ÷ 0.200 = 3.27 × 10⁷ Moles of NaOH = 9.45 × 0.100 ÷ 1000 = 9.45 × 10⁻⁴ = moles of ibuprofen Mass of ibuprofen = 9.45 × 10⁻⁴ × 206.0 = 0.1947 g (194.7 mg) Percentage = 194.7 ÷ 200 × 100 = 97.3% 10 The six H atoms of the two equivalent CH₃ groups in the 2-methylpropyl group, (CH₃)₂CH– The adjacent carbon atom has one H atom, so the peak is split into n + 1 = 2 lines
items.why: Section C often takes an industrial or unfamiliar synthesis with yield, atom economy and titration calculations (Jan2026 Cativa process, Oct2025 carminic acid, Jan2024 Q14(d)); the BHC route links route evaluation with Friedel–Crafts (C18.5) and heterogeneous catalysis (C17.27).

items.question: Aspirin is made by reacting 2-hydroxybenzoic acid with ethanoic anhydride. One mole of 2-hydroxybenzoic acid forms one mole of aspirin. A student needs to make 5.00 g of aspirin. The expected percentage yield is 65.0%. [Mr: 2-hydroxybenzoic acid = 138.0; aspirin = 180.0] Calculate the minimum mass of 2-hydroxybenzoic acid that the student should use.
items.ms: Moles of aspirin = 5.00 ÷ 180.0 = 0.02778 (moles of 2-hydroxybenzoic acid needed at 100% yield) Mass of 2-hydroxybenzoic acid = 0.02778 × 138.0 ÷ 0.650 = 5.90 g
items.why: Aspirin yield calculations recur (Oct2023 Q21(b)(iii), Jan2025 Q11, Jun2025 Q15(b)); working back from the yield ('divide by the yield', Jun2022 examiner report) has not been asked for aspirin.

The structure of 2-hydroxybenzoic acid is shown. Write the equation for the reaction. Use structural or skeletal formulae for the organic compounds. Iron(III) chloride solution forms a violet complex with compounds that contain a phenol group (an OH group bonded directly to a benzene ring). Explain how iron(III) chloride solution could be used to show whether a recrystallised sample of aspirin still contains 2-hydroxybenzoic acid.
items.ms: Aspirin shown correctly: the phenol OH converted into an ester group, CH₃COO–, on the ring carbon next to the COOH group (CH₃CO)₂O on the left and CH₃COOH on the right, with the equation balanced 2-Hydroxybenzoic acid has a phenol group, but in aspirin this OH group has been converted into an ester, so pure aspirin does not give the violet colour Add iron(III) chloride solution to a solution of the sample: a violet colour shows that 2-hydroxybenzoic acid is still present; no violet colour (the solution stays yellow / orange) shows that it has been removed

items.question: Steam distillation is used to separate some organic compounds from reaction mixtures. Which compound would be separated most effectively by steam distillation? ethanol (boiling temperature 78 °C) phenylamine (boiling temperature 184 °C) sodium benzoate 2-aminoethanoic acid (glycine)
items.ms: B: phenylamine is volatile and almost immiscible with water, so it distils with steam below 100 °C, well below its boiling temperature. A: ethanol is miscible with water, so it is separated by fractional distillation instead. C is ionic and D exists as zwitterions; neither is volatile, so neither distils with steam.
items.why: Steam distillation is in the spec (20.5(vii)) but has not been examined in any of the 17 sessions.

items.question: Butan-1-ol (boiling temperature 118 °C) is oxidised to butanal (boiling temperature 75 °C) by acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Which conditions give the highest yield of butanal? heat under reflux, with excess oxidising agent heat under reflux, with a limited amount of oxidising agent distil off the product as it forms, with excess oxidising agent distil off the product as it forms, with a limited amount of oxidising agent
items.ms: D: butanal has a lower boiling temperature than butan-1-ol, so it distils out as soon as it forms and is not oxidised further; limiting the oxidising agent also prevents oxidation to butanoic acid. A and B: under reflux the butanal returns to the flask and is oxidised to butanoic acid. C: the excess oxidising agent oxidises some butanal to butanoic acid before it distils off.
items.why: Distilling an aldehyde out as it forms was asked in Oct2022 Q23(b), Jan2024 Q15(b) and Jun2025 Q18(d), and the examiner reports say candidates confuse it with reflux.

items.question: Eugenol is the main compound in oil of cloves. Its structure is shown. Eugenol has a boiling temperature of 254 °C, is almost insoluble in water and decomposes slowly when heated close to its boiling temperature. Eugenol is extracted from cloves as follows. Step 1 Ground cloves and water are steam distilled. The distillate is cloudy. Step 2 The distillate is shaken with dichloromethane in a separating funnel and the layers are allowed to separate. This is repeated with a second portion of dichloromethane. Step 3 The dichloromethane extracts are combined and anhydrous magnesium sulfate is added. Step 4 The mixture is filtered and the dichloromethane is removed by distillation, leaving eugenol. Explain why eugenol is obtained by steam distillation rather than by heating the cloves and distilling at the boiling temperature of eugenol. Explain why the distillate in Step 1 is cloudy. The density of dichloromethane is 1.33 g cm⁻³. State which layer in the separating funnel contains most of the eugenol in Step 2. Justify your answer. In Step 3, anhydrous magnesium sulfate is added. State the purpose of the anhydrous magnesium sulfate. State how you would know that enough anhydrous magnesium sulfate had been added. Dichloromethane boils at 40 °C. Its vapour is harmful if inhaled and it is suspected of causing cancer. Using this information, explain why the dichloromethane in Step 4 is removed by distillation in a fume cupboard using a warm water bath, rather than by leaving the solution to evaporate in an open dish on the bench. From 25.0 g of cloves, 3.20 cm³ of eugenol was obtained. The density of eugenol is 1.07 g cm⁻³. Calculate the percentage by mass of eugenol in the cloves. State what you would see when bromine water is added to a sample of eugenol.
items.ms: Eugenol would decompose if it were heated to (or near) its boiling temperature of 254 °C Eugenol is immiscible with water, so in steam distillation it distils with the steam at a temperature below 100 °C (well below 254 °C) Eugenol does not mix with (is immiscible with) water, so it forms tiny droplets (an emulsion) in the water The lower layer, because dichloromethane is denser than water (and immiscible with it) Eugenol is more soluble in dichloromethane than in water, so it moves into the dichloromethane layer To remove water / to dry the solution (it is a drying agent) The liquid changes from cloudy to clear / the solid no longer clumps together and moves freely when swirled Distillation condenses the dichloromethane vapour, so little escapes and the harmful (possibly carcinogenic) vapour is not breathed in; the fume cupboard removes any that does escape A warm water bath is hot enough because dichloromethane boils at only 40 °C, and it does not overheat the eugenol (which would decompose) The dichloromethane is collected and can be reused Mass of eugenol = 3.20 × 1.07 = 3.424 g Percentage = 3.424 ÷ 25.0 × 100 = 13.7% The orange / yellow / brown bromine water is decolourised (turns colourless)
items.why: Solvent extraction and drying recur (Jan2026 Q17(a), Oct2025 Q14(e)(iii)), but steam distillation has not been examined in 17 sessions, so a whole isolation sequence from a natural product is a likely surprise.
